OBJECTIVE:

Students will

  • learn the purpose and objectives of the LIA course.
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness, Social Awareness))
  • continue developing effective communication skills (Self-Management, Relationship Skills)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION (Welcoming Activity)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Purpose: To use Class Introductions, Developing Relationships, and Express Care with one another to further enhance relationships and support for one another. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Class Introductions and Developing Relationships activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (4 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Introduce yourself to the students. Go over the purpose and objectives of the lesson. 
  • Choose 1 - 2 ideas to facilitate from the Teacher Introduction Activities. (See Bright Ideas.)
    • Self-image and identity (Exploring your online versus your offline identity) 
    • Invite students to tell their personal stories (they may use digital tools to visually represent with images, recordings, etc.)
  • Introduce and lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices (3 minutes) (See Bright Ideas) 
  • Go over Class Norms of Collaboration and Shared Agreements (Virtual)
    • Be Present and visible (virtual)
    • Be Respectful
    • Empathic Listening
    • Equal Time
    • Give Me Five - Pause Activity, Eyes on Speaker
    • Digital footprint and reputation (How to protect your own privacy and respect others’ privacy and remind students to “self-reflect before they self-reveal” – in-person and online)

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ways to build community? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about community building today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better. INSTRUCTION (Engaging Activities)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text text_direction="default"]Model

What is LIA?

  • View the 10-minute video “What is LIA?”
  • Ask the students the following questions. (Use pair-share or small groups in person; chat in virtual)
    • Why did you register for LIA?
    • How has LIA made a difference for these students?
    • How do you think LIA can make a difference in your life?
    • How can your cultural and language be of benefit to the LIA community?
  • Use LIA Introduction to introduce LIA’s mission statement and purpose.
  • See examples and video clips embedded within the PPT.

Guided Practice

  • Divide class into groups of 3 to 4 students - Review Norms of Collaboration, Group Roles (Leader, Reporter, Recorder, Timekeeper) 
  • Pass out LIA Reflection (English) to each group.
  • Instruct them to discuss the questions and record their answers and reflections.

Teacher Notes

  • If the majority of students have taken LIA in previous years, teachers may want to forego this lesson, just watch the video clips as highlights, concentrate on extension activities, or spend time debriefing on lessons learned from prior years, goals accomplished and new goals for the current year. (Create a K-W-L Chart for students to complete: Begin with students independently completing “What I Know” in the “K” column; students in pairs/small groups input “What I Want to Know” in the “W” column; prior students sharing  “What I Learned” in the “L” column) 
  • Spend additional time in building class community through journal writing and pair-share. 
  • Share aloud group responses - Report out by group (assigned reporter)

  • Conduct this lesson in Spanish or have a student translate each slide.
  • Use LIA Reflection (Spanish) as an additional option.
  • Debate: The Most Important Part of LIA
    • Divide students into small groups and assign each one an important function of LIA (Service, Tutoring, Activities, Leadership, etc.). Ask each group to investigate and develop an argument about why their assigned function should be considered the most important. Hold a mini-debate between two groups or allow students to create a presentation and ask the class to vote on who gave the most compelling argument.
    • Presentation format creates an atmosphere for students to display visual, auditory, reading, writing, and kinesthetic modalities.
  • Review Norms of Collaboration, Roles and Responsibilities 
    • Online debate can occur within the synchronous class session (Google Meet, Zoom, etc.)
    • Online debate can occur on a virtual discussion board with the initial posts and responses in affirmative and negative discussion threads.

Extension

  • Ask students that have taken LIA in the past to prepare and present this lesson to the other class members.
  • Ask an LIA Alumni member to prepare and present this lesson.
  • If all students have already taken LIA in the past, ask students to organize/write a five-paragraph essay to demonstrate the benefits of LIA. Use this template Essay Outline Guide (English) or Essay Outline Guide (Spanish) as a guide.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why did you take LIA?
  • What are you hoping to get out of LIA?
  • Reflections on Personal Goals and Professional Goals

Students will:

  • get to know their classmates by participating in “icebreaker” activities and to create a class motto.
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY 

Purpose: To use Ice-Breakers to build community and create a class motto. Students will be practicing Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Responsible Decision Making

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Ice-Breaker activities further enhance students’ competencies of Social Awareness and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Facilitate My Name, My Identity Activity (see Greetings) - pair share, large group (layered and process)
    • Share the story about how you were given your name and the meaning behind it.
    • Has anyone ever made assumptions based on your name? What was that like for you? 
    • Is your name easy or difficult for other people at school to pronounce? Do other students in your school have the same name? What is that like? 
    • What can you do if someone’s name is difficult to pronounce?  If you have a name that is challenging for other students to pronounce, what can you do to help them learn your name?
    • The Native Americans often had names which described something about the person or compared the person to something in nature. Examples are White Elk, Thunder Cloud, or Spotted Deer. If you could make up a Native American name for yourself, what would it be? How to do it Respectfully?
  • Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.”

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore our names and how people respond to them? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about names today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better. Include Hand Raise, Chat, Breakout Rooms, and Gallery conversations to engage students throughout the lesson.  

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Protocol and procedures used in the classroom.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Explain to students that today’s lesson will help us get to know each other better and develop a class motto. If we know each other better, we are more likely to be respectful of others’ challenges, work better as a team, and more effectively create common goals that we can help each other achieve. 
  • Begin with community building and introduce one of the ice breaker activities described in 1.02 Video Icebreakers 1-Teacher Materials or 1.02 Weblink Icebreakers 2 Teacher Materials or 1.02 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials. (See questions for each activity listed for discussion in 1.02 Ice Breakers 2-Teacher Materials) 
  • Debrief activity using questions noted in each icebreaker.  See 1.02 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials.  This document has 4 pre-selected icebreakers that may work well for the LIA classroom setting with debriefing questions identified in a simpler format.
  • Select another icebreaker activity as time allows and then debrief.

Guided Practice

  • Students will create a class motto. 
  • Explain what a motto is and how it is important to promote a positive organizational culture in the LIA class. Provide examples of mottos/slogans (Use Ideas for Introducing Mottos - Bright Ideas) 
  • Facilitate a non-sequential Community Circle. Ask students to share one word they think could be in a class motto. Chart their responses or make available in the Chat. 
  • Divide students into groups of 3 - 4. Go over Group Norms and assign Group Roles.
  • Invite groups to consolidate the words that have been shared and come up with a one-sentence draft of a class motto. Ask Reporters to put their draft motto on a shared electronic document or in the Chat.
  • Invite Reporters from each group to share their first draft of mottos and make an argument for their motto. Display all mottos.  
  • Lead students in a discussion about their favorite parts of the mottos that have been shared. Discuss the big ideas from each chart and either create a class motto that includes them from all the charts OR vote/select from the mottos and choose one that best describes LIA’s purpose, goals, and class ideas. If available, use the voting app.
  • Refine until the class gives a thumbs up to the final product. Write it on butcher paper and have the class sign it.  

Reflection

  • Ask the students to pair-share the following questions, then have volunteers share with the large group. 
    • What have you learned about what it takes to be a part of LIA? To create a common purpose statement or motto? 
    • What do you like about our class motto? What does it mean to you personally? 
    • How can we use the class motto to build our commitment to LIA? How can we use this motto to reach out to other friends and classmates who would benefit from taking LIA? How can we be more inclusive and welcoming in general?

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

  • Review
    • Create a classroom website and blog (For example - Google Sites, Weebly for Education, Blogger, WordPress, Edublog, etc.)
      • Post the class motto on the website. Have each student respond to a blog post: “What does the motto mean to you?”
    • Small Group Option: Create small groups and rotate groups through 3-4 stations with different ice breaker activities at each station (this is especially effective for students that have anxiety participating in large groups).

Students will:

  • be able to research current events that have a direct impact on their school, local, student body and administration and complete a current event bell ringer
  • analyze beliefs, mindsets and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)
  • explore the impacts of cultural awareness on effective team building (Relationship Skills)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To reflect on a statement, image, or prompt that relates to a characteristic, quality or preference of their culture, language, history or personal interest and move to a "corner" that matches their choice so they can share their rationale for choosing that corner. “Corners” is helpful in promoting the importance of divergent perspectives and the value of having all voices heard. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Reflecting on a statement, image, or prompt students will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students – lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Before the activity, mark four to five areas in the room with a large image, number, or word that corresponds to the choices from cultural characteristics that you will be giving in the areas of music, food, art, history or language.
  • Ask participants to silently reflect on a statement or question prompt that is aligned with the content of the current event.
  • Share 4-5 choices with the group on a poster/slide (quotes, pictures, etc.).
  • Instruct participants to choose one of the responses, then ask them to move to that designated "corner" of the room, find a partner or trio within the group that forms in that area, and share what drew them to that choice.
  • NOTE: If you end up with a solo participant in a “corner,” join that person to hear their thoughts, using a timer to keep on track.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings about language, history, and other characteristics as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore each other's thoughts or ideas regarding personal preferences and interests? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do to continue building your relationship with others who were in your corner? (Relationship Skills)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing their interest in a certain response or topic in their own areas of interest. Send students to Breakout Rooms for the Corners activity to discuss their reasons for selecting their response.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “Empowering youth to lead and strengthen their communities.”
  • The purpose of this current event lesson is to establish the routine of the current event bell starter activity which is the first activity in the Introduction of every lesson.
  • The importance of knowing the current events occurring locally, in the U.S., and in the world, will help students meet the LIA mission to become more knowledgeable of culture to serve more effectively and broaden their education.
  • Write “ignorance is bliss” and “knowledge is power” on the board. Ask students to express their thoughts on each quote.
  • Ask the students if they agree or disagree with these quotes. Encourage students to support their argument with examples.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Teachers may choose either current event bell ringer option 1 or option 2 or alternate between the two options (hybrid) throughout the year. If teachers choose to do a hybrid option, please use two class periods to complete this lesson. Daily, current event bell ringers are highly encouraged. 

  • Connect the curriculum to current events by focusing on timely topics from pop culture through articles, videos, social media, and podcasts.

Option 1 Model – demonstrate a current event graphic organizer bell ringer        

  • Display 1.03 HO Current Events GO (English).
  • Distribute 1.03 Weblink Article 1 to students.
  • Display 1.03 Current Events Graphic Organizer Teacher Model.
  • Demonstrate how to complete sections 1, 2, & 3.  Ask students the following questions. Record students’ responses on the handout.
    • What are e-cigarettes?
    • Why is traditional smoking declining?
    • What are the health risks when using e-cigarettes?
    • What is your opinion?
  • Read the article as a class.
  • Identify challenging vocabulary and discuss student-friendly definitions. List the vocabulary words and definitions in section 4.
  • Answer the questions (5 Ws and an H) in section 5 as a class.
  • Model writing a sentence describing a summary of the main point of the article in section 6.

Option 1 Guided Practice

  • Divide students into groups.
  • Choose an article, video, social media, or podcast, (chosen by the teacher), to share with each group.
    • See 1.03 HO Current Event Resources.
  • Guide students in completing 1.03 HO Current Events GO (English) or 1.03 HO Current Event GO (Spanish) in their groups.

Option 2 Model – demonstrate a five-minute fact or fiction bell ringer

  • Display 1.03 HO Five Minute Fact or Fiction Outline (English)
  • Distribute 1.03 Weblink Article 2 to students.
  • Use 1.03 Five Minute Fact or Fiction Teacher Model.
  • Demonstrate how to complete the “Article Description” section. Ask students the following question and emphasize the following. 
    • What is this article about?
    • As we read the article, think about the main points the author makes.  We will be writing a summary, so you may want to highlight important facts.
  • Read the article as a class.
  • Identify challenging vocabulary and discuss student-friendly definitions. List the vocabulary words and definitions on the outline.
  • Ask students what they learned from the article, any thoughts, and how the subject relates to LIA.
  • Record student responses on the outline.
  • Model writing a summary paragraph for the article.
  • Model forming questions and fact and fiction statements for student discussion.

Option 2 Guided Practice

  • Divide students into groups.
  • Choose an article, video, social media, or podcast, (chosen by the teacher), to share with each group.
    • See 1.03 HO Current Event Resources.
  • Guide students in completing 1.03 Five Minute Fact of Fiction Outline (English) or 1.03 HO Five Minute Fact or Fiction Outline (Spanish) in their groups.
  • Student groups present articles to the class.

Activity

  • Students choose a historical event for their “What if?” history project
    • Students research an actual historical event, describe and explain the point of divergence, and create a timeline of newly imagined events in history leading to a new current event.
    • Students use an online tool for creating a Timeline to show their project (For example - Enwoven, Time. Graphics, story, Knightlab Timeline, etc.)
  • Students conduct research on a topic and create a virtual public service announcement to educate others about recent trends in their communities or society in general.

Students will: 

  • gather information about ancestors, family and self and prepare a presentation on their personal history and background to develop a better understanding of self
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • build understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Mix and Mingle activity to have students move around the room and share ideas with a partner or small group. This is designed to build community by encouraging participants to interact with each other with the expectation that everyone's personal history, language, culture, and voice are valued. Skills for Life and Learning Signature Practices Playbook(optional)

Skills for Life and Learning Focus: This Mix and Mingle activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness and Social Awareness.

Overview (3 min): 

  • Welcome students – lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Life and Learning Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • On a card or half-sheet of paper, ask participants to write down a response to a prompt you give related to their own personal history. (Begin with a low-vulnerability prompt such as, “Where were you born?” or “How would you describe the family and culture you were born into?” or something connected to upcoming work like “What’s one thing you like most about [insert LIA topics such as tutoring, leadership, bootcamp, LIA class, etc.]?”
  • When you announce, "Mix and mingle!" and turn on music (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, Norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc) participants move around.
  • When the music stops, participants find a partner near them. Help with pairing if needed.
  • Partners share their responses, listen actively to each other, and ask follow-up questions.
  • Start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as your time permits.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own personal history with other people? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people's personal history? (Self Management)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better. Include Hand Raise, Chat, Breakout Rooms, and Gallery conversations to engage students throughout the lesson. “Mix and Mingle” also works as an Optimistic Closure activity. Provide a prompt that draws from the content, experience, or process of your activity.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • In order to more fully understand yourself, each of you are going to explore your background by learning more about your family.
  • Watch Video Mejiafricana (2 min) and discuss the following questions.
    • Write down any Spanish words you hear or any English words you are unfamiliar with. Discuss their meaning as well as their significance.
    • How can personal history make you a stronger individual?
    • How can you become more passionate and educated about your personal history?
    • What can you do to preserve, uphold, and celebrate identity for future generations?
  • Alternate Video: The Danger of a Single Story (with closed captions, 18:21 min), video to be shown in parts.
    • Video clip - 0:00 - 2:49
      • What do you believe is the meaning of the term “a single story?” 
      • In what ways do you relate to her experiences? 
      • Do you see yourself and/or your identity represented in the books and curriculum in your school?
    • Video clip - 2:50 - 5:10
      • Identify challenges Chimamanda Ngozi Adichie faced as an immigrant when attending college in the U.S. Why do you think she faced those challenges?
      • Describe the elements of the single story that made her roommate believe she was not equal to her?
    • Video clip - 5:47 - 9:27
      • How did the political climate in the U.S. shape her views?
      • Have you found yourself having a single story about someone? 
      • In what ways do “single stories” impact our own personal stories, how we view others, and the choices we make?

  • Distribute Personal History HS: Part I of 2 (English) to each student.
  • Explain to students that they will complete the handout and then decide how they want to present this information to the class.  Some ideas include creating a poster, Powerpoint, or collage.
    • Display Personal History HS: Part I of 2 (English) (completed by classroom teacher).
    • Discuss each requirement and share-out teacher responses.

Guided Practice

  • Allow students time to complete Personal History HS: Part I of 2 (English).
  • Instruct them to choose a presentation format. 
  • Ask students to take the assignment home in order for family members to assist them in completing the assignment.
  • Students will create a digital storytelling presentation about their personal history by interviewing and recording their own family history. Empower students to create and publish multimedia resources such as videos, podcasts, and e-books to help them organize and communicate their ideas more clearly and effectively.  Students can use tech devices to record images, audio and video to provide a multisensory experience for the learner. Here are sample interview questions and prompts:
    • Tell me about your childhood home/country?
    • What is your first memory of your childhood?
    • Do you share a name with someone else in the family?
    • What was your school like?
    • What was your favorite subject and why?
    • What did you want to be when you grew up?
    • Tell me a funny story about your family.
    • Did you move around much?
    • Why did you move and to where?
    • How did you feel about moving to another place?

Purpose: To use the Clock Buddies tool to facilitate student interaction so that students will have specific partners for various activities throughout the period or week. This is a quick and easy way to create pairs for future partnered activities that offer a break from continually turning to an elbow partner. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Life and Learning Focus: Interacting with Clock Buddies will further enhance students’ competencies of Relationship Skills, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students – lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Life and Learning Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Make copies of a Clock Buddy handout.
  • Distribute a handout to each participant and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  • Instruct participants to stand up with their papers and a pencil and move quietly around the room until you use your attention signal, at which point they should stop and find a partner. Make sure that they select someone who they are not familiar with or from a different country of origin.
  • When everyone has a partner, ask them to make sure that they can pronounce each other’s first and last names properly. Sign each other’s paper on the 3 o’clock line. It is very important that they all start on the same line.
  • Give the signals to mix, stop, and find a new partner, making sure that  they pronounce each other’s first and last name properly. Check to be sure everyone has a new partner before you ask participants to sign each other’s papers on the 6 o’clock line.
  • To complete the activity, have partners mingle and pair up two more times. They’ll sign next on the 9 o’clock line and finally on the 12 o’clock line.
  • After all lines are signed, invite participants to return to their seats.
  • Each time you need participants to form pairs during the engagement, have them take out their appointment clocks and announce one of the times to designate their partner for this activity. For example, “Now meet up with the person who is your 9 o’clock appointment to reflect and discuss..." Do this as a practice exercise.
  • You will use the Clock Buddies for the Current Event Bell Starter, Guided Practice, Google My Maps Activity, Review and Assessment, and Adaptations.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you signed up for your Clock Buddies? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to get to know other students who you do not know very well or from a different country of origin? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about different names, histories, and origins? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer to access the Clock Buddies and facilitate a virtual Clock Buddie list. Manually place Clock Buddies in Breakout Rooms to get to know each other and their histories. Emphasize Norms of Virtual Collaboration and Shared Agreements.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Pair students up with their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy
  • Display the 1.04 HO Presentation Rubric (English) or 1.04 HO Presentation Rubric (Spanish).  
  • Have students work with Clock Buddies to fill out the HO Presentation forms. Remind students of each area they need to include in the presentation. 
  • Have students practice their presentations with each other before presenting to the whole class.
  • Hand out index cards.
    • Today we are going to listen to each class member’s presentation.  As we listen to each presentation, write down one new thing you learned about each peer’s background or family on your index card.

  • Ask students to volunteer to give their presentations.
  • May need to continue presentations during the following class period as well.

Activity

Google My Maps Activity – Personal Student Stories

  • Google My Maps is an online mapping tool, that allows students to create and share their own maps or collaborate simultaneously on the same map. Students are going to use the multimedia environment to tell their story and present their research to the rest of the class. Have students work in pairs with their 6:00 O’Clock Buddies.
  • Teachers and students log in or create an account on Google My Maps. Begin by preparing a completely new Google My Maps with the share setting editable by anyone with the link. You can create and store My Maps directly in Google Drive. It is recommended that collaborative groups working on the same map are between 4-5 students. 
  • Students will use My Maps to write a story about their personal history. They will map the route of their personal journey by adding a pin for each location and include pictures, images, and videos. The final product will serve as a resource for others in the class to find out where everyone is from and to identify the diversity among the class members. Below are some sample steps to follow:
    • Build prior knowledge - Ask if anyone has ever used My Maps or GPS
    • Students will begin to explore the map and search for a location
    • Edit the My Map title and description
    • Add a pin on their hometown or native country
    • Students complete a description on the pin location
    • Students can add an image or a video to the pin location
    • Students can use the measurement tool to show the distance from their hometown to their school’s location
  • Encourage students to share what they’ve discovered about My Maps and the tools available. Students will share with their 6:00 O’Clock Buddies about their hometown or native country and their school community demographics (making connections between the two). Students will explain the differences between the communities.

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

  • Each student creates their own digital trivia quiz about their personal stories shared during lesson 1 with their 9:00 O’Clock Buddies. (For example - Kahoot, Quizlet, Quizzizz, GimKit, Mentimeter, etc.)
  • Have each student respond to a blog post: How does your classmates’ personal story help you to understand a different viewpoint?

Review

  • Ask students that created posters, collages or other visual aids to display them in the classroom

  • explore elements of self-confidence and self-efficacy (Self-Awareness)

Purpose: To use the SELFie activity to allow students to be reflective of their emotional response to challenges and identify personal strengths and assets through the use of a SELFie. A SELFie is a picture of a person taken by that person (selfie), to show a facial expression representing the social and emotional state at any given time.

Skills for Life and Learning Focus: Interacting with the SELFie activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Make copies of a Clock Buddy handout and ask students to fill it out and find Clock Buddies (see Lesson 1.05)
  • Ask for the meaning of an emoticon - the little emotional faces that some people attach to emails. 
  • Then asked for the definition of a "selfie." Give examples on the board/screen and ask students to take a selfie with their own devices and share it with their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy.
  • Define the meaning of a SELfie as a picture of a person taken by that person (selfie), to show a facial expression representing the social and emotional state at any given time.
  • Have the students take out their cellphones/devices and take two SELFies, one representing happiness and the other representing anger or sadness. With their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy, have them share each SELFie, describing the things that make them happy and the things that make them sad or angry.
  • Have them take another SELFie representing feelings of self confidence and self-esteem. With their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy have students describe their personal strengths and assets associated with their own feelings of self confidence and self-esteem.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore our own feelings and thoughts about yourself? (Self-Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about yourself today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Have students work with their Clock Buddies or in groups of 4 in Breakout rooms to complete the activity.  

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.”
  • Explain that today’s lesson will help us each to evaluate our self-esteem by taking an inventory of our strengths and weaknesses.
    • Today we are going to take a personal inventory to help us each evaluate our strengths and weaknesses.  Knowing our talents will help us work more effectively as a team.
  • Ask students the following questions and have them discuss with their 6:00 O’Clock Buddy.
    • What strengths or talents do you bring to our class?
    • How has your background helped you develop these talents?

  • Display 1.06 Weblink HO Advanced Personal Inventory on a projector screen or smartboard.
  • Read several examples aloud for students and explain how to complete each section of the handout.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute 1.06 Weblink HO Advanced Personal Inventory.
  • Allow students time to complete the task with their 9:00 O’Clock Buddy.
  • Once completed, divide class into same-gender groups of 2-3 students.
  • Ask them to discuss selected items on the handout in their groups. (May want to ask each student to share one item to encourage participation from every class member).
  • Bring the class back together and have volunteers share any final thoughts.

Activities

  • Pass out colored strips of paper (3 to each student).
    • Ask students to write one positive thing about each person in their group on the separate strips of paper.
    • Instruct students to make a paper chain out of their strips and then join them with all other students’ chains.

Agree/Disagree Virtual Activity: 

  • In the Agree/Disagree Virtual Activity, the teacher prepares 12 statements that show various levels of agreement or disagreement. Students prepare 4 pieces of paper in 4 different colors:
    • Blue = Agree
    • Green = Strongly Agree
    • Orange = Disagree
    • Red = Strongly Disagree
  • The teacher virtually shares one by one the 12 statements with the students. Students start by identifying the level of agreement or disagreement by showing on their camera the colored paper that represents agree, strongly agree, disagree or strongly disagree after each statement. Next, students write in the chat box whether they agree, strongly agree, disagree, or strongly disagree with the statements by writing a sentence about their opinions. In a breakout room, students are paired or work in small groups to discuss their opinions.

Purpose: To use the Fishbowl activity to strengthen listening skills and encourages everyone to participate in a discussion. It can be used during a session to discuss content, or at the end of an engagement to give airtime to everyone about what they learned or found useful. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Fishbowl activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (10 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • In this Fishbowl activity, participants are divided into two groups that are seated in concentric circles, all facing the center. The outside circle listens while the inside group has a discussion about a topic. Then the groups switch places so the listeners become the speakers, and vice versa. 
  • Make sure the audience knows you will hold them accountable for sharing their observations. Use equity sticks (a cup of sticks with each student’s name on one) to increase audience participation and accountability.
  • Provide the question prompt or discussion topic. These would vary depending on the theme of the lesson. The prompts for this activity would be: 
    • What are some of the positive characteristics of healthy relationships?
    • What are some of the negative characteristics of unhealthy relationships?
  • Only the inside group members may speak during this time (4 minutes). Instruct the outside group to quietly listen and notice their own ideas that surface during the discussion. Note-taking on a graphic organizer may be helpful.
  • When the time is up, ask the groups to trade places so that the outside group is sitting on the inner circle chairs and vice versa. Set the timer again for four minutes and let the new inside group discuss the topic. 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore your feelings about healthy and unhealthy relationships? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about relationships today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Divide students into two groups on paper, Group 1 and Group 2. Either assign students a number or ask them to choose a group to belong to. Have them write their number on a card. Those with number “1” will hold up their cards to the screen and they will symbolically be in the inner circle. Call their names using the equity sticks for them to share thoughts on the prompts. Switch numbers for the next group.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 1.07 Video “The Line” (1 min).
  • Ask the students the following questions and have them write their feelings and responses to the questions.  Reassure them they do not need to share out these responses.
    • Write down your response to the video clip.
    • Have you ever felt like the guy in this clip? Jealous or controlling?   Have you ever felt like the girlfriend on the other line?  Has your girlfriend or boyfriend ever been overly suspicious and untrusting?
    • Where is the line?

  • Reference 1.07 Weblink Dating Abuse Teacher Materials and 1.07 Weblink Warning Signs Teacher Materials
  • Lead the class in a discussion about the definition of dating abuse.
    • Dating abuse is a real problem.
    • How would you define dating abuse?
    • What are some warning signs of dating abuse? (List on the board:  i.e. extreme jealousy, constant belittling, possessiveness, etc.)

Guided Practice

  • Ask students to take 1.07 Weblink Quiz “Is My Relationship Healthy”.  Students can take the quiz online in the computer lab or take the text version.  If they take the text version, ask them to calculate their score.
  • Discuss the meaning of the scores (see explanation at the bottom of the quiz).
  • Remind students that they can also talk to the School Psychologist or School counselor if they have further questions or need help.

Activities: Adapted from Break the Cycle Activity Guides

#3: Stay/Talk/Go (Virtual Class Activity)

  • The teacher develops up to 30 dating relationship scenarios that name either a healthy, unhealthy, or abusive behavior that could be found in a teen dating relationship. The teacher shares a digital graphic organizer divided into 3 categories: Stay, Talk, or Go. Each student is assigned one of the dating relationship scenarios. Students read their cards and consider what they might do in that situation: “stay together” “talk about it” or “get out of the relationship.” Students will read aloud their card and explain to the class which category they think the behavior should be placed in and why. Students' answers are recorded on the digital graphic organizer.

#6: PSA (Public Service Announcement) Making

  • The teacher selects and shows some examples of what healthy relationships look like in the media. This can include popular TV shows, social media apps, or celebrities. Students find other examples and create their own examples of healthy relationships. Students will create a multimedia PSA presentation including pictures, video, and/or sound to support healthy relationships in their school and community. 

#7: Music Lyrics

  • The teacher selects 3-5 popular songs that students are familiar with and provides the lyrics to the students. Students will listen to the songs and discuss whether the lyrics to the songs support healthy relationships. Students will write down in the chat box healthy and unhealthy words and behaviors they hear in the song. Students will then search their music idols to discuss the negative messages that impact the way they talk about relationships.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Save the Last Word activity to help students to further develop their communication skills by following an established protocol to share and discuss their responses to a text, quote, image, or video clip. By creating a clear structure for discussion, this strategy encourages everyone to be both an active speaker and an active listener and supports equity of voice by ensuring that frequent speakers give space for others to share. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Save the Last Word activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students – lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Identify a relevant reading passage, quote, image, or video clip that will serve as the catalyst for this activity.
  • Have participants read/view the selected text/quote/image or video and highlight three sentences or make note of three ideas that particularly stand out for them.
  • Ask participants to write each sentence/idea on the front of an index card. On the back of the card, ask them to write a few sentences explaining why they chose that quote (what it meant to them, reminded them of, how it connects to their own experience, background, language, history, etc.).
  • Divide the participants into groups of three, identifying one person as A, one person as B, and one person as C.
  • Invite the A participants to read one of their chosen quotations or ideas to their group. Then persons B and C discuss the offering while person A listens. (For example, What do they think it means? Why do they think these words/ideas might be important? To whom?)
  • After several minutes, ask Participant A to read the back of their card (or to explain why they picked the quotation or idea), thus having “the last word.”
  • This process repeats with B sharing and others reflecting before B gets “the last word,” then is repeated again with C sharing.

 Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to be able to communicate ideas and opinions effectively and to be able to listen effectively? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about communication skills today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Divide students into groups of three on paper, Groups 1, 2...etc. Either assign students a number or ask them to self select by choosing two other students they want to work with. Have them write their number on a card. Those with number “1” will hold up their cards to the screen and they will be assigned to a Breakout room.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 1.08 Video Spoken Word Poet Smego (min. 5-7).
  • Ask the students the following questions and have them write their responses. May want to post and read these questions ahead of watching the clip to enable students to listen for the phrases.
  • Introduce vocabulary before watching the clip if the students aren’t familiar with these terms (Smego uses several of these terms in the clip.).
  • Ask the students the following questions and have them write their responses (You may want to post and read these questions ahead of watching the clip to enable students to listen for the phrases):
    • Smego uses words to communicate his feelings and experiences.  What do you think he means when he says “words come out to play”?
    • What did Smego say is like finding a “needle in the haystack”?
    • Smego wants us to elevate our __________?
    • How can words be powerful?
    • What is the overall message?
    • How does knowledge of vocabulary influence communication at school, home, work, and in the community?
  • Ask students to share out their written responses.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Model

  • Introduce the key parts of communication.
    • Communication involves two parts, speaking and listening, or in other words, sending and receiving a message. Sometimes we can “send” a message, but the other person does not “receive” it in the same way that it was sent. Why might that be?  We are going to complete an exercise to demonstrate how this works.

Activities

  • Distribute blank pieces of paper.  Explain that you are going to read instructions to draw an animal. See 1.08 Communication Activity HS: Teacher Materials.
    • As we saw in the previous activity, listening is a critical part of communication, but it was missing an important part, so most of you were unable to draw the chicken.  Asking questions (speaking) is an important part of communication that would have made this activity much easier.  Speaking and listening are both critical for communicating effectively.
  • MYSTERY SKYPE/ZOOM/GOOGLE MEET
    • Create a virtual mystery game with another LIA class in an unknown location. Your students' goal is to guess the other school and their location (country, state, city, school name) before they guess yours. (Students are provided a list of the states and school names participating in LIA). The mystery guessing game helps build cultural awareness, critical thinking skills, and listening and speaking skills by challenging students to guess the location of the other classroom through a series of yes/no questions. This is a student-led activity.
    • It's important to prepare the students at least a few days in advance so they can gather materials, such as maps, or ask questions about their responsibilities.
    • Assigning roles or jobs prior to the virtual mystery game spreads out the responsibility and gives all students a sense of involvement and purpose. Below are some sample roles for students:
      • Facilitator – This student introduces the class to the other class and shares some cool facts about their own class without giving away the location.
      • Investigators – These students ask questions that were prepared before the event.
      • Responders – These students respond yes or no to the questions. These students need to know their state/geography facts.
      • Think Tank – These students work on figuring out the clues based on the yes/no answers from the other LIA class.
      • Recorders – They record all of the answers to the questions asked by their class.
    • Encourage students to collaborate before guessing, and set ground rules for how quickly they can guess the school and location. Watch the excitement build as they eliminate schools as they make their guesses. At the end of the game, give students time to reflect on what worked and what didn’t. This activity can lead to other virtual collaborations for future projects. 

Model

  • Emphasize the importance body language plays in communication as well.
  • Listening and speaking are obviously key pieces of communication.  However, body language plays an important role as well.

Guided Practice / Activity

  • Partner students.
  • Distribute 1.08 HO Making a Good First Impression to one individual in each partnership.
  • Ask students with the HO to act out one of the actions on the list (i.e. “Be on Time”–look at watch, quickly get ready etc.).  The other partner guesses the action that one should do to make a good first impression.  As soon as the partner gets the action correct, the duo moves on to the next item.  The pair that finishes first, wins the game

  • Emphasize the following points.
    • Effective communication requires two parts, listening and speaking.
    • Word choice and gaining a greater knowledge of vocabulary, as Smego demonstrated in the video, can help us become better communicators.  
    • Even when we don’t say anything, our body language communicates with others, too.

  • Divide the 4 questions in the Relevancy / Linkage section of the lesson among 4 different groups in the classroom.  Watch 1.08 Video Spoken Word Poet Smego (min. 5-7). Ask students in each group to discuss their question and share out their group’s thoughts.

Extension

  • Use 1.08 Understanding Self-Efficacy Teacher Materials and 1.08 HO What is Self-Efficacy? / Confidence to build a lesson on Self-Efficacy and Confidence. Students that have a high level of self-efficacy and confidence are better communicators. See also 1.08 Weblink Self-Efficacy Scale.  Display the scale on the board and ask students to rate themselves on a separate piece of paper.
  • Watch 1.08 Video “Look Up” (5 min).  “Smart phones and dumb people”.  Ask students to discuss these questions. How have we become a society without “spoken word”? What are the disadvantages of relying only on technology to communicate?

  • How can you communicate better?
  • What are body language cues that are different in different cultures?

Purpose: To use the Resolve Differences Quickly to help students learn how to participate in discussions and activities to learn how to initiate a compromise or a mutual agreement that is mutually beneficial when a conflict arises with another individual or group.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Resolve Differences Quickly activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (8 min):

  1. Welcome students – lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas).
  2. Engage students in a discussion on the meaning of “compromise” as a way to settle differences by coming to a mutual agreement that benefits all parties in some way. Explain that reaching a compromise requires a degree of cooperation in order to “meet in the middle” especially when you feel that you are right. It is necessary if they want to move past the conflict. It is a skill that needs to be practiced and it is also one of the most mature actions that they can take to show that they can make adult decisions. 
  3. Ask students to discuss with two other partners the following questions:
    • What are some of the potential benefits of reaching a compromise in resolving conflicts and differences respectfully and swiftly? 
    • Give an example of a disagreement you have been involved with personally such as differences of opinion, beliefs, or even conflicts between groups of different backgrounds.
    • Visualize a time when you helped dissolve a disagreement between friends or family members. What was the cause of the disagreement and what did you say or do to help resolve the conflict? What were the terms of the compromise? 
    • What were the long term benefits of resolving this conflict? Did it eliminate the conflict and restore the relationship? What were the long term benefits in terms of eliminating stress, anxiety, fear, and anger?
  1. Ask students to write out the most important steps in resolving a conflict and reaching a compromise. Have them share with their partners and then with the larger class.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ways to resolve a conflict or disagreements? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about reaching a compromise today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Give students several scenarios of conflict and divide the class into groups of four. Make sure that each team is representative of the class diversity, cultures, and languages. Manually assign students to Breakout rooms to respond to the questions. Have students take on roles as Timekeeper, Recorder, Facilitator and Reporter. This should take them about 8 minutes. The Recorder enters the summary in the Chat box while the Reporter gives a verbal summary when called on by the teacher. 

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  1. Watch 1.09 Video Waterboy Conflict (2 m)
  2. Ask the students the following questions:
    • Identify the conflict.  Who is the conflict between and what are they disagreeing about?
    • What should Adam Sandler’s character do to resolve the conflict with the teacher?  What about the teacher?  How did the teacher make the situation worse?  
    • Have you ever had a conflict with a teacher?  What did you do?  Was it a good choice?

  1. Display 1.09 Case Study Resolving a Conflict: Teacher Materials.
  2. Read aloud to students or ask a student to read the scenario.
  3. Discuss each point listed in the problem-solving steps while brainstorming solutions.
  4. Write final actions/solutions on the board (i.e. 1. Cool Off–Go to my room and listen to music to calm down.)

Guided Practice

  1. Divide class into groups of 3-4 students.
  2. Distribute 1.09 HO Resolving a Conflict to each group.
  3. Ask students to write a skit demonstrating a conflict and a resolution using the steps listed in the HO. Make sure to include parts for all group members.

Activity

  1. Students will work in small groups to role play and record a skit demonstrating a conflict and resolution. The videos will be posted in the digital classroom for all students to watch. Students will resolve the conflict using 1.09 HO Resolving a Conflict. 
  2. Students discuss reasons why people address conflict via social media rather than in-person and discuss the pros/cons of doing so. Students complete and share a pros and cons list on a digital handout.

  1. Ask some of the student leadership in the class to prepare ahead of time to role play the scenario in 1.09 Case Study Resolving a Conflict: Teacher Materials.  Instruct students to lead the discussion on how to solve the conflict using the steps in the hand out.
  2. Practice paraphrasing others feelings, taking responsibility, using “I messages”, etc. in Spanish. How does a language barrier sometimes create conflicts? Which steps can help eliminate language barrier issues?

Extension

  1. Ask students to create problem-solving steps for elementary age students.  Create a worksheet with simple language and pictures.  Share with the local elementary school where students tutor.
  2. Extend this lesson an extra day and ask students to perform their skits for the class.
  3. Video record the skits for a future assembly or LIA activity.
  4. Watch and discuss 1.09 Video - Conflict Resolution. 

Language Enhancement

  1. Watch 1.09 Video El Chavo (9 min). Ask students to identify what steps Chavo uses to resolve the conflict using 1.09 HO Resolving a Conflict.  What does he do well?  What does he not do well?

Journal Entry Suggestions

  1. Define conflict. Does conflict have a positive or negative connotation? How are conflicts beneficial?
  2. Describe a conflict that you saw resolve positively, what made it end well?
  3. How can you teach elementary students to become better at resolving conflicts?

Students will complete a personal history hand-out and presentation to the class

  • Explain that understanding your personal history is an important step to being prepared for college and career opportunities. As part of an application or recruitment process, candidates will often be asked to explain about themselves, their lives, families, motivations, strengths, weaknesses, and goals. This assessment gives an opportunity for students to research and craft their message.
  • Distribute Personal History HS: Part I of 2 (English) to each student.
  • Explain to students that they will complete the handout and then decide how they want to present this information to the class.  Some ideas include creating a poster, Powerpoint, or collage.

Presentation

  • Allow students time to complete Personal History HS: Part I of 2 (English).
  • Instruct them to choose a presentation format.
  • Ask students to take the assignment home in order for family members to assist them in completing the assignment.

Grading

  • Presentations will be graded using the following rubric: Presentation Rubric (English)

*These forms are also available in Spanish: Personal History HS: Part I of 2 (Spanish) and Presentation Rubric (Spanish).

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • create at least 2 SMARTE goals centered on LIA standards.
  • identify and explore ways to develop skills and talents (Self-Awareness) 
  • develop skills in planning and organizational skills (Self-Management)
  • work collaboratively with others (i.e., listen, encourage, acknowledge opinions, compromise, reach a consensus) (Relationship Skills)

Purpose: To use the Mix and Mingle activity to have students move around the room and share ideas about personal and professional strengths and goals with a partner or small group. This is designed to build community by encouraging participants to interact with each other with the expectation that everyone's personal history, language, culture, and voice are valued.  See an example of the Mix and Mingle activity in the Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook.(optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Mix and Mingle activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Prepare index cards with one question per card from the list below (feel free to modify or add additional questions as needed). Randomly hand them out to the students while they are sitting in their community circle. Give them a minute to read their card and think about their response. Index Cards:
    1. What are your personal strengths?
    2. If one of your personal strengths was a superpower, what would it be?
    3. If you had to describe one of your strengths as a body of water (stream, a waterfall, a river, a tidal wave, etc) what would you be and why?
    4. How does your mood affect how you learn?
    5. Describe your mood as an outfit.
    6. What is a dish/food you like to eat on a special occasion?
    7. If you could serve one dish that would represent who you are, what would you serve? 
    8. If you were a flavor of ice cream, what flavor would you be?
    9. What are some examples of your personal goals? 
    10. What are you personally responsible for?
    11. What is great about being in charge?
    12. What are some skills you will need to develop in order to reach your personal goals?
    13. What are some examples of professional goals you have considered?
    14. What are some skills you will need to develop in order to reach your professional goals? 
    15. What is something you were blamed for that you did not feel responsible for?
    16. When was the last time you needed help?
    17. What do you need help with in your life today?
    18. Who do you turn to for help? Why?
    19. Who can you ask for help at home?
    20. What is one time you asked for help at school?
    21. Who can you ask for help in the community?
  2. When you announce, "Mix and Mingle!", turn on the music and have students move around the room greeting each other (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc).  When the music stops, students should find a partner near them. Help with pairing if needed. This activity also can be done without music by ringing a chime when it is time for students to stop walking around.
  3. Partners share their responses to the question on the cards.
  4. Have them exchange cards when you start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as time permits.
  5. Reconvene a community circle. Ask for volunteers to share out one thing that surprised them or one thing that they learned from this activity.
  6. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your personal and professional strengths and goals? (Self-Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ personal and professional goals? (Relationship Skills)

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • View 2.01 Goals Video  (1 min) and ask the following questions.
  • Explain and review the goals of LIA. They are lofty and can be demanding.
  • Why do you think LIA is offered at your school?
  • Have students reflect on what they are willing to put into reaching those goals?
  • View 2.01 HO LIA Standards – Student as a class, go over LIA’s purpose and standards.
  • LIA class materials were created to help you reach these goals; however, you all have individual talents and dreams. Today you will have time to set individual LIA goals.

  • Choose an LIA standard from 2.01 HO LIA Standards – Student and complete 2.01 HO SMARTE Goal Template as a class.

Guided Practice

  • Instruct each student to choose at least 2 goals that are centered around any of the LIA standards. Encourage the students to set at least one goal that is related to post-secondary education.
  • Discuss a few chosen goals as a class.

Create breakout pairs or groups of students in Jamboard and have students research and share ideas about two educational goals on their Jamboard page. Students will then report back to the whole class at the end of the session.
  • Tap into Miro for free digital whiteboard templates for education and increase participation for ELs. Students can collaborate and engage in online assignments and group projects.

  • Project 2.01 LIA Standards With Definitions – Student from a computer or allow students to view from a computer when viewing LIA standards.

Extension

  • Watch 2.01 Video LIA Conference Footage (0-2:00) and discuss as a class (1) educational goals you have previously set and reached and (2) educational goals you want to set and how you plan to reach them.
  • Watch 2.01 Video Philosophy For a Happy Life and discuss the three philosophies discussed.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What will help me achieve my goals?
  • How can I help my elementary students to set and achieve goals?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • identify multiple bilingual career options of interest
  • recognize qualities of positive role models (Self-Awareness)
  • identify personal, cultural, and linguistic assets (Self-Awareness)
  • recognize various jobs and the responsibilities the jobs hold (Self-Management)
  • identify future careers that are aligned to personal interests, skills, and goals (Self-Management)
  • Identify and value similarities and differences among different social and cultural groups (Social Awareness)
