ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiation Ideas

  • Guide students to realistic, achievable school options. Community and technical schools are good options if students have special circumstances. Direct students to 3.07 Weblink Technical Schools to search for technical schools by state, then model a technical school choice by using 3.07 HO College Exploration – Teacher Model (Differentiation). Invite the students to complete the remaining two choices using 3.07 HO College Exploration.
  • Allow students to look at postsecondary education options in the country where they have citizenship if they so choose (be cautious to not single any students out with this invitation). 
  • Invite the students to listen for college terms they’re unfamiliar with during the lesson. Invite them to look through Weblink Spanish College Terms for more information. 
  • Read “The Role of the ELL Teacher” in 3.07 Getting Ready for College: What ELL Students Need To Know. If you have time, read the whole article before class and share statistics, steps, tips, and other pertinent information with students.

Extension

  • Share your path and story to higher education with the class.
  • Invite an LIA alumni or a community professional to share their path and story to higher education with the class.
  • Invite the students to write a short essay or other form of expression to explain why they want, or do not want, to go to college.
  • Host an in-person multilingual parent informational session on post-secondary education. The post-secondary informational session can be hosted as a series of small group presentations where parents can choose from various workshops to gather information and ask questions. Guest speakers should include guidance counselors, college personnel, work-based coordinators, etc. Quality information and/or resources can be shared on college/career preparation and options.
  • Host a live virtual multilingual parent informational session on post-secondary education utilizing Google Meet or Zoom. The live virtual session allows parents the flexibility to join from their own home at a pre-scheduled time. The post-secondary informational session can be hosted as a series of small group presentations where parents can choose from various online workshops to gather information and ask questions. Guest speakers should include guidance counselors, college personnel, work-based coordinators, etc. Quality information and/or resources can be shared on college/career preparation and options. The event can also be recorded and later distributed to allow the information to be provided to parents who were unable to attend in person or live online.  

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What can a postsecondary education do for you? Is it beneficial for the career path you’ve chosen?
  • Did any of the information you learned today change your ideas about postsecondary education? Why or why not?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • explore different academic, social, health, and recreational services offered at a school of their choosing.
  • understand that effort and practice help build confidence and that feeling confident helps you do your best and makes you proud (Self-Awareness)
  • understand the impact of developing self-discipline and self-motivation (Self-Management) 
  • demonstrate appropriate social behaviors to improve success, i.e., ask permission, ask for help, offer help to others, and contribute to the community. (Self-Management)
  • recognize the importance of effort in goal attainment (Self-Management)

Purpose: To build a positive class community by encouraging students to work together to find information about a college or university. Students will work together in pairs to complete the My College Scavenger Hunt (Part 1) activity through the use of the Periodic Table Partners (Single) activity.  

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This My College Scavenger Hunt activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Dedicate time in your Community Circles/ Class Meetings to establish norms of collaboration on:
    1. how to greet each other once they meet their new Periodic Table Partners, 
    2. have them practice pronouncing each other's first and last names properly, 
    3. how they will ensure that each partner has equal time, and 
    4. how to thank each other once they have completed their activity instead of just walking away once the time is up. 
  2. Make copies of the Periodic Table Partners (single) and distribute to each student and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  3. Distribute the Periodic Table Partners handout to each student and follow the procedures for HS Lesson 3.02 on Clock Buddies. However, have them find a partner only for Boron and Americium. Once they have two Periodic Table Partners, hand out the My College Scavenger Hunt (Part 1) worksheet.  
  4. Call out which Periodic Table Partners they will be working with (ex., Boron) so that they can begin the scavenger hunt on their computers, collecting data from the same college or university. Each student fills in their own worksheet. 
  5. Once completed, have the students get together with their 2nd Periodic Table Partner (ex., Americium) to compare worksheets and their findings.
  6. Once done, return to the community circle and invite a few participants to share their findings and something they learned working with their partners on this scavenger hunt. 
  7. Before the period ends, have students turn in their Periodic Table Partners sheets for safekeeping to be used in future activities.
  8. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to work with a partner to complete the My College Scavenger Hunt worksheet? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about a virtual college scavenger hunt? (Self Management)

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
  • Last time we researched a few postsecondary schools of interest and looked at affordability, deadlines, admissions, etc. Today we will take a more in-depth look at academic, social, and recreational options available at the school of your choice.
  • Show the students 3.08 Video UCF Spirit Splash and/or 3.08 Video USU Basketball Chant and ask them the following question:
  • One main focus in choosing a college should be academics. However, there are many other aspects of college that are important to explore as well. What other aspects of college life may or may not influence your decision to attend a certain college?

  • Please select one of the following Virtual Campus Tours or choose your own. Keep in mind that you may need to create a free account before being able to view the virtual tour videos and resources listed below:
    • Weblink - Campus Tours Interactive Maps and Virtual Tours
    • Weblink – YouVisit College Search Virtual Tours (Nationwide List)
    • Weblink – Florida Colleges Virtual Tours List
    • Weblink – University of Utah Virtual Tour
  • Take the virtual tour as a class.
  • During or after the Virtual Campus Tour, facilitate a discussion about different academic, recreational, and social services offered at the college.

Guided Practice

  • Place students in pairs or groups based on their ideal college choice, interested major, or other similar interests. 
  • Distribute 3.08 HO Virtual College Tour (English) or 3.08 HO Virtual College Tour (Spanish) to each student group and invite them to complete the information using the school website of their choice.
  • Inform students that they will receive additional time in the next lesson to complete the handout. Each student team will choose something from each category in the handout to share with the class tomorrow.

 

Independent Practice

  • Read the blog post Using Social Media to Research Colleges to better understand the positive presence social media can play when searching schools. 
  • Invite students to visit a school’s social media channel like Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, or LinkedIn. Students can now connect with schools through the power of social media. Many schools are sharing photos on Instagram, YouTube videos, tweets, and more. Hashtags, blogs, and specific groups on social media channels are great ways to connect prospective students with schools and facilitate conversations around specific topics.
  • Have students search specific college groups such as new students, freshman, current students, and alumni. Students can post questions on the social media channel or specific group’s page regarding academics, dorms, food, clubs, extracurricular activities, etc.  Students will then share with the class what they have learned about a particular school.

Extension

  • Use 3.08 PPT USU Services Offered, or create your own presentation showcasing services at a local college. Share what you learned with the class about the different academic, recreational, and social services offered.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Based on your Virtual College Tour research, do you meet the admission requirements? Does the college offer the major you want to pursue? Do tuition and living expenses fit within your budget? Explain your answers.

  • Do they have programs that support me and my goals? What programs do?

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • teach the class about different academic, social, health, and recreational services offered at a school of their choosing.
  • understand that effort and practice help build confidence and that feeling confident helps you do your best and makes you proud (Self-Awareness)
  • understand the impacts of developing self-discipline and self-motivation (Self-Management) 
  • demonstrate appropriate social behaviors to improve success, i.e., ask permission, ask for help, offer help to others, and contribute to the community. (Self-Management)
  • recognize the importance of effort in goal attainment (Self-Management)

Purpose: To build a positive class community by encouraging students to work together to find information about a college or university. Students work together in triads to complete the My College Scavenger Hunt (Part 2) activity through the use of the Periodic Table Partners (single) activity.  

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This My College Scavenger Hunt activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Dedicate time in your Community Circles/ Class Meetings to establish norms of collaboration on:
    1. how to greet each other once they meet their new Periodic Table Partners, 
    2. have them practice pronouncing each other's first and last names properly, 
    3. how they will ensure that each partner has equal time, and 
    4. how to thank each other once they have completed their activity instead of just walking away once the time is up. 
  2. Make copies of the Periodic Table Partners (single) and distribute to each student and follow the procedures for HS Lesson 3.02 on Clock Buddies. However, have them find two new partners only for Boron. Once they have two new Periodic Table Partners, hand out their original My College Scavenger Hunt worksheet that they used in Lesson 3.08.  
  3. Call out which Periodic Table Partners they will be working with (ex., Boron) so that they can begin a round-robin process of sharing out each item on their worksheets. 
  4. Once done, return to the community circle and invite a few participants to share their findings and something they learned working with two new partners on this scavenger hunt. 
  5. Before the period ends, have students turn in their Periodic Table Partners sheets for safekeeping to be used in future activities.
  6. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to work with two other partners to review the My College Scavenger Hunt worksheet? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about a virtual college scavenger hunt? (Self Management)

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
    • Last time we began to take a more in-depth look at academic, social, and recreational options available at the school of your choice. Today we will continue to look at services offered at your school of choice and learn services offered at your peers’ school of choice.
  • Show the students 3.09 Video – A Mile in Someone Else’s Shoes (4 min).
  • Ask a student to share about a time they had ill-fitting shoes that hurt their feet.
  • Share the following with the students:
    • Just as there are many things to consider when choosing the right shoe for an occasion, there are many things to consider when choosing which college you want to attend.
  • Ask the students the following questions:
    • What must a college have to make it a good fit for you?
    • What aspects of a college are most important to you? Which aspects are not as important to you?

  • Review 3.08 USU Services Offered or answer any questions the students may have if needed.

Guided Practice

  • Allow each student group additional time to complete 3.08 HO Virtual College Tour.

Independent Practice

  • Read the blog post Using Social Media to Research Colleges to better understand the positive presence social media can play when searching schools.
  • Invite students to visit a school’s social media channel like Instagram, Facebook, Twitter, or LinkedIn. Students can now connect with schools through the power of social media by viewing photos and videos on Instagram, YouTube, tweets, and more. Hashtags, blogs, and specific groups on social media channels are great ways to connect prospective students with schools.
  • Have students search specific college groups such as new students, freshman, current students, and alumni. Students can post questions on the social media channel or specific group’s page regarding academics, dorms, food, clubs, extracurricular activities, etc.  Students will then share with the class what they have learned about a particular school.

Purpose: To build a positive class community by encouraging students to work together to create their own ideal college or university. Students will work together in triads using the Periodic Table Partners (double) to complete the My College Scavenger Hunt (Part 3) activity from Lesson 3.09 to create their own ideal college or university. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This My College Scavenger Hunt and Periodic Table Partners (Part 2) activities will further enhance students’ competencies of Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Dedicate time in your Community Circles/ Class Meetings to establish norms of collaboration on:
    1. how to greet each other once they meet their new Periodic Table Partners, 
    2. have them practice pronouncing each other's first and last names properly, 
    3. how they will ensure that each partner has equal time, and 
    4. how to thank each other once they have completed their activity instead of just walking away once the time is up. 
  2. Return their copies (or make new copies) of the Periodic Table Partners (double) from Lesson 3.09. Have them find two new partners they have not had a chance to work with for the element Americium (or any other element that you choose). Once they have two new Periodic Table Partners, have them use their original My College Scavenger Hunt worksheet that they used in Lesson 3.08.
  3. Give students instructions to create their own ideal college or university using the characteristics from the scavenger hunt or other materials as needed. Here are the steps:
    1. They will need chart paper or 8.5x17 sheets of paper and markers to diagram their own university or college. They should include buildings and labels of offices, different theme houses, and activity centers that would be the ideal campus for them.
    2. Create a humorous name for the school. Encourage humor and creativity in the lettering. The acronym should represent something funny such as SWAGU = Showing the World All Your Greatness University; UFO = University of Fancy Outfits; LOLU, UFBI, etc. Let them know the acronyms have to make sense and be respectable.
  4. Call out which Periodic Table Partners they will be working with (ex., Americium). so that they can begin their projects. Give them 5-8 minutes (they can continue their project over a period of a few days if they need more time)
  5. Once done, have them post their charts around the room and return to the community circle. Invite a few participants to share their creations. Give students the opportunity to improve on their charts and present their final versions over the next few days. 
  6. Before the period ends, have students turn in their Periodic Table Partners sheets for safekeeping to be used in future activities.
  7. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to work with two other partners to create their own college or university campus? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about creating your own college or university? (Self Management)

 

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson:
    • Last time we explored academic, social, and recreational options available at multiple colleges or universities. Today we will talk about how to save money for college NOW.  
    • Invite each student to estimate the cost of a three-credit university class.
    • Discuss the cost of three credits by displaying 3.10 Weblink – Tuition Estimator at UofU, 3.10 Weblink – Tuition Estimator at FAU, or another local university tuition calculator of your choosing.
    • Ask the students if they are aware of college courses available in their high school, and if so, which ones. Make a list and invite students to share what they have experienced or heard about these classes.
    • Ask the students about how much money they will save if they take 2, 4, or 6 college courses in high school.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Model

  • Invite a guidance counselor or administrator to discuss with the class the Course of Studies Catalog available at your high school. The guest speaker will review the proposed academic and college level course offerings and descriptions of each course. LIA students will create a digital flowchart, using Canva or Miro, of their selected programs of study in high school, grade-level requirements, prerequisites, and credits granted for successful completion. Students should understand the requirements for graduation and the opportunities to take college courses and earn college credits while in high school. The session should be offered in English and the students’ home language. 
  • Give each student a high school registration booklet or an information sheet where they can access all post-secondary courses available to them.
  • Use 3.10 Teacher Model CE, AP and TECH Info to guide a discussion around the differences and similarities between concurrent enrollment, AP courses, and courses offered at a technical school. Instruct the students to take notes on new information.
  • *NOTE: 3.10 Teacher Model CE, AP and TECH Info is only a general guide. Course titles, prerequisites, and mechanics of how these courses work will vary depending on your school and state. If you are unclear about the options available at your school, please speak with the school counselor.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute 3.10 HO CE, AP, and TECH Info (English) to each student and complete the first seven questions as a class.

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

  • Invite students to share which courses they want to take and why.
  • Inform the student that next class period we will be working on college admission applications. If they would like to submit an application during class they will most likely need to bring their driver’s license and a form of payment. Encourage them to check out the application beforehand.
  • Quickly go over or distribute 3.11 Student Sample – College Application Suggested Materials and Information and inform students that next lesson they will have time to apply for college. Encourage students to take a look at the sheet so that they are prepared to jump in during the next lesson.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiation Ideas

  • Invite students to share what high school post-secondary course options were available at their previous high school(s).  
  • Use 3.10 HO CE, AP, and TECH Info (Spanish).
  • If students do not meet the minimum requirement(s) to take college courses, invite them to explore courses offered through a technical school or set a SMARTE goal using the 2.01 SMARTE Goal Template centered around passing current classes, remediation courses, study habits, etc.  

Extension

  • Use 3.10 Weblink – USU General Education Requirements to assist in teaching students about general education requirements in college. Note that this is Utah State University’s website. You may use a different source if you prefer. 
  • Just like in high school, in college, you are required to take certain courses or certain courses within an umbrella category like “creative arts”. It is important to understand this so you do not take classes in high school that are not needed.
  • Example: Unless you want to go into the music field, it may not be wise to take Music 1010, AP Music, and AP Art. You will most likely only be able to use one of them, the rest will go to elective credit.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What programs are available to me now to help me prepare or even receive college credit?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • fill out a college application of their choice.
  • Understand the impact of developing self-discipline and self-motivation (Self-Management) 
  • demonstrate appropriate social behaviors to improve success, i.e., ask permission, ask for help, offer help to others, and contribute to the community. (Self-Management)
  • recognize the importance of effort in goal attainment (Self-Management)

Purpose: To create opportunities for students to define steps towards accomplishing their goal of attending college. Students will work together in triads (3 people) to complete the Step by Step Map (Part 1) through the use of the Periodic Table Partners (double) activity. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: These Periodic Table Partners (double) and  Step by Step Map activities will further enhance students’ competencies of Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Self-Management.

Overview: 

  1. The Step by Step Map is used to sequence events and information. The substages are the smaller boxes underneath the regular boxes so that students can add additional details of each major step. Students can also have the option of drawing pictures or anything that shows a sequence instead of the boxes.
  2. Return their copies (or make new copies) of the Periodic Table Partners (double) from Lesson 3.09. Have them find two new partners, whom they have not had a chance to work with, for element Krypton (or any other element that you choose). Once they have two new Periodic Table Partners, distribute copies of the Step by Step Map.
  3. Give students instructions and examples on filling out the Step By Step Map on how to go to college (another option is to have the students select a topic of interest to them to get used to using the map). Below is a list of possible steps for students to begin their planning using the Step By Step Map. These could be posted on the board or screen. Allow them to use their computers:
    • support of family members
    • college planning timeline
    • taking college entrance exams - ACT/SAT
    • choosing a college
    • the college application process
    • campus visits
    • writing a college essay
    • college interview
    • paying for college (2 or 4 year)
    • applying for financial aid
    • And other possible steps students may think of.
  4. Call out which Periodic Table Partners they will be working with (ex. Krypton) so that they can begin working on their maps. Give them 5-8 minutes (they can continue their project over a period of a few days if they need more time)
  5. Once done, have them return to the community circle. Invite a few students to share their creations. Give students the opportunity to improve on their maps and present their final versions over the next few days. 
  6. Before the period ends, have students turn in their Periodic Table Partners sheets for safekeeping to be used in future activities.
  7. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to work with two other partners to map out the steps to get into a college or university? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about mapping out your own college or university plans? (Self Management)

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
  • The last few lessons have been focused on preparing for and exploring post-secondary education options. Today you will be given time to apply to your chosen school.
  • Hold a class discussion around the following questions.
  • Has your top school choice changed or stayed the same, what has or hasn’t influenced your choice?
  • What are some barriers you or your friends might be facing that may influence your decision to attend college? What are some solutions?

Differentiation Ideas

  • Allow students to make phone calls during class. Some technical colleges do not have online applications and need to be contacted to begin the admissions process.
  • Encourage ALL students to apply for some type of post-secondary education (e.g., technical school, certificate, community college, etc.) that fits their financial, learning, and citizenship circumstances.

Extension

  • Send in an application to a second college.
  • Find and apply for school-sponsored scholarships.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • When do I need to start college applications?
  • Who and what resources are available to help me with the application process?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • search and apply for at least 2 scholarships
  • understand that effort and practice help build confidence and that feeling confident helps you do your best and makes you proud (Self-Awareness)
  • understand the impact of developing organization skills (Self-Management) 
  • recognize the importance of effort in goal attainment (Self-Management)
  • demonstrate appropriate social behaviors to improve success, i.e., ask permission, ask for help, offer help to others, contribute to the community. (Relationship Skills)

Purpose: To strengthen students' listening skills and encourage all to participate in a discussion based on the steps they’ve defined in their own Step by Step Map (Part 2) . The Fishbowl activity (optional: see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook p.25-26) will be used to facilitate discussion among the groups. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Fishbowl and the Step by Step Map activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
  • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
  • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
  • Greetings
  1. In this Fishbowl activity, participants are divided into two groups that are seated in concentric circles, all facing the center. The outside circle listens while the inside group has a discussion about career exploration. After 5 minutes, the groups switch places so the listeners become the speakers, and vice versa. 
  2. Consider using equity sticks (a cup of sticks with each student’s name on one) to increase student participation and accountability.
  3. Have students prepare their comments about their Step by Step Map and the meaning of each step and why they are important before engaging in the Fishbowl. Here are a few questions that could be used to stimulate further conversation (feel free to consider other questions): 
    1. Why is it important to get the support of family members to attend college?
    2. Name a few examples of professional/career goals you have considered?
    3. What would you include in writing a college essay?
    4. What are some options you have considered for paying for your college education?
    5. Why is a college education important in order for you to reach your professional goals?
    6. What are some courses in college you will have to take in order to reach your professional/career goals?
  1. Only the inside group members may speak during this time (5 minutes). Instruct the outside group to quietly listen and notice if any of their own ideas surface during the discussion. Encourage everyone to add additional notes to their Step by Step Map.
  2. When the time is up, ask the groups to trade places so that the outside group is sitting on the inner circle chairs and vice versa. Set the timer again for five minutes and let the new inside group discuss the topic.
  3. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  1. So What? Why do you think it’s important to share your thoughts about the steps to get into a college or university?  (Self-Management) 
  2. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about mapping out your own college or university plans?  (Responsible Decision Making)

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
  • Last time we applied for college.  Applying is important, but we also need to get finances in order. Tuition expenses can be a major barrier to attending college. There are many different ways to pay for college. Today we will be exploring and applying for scholarships as a means to pay partial or full college expenses. In the financial freedom unit, we will discuss loans, grants, etc.
  • Watch 3.12 Video Scholarship Overview (2 min) and invite the students to answer the questions below.
  • What is the best search tool for finding scholarships?
  • Besides the internet, where are other good places to look for scholarships?
  • Hold a class discussion around the following questions.
  • How have your family members, friends or others you know paid for college?
  • How do you plan on paying for college?
  • Have you ever applied for a scholarship? If so, which one(s) and what was required to apply?

  • Display 3.12 Weblink Scholarship Essay Writing Tips.  Some, not all, scholarships require essay submission. Let’s go over a few essay tips to help prepare you for your scholarship hunt today.
  • Choose a few tips to discuss as a class. Encourage discussion and student examples.

Independent Practice

  • Create an interactive class digital bulletin board using Google Slides, Padlet or Wakelet. Using a digital bulletin board allows ELs to consolidate information in an organized manner. Students start by locating scholarships and use the digital bulletin board to digitally bookmark scholarships that can be shared, collaborated on, and accessed by all students. Information for each scholarship should include type of scholarship, scholarship criteria, and scholarship funding, etc.
  • Distribute 3.12 HO Scholarship Websites Resources to each student or allow them online access to the doc so they can click on the links.
  • Go to the computer lab and allow students adequate time to research and apply for at least two scholarships.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Differentiation Ideas

  • Encourage students of all grade levels and citizenship to apply for scholarships. The best time to apply for scholarships is NOW. Use the following links as suggestions: 3.12 Weblink – HS Freshman Scholarships, 3.12 Weblink – Undocumented Scholarships. 
  • Teach how to write a scholarship essay by using 3.12 Weblink Tips. Invite the students to take notes and write down the essay outline given in this 3.12 Scholarship Essay Outline.

Extension

  • Browse local high school websites. Most high schools have a scholarship page.
  • Visit the counseling center, often scholarships or additional resources can be found there.
  • Invite the school counselor to class and discuss different scholarships available.
  • Encourage students to apply for scholarships that require an essay submission. Allow students time to write the essay and encourage peer reviews before submission.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What scholarships are available to me?
  • Is there a person/resource that I can use to help me find other scholarships?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • learn basic overview and eligibility requirements for FAFSA.
  • understand that effort and practice help build confidence and that feeling confident helps you do your best and makes you proud (Self-Awareness)
  • uUnderstand the impact of developing self-discipline and self-motivation (Self-Management) 
  • demonstrate appropriate social behaviors to improve success, i.e., ask permission, ask for help, offer help to others, contribute to the community. (Relationship Skills)

Purpose: To strengthen critical thinking skills and encourage all students to participate in conversation.  Students will use their completed Step by Step Map (Part 3) and the 4Ws and 4 Corners activities to guide group discussion about [INSERT TOPIC OF DISCUSSION] strengthen critical thinking skills and encourage all students to participate in a discussion using their own Step by Step Map (Part 3) that they have completed.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The is 4Ws and 4 Corners activities and with their Step by Step Map activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Prepare 4 sheets of paper of four different colors with one of the 4Ws in large visible type on each sheet. Post one sheet in each of the 4 corners of the classroom. For example, the blue sheet would have the WOW!!!, the green sheet would have the I Wonder???, etc.  
  2. Make copies of the 4Ws worksheet (or 5x8 cards) in equal number of 4 different colors. For example, if you have 20 students, then there would be 5 blue, 5 green, 5 yellow and 5 orange color worksheets (or cards). Distribute one worksheet or card per student, making sure that the four colors are evenly divided by the number of students and that they are randomly distributed. One option is to pre-assign the color worksheet/cards to ensure diversity in language ability, national and cultural background so that they will be able to meet new friends. 
  3. If using cards, have the students fold the cards in half and have them add the 4Ws as a header on each of the cards (the worksheets are already labeled):
    • WOW!!! - [INSERT AN EXAMPLE OR WHAT STUDENTS ARE TO BE RESPONDING TO]
    • I Wonder??? - [FOR EXAMPLE, I WONDER HOW…]
    • I Wish* * * - [INSERT EXAMPLE]
    • I Worry About. :O - [INSERT EXAMPLE]
  4. Take three minutes for students to write one sentence for each of the 4Ws on their worksheet/card regarding their work with the Step by Step Maps.
  5. Once completed, explain to the students that they will be going to the corner that corresponds to the color of their worksheet/card. Once in the corner, they will select a Recorder and Reporter for each group. Studnet will then sshare their thoughts (round robin style) about the one 4Ws that corresponds to their assigned corner. For example, students in the I Wish*** corner will only discuss their notes on I Wish***. Have them select a Recorder and Reporter for each group. Allow 5 minutes for this activity.
  6. Once done, return to their community circle and the Reporter from each corner to share their findings. 
  7. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  1. So What? Why do you think it’s important to share your thoughts about the 4Ws?  (Self-Management) 
  2. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about the 4Ws and 4 Corners activity?  (Responsible Decision Making)

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
  • Last time we applied for scholarships or free money. Today we are going to learn about FAFSA, a potential additional option to support scholarships and individual funds.
  • Display 3.13 Article – How Much Does College Cost? Talk through some of the highlights, prices, and graphics.
  • Discuss the following questions:
  • Do you think scholarship searches were successful?  Why or why not?
  • Do you feel you have enough funds to attend college? What are other barriers might you face?
  • If you don’t receive a scholarship, how do you plan to pay for school?
  • Aside from scholarships, what other forms of financial assistance are available?

  • If students are not eligible to apply for FAFSA invite them to continue to search and apply for scholarships. Try 3.13 Weblink Scholarships 1 or 3.13 Weblink Scholarships 2 to get students started.
  • If students are not eligible to apply for FAFSA invite them to look at alternative options. Some examples include the following: attending a less expensive college; seeking some type of trade or certificate to earn money to pay for college; researching a college in their home country, etc.

Extension

  • Invite students to explore the official FAFSA website: studentaid.gov/h/apply-for-aid/fafsa
  • Invite a financial representative from a local college or your school counselor to help answer student questions.
    • Introduce students to FAFSA by taking them to a computer lab and inviting them to complete the 3.13 Weblink Federal Student Aid Estimator.
  • Host an in-person multilingual parent informational session on financial aid and an overview of the FASFA. The informational session can be hosted as a series of small group presentations where parents can choose from various workshops to gather information and ask questions. Guest speakers should include guidance counselors and college financial aid advisors. The high school should ensure that information is communicated to parents in a language that they understand. Translation or interpretation services should be provided.
  • Host a live virtual multilingual parent informational session on financial aid and an overview of the FASFA.  The live virtual session allows parents the flexibility to join from their own home at a pre-scheduled time. The informational session can be hosted as a series of small group presentations where parents can choose from various online workshops to gather information and ask questions. Guest speakers should include guidance counselors and college financial aid advisors. The high school should ensure that information is communicated to parents in a language that they understand. Translation or interpretation services should be provided. The event can also be recorded and later distributed to allow the information to be provided to parents who were unable to attend in-person or live online.
  • The event can also be recorded and later distributed to allow the information to be provided to parents who were unable to attend in-person or live online.  
  • Use 3.13 UHEAA FAFSA DIY Kit FLAG for assistance in planning a FAFSA night or answering FAQs about filling out FAFSA, resources, dependency status, glossary, unique situations, tips for undocumented students,  etc.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What could I have done in elementary school or junior high to prepare for college? How could you use this perspective to influence the student you tutor?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVE:

Students will: 

  • begin to apply for FAFSA
  • understand that effort and practice help build confidence and that feeling confident helps you do your best and makes you proud (Self-Awareness)
  • demonstrate positive behaviors and self-regulation skills such as organization, completing tasks independently, bringing materials needed, planning projects, and making corrections (Self-Management)
  • evaluate the consequences of various actions and decisions and consider the long term well-being of oneself and others (Responsible Decision Making)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To engage students in structured academic discussion with peers by using the Give 1! Get 1! activity. This will encourage students to reflect on any significant learnings, strategies or ideas they have learned from Unit 3 on College and Career Exploration. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Give 1! Get 1! activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Make copies of the Give 1! Get 1! worksheet and give students a copy. Make sure that they add their names to the sheet.
  2. While in the Community Circle, explain the following steps for Give 1! Get 1! activity (this activity can be used for any topic in any subject area or grade level:
    1. On your own, write down four significant learnings, strategies, or ideas you have learned from Unit 3 on College and Career Exploration. They should be one sentence long and could refer to their Step by Step Map and/or 4Ws cards for ideas. 
    2. Once students have listed four learnings, strategies, or ideas, play soft music to mark the start of the activity and so that students can begin walking around the class sharing to share one of their ideas with a partner (Give 1!) and add one unique idea from their partner (Get 1!) to their sheet. Students should read their sentences directly from their notes and they should add the sentence and name of the partner who gives them one to their sheets. Students continue the process of getting one idea from another student until their sheets are filled, at which time, they should return to the community circle.
    3. Students must follow a specific discussion structure and use sentence starters when first introducing Give 1! Get 1! It is important to model how to share using good academic speech. Here is an example of how a good discussion might look like:
      1. Student 1: Hello ____. May I share with you?
      2. Student 2: Yes
      3. Student 1: I feel that music is important because it can unite people.
      4. Student 2: In other words, you think that music brings people together?
      5. Student 1: That's right. What's your idea?
  3. Once students are back in their community circles, begin the process of sharing out by having students invite another student who they exchanged an idea with to share with the community. Continue this process for a few minutes. This should go smoothly because each student has already practiced sharing an idea with a few peers. 
  4. This Give 1! Get 1! strategy takes some prep and may take time it can be tough to teach students the procedure the first few times around. However, it gets students to engage in academic conversation in a low-risk environment. It keeps every student accountable and is a great way to increase the energy of the class! 
  5. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own ideas about college and career exploration with your peers? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned through this Give 1! Get 1! activity? (Self Management)

 

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
  • Last time we learned some basics about FAFSA. Today you will have class time to start and potentially submit your applications. We have invited a guest (introduce the guest) to assist with FAFSA questions.

  • Display 3.14 Weblink Official FAFSA Application.
  • Invite the school counselor or FAFSA specialist to walk the class through creating an account and/or an FSA ID. Suggest that students write their account information down for easy future reference.

Guided Practice

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiation Ideas

  • If students are not eligible to apply for FAFSA invite them to continue to search and apply for scholarships. Try 3.13 Weblink Scholarships 1 or 3.13 Scholarships 2 to get students started.
  • If students are not eligible to apply for FAFSA invite them to look at alternative options. Some examples include the following: attending a less expensive college; seeking some type of trade or certificate to earn money to pay for college; and researching a college in their home country, etc.  
  • Ask your school counselor when and where the nearest FAFSA Application Night is and encourage students to attend for additional individual attention.
  • If a counselor is unavailable, direct students to 3.14 Weblink – FAFSA Help for FAQs, chat, email, and phone contact information.

Extension

  • Host an in-person multilingual parent informational session on financial aid and an overview of the FASFA. The informational session can be hosted as a series of small group presentations where parents can choose from various workshops to gather information and ask questions. Guest speakers should include guidance counselors and college financial aid advisors. The high school should ensure that information is communicated to parents in a language that they understand. Translation or interpretation services should be provided.
  • Host a live virtual multilingual parent informational session on financial aid and an overview of the FASFA. The live virtual session allows parents the flexibility to join from their own home at a pre-scheduled time. The informational session can be hosted as a series of small group presentations where parents can choose from various online workshops to gather information and ask questions. Guest speakers should include guidance counselors and college financial aid advisors. The high school should ensure that information is communicated to parents in a language that they understand. Translation or interpretation services should be provided. The event can also be recorded and later distributed to allow the information to be provided to parents who were unable to attend in-person or live online.   
  • Allow students additional lesson time to complete the FAFSA application.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What do I wish I would have done when I was in elementary or middle school to prepare for college? Write down your thoughts and share them with the students you tutor at your next session.
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

The tip of the iceberg is the only easily visible part, yet it would be foolish to make a judgement on its overall size based on that alone. You already know that the majority of an iceberg is beneath the surface of the water.

This phenomenon applies to you and your students. There are certain characteristics we can easily see, but stopping there would only give us a surface or shallow understanding of that person. A CRT teacher will strive to learn the qualities beneath the surface. A teacher who champions his or her students will need to understand and connect with them through deep relationships. At that point, you will know how put them in situations where they will connect with your teaching and succeed in your class.

There a many human examples of this concept and surely you have been on both ends, as someone who misjudged or has been misjudged.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain: Last time we discussed personal, family, and celebrity spending and saving habits. In addition to saving personal money for college, today we are going to explore multiple ways to pay for college.  
  • Discuss the following questions:
    • Who knows how much it costs to go to Stanford University for one year? (about $45,000)
    • What about the University of Utah? (resident $8,240 versus non-resident $26,180)
    • How do you plan on paying for school?

Model 

  • Explain: We are going to split into 6 groups. Each group will have the same tuition costs, but will each have a different method of paying for college. Each group will explore and teach a different method of payment to the class.
  • Display Option 1 (Teacher Model) on 4.02 Paying for College Activity. *Note: interest rates change every year, these total costs are ESTIMATES.
  • Explain the information in Option 1, calculate the total cost and discuss the pros and cons as a class.
  • Give each student a copy of 4.02 HO Paying for College Handout and complete Option 1 - Subsidized Loan together.

Guided Practice

  • Split students into 6 groups and give them each a different option to explore and discuss.
  • Invite each group to review their information, calculate the total cost and discuss the pros and cons.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain  Last time we invited a guest speaker to class to discuss the importance of saving money and the different costs associated with graduating from high school.  Today we are going to take the knowledge we have learned and create a college budget.

Model

  • Give each student the 4.04 Weblink HO College Budget.
  • Discuss possible income sources and help the students categorize their income suggestions (e.g., babysitting, student loans, grants, scholarships, birthday money, etc.).
  • Discuss items explored in previous financial responsibility lessons such as saving habits, spending habits, guest speaker advice, etc. Invite students to incorporate these ideas into their budget.
  • Go to the “transportation” category and ask the students to estimate how much an average car payment or average car insurance will be in college.
  • Show students how to find this information by doing a Google search as a class.  Example: type in “average used car cost” or “average car insurance cost for a college student in Utah.”

Independent Practice

  • Invite each student to complete the remainder of the worksheet individually according to the location and college they plan on attending.

Students will:

  • learn about leadership styles  
  • learn the purpose and responsibilities of LIA leadership committees 
  • build an understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-management)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
  • determine common social goals and interests related to LIA leadership committees (Responsible Decision Making)

column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use this Stand Up / Hand Up activity to help students get to know one another better, visually see how others are similar to and different from self and build confidence within the community to share who we are and to interact with growing ease.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This The Stand Up / Hand Up activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Management, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (5 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Teacher reads a series of statements aloud. Students stand up or raise their hand to indicate that the statement applies to them. 
    • When explaining the activity to students, explicitly encourage them to ‘boldly look around, don’t just sneak a peek!’ to see how others are responding, since our goal is to learn about each other.
    • Keep the pace lively and fun—read each statement with an equally upbeat expression so students can feel positive about any they respond to; do a quick look around, acknowledging the responders by nodding, smiling, eye contact; zip on to the next statement.
    • Some students enjoy the option for more movement (stand up) while others prefer less (hand up). Teachers know best about their own comfort level and about their class, so might choose to offer only one response option.
  • First round of Statements (Stand up, hand up if you…)
    • Did something fun outdoors in the past two days
    • Listened to music that helped you feel good
    • Read for pleasure, not an assignment
    • Laughed out loud about something
    • Wrote in a journal
    • Played any kind of game (inside, outside or online)
    • Prepared some food for yourself and/or others
  • Second round of Statements (Stand up, hand up if you…)
    • Belong, use to belong, to any kind of organization, club, committee, or group that meets regularly 
    • Held a position in a club or organization such as president, VP, captain, secretary, reporter, etc.
    • Lead a meeting or activity where others followed your direction
    • Were responsible to organize materials, supplies, and resources of a club or organization
    • Know what an agenda is and why it is important to have one
    • Were responsible for resolving a misunderstanding, conflict, or disagreement where you were able to reach a compromise
  • Have students form a trio and tell them the name of the club, committee, or organization that you belong to now or have in the past, or one that you would like to belong to someday. After each partner names their club or organization, explain why they want to belong to it.
  • Have them share with the larger class.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ways to be a leader of a club, committee, or organization? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about leadership today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkages

  • Discuss the need for organization and leadership by discussing the following questions.
  • What do you think would happen if the school did away with teachers, principals, and other leadership?
  • What do you think would happen if teachers did not follow through with school, district, and/or state requirements?
  • What about on a larger scale (e.g., state or national level)?
  • What if the president decided he no longer wanted to attend any of his meetings?
  • Why are organization and leadership important?

Video

  • Watch 5.01 Video Leadership Styles (2 min).
  • Ask students to think about the following questions:
    • Which leadership style do you think is the most effective?
    • Do any of them come across as condescending, why or why not?
    • What leadership style would you respond best to?
  • How does being a member of LIA place you in leadership positions in the school and community?

column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Committee Overview

  • Display and discuss each committee’s purpose, responsibilities and resources/ideas:
  • 5.01 LIA Leadership Committee Overview
    • Professionalism
    • Service
    • Social Activities
    • President, Historian and Secretary
  • Explain that students will elect leadership positions and be placed in committees during the next class period. Reference 5.01 LIA Leadership Selection Guidelines. Note: Depending upon how the teacher chooses to run the election, elections may extend over 2 or 3 class periods.

Model

  • Explain that each LIA student will participate in regular committee meetings.  
  • Ask the students what they picture an LIA leadership meeting to be like.
  • Discuss and model what an LIA meeting would look like using 5.01 LIA Meeting Agenda Teacher Model.
  • Students will use 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline for this activity.

Activity

  • Challenge small groups of students to simulate a campaign for an assigned LIA leadership role by building arguments to support issues that are relevant to the specific role. Students research sample slogans to create a campaign slogan and digital poster.
  • Host a mock election based on the simulated campaign developed by the small groups of students. Students choose the electronic resource to be used for the voting process.

  • Place students in pairs and assign each group a leadership style.  Have each group fill out 5.01 HO Leadership Styles: Frayer Model and then share their finished model with other groups.

Extension

  • Have the students split into small groups and use the computer to research what leadership styles specific world leaders are using 5.01 HO Leadership Style Examples.
  • Watch 5.01 Video Book Drive and 5.01 Video Fundraiser to view previous LIA events.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Think of a current leader. What specific, admirable qualities does that leader possess?
  • What leadership qualities do you possess?  Where/who did you learn these qualities from?

Students will:

  • choose committee leaders and individual leadership committee meetings.
  • develop understanding of how social interdependence affects trust (Self-Awareness)
  • recognize opportunities and demands that exist in current setting (Social Awareness)
  • continue developing effective communication skills (Relationship Skills)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use this Leadership Shout Out activity to help students identify positive leadership characteristics of a specific person who is personally admired. Students will discuss perspectives about what constitutes admirable qualities in a leader.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Leadership Shout Out activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (5 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Before students arrive, write directions on the board or screen. As they arrive, greet them warmly at the door by preferred name and correct pronunciation. Point them toward the posted Welcoming Activity.
  • Use a pairing activity to group students intentionally ensuring that English-dominant students are paired with ELs. 
  • Welcome! In the next five minutes:
    • THINK ABOUT a leader in your family, community, or the world, who you admire. What qualities does that leader (show?) (demonstrate?)
    • CHAT with at least two other people and share your thinking about the leader and their admirable qualities.
    • PREPARE to share with the whole group.
  • Chart their responses on the board, looking for similarities and differences. 
  • Ask students to reflect on the leadership qualities that they would like to develop for themselves. Share with a partner.
  • When the time is up use an attention signal to bring the group to quiet focused attention. Invite volunteers to share their own thinking (not their partner’s—although they may want to encourage their partner to share!).  

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore characteristics of a leader? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about leadership today? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Use breakout rooms for partner/trio conversations. Relevancy/Linkages

  • Review the previous lesson by asking the following question.
    • What are the 3 main leadership styles and give an example of each.
    • If needed, review 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline.
    • Watch 5.02 Video Latinos In Action and consider the following questions.
    • How can you serve others?
    • How does serving others in turn benefit you?
    • How do LIA Leadership Committees help you develop qualities you need to be successful during and after high school?

Committee Business

  • Review your chosen class election process and, if needed, 5.01 LIA Leadership Selection Guidelines.
  • Hold your class election.
  • Announce the leaders and committee members.
  • As each class election process is different, the time needed may vary. Adjust the lesson accordingly.

INSTRUCTION

Model

  • Explain that committee leaders should prepare an agenda for each meeting and use the information and meeting time to create an LIA Activity Proposal Form for each activity.
  • Guide students through the 5.02 LIA Activity Proposal Form Teacher Model.

Guided Practice

  • Students split into their committees.
  • Pass out the corresponding 5.01 LIA Leadership Overview handout to each committee (Professionalism, Service, Social Activities, President, Historian and Secretary)
  • Students may use the 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline or create their own agenda.
  • Students may use the 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline or create their own agenda.
  • Give each committee 5.02 HO LIA Activity Proposal Form to fill out when they are ready.
  • Students have the remainder of class time to hold their first committee meeting.

Alternate Activity

  • Explain to the class that some social platforms are designed specifically for professional networking. Colleges and employers look for individuals that stand out from other applicants. In order to set themselves up for college and career success, students will create a LinkedIn profile to post their skills, interests, LIA leadership roles, and accomplishments. Provide students with the LinkedIn Profile Checklist.

  • learn how to work well with others through an interactive game and situational practice
  • notice how they integrate personal and social-cultural identities (Self-awareness)
  • practice acknowledging diverse norms (Social Awareness)
  • develop teamwork and leadership skills (Relationship Skills)

WELCOMING ACTIVITY  

Purpose: To use this 1-2-3 CLAP! skill-building activity to help a group quickly bond in preparation for collaboration, cooperation, and team building that would encourage innovation and creativity during class activities. It demonstrates how making mistakes together can be a fast track to generous, creative collaboration. (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This 1-2-3 CLAP! activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (7 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Use one of a number of pairing strategies to assign students in pairs that are inclusive, equitable, and diverse. 
  • Once students have been paired, the same partners face each other during each of the three rounds of this activity. When modeling with a student partner, it’s always the teacher who ‘makes the mistake.’

Round 1:

  • Explain that pairs will count to three over and over again, with each player saying the next number in the sequence.
  • Model slowly with a partner.
  • Once everyone has had a minute or two to play, call the game to a close with your agreed-upon attention signal. Ask, "How many of you made a mistake?" "What did you do when you made a mistake?" (Common answers: “Laughed” or "Said sorry" or “Pulled back.”)
  • Explain that these are all ways that people give cues to the group that say, "I've got this. I'll laugh at myself or apologize as my way of handling making a mistake."
  • Tell the group that during the next round, whenever they make a mistake, they should raise their hands in the air and say, "Tah-dah!"

Round 2:

  • Explain that for this round, pairs should replace the number “1” with a clap and then continue the number sequence “2-3" counted out loud (Clap-2-3, Clap-2-3, etc.).
  • Model slowly with a partner. During the modeling purposefully make a mistake, such as saying “1” instead of clapping after “3.” Raise your hands in the air and say, "Tah-dah!"
  • Once everyone has had a minute or two to play, use your attention signal to call the round to a close. Ask, "Was anyone glad that they weren't the one making a mistake?"
  • Tell the group that in the next round when one person makes a mistake, both partners will raise their hands in the air, give each other a double high-five, and both say, "Tah-dah!"

Round 3:

  • Explain that in this round, participants should clap for “1,” replace the number “2” with a foot stomp, and say “3.” (Clap, stomp, 3; Clap, stomp, 3; etc.).
  • Model this with a partner while YOU purposefully make a mistake, such as saying “two” instead of stomping. You and your partner now give each other double high-fives and shout, “Tah-dah!” together, and start over again.
  • Once everyone has had a minute or two to play, call the round to a close with your usual attention signal.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to participate in team building activities that require cooperation such as this one? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about cooperation when working with another person? (Responsible Decision Making)

  • Students self-select a situation and the best possible solution and role play in front of the class or another group(s).

  • Watch 5.03 Video Working Together (1 min)
  • Ask the students the following questions:
    • Give an additional example of how a group came together and accomplished something they couldn’t do individually.
    • What essential qualities must all group members possess to make a project more successful?
  • Watch 5.03 Changing a Light (1 min).
  • Students answer the following questions in small groups or in their journal:        
    • Does cooperation always equal success? Why or why not?

  • What are some examples of cooperation that you have seen from two different cultures?  Are they different?  Why do you think that is?
