INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Activity

  • Show one of the following videos: Example of a Dysfunctional Meeting or Why Everyone Hates Bad Meetings.
  • Ask students if they can relate to the personalities in this video with experiences they have had working in groups. Can they identify additional challenges?
  • As a teacher can you point out examples from a group you have? A club, team, faculty meeting, and even your own class? (Who is the social medialite, always late, the class clown, then fervent note-taker, etc.?)
  • Review the strategies your committees can use that encourage all students to participate. Choose one that you would like to use/practice in your LIA committees.
    • Think-Pair-Share
    • Last Word
    • My Two Cents

Guided Practice

  • Review and agree upon the possible roles students can have in a committee. Some options are:
    • Secretary- Person who keeps copies of all documents and submissions
    • Scribe/Recorder- Person who writes the minutes and/or completes the agenda.
    • Spokesperson- Person who reports to the teacher or class if needed
    • Time Keeper- Makes sure the group is aware of time and pacing of the meeting
    • Runner- Person who runs to ask questions or gather materials
    • Explorer- Person who speaks with or asks questions of others outside the LIA classroom
    • Facilitator- The person who opens the meeting and guides the discussion
  • Allow students to create a poster or display that define these roles and make them visible to the class.

  • Use a current event topic to practice organizing students into groups, assigning roles, and producing a finished product. For example, groups can be assigned to review a certain current event, allow each member to give a reaction, appoint a scribe to write down the main points, and a spokesperson to report a summary of the event and discussion to the class.

  • Use the video How Teamwork Works to reinforce students' understanding of what makes a successful team. After viewing, facilitate a discussion or reflection activity where students identify key teamwork behaviors shown in the video (e.g., communication, collaboration, shared responsibility).
  • Rotate committee roles among students in order to develop different skills and responsibilities. All minutes from the committee meeting should be posted in the electronic classroom or website. 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How do the different committee roles work together to achieve goals and objectives?
  • What are some ways you could fairly assign committee roles to your classmates?

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use this Attention Signal skill-building activity to bring the group’s attention back to the facilitator or team leader during a meeting. A well-practiced and consistently implemented attention signal is essential in group-learning, interactive team meetings, and special project situations. Whether adults or students, any gathering of engaged participants is going to be deeply immersed in meaningful, task-oriented conversations during which you will need to get their attention. (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Attention Signal activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • There are many versions of attention signals (flashing the lights, clapping, raising or lowering your voice) but one that has been most consistently effective is to raise your hand in the air and wait for everyone else in the room to raise their own hand and be silent before you proceed with directions, information or the next agenda item.
  • Teacher explains: When you see me raise my hand, you’ll have two jobs. One is to raise your hand too. That gives others around you a visual cue that they should quietly look my way. The other is to bring your conversation to a close. That will help the room quickly become silent so you can hear the next direction or announcement.
  • Allow students to self select into teams of three. Once they cluster in a group, have them come up with topics or themes that are of greatest interest to them at the time. Select up to five themes and post them on the board or screen. Another option is to post a teacher made list.
  • Have students select one of the topics they will discuss with their group of three. Each one selects a different topic. 
  • To determine the order that students will discuss their topic, have them arrange their first names alphabetically. They will proceed in alphabetical order. 
  • Begin the activity by holding your hand up and drop it as if signaling the beginning of a race. Each student will have 60 seconds to talk about the topic of choice. After the first 60 seconds raise your hand and wait until all students give you their full attention. Drop your hand down to begin the second round of sharing out. Repeat the activity for the third round. 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore attention getting signals? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about attention getting signals? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: The hand raising activity can be done during Gallery View large group activities in a virtual environment.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Link the idea behind an agenda by introducing students to a map of a theme park and ask students why the park provides these to their guests. Ask students who have been to large parks to describe their experience walking around and trying to find attractions. Is there an advantage at Disneyland if you know where you are going and what you are doing? Use this Disneyland Map as an example. 
  • Share any experiences where you did not have clear directions or a destination point.
  • Explain to students that today’s lesson will focus on using an agenda as a tool to know where they are going in their classroom activities.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Show the video Effective Meetings that highlights how agendas are meant to avoid the very reasons people often don’t like meetings.
  • Use one or both of the following sample agendas: Trevor Beck's Meeting Agenda Sample; 5.06 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Teacher Model.    
  • Explain to the students that an agenda is their map for their committee meetings.
  • Explain the parts of an agenda and what each space should be used for.

Guided Practice

  • Demonstrate for students that they have likely interacted with agendas in other activities outside of school. Programs handed out for performances, funerals, and church are all types of agendas. 
  • Show students a few different examples of agendas:
    • Summer Day Camp Agenda Example
    • Music Recital Program Example
    • Funeral Program Example
  • As a class or in smaller groups, have the students analyze the differences between the 3 Examples above. Use the following questions to help guide the discussion:
    • Is the speaker identified?
    • Are time limits identified?
    • Do they specify people’s roles?
    • Are topics written out?
    • Which agenda do they like best?
  • Display 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline.
  • Lead students in filling out 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline to plan a service project or activity as a class. A great starting point could be your upcoming parent night activity.

  • In committees, have students fill out 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline Sample for their committee's role in the previously discussed activity. 
  • If needed, remind students that the objective of this activity is to practice using the agenda outline correctly.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Extension 

  • All committees should agree on the format of an electronic shared agenda that will be used for all meetings (Google Doc, OneDrive, etc.). Students can add items, comments, notes before, during, and after each meeting. At the end of the meeting, students can rate how they felt the meeting went using an electronic survey. 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can using an agenda help to guide committee meetings?
  • Why is it important for everyone's voice to be heard in a meeting?
  • Why do you think it is important to prepare and follow an agenda during a meeting?

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain: We have discussed many important leadership qualities in this class. This lesson will help you learn more about the important work of Chavez and how to use the main ideas in a text to create a summary of his life.
  • Ask students the following questions:
    • What are the leadership qualities we have explored? (cooperation, courage, positivity, dependability, & patience)
    • As we watch this clip on the life of Cesar Chavez, what is at least one leadership quality that we have discussed that Chavez demonstrates?
    • How does he demonstrate this quality?
  • Watch 5.08 Video Cesar Chavez (4 min).
  • Discuss the questions mentioned before watching the video.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson:
    • In the last lesson, your groups completed an outline about a leader that helped to shape U.S. history.
    • Ask students the following questions:
      • Was working in groups more difficult or easier than working independently?  Why?
      • This lesson will give all of you the opportunity to present your group research findings and evaluate each other's presentations.

Model

  • Display 5.10 Weblink Oral Presentation Rubric.
  • Discuss the requirements for the presentation grade.
  • Explain that students will grade each group based on the rubric.

Guided Practice

  • Pass out index cards to each student (i.e. if there are 5 groups total, each student will receive 5 index cards).
  • Groups practice their presentation.  Each group member is responsible for telling about the area they researched.
  • Monitor groups & give feedback to improve group presentations.

Independent Practice                                                                                    

  • Groups present their research to the class.
  • Class members grade each group using the 5.10 Weblink Oral Presentation Rubric and record the grade and comments on the index cards.

Computer

  • Students may need access to projector or smartboard to display visuals for presentation.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Strategy Grouping--Partner highly skilled students with mid-level skilled and/or partner mid-level skilled students with lower skilled ones.

Extension

  • Presentations may need to extend to the following class period based on class time.
  • Create a presentation with student-friendly pictures and present it to elementary school students.

  • Student groups of 2-4 will choose a research study that is centered around principles or qualities of leadership.
  • View the documents below for project details and expectations:
    • 5.11 HO List of Research Ideas
    • 5.11 HO Project Criteria
    • 5.11 HO Grading Rubric 
  • Students will focus only on part 1 today and will have time tomorrow to finish part 1 and begin on part 2.

Model

  • Use the 5.11 PPT Research Project Teacher Model as an example to show students.
  • Allow time for students to ask questions.

Teacher note: Due to picture copyrights within the curriculum, no pictures are included in the teacher model. Please encourage your students to appropriately cite visuals.

Independent Practice

  • Either assign or allow students to choose groups.
  • Give students the remainder of the time to choose a research study and begin part 1 of their presentation.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Require only select portions of the assignment/project for students that are unable to complete the entire project within the time allotted or reduce the length of the assignments.
  • 5.11 Weblink Experiment Summary provides short summaries of recent psychology studies. Have students select one that relates to leadership qualities.

Extension

  • Explore Milgram’s study further by reading his published article: The Milgram Experiment (7 pages)
    • Split students into groups to read and discuss or split the article into sections for students to read and discuss. Have the groups answer the following questions:
      • What additional information did you learn about the study from reading the article versus watching the video?
      • What new vocabulary words did you learn?
    • Instruct students to circle and look up vocabulary words they are unfamiliar with.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can a leader have a positive impact on others?
  • Who can I have a positive impact on (of those around me), and how?

  • Pair two groups together, one group will play the presenting group while the other board of directors.
  • Give a 3 min. warning when the Q/A session should begin, and then another notice when time is up. Instruct the presenting and board of directors group to switch roles.
  • Mix up the groups. Each group should deliver their presentation at least twice.

Preparation for tomorrow

  • Have each board of directors group (every group) select a presenting group to fund.  Allow time for the groups to swap any additional information or project materials they would like to share. Remind students that each group will be giving the entire company, the class, a brief summary of the group they have chosen to fund tomorrow during class.

Model

  • Display 6.02 Weblink “Learning by Doing” (p. 2) Environmental Topics.
  • Discuss the points emphasized in 6.02 Video Service Learning Definition and how they relate to the  6.02 Weblink “Learning by Doing”. Use the environmental topics listed to generate ideas for possible service activities. 
  • Explain that students will have the opportunity to propose a service learning project in groups.
  • Display 6.02 HO Service Learning Brainstorm Teacher Model.
  • Introduce the four different types of service learning projects: Improving Our School, Improving Our Partner Schools, Environmental Service Learning Projects, and Community Improvement.
  • Share the teacher model examples.

Guided Practice

  • Divide students into groups of four.
  • Distribute  6.02 HO Service Learning Brainstorm.
  • Give students 5-10 minutes to produce as many ideas as possible.

Model

  • Stop brainstorming activity.
  • Instruct groups to choose their favorite service learning project.
  • Display 6.02 HO Service Learning Proposal Form Template.
  • Discuss each section of the project proposal template.  Teacher Note:  Ideally, this activity/process has been previously modeled during the formation of leadership committees.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute 6.02 HO Service Learning Proposal Form Template.
  • Instruct student groups to fill out the template with their groups.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Show students further examples of LIA service learning projects to assist in the brainstorm activity.  See 6.02 Weblink Service Learning Example 1, 6.02 Weblink Service Learning Example 2, and 6.02 Weblink Service Learning Example 3.

Extension

  • Watch 6.02 Video Service Learning Example (5 min) or other examples like this.  Discuss the benefits students discovered during this project.

Model

  • Instruct students to sit with their group.  
  • Distribute 6.02 HO Service Learning Proposal Form Template (completed).
  • Display 6.03 HO Action Plan Template.
  • Explain & model completing the template.
  • Use examples from the students' completed 6.02 HO Service Learning Proposal Form Template.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute the 6.03 HO Action Plan Template to each group.
  • Instruct student groups to fill out the action plan and to be as specific as possible in each category.
  • Assist student groups as needed.
  • Student groups that complete their action plans, should start contacting the necessary individuals to put their plans into motion.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 6.04 Video Youth Making a Difference (4 min).
    • If you had no limitations on what you could do to make an impact in this country or your native country, what would it be?
  • Introduce service learning by discussing what changes students would want to see to make improvements in the state or country.
    • What are some problems you see?
    • Do you know of an issue where you want to make your voice heard?
    • Today, we are going to research different topics or issues that are relevant to you and identify what you can do to make a difference.

Model

  • Display 6.04 HO Service Learning Brainstorm (Country).
  • Introduce the three different areas to help students brainstorm ideas.
  • Share the teacher model examples.

Guided Practice

  • Divide students into groups of three to four.
  • Distribute 6.04 HO Service Learning Brainstorm (Country).
  • Allow student groups computer access to research issues.
  • Give students 5-10 minutes to produce as many ideas as possible.

Model

  • Stop brainstorming activity.
  • Instruct groups to choose their activity.
  • Display 6.04 HO Service Learning Proposal Form Template (Country).
  • Discuss each section of the project proposal template.  Encourage letter or email contact.  Teacher Note:  Ideally, this activity/process has been previously modeled during the formation of leadership committees and/or 6.02 Impacting Your Community.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute 6.04 HO Service Learning Proposal Form Template (Country).
  • Instruct student groups to fill out the template with their groups.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain: Yesterday all of you found worthy issues or causes to pursue in areas that you want to make a difference.  Today we are going to vote on the cause that we will pursue together.  With our combined efforts, we can make more of a difference than pursuing our causes on our own.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Activity

  • Instruct students to sit with their groups.
  • Each group should appoint a group leader to share their issue or cause.
  • Use 6.04 HO Service Learning Proposal Form Template (Country) (completed) to share all main points of the proposal (Roman Numerals I-V).  Students should explain if this proposal is to contact state or national leaders regarding an issue, or if they have chosen to raise money for an organization.  All groups should present.
  • Instruct students to write on a piece of paper which group’s proposal they would like to pursue for the class project.
  • Read the votes to determine the proposal with the highest votes.

Model

  • Ask the group leader of the winning proposal to write the contact information for all students to include in their individual letter.
  • Model letter writing using 6.05 Weblink Sample Letter to Your Senator (click on the link & it downloads a Word document that can be edited) and/or 6.05 HO Letter Template depending on the issue/cause.
  • Discuss what information should be included in each paragraph.

Teacher Note:  Students may need additional time to research the issue to enable them to write knowledgeable letters.  May need to provide additional resources depending on the topic.

Guided Practice

  • Instruct students to begin writing a letter using 6.05 HO Letter Template.  

Independent Practice

  • Students may complete their individual letters as a homework assignment.
  • Remind students to edit and proofread the letter as well.

  • Debrief by asking the students the following questions:
    • Why do you feel _______________ (the issue/cause students are addressing) is important enough to contact ____________________________?
    • What should be our next steps in following up with our letters?
    • Did you learn anything new today about _____________________?

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Differentiation Ideas

  •  If the class chose an organization where they wish to sponsor a fundraising activity, it may be more appropriate to write a class action plan using the 6.03 HO Action Plan Template.  One class letter could be written to the development officer of the organization.

Extension

  • Read 6.05 Weblink Effective Letters to Congress as a class.  Discuss the steps to write effective letters to our state and national leaders.  
  • Ask students to find a current event article (online or in a newspaper or magazine) that discusses the issue/cause students are interested in pursuing.  Instruct student groups to prepare and then present these articles to the class before voting on the class proposal.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Who would you like to write a letter of change to?  Do you think a letter can make a difference?

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

Instruct the students to take out a piece of paper. Allow students 30 seconds to answer each question below:

  • Question 1: What qualities do you think one must possess in order to become a successful professional?
  • Question 2: List as many successful professionals as you can.

Discuss student answers to Question 1.

Discuss student answers to Question 2.

Ask the following follow-up questions:

  • How many professionals were listed that look or speak like you?
  • Why do you think this number is high or low?

  • View 8.01 Weblink Influential Latinos as a class. Scroll through and choose 2 or 3 of the 25 individuals that stand out to the students. Skim through the individual's short biography with the students and discuss interesting facts, qualities possessed, and accomplishments.

Independent Practice

  • Watch 8.01 Video Richard Montanez  as a class and ask the students to write down interesting facts, qualities possessed, and accomplishments that Mr. Montanez mentions. 
  • The LIA teacher may choose a different video of a successful Latino/a business person if they would prefer.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Allow students to use 8.01 Weblink Influential Latinos - Spanish Version as a reference for the 2 or 3 individuals that the teacher reviews from the English list in the Modeling portion of the lesson. 
  • Invite a professional guest speaker to discuss the professional skills necessary to be successful in the workforce. You may need to use this option if computers/internet are not available.

Extension

  • Invite students to choose an individual from 8.01 Weblink Influential Latinos to research. Give each student 10-15 minutes to briefly research their chosen individual's story, interesting facts, and what the individual did to become a successful professional. Place students in groups of four and have each student present their chosen individual to their group.
  • View 8.01 Video - Professionalism in Soccer 1 (15 sec) or 8.01 Video - Professionalism in Soccer 2 (4 min) and discuss how a soccer player's unprofessional behavior may change a teammate or opposing team member's view of that player. How does this relate to professionalism in the workplace?

Journal Entry Suggestions

Answer the following questions in relation to LIA Tutoring, your LIA Class, and in general:

  • How do your behaviors reflect positively or negatively? What does that say about you?
  • Is your attitude professional?  
  • What could you change or do differently to improve your professionalism?

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous lesson:

  • Last time we learned about a few professionals. What parts stood out to you?
  • One of the first steps in joining the professional field is finding a job. In order to find a job of interest, you need to submit a competitive, standout resume.

Display 8.02 High School Resume Example Teacher Model and 8.02 High School Resume Non-Example Teacher Model.

  • Let’s pretend you are an employer and these two resumes come across your desk.
  • Ask the students which candidate they would hire and why.
  • Discuss the importance of submitting a clean, concise resume.

Model

  • View the resume tips from 8.02 Weblink Resume Tips, or another similar website, as a class.
  • Use 8.02 HO High School Resume Template to create one sample resume as a class, choosing the name and other details together. Use 8.02 High School Resume Example Teacher Model, if needed.

Guided Practice

*Teacher Note 1: You may have some students who already have a resume or even a job. However, this resume assignment will be used as the unit assessment so everyone will need to participate. 

  • Instruct each student to choose a job they would like to apply for.
  • Have students begin to draft their own resumes, using the resume example as a reference. 
  • Encourage students to use specific, powerful language.
  • Invite the students to share their resumes with a peer and ask for feedback.

**Teacher Note 2: You may invite students to use 8.02 Weblink - Canva Resume Templates as a guide to creating a final draft of their resume if they would prefer to have a modern finish.   • Invite students to share sections of their resume with the class.
  • Inform students that next class period you will be holding mock interviews. Students will need to come to class with a resume in hand and dressed for a professional interview.
  • Review with students what is and is not professional dress. You may use Visual - LIA Conference Dress Code as a guide.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Invite students to write their resume in Spanish, then have a peer assist in translating it to English.
  • Use 8.02 Weblink Resume Assistant for a step-by-step guide, additional templates, vocabulary helps, etc. Note that in order to download your completed resume you will need a paid account. 

Extension

  • View 8.02 Video Resume (2 min) and discuss the importance of submitting honest, accurate information on a resume in a group. 
  • Have students review their peers' resumes for grammatical errors, suggestions, additions, etc.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why is it important to have a resume?
  • How can you make your resume stand out?
  • What can you do to strengthen your resume?

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous lesson:

  • Last time we learned how to make a more competitive resume. Today we are going to hold mock job interviews.

View 8.03 Millennial Interview and discuss whether or not it accurately depicts teenagers today.

View 8.03 Video Interview Tips (5 min) and ask the following questions:

  • What tips stood out to you?
  • Has anyone had an interview experience they would like to share with the class?
  • Any additional tips?
  • How can being bilingual give you an advantage in a job interview?

Model

  • Display 8.03 HO Mock Interview Questions for students to view.
  • Using 8.03 Teacher Model Mock Interview Questions as a guide, model a job interview by reading through these common interview questions and responding to them. 

Independent Practice

  • Instruct students to gather their thoughts and write down notes, examples, and ideas under each question in the 8.03 HO Mock Interview Questions to prepare for mock interviews.
  • Invite students to use their completed 8.02 HO High School Resume Template to assist them. You may need to pull up and display 8.02 High School Resume Example Teacher Model as a reference for students.  

Activity 

  • Pair students up to conduct mock interviews, using the notes they prepared with 8.03 HO Mock Interview Questions and their resumes from the previous lesson.   
  • Tell students how long they have for their interview before switching roles. 
  • The teacher may walk around offering support as needed.

  • Direct students to 8.03 Weblink Interview Vocab Helps, or another similar website, and allow students time to learn or review job interview vocabulary in English and/or Spanish. Hold portions of the job interview in Spanish if needed.

Extension

  • Watch 8.03 Video Additional Questions and have students choose additional surprise interview questions to ask their interviewee.

  • What can you practice and work on to strengthen your interviewing skills?
  • What skills do you possess that make you a strong interviewee?

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
    • So far we have discussed professional qualities, resumes, and interviews.  Today we are going to explore alternative ways to find job openings besides the traditional online job search.
  • Ask students what they think about the phrase, “Be nice to the nerds in high school because they will be your future boss."
  • View 8.04 Weblink Networking in High School as a class, focusing on the five takeaways:
    1. Eat lunch at a different table each day.
    2. Connect with the “untouchables.”
    3. Stop thinking that everything is about you.
    4. Interact with people who are not just like you.
    5. Have a life outside of high school.
  • After reviewing the list above, ask the following questions:
    • Which of the five tips stood out to you?
    • Do you agree or disagree with these suggestions? Why or why not?
    • How could these tips potentially benefit you?

Activity

  • Give each student a copy of 8.04 HO Networking Activity (English).
  • Instruct the students that they will complete this activity twice. 
  • Point out that there is a column for Round 1, and a second column for Round 2.
  • Give the students two minutes to complete Round 1 of the handout without speaking.
  • After students have completed Round 1, give them two more minutes to complete Round 2, allowing for speaking and interactions.
  • Once the activity has been completed, discuss the following questions:
    • Which activity was more successful and why?
    • Were you able to complete either activity? Why or why not? What other tools or contacts would have been helpful?
    • How does the first activity relate to finding a job through the newspaper or advertisement? How does the second relate to networking?
    • Do you think networking is simple or difficult? Please share any networking experiences you may have.

Model Practice

  • Share the following with the students:
    • Face-to-face talking, using social media, texting, etc. are all very effective networking tools. We are now going to begin a brief networking project to test out these tools.
  • Display 8.04 Teacher Model Networking Project and discuss the first three examples together.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Allow students to network with each other for different personal or educational goals (e.g., scholarships, internships, job shadowing, etc.).
  • Use 8.04 HO Networking Activity (Spanish) for the application/engagement activity section if needed.

Extension

  • See 8.04 Weblink Networking Lessons for additional resources and practice activities on networking.
  • Invite a professional to speak to the class about their experience with networking.
  • Watch 8.04 Video Networking Tips and discuss the 10 tips shared in the video as a class.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What can you do to network?  
  • How does networking help you in your personal goals?

Students should create a resume following these guidelines:

  • Professional Formatting
    • The format is easy to read and follow.
    • The font is appropriate.
    • The layout is printer-friendly.
  • Includes Important and Relevant Content
    • Name and contact information.
    • Education, skills, and certifications.
    • Work, volunteer, and service experience.
  • Reviewed and Proofread for Errors
    • Reviewed by an adult besides the LIA teacher.
    • Checked for spelling, grammatical errors, and clarity in writing.

* After submission and review, students should incorporate their resume into their digital or paper LIA portfolio.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Discuss the following questions as a class or in small groups:
    • What are your daily needs and what must you do in order to meet those needs?
    • What were daily needs 100 years ago and what did people need to do in order to meet those needs?  
    • What is self reliance?
    • Are we more or less self reliant than people 100 years ago?
    • How can we become more self reliant as a member of our home, school, and community?

Computer Lab Research

  • Explain that there are many ways to become self reliant. Today we are going to research a modern day story of self reliance.
  • Divide the students into pairs and give each partnership a copy of 9.01 HO A Life of Self Reliance.
  • Instruct the student to be self reliant and search for sources to use to complete the handout.
  • Give the students the remainder of the class to use the computer lab to complete the handout.

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or  Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

Project/Activity Overview

  • Paired student groups will receive real life situations and brainstorm ways self reliance would help the situation become more successful. Groups will learn a new skill and then teach multiple groups the skill during the 9.03 lesson tomorrow.

Model

  • Display 9.02 Self Reliance Situations
  • Model completing the handout by using Problem #1 information provided in 9.02 Self Reliance Activity Teacher Model.

Guided Practice

  • Invite the students to assist in completing Problem #2 on  9.02 Self Reliance Activity Teacher Model.

Independent Practice

  • Assign or allow pairs to select a situation from 9.02 Self Reliance Situations and being filling out 9.02 HO Self Reliance Activity Outline.
  • Invite student pairs to complete 9.02 HO Self Reliance Activity Outline, using the internet to search for help as needed.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Require only select portions of the assignment/project for students who are unable to complete the entire project within the time allotted, or reduce the length of the assignments.
  • Allow students to ask other class members to assist them in learning how to solve the problem if computers are unavailable.

Extension

  • Watch 9.02 Video El Chapulin Colorado and ask the students the following questions: 
    • “Who could possibly help up now?” (1:50) Explain your answer. (¿Existe la autosuficiencia en la declaración "y ahora quien podra defenderme?" Explica.)
    • How can being self reliant benefit members of a group such as LIA? (¿Cómo puede la autosuficiencia beneficiar a los miembros de un grupo como el de LIA?)
    • El Chapulin Colorado demonstrated qualities necessary to be self reliant, can you identify them? (El Chapulin Colorado demostró cualidades necesarias para ser autosuficiente, ¿puedes identificarlas?)
  • Students may choose additional skills to research and learn.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • List five things you can do to become more self reliant as a student, family member, and as a young adult living in America.

OBJECTIVE:

Students will learn and teach skills to be more self reliant in different situations.

PURPOSE

Students explore the importance of self reliance.

PREPARATION

  • Sign up for computer lab
  • Copy student handouts

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 9.03 Video Daily Life and 9.03 Video Daily Life 2
  • Ask the students the following questions:
    • How does money influence self reliance?
    • Discuss the statement that follows. Which is true and why?
      • More money increases one’s ability to be self reliant, or having less money increases one’s ability to be self reliant.
    • How does one increase their ability to be self reliant? (i.e., knowledge, experiences, etc.)

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • Model how to teach one of the skills from 9.02 Self Reliance Activity Teacher Model or choose your own skill to model.

Independent Practice

  • Allow pairs a few minutes to go over their completed 9.02 HO Self Reliance Activity Outline.
  • Give each group about 5 minutes to teach their skill to another group and then switch. Rotate groups as many times as time will allow.

  • Strategy Grouping--Partner high skilled students with students with mid-level skills and/or partner mid-level skilled students with students with lower skills

  • Have the student pairs discuss their scenario and teach the second skill they researched from 9.02 HO Self Reliance Activity Outline.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What skills or talents do I want to learn to become more self reliant at home, school, work, and my community?

Differentiation Ideas

  • Divide students into groups of 5 and arrange for 3-5 different activities around the school. Have each group rotate working on each activity for 10 minutes. Turn it into a competition and see which group can get the most done within the given time period.

Extension

  • Instruct students to continue to work on the chosen task, but give them an injury or a disability (e.g., can’t see, can’t hear, can’t speak, no use of one hand, no use of feet, etc.). Discuss student thoughts and experiences.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Do you consider yourself a hard worker? Why or why not?

BRIGHT IDEAS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][toggles style="default" accordion="true" accordion_starting_functionality="default" border_radius="none"][toggle color="Default" heading_tag="default" heading_tag_functionality="default" title="INTRODUCTION"][ultimate_modal modal_title="Create a Personal Mantra" modal_on_align="left" btn_text="Create a Personal Mantra" modal_size="medium" overlay_bg_opacity="75" content_bg_color="#ffffff" header_bg_color="#e5e5e5" img_size="80"]

A personal mantra is an affirmation to motivate and inspire you to be your best self. It is typically a positive phrase or statement that you use to affirm the way you want to live your life. Its purpose is to provide motivation and encouragement to you when you need to focus your mind to achieve a goal.

Explain that students will be creating their own Mantra.  Have students read in groups of 2 or 3, or read and discuss as a class, the following article:  https://greatist.com/live/mantras-how-to-create-a-mantra-for-personal-growth 

Share your own personal Mantra with the students, and then have students write and share their own Mantra.  Encourage them to hang it up somewhere they can see it daily, their locker, their bedroom etc.

An ELL option could be to do this in Spanish, or through pictures.

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Say: Last time we learned to not sit and dream, but to go out and work hard! Today, we are going to discuss relevant life issues that require perseverance and self-discipline.
  • View 10.02 Fast Workers (3 min) and ask the students the following questions:
    • What do you think these individuals had to do in order to master these tasks?
    • What sports, academic subjects, activities, etc., have you needed to show self-discipline or perseverance to succeed?

Class Discussion

  • View 10.02 Video Spoken Word (3 min) as a class.
  • Use 10.02 Discussion Guide Teacher Materials to lead a class discussion.

Class Debate

  • Now that we have discussed different aspects of self-discipline and perseverance as a class, we will explore your personal views of them.
  • View 10.02 Video Bullying (6 min) as a class. Invite students to choose one of two sides and hold a class debate. Instruct students to use topics and examples brought up in the earlier class discussion, along with additional information:
    • Persevering through criticism or bullying builds character and is the best option.
    • Changing your situation to prevent criticism or bullying is the best option.
  • Hold a class debate.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Review some or all of the words from 10.02 Spoken Word Vocabulary before viewing  10.02 Video Spoken Word. Also, see "Language Enhancement" below.
  • Before beginning the debate, instruct students to pair up with someone with the same point of view. Give each pair 5 minutes to brainstorm and write down key points, examples, stories, etc. to back up their chosen side.
    • During this time, feel free to use any response protocol to assist students in forming ideas and helping them verbalize information correctly. Use the 10.02 Response Protocol Article for more details.

Extension

  • Review or teach the students about the Inner Circle/Outer Circle Debate Strategy using 10.02 Weblink Debate Tips. Use this strategy to hold the class debate.
  • Skim over or read portions of 10.02 Story of Perseverance 1 or 10.02 Story of Perseverance 2. Discuss as a class how these people displayed perseverance.  

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can having self-discipline make a positive impact on my life?
  • Who do you know who shows perseverance?  What example supports this idea?

Language Enhancement

  • Invite the students to assist each other in translating portions of 10.02 Video Spoken Word from English to Spanish, and ask the following questions:
    • What parts were the most difficult to translate?
    • What meanings, feelings, etc. were changed or lost in translation?
    • Memorize a portion of this spoken word poem and share it with a family member.

Purpose: To help students explore their multilingual abilities by responding to critical questions related to the factors that shaped their values, ideas, actions, and associations with others.  Using the Bilingual Index Card activity, students will ask themselves the questions “What are my language assets?” and ”How has my bilingualism shaped my identity and defined my friends?” By having students examine and share their own language abilities, students are able to build positive relationships that are more accepting, patient, understanding, and value diversity among themselves. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Bilingual\Multilingual activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Prepare index cards with the questions listed below:
  2. Index Cards (feel free to modify or add additional questions as needed):
    1. How has your first language shaped your identity and who you associate with? 
    2. To what extent are you defined by your language/multilingual abilities? 
    3. To what extent are you defined by your family or community background?
    4. To what extent are you defined by your social and financial background? 
    5. To what extent are you defined by your beliefs? 
    6. To what extent are you defined by your nationality?
    7. How do you label yourself and how are we labeled by others? 
    8. How are your decisions and actions influenced by how you think others see you? 
    9. How do your language abilities shape your values, ideas, and actions toward others and social interactions with peers and adults? 
    10. In what ways would your life be different if English was/wasn't your first language?  
    11. How do you adapt when interacting with people from various language backgrounds?
    12. What are the benefits of knowing more than one language?
    13. What is the difference between being bilingual and bicultural?
    14. What are the economic advantages of being bilingual or multilingual?
  3. Randomly distribute the cards to the students as they are sitting in their community circle. Give them a minute to read their card and think about their response. 
  4. When you announce, "Mix and mingle!", turn on music to cue when participants are to move around the room (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc). 
  5. When the music stops, participants find a partner near them. Help with pairing if needed. *Note: This activity can also be done without music by ringing a chime when it is time for students to stop walking around the room and find a partner.
  6. Partners share their responses to their questions and then exchange cards. 
  7. Start the music again and have students repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as your time permits.
  8. In the end, ask for volunteers to share one thing that surprised them or one thing that they learned about themselves. 
  9. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own personal story, language abilities, and values with other people? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about being bilingual or multilingual? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

Current Event Bell Starter

  • Watch one or more of the following videos on bilingualism: 
    • 11.01 Article Bilingualism
    • 11.01 Video Santa Claus
  • Is being bilingual beneficial? Why or why not?
  • If bilingualism is advantageous, what advantages do you have over someone who is monolingual?

    • Display the infographic from this link: 11.01 Weblink Infographic $ to be Bilingual. Distribute & display 11.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes.
  • Many students don’t fully grasp the benefits of being bilingual. Look at this infographic.
    • Explain that this infographic displays a lot of information and our goal is to summarize the information in the most efficient way possible.
  • Take notes on 1.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes as we are discussing the infographic. We are going to try and use our own words and not just copy the vocabulary or summaries on the graphic.

Possible ways to model:

  • Ask students to identify vocabulary from the infographic.
  • Write down three vocabulary words from student suggestions and record them on 11.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes.
  • Help guide students to come up with definitions and record them.
  • Lead a class discussion on the other information on 11.01 Weblink Infographic $ to be Bilingual.
  • Write a summary of the information on 11.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes by asking for student ideas. Emphasize the importance of concise summaries.
  • Demonstrate a drawing that represents the summary on 11.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes

Guided Practice

Ask students to choose one of the following articles on bilingualism:

  • 11.01 Weblink Article 1 Resilient Brain
  • 11.01 Weblink Article 2 New Language
  • 11.01 Weblink Article 3 Languages Smarten
  • Distribute a blank copy of 11.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes. Instruct students to read the article and complete the HO.

Independent Practice

Option 1

  • Students begin by creating audio podcasts based on their experiences of growing up bilingual. Podcasts not only provide ELs opportunities to produce language but it allows them to share their voices in a public and authentic way. Create a space where languages and cultures are valued and invite students to record their podcast in the language they are most comfortable in. Edit and revise podcasts and launch an anonymous classroom podcast on Hidden Voices on Apple Podcasts. Keep in mind that all podcasts must meet Apple Podcasts' requirements and pass technical validations and a review process before they’re made available on Apple Podcasts.

Option 2

Padlet encourages ELs to practice organizing their thoughts and encourages classroom interaction and communication by having students post video responses to a classroom Padlet Board topic. The Padlet topic videos are short and allow ELs unlimited retakes when recording. Begin by creating a Padlet Board for students to share their experiences of growing up bilingual. Students post video responses to the prompt and reply to each other’s videos. Create a space where home languages and backgrounds are valued and invite students to record their podcast in their home language.

  • Divide the class into three groups.  Distribute one of the following articles to each group (11.01 Weblink Article 1 Resilient Brain, 11.01 Weblink Article 2 New Language, 11.01 Weblink Article 3 Languages Smarten). Assign students to fill out the 1.03 HO Current Events GO as a group. Each group then presents their article to the class.
  • Complete the article reading and 1.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes in small groups or partners.

Extension

  • Use 11.01 Weblink Articles Advantages of Bilingualism and the references listed on the webpage to conduct their own research about the benefits of being bilingual. Ask students to write an essay presenting this research.
  • Create presentations (PPTs or poster board) to give to classes at the elementary school where they tutor.  
  • Create a large class poster highlighting the benefits of being bilingual using the student picture summaries from 11.01 HO Infographic & Article Notes.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • In the past, how has bilingualism been seen, as a benefit or a curse? How is it viewed now?
  • What are some advantages you have experienced about being bilingual?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • define prejudice, stereotype, and discrimination, and identify strategies to respond to potential conflicts.
  • analyze and examine prejudices, beliefs, mindsets, and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  • accept feedback or consequences without getting upset or defensive (Self-Management)
  • identify diverse social norms, including unjust ones (Social Awareness)
  •  deepen understanding about the power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • define the term “ally” and identify when and how to be one (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrate “I” messages to state how one feels, why they feel that way, and what they want to change(Relationship Skills)
  •  demonstrate acknowledging mistakes, making an apology, and offering to make amends (Responsible Decision Making)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To have students explore the factors that divide a community by devaluing, disrespecting, and dishonoring each other's diverse backgrounds and lived experiences. This Examining Stereotypes (Part 1) activity will have students defining, illustrating, and exploring personal experiences of Racism, Prejudice, Stereotypes, and Discrimination. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Examining Stereotypes (Part 1) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview: 

  1. First label the four corners in the room with four chart papers with the headers Racism, Prejudice, Stereotypes, and Discrimination. Then randomly select students' names written on a sheet of paper from a bowl, hat, or bag and assign them to one of the four corners in numerical order. Another option is to pre-select the teams by intentionally diversifying each group by English language ability (evenly mixing ability levels in each group), gender, national origin, etc.
  2. Each of the four teams will be responsible for exploring a formal definition of each assigned word, identifying scenarios whether through personal experiences or examples from other sources, defining how their class, school, or greater community can address these negative behaviors, and suggesting how they can repair harm (restorative practices) caused by these negative behaviors. 
  3. Each chart should be divided into four quadrants with the subheaders of:
  1. Definition
  2. Personal Experiences
  3. Addressing Negative Behaviors
  4. Repairing Harm
  1. Delegate the responsibility of researching and responding to each subheader by either randomly assigning students a subtopic or giving them the option to select the subtopic they will work on.
  2. Conclude the activity by having students do a gallery walk clockwise to each poster. One student from each group should either volunteer or be selected by the group to present their findings three times to their classmates from the other groups.
  3. Once completed, take a group photo of students from each corner holding up their final chart with the information posted in each quadrant. These charts could be displayed on the walls either in the classroom or hallway. 
  4. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own definition, experiences, and solutions to the problem of Racism, Prejudice, Stereotypes, and Discrimination? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about addressing this problem and repairing harm? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 11.02 Video Racism (23 sec-2.23 min).
  • From what you could tell from the clip, how many students were NOT affected by racism or prejudice?
  • At what point did the football player realize he was being racist or prejudiced against his teammate, Dorian?
  • What did he do about it?
  • Do you think you have experienced racism or prejudice?  Why or why not?
  • What would you say or do if you were the victim of discrimination?

  • Display the Physical Appearance worksheet from 11.02 Weblink Breaking Prejudice.
  • Ask students to write down their answers.
  • Debrief by asking students to share their answers.
  • Continue the discussion by using  11.02 Weblink Discussion Questions.
  • Ask students to brainstorm some common examples of racism, prejudice, stereotypes, OR discrimination.
  • List student ideas on the board.
  • What are some examples of ways to address these problems?

Guided Practice

  • Create groups of 3-4 students. Note:  Make sure to include a mix of genders in each group.
  • Distribute 11.02 HO Definitions to each group.
  • Sometimes we think of racism, prejudice, stereotypes, & discrimination being words from the past.  Unfortunately, even in today’s world, we see these “words” play out in many different situations.
  • During the previous activity, we all made judgments based on an individual’s physical appearance and possibly stereotyped individuals based on what we saw.
  • Using the knowledge you gained from the vocabulary introduction and our discussion today, write definitions in your groups for each term.
  • Read the rest of the directions on the HO carefully and complete it together in your groups.  
  • Teacher Note:  Make sure all terms are represented at least once in the group case studies.

  • Instruct student groups to read their case studies aloud.
  • Class members identify which term is being demonstrated in the case study (racism, prejudice, stereotypes, or discrimination).

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiation Ideas

  • Explain to students that we all have internalized cultural stereotypes which cause us to make judgments of people who are different from ourselves. These cultural stereotypes can often lead to discriminatory practices.

Each LIA student will select a random person to interview who they do not know within their school. Without speaking, students will complete the following questions about the random person based on their appearance only. Using their electronic devices, LIA students will record their answers on an online word processor, such as Google Docs or Evernote. Once they have silently completed all of the questions, the random person will provide the correct answers to the questions.

  1.     Which languages do you speak?
  2.     Who do you live with?
  3.     What do you like to do in your spare time?
  4.     What is your favorite food?
  5.     What is your favorite sport?
  6.     What kind of music do you listen to?
  7.     What is your favorite subject to learn?
  8.     What is your favorite movie/show?
  9.     What is your favorite thing to do over the weekend with your family?
  10. How do you connect with your friends? In-person, social media, calling, or texting?

Discuss: What have you recognized about your internalized cultural stereotypes? How can we improve our unconscious beliefs and attitudes toward people who are different from ourselves?

  • Instead of showing the video clip 11.02 Video Racism, provide a similar activity for the class by putting a piece of tape in the middle of the floor.  State the following examples or create your own:
    • Walk across the line if you have ever been teased because you wear glasses, speak Spanish, have a different color of skin,  are not strong enough, skinny enough, too small, etc.
  • Debrief by discussing what happened during the activity.
  • Strategy grouping (See differentiation strategies in Teacher Guide).

Extension

  • As an alternative introductory video, consider clips from What Would You Do? YouTube has many clips that feature racism, discrimination, and stereotypes. Consider and preview this example, although others are easily found as well: Example – Bike Theft
  • If time allows, invite your students to complete the Mi Herencia Project Portfolio.  (See the Middle School Lesson 11.01 Mi Herencia: What is Culture?) for more activities on exploring definitions of culture and for the introduction of the Mi Herencia Project (Middle School Unit 11 Biculturalism lessons 11.01-11.07).
  • See 11.02 Weblink Understanding Prejudice for more guided activities and worksheets.
  • Invite students to talk with parents, classmates or research on the internet how their home country defines and addresses and racism, prejudice, stereotypes, & discrimination. Discuss: How is this different or similar to the US? Which view(s) do you favor and support?

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What are some specific ways you can confront racism, prejudice, stereotypes, and discrimination?
  • When have you stood up to racism, prejudice, stereotypes, or discrimination? What happened?
  • When have you felt the effects of racism, prejudice, stereotypes, or discrimination? What happened?  How did you feel, and react?

Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • learn and demonstrate how to conduct an ethnographic interview.
  • analyze and examine personal beliefs, mindsets, and preconceptions (Self-Awareness)
  •  deepen understanding about the power of compassion and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrate “I” messages to state how one feels, why they feel that way, and what they want to change (Relationship Skills)
  • deepen their understanding of the structures for co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
  •  foster ethical responsibility by creating spaces for voice (Responsible Decision-Making)

Purpose: To have students practice the process of an Ethnographic Interview with a buddy to further explore their lived experiences through the use of Examining Personal Experiences (Part 2) Activity.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Examining Personal Experiences (Part 2) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview: 

  1. As a follow-up from the four corners activity, use a pairing strategy that matches partners from different corners. Options for pairing from different corners could be teacher-assigned by intentionally assigning groups, the use of Clock Buddies (Unit 2, Lesson 4) or allowing them to self-select. 
  2. Each pair should sit by the chart that the interviewee participated in. Decide if the interviewer should take notes (note-taking on a graphic organizer may be helpful) or audio record the interview. When they switch roles in the ethnographic interview, have them move to the chart of the other partner so that they can refer to the notes. 
  3. Using the four quadrants, here are the questions that could be asked:
  1. What is the Definition of the word your group defined?
  2. Please share any Personal Experiences you have had with this type of behavior. 
  3. How did you or would you address these Negative Behaviors?
  4. What would you recommend as the next steps to Repairing the Harm done?
  1. Conclude the interviews by having teams pair up with another pair so that they can report out on what their partners shared.
  2. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Do you think it’s important to share some of your personal experiences with someone? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about addressing this problem and repairing harm? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 11.03 Video Interview Katie Couric (5 min).
  • Why do journalists conduct interviews?
  • Why is the interview a “powerful tool”?
  • Katie Couric talks about making the subject “comfortable”.  How can one do that?
  • Anthropologists use a method called “ethnographic interview”.  You will be conducting this type of interview and writing a reflection paper sharing what you learned.

  • Explain that small groups will become experts on each tip presented in 11.03 Weblink Interview Tips and share what they learn with the class.
  • Instruct students to read the section they are assigned and complete the following activities in their groups:  
    • Highlight important information.
    • Write a main idea sentence for each paragraph.
    • Using the main ideas, write a summary paragraph.

  • Divide the class into five groups.
  • Distribute 11.03 Weblink Interview Tips giving one section (1-Framing the Interview, 2-Conducting the Interview, 3-Taking Notes, 4-Ending the Interview, 5-Organizing Your Notes & Becoming an Expert) to each group.

  • Establish a check-in opportunity where ELs can meet in-person or virtually using tools such as Zoom, Google Meet, or Microsoft Teams. The check-in provides ELS with one-on-one time with the facilitator to ask questions, discuss concerns, or share successes and failures related to the ethnographic interview. The goal of the check-in is to help ELs develop contextually rich language practice and confidence in a welcoming and inclusive environment.
  • Strategy Grouping–Partner high skilled students with students with mid-level skills and/or partner mid-level skilled students with students with lower skills.

Extension

  • See Middle School Unit 11 Biculturalism for directions on completing the Mi Herencia Project Portfolio and Visual Presentation.  The Etnográficas Interview & Reflection Paper would be a good addition to the project.  High School students could complete the Mi Herencia Project in addition to the Etnográficas Interview & Reflection Paper.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What is one advantage of an ethnographic interview compared to other resources?
  • What are some questions you could ask in an ethnographic interview?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • demonstrate their understanding of ethnographic interviews by conducting an interview and writing a reflection paper on the process
  •  analyze and examine prejudices, beliefs, mindsets, and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  •  deepen understanding about the power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrate “I” messages to state how one feels, why they feel that way, and what they want to change(Relationship Skills)
  • deepen their understanding of the structures for co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
  •  foster ethical responsibility by creating equity of voice (Responsible Decision-Making)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To strengthen listening skills and encourage everyone to participate in the discussion about mindsets, beliefs, preconceptions, and compassion. Students will use the Examining Personal Experiences (Part 3) activity to participate in a Fishbowl (Unit 2, Lesson 3 also Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional). 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Examining Personal Experiences (Part 3) activity using the FishBowl activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview: 

  1. As a follow-up from the interview activity, divide the class into two groups that are seated in concentric circles, all facing the center. The outside circle listens while the inside group has a discussion about mindsets, beliefs, preconceptions, and compassion. Then the groups switch places so the listeners become the speakers and vice versa. 
  2. Make sure the audience knows you will hold them accountable for sharing their observations. Use equity sticks (a cup of sticks with each student’s name on one) or have them pass a talking stick/object to increase audience participation and accountability.
  3. Provide the question prompts related to four subheaders on the charts. 
  1. What is the Definition of the word your group defined?
  2. Please share a personal experience you have had with this type of behavior. 
  3. What are some indicators that this behavior is present?
  4. What are some ways you can identify this in yourself?
  1. Only the inside group members may speak during this time (4-6 minutes). Instruct the outside group to quietly listen and notice their own ideas that surface during the discussion. Note-taking on a graphic organizer may be helpful.
  2. When the time is up, ask the groups to trade places so that the outside group is sitting on the inner circle chairs and vice versa. Set the timer again for 4-6 minutes and let the new inside group discuss the topic.
  3. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this Fishbowl activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to share your own experiences with mindsets, beliefs, preconceptions, and compassion with a larger group? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about these behaviors and how you can repair harm? (Responsible Decision Making)

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Introduce today’s lesson and ask students if they have questions or need clarifications.
  • Yesterday we learned the importance of using interviews to collect information.  Student groups presented interview tips.  What were the five areas of tips presented?
  • Today we are going to use those guidelines to write interview questions and practice our interviews.
