INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Model

  • Distribute 11.03 HO Interview Tips Notes and explain the following:
  • The (teacher model below) questions that I will show you are based on an ethnographic interview that was between a graduate student and a Chinese couple that live in Utah.  They do not speak English and have two young children.  The interviewer wanted to find out the couples experiences navigating the school system here in the U.S.  
  • I want you to think about someone in your family or a family friend that would offer an interesting perspective about living in the United States compared to their native country.  It would be great to interview a first-generation immigrant or someone that has a different ethnic background than you. 
  • On the back side of your notes, please write at the top of your page some ideas about who you would like to interview.  
  • Write an opening interview question based on what you have learned about interviewing.  Make sure to make it open-ended.
  • Ask for students to share out their opening interview question.
  • Display 11.04 Interview Questions Teacher Model.
  • Explain that these are some examples of the types of interview questions the students may want to ask.
  • Discuss other examples of interview questions.  
  • Make sure to emphasize the importance of including questions about key life experiences that have shaped the interviewee’s perspective.

Guided Practice

  • Provide students time to write approximately 10 interview questions.  Students may use some questions from the teacher model or they can create their own.
  • Partner students.
  • Guide students to practice interviewing each other by using their notes and their interview questions.
  • Remind them to take notes and to use follow-up questions as appropriate (i.e. Tell me more about that?)
  • Teacher Note:  Students may want to pretend to be a family member or friend that is a first-generation immigrant for the practice interviews, or they may choose to tell their own story.

Independent Practice

  • Ask students to conduct the interview as a homework assignment.  Students may need several days or a weekend to complete this assignment.  The teacher may want to encourage students to record the interview as well.

Create a rubric with the students to assess the performance of the presentations for the ethnographic interview project. Determine the criteria, ratings, and scores to be used with the students.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiation Ideas

  • Establish a check-in opportunity where ELs can meet in-person or virtually using tools such as Zoom, Google Meet, or Microsoft Teams. The check-in provides ELS with one-on-one time with the facilitator to ask questions, discuss concerns, or share successes and failures related to the ethnographic interview. The goal of the check-in is to help ELs develop contextually rich language practice and confidence in a welcoming and inclusive environment.
  • Require only select portions of the assignment/project for students that are unable to complete the entire project within the time allotted or reduce the length of the assignments.
  • Conduct the interview in Spanish.
  • Share the following presentation as a completed sample for students: 11.05 PPT Interview Teacher Model

Extension

  • Consider extending the lesson over 1-2 more class periods to allow students to write the reflection paper in class.  Follow up the writing activities with a peer editing and proofreading activity using the 11.04 HO Editing & Proofreading Rubric.  Students can type their final draft.
  • See Middle School Unit 11 Biculturalism for directions on completing the Mi Herencia Project Portfolio and Visual Presentation.  The Etnográficas Interview & Reflection Paper would be a good addition to the project.  High School students could complete the Mi Herencia Project in addition to the Etnográficas Interview & Reflection Paper.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What made you feel comfortable or uncomfortable when your partner was interviewing you? 
  • What do you think would make the person you interview more comfortable?
  • What did you learn about the person being interviewed?  Is this information important?  Why?  
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • share their findings with their class.
  •  deepen understanding about the power of compassion and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • practice perspective-taking, curiosity, and listening (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrate “I” messages to state how one feels, why they feel that way, and what they want to change(Relationship Skills)
  • deepen their understanding of the structures for co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
  • foster ethical responsibility by creating spaces for voice (Responsible Decision-Making)

Purpose: To further build community and confidence by encouraging participants to interact with each other with the expectation that everyone's personal history, experiences, language, culture, and voice are valued. The Community Circle/ Class Meeting activity will have students gather in a community circle and share emotions, thoughts, and new relationships with other students in the class. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Community Circle/ Class Meetings will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Facilitate the community circle by reminding students of the shared agreements that have been established in prior meetings regarding the use of the talking stick/object, empathic listening skills and acknowledging, respecting the opinions and personal stories of others, and allowing students to pass on a turn if they are not ready to share. 
  2. Using the talking object, begin the discussion with the following prompts:
    1. What was one significant learning or takeaway from this activity with the four corners and the interviews?
    2. How did it make you feel?
    3. What is one new thing you learned about a peer?
  3. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this Fishbowl activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to share your own experiences with mindsets, beliefs, preconceptions, and compassion? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about addressing this problem and repairing harm? (Responsible Decision Making)

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Follow-up with students regarding the interviews and writing the reflection paper.
  • Was interviewing this individual challenging, why or why not?
  • Sometimes interviews go in a totally different direction than you planned.  Did any of you gain information that surprised you or you weren’t expecting?

  • The facilitator and students will use the presentation rubric to evaluate the ethnographic interview presentations and to provide timely, effective feedback in order to motivate students to improve their work. Feedback for ELs should motivate them to keep trying and improving their work.

Please see the following teacher resource for more information about supporting EL students:

Why is feedback important for English language learners in the online ESL classroom?

  • Highlight some of the key “takeaways” students learned.

  • Establish a check-in opportunity where ELs can meet in-person or virtually using tools such as Zoom, Google Meet, or Microsoft Teams. The check-in provides ELS with one-on-one time with the facilitator to ask questions, discuss concerns, or share successes and failures related to the ethnographic interview. The goal of the check-in is to help ELs develop contextually rich language practice and confidence in a welcoming and inclusive environment.
  • Conduct the presentation in Spanish or have a fluent bilingual student translate another student’s presentation.

Extension

  • See Middle School Unit 11 Biculturalism (Identity Through Art 11.08-11.11) for an additional bicultural project option.
  • Present to other high school classes (Spanish or Social Studies).

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • If someone was to interview you, what stories, experiences, or events would you share?  What makes your perspective unique?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Students will conduct an ethnographic interview, reflection paper, and presentation. Note this assignment may take several days to complete.

  • Interview
    • Students will interview someone in their family or a family friend that would offer an interesting perspective about living in the United States compared to their native country.  It would be great to interview a first-generation immigrant or someone that has a different ethnic background than you.
    • The interview should have at least 10 questions and use follow-up questions as appropriate.  Some questions may come from the teacher model or students can create their own.
    • Students should take notes and/or record the interview as evidence of a completed interview.
  • Reflection Paper and Presentation
    • These should be assigned following the completion of the interview.
    • Students should follow the instructions found in the Reflection Paper & Presentation Guidelines.  
  • Students should include their notes, reflection paper, and if applicable a copy of their presentation slides in their print or digital portfolio.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Display 12.01 Weblink Alliance for Education and scroll down to page 1.
  • Read the introduction paragraph together.
    • In what type of schools are ⅓ of the students not graduating?
    • Why do you think that is the case?
  • Explain that when students are more aware of what it takes to graduate from high school and check regularly on their progress, they are more likely to graduate from high school on time and be better prepared for postsecondary education or training.
    • In today’s lesson, we are going to explore our strengths and weaknesses and identify how we can improve our weaknesses to further our academic achievement.

Model

  • Ask students to go to 12.01 Weblink Online Student Questionnaire.  Note:  Each student will need a computer for this activity.
  • Instruct students to carefully read each question and rate themselves from 1-5 (1 = “doesn’t describe you at all” and 5 = “describes you exactly”).
  • Submit the questionnaire. Note:  Students may want to print the results to take back to class to complete the remainder of the lesson.
  • Display 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses HS.  Note:  Ideally, teachers will model filling out the HO based on their own questionnaire results.
  • Distribute 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses HS & Individual Grade Printouts (for this school year) and/or Progress Towards Graduation.
  • Ask students to highlight grades/subjects where they excelled and highlight (using a different color) grades/subjects they need to work to improve.
  • Instruct students to circle the number of credits they have earned and the number required to graduate.
  • Explain how many credits students need in each area by the time they complete their senior year.

Guided Practice

  • Instruct students to complete the 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses HS using the information they received from 12.01 Weblink Online Student Questionnaire.

Independent Practice

  • Ask students to complete the remainder of the HO independently.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Use 12.01 Weblink Student Questionnaire PDF instead of the online questionnaire.  Print & distribute.  Students will identify their strengths by looking at all items that were answered “No” and identify their weaknesses by looking at all items that were answered “Yes”.

Extension

  • Ask students to “pair up” with someone in the class they know well.  Students can help each other identify additional educational strengths for 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses HS.
  • Research ways to improve specific educational weaknesses.  Write a paragraph describing the specific suggestions discovered.
  • At the end of each term, ask students to complete 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses HS based on their performance for the term.  Save this information for the year in order to allow students to compare every term/semester’s performance.
  • Ask students to identify what school supports can help them improve their academic achievement?  Write a paragraph describing these supports.
  • Watch 12.01 Video Immigrant Surgeon. Debrief by discussing how Dr. Alfredo Quinones overcame great odds to become a surgeon.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What are my academic strengths?
  • How can I help the students I work with to learn their academic strengths?
  • How can knowing my academic strengths help me in the future?

Activity

  • Distribute 12.02 Weblink Study Habits Questionnaire.
  • Ask students to read and carefully evaluate each statement, then circle the corresponding answer. (A= Always, B= Generally, C= Sometimes, & D= Rarely)
    • Say: Once you have completed the questionnaire, record your scores on 12.02 HO Study Skills.
    • Do you have an area that needs improvement?
    • Reflect, brainstorm, and write ideas on what you can do to make a change in the area you identified.
    • Share some of your ideas with a partner.

Model

  • Explain that one thing that can help improve study skills and make students more aware of their learning is to use a learning log.
  • Distribute 12.02 HO Learning Log.
    • Say: Look at the learning log.  This log is designed to help you identify content and skills you learn daily and help you keep track of homework assignments.
  • Read the example aloud.
    • Say: Sometimes it is most effective to only record subjects/courses that are the most challenging for you.  Other times, students may want to record all subjects.  Today, for practice, we will record all subjects.

Guided Practice

  • Complete the learning log for all subjects (with yesterday's or today’s lessons).
    • Say: Once you are comfortable with the format, feel free to use a regular notebook for your learning log.

Independent Practice

  • This week, as a homework assignment, I want you to keep a learning log.  This assignment will be due next _________________.

Model

  • Good note taking is also critical in developing effective study skills.  One popular and effective method for note taking is called Cornell Notes.  Ask: 
    • Has anyone used Cornell Notes?
    • What is your opinion about this note taking system?
    • This video clip gives a good introduction on how to take notes using the Cornell method:
  • Watch 12.02 Video Cornell Notes (2 min).
  • May want to emphasize that any type of graphic organizer, like Cornell Notes, can help students with reading and writing tasks.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute 12.02 HO Note Taking.
    • Say: Now we are going to watch the clip again (12.02 Video Cornell Notes).  This time, I want you to take notes on the HO using this method.  
  • Ask students if they have questions or need clarification.
  • Review student work to make sure they have grasped the concept.

Teacher Note

  • The teacher may want to review the learning log and note taking skills once a term, and ask students to show them to you for a grade/feedback.  These study skills will not be helpful to students unless they are used repeatedly and become second nature to students.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Check ahead of time to see if some students are familiar with Cornell notes.  Ask these students to plan a lesson to present the “how to” portion of note taking.

Extension

  • Divide students into groups of 3-4.  Ask student groups to research online and locate a Spanish news story.  Show the different groups’ news clips in class.  Require students to take notes on these news stories using the Cornell method.  

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What effective study skills do I possess?  
  • How can I more effectively study and prepare for high school and college?

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 12.03 Video Mr Bean Taking a Test (5 min).
    • Ask students if they have ever felt “Test Anxiety.” Define it and relate examples from your own experience about being nervous for a test (College finals, Driver’s Test, Principal Evaluation).
    • Today we are going to discuss test anxiety and how we can manage that by using different test taking strategies.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Model

  • Show 12.03 Weblink PPT Test Taking Questionnaire (slide 1)
  • Describe the Likert scale students will use (slide 2).
  • Read each statement aloud (slide 3).
  • Ask students to rate themselves using the Likert scale and record their answers (slide 3)
  • Read the last slide to determine students’ results (slide 4). Ask: 
    • Do you have test anxiety based on the results of this questionnaire? 
    • What would it take to alleviate some of this stress and anxiety?
    • Some anxiety is good because it helps motivate us to prepare.  Too much anxiety can prevent us from doing our best.  However, preparing well and having strategies to successfully approach a test will help get rid of some of the unnecessary anxiety.
    • One way to improve your test taking is by using a mnemonic called PIRATES.  This mnemonic will help you remember what to do when you begin a test.
  • Display and distribute 12.03 HO PIRATES Mnemonic.
    • Ask individual students to read the description for each letter.

Guided Practice

  • Partner students.
  • Ask them to take turns rehearsing the PIRATES strategy.
  • Practice writing the strategy.

Teacher Note

  • It is important to remember that students need extensive practice when using a new mnemonic or other strategy.  Try to incorporate this strategy often.

  • Watch 12.03 Video - Test Taking Vocabulary at the beginning of the lesson. This clip uses “test-taking” vocabulary words to help students who may be unfamiliar with their meanings.  

Extension

  • Instruct students to complete a practice test using the PIRATES strategy.  
  • Complete a follow up lesson, or if the majority of students know the PIRATE strategy, teach the ANSWER strategy for essay tests found at 12.03 Weblink HO PIRATES Mnemonic (page 2).

Current Event Bell Starter

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Display 12.04 Weblink Adol. Literacy Fact Sheet.
  • Select 1 to 2 paragraphs to read together. Ask: 
    • What does the term “literacy” mean?
    • Why is literacy so important for high school and middle school students?
  • Scroll down the fact sheet to display the graphs on page 2. Ask: 
    •  What do these graphs tell us?
  • Read points 4, 5, and 6 on page 3 of the fact sheet. Ask: 
    • What patterns do you notice? 
    • What is the number one predictor of college success?
  • Explain to students that today we are going to learn some comprehension strategies that will help strengthen our reading skills.
    • Throughout your middle, high school, and postsecondary education, good reading skills are critical for your success.

Teacher Note

  • The teacher may want to divide students into groups based on the text they will read.  Students create example sentences in their groups with their defined vocabulary.

Model

  • Display 12.04 Weblink QAR Question Types.
  • Using the weblink above, discuss the four types of Question-Answer Relationship Types:  1) Right There; 2) Think & Search; 3) Author & Me; 4) On My Own.  
  • Demonstrate creating each type of question using 12.04 Weblink Article QAR Teacher Model.  Use labeled sticky note tabs (1-4) to identify each area in the reading that will be used to write the question.
  • Write an example of each type of question using 12.04 Weblink Article QAR Teacher Model.  Fill out the 12.04 HO Article QAR (English) with these model questions.

Guided Practice

  • Divide students into leveled groups.
  • Distribute 12.04 Weblink Article 1-Easy, 12.04 Weblink Article 2-Intermediate, or 12.04 Weblink Article 3-Difficult to each group.
  • Instruct them as a group to identify the vocabulary, read the article, and then create the 4 types of questions and record them on 12.04 HO Article QAR HS.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Use 1.03 HO Current Event Resources to find other articles for student groups.
  • Use 12.04 Weblink ReadWorks to find leveled passages and comprehension activities for up to grade 8.  A few passages are available for 9-10 grade-level readers.  Teachers can sign up for a free account.
  • Print or have students access Spanish articles from 12.04 Weblink CNN Español and 12.04 Weblink Fox News Latino.  Complete the same activities listed above in Spanish using 12.04 HO Article QAR (Spanish).
  • For more detailed instructions on the QAR strategy, see 12.04 Weblink QAR Teacher Resources.  Teachers can sign up for a free account.

Extension

  • This lesson can easily be expanded over 2-3 class periods.  Once student groups have written each type of QAR question, ask students to discuss each question in their groups.  Students may form opinions about the article and draw final conclusions.  Student groups can present their opinions and final conclusions to other groups.  Repeat the activity with a different article to allow students to further practice the skill.
  • Ask students to create a SMARTE goal using 2.01 SMARTE Goal Template - Word around improving reading comprehension.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What do you enjoy reading (fiction, non-fiction, history, articles, etc.)?  What benefits does reading bring to your life?
  • How successful do you think you are with grade level reading and writing activities?  Do you struggle reading texts for your classes?  Or is the reading “too easy” for you?  How can you improve your literacy skills if school tasks are difficult?  How can you challenge yourself if you find the reading and writing tasks too easy?

Students will:

  • understand the purpose of reading and the elements of reading so they can be effective reading tutors
  • develop understanding of how social interdependence affects trust (Self-Awareness)
  • understand impacts of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • deepen understanding about power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use this Gallery Walk activity to help students brainstorm about the role of a tutor and expectations on helping tutees with their reading skills. Like viewers at an art gallery, small groups of students will rotate from poster to poster, stopping to view, discuss, and add ideas at each station (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Gallery Walk activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self Management, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (15 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Establish the goal of developing clarity of the roles and responsibilities of effective tutors. A good prompt would be: "What skills do you need to become an effective tutor in helping your tutee further develop their reading skills?
  • Hang four posters with headings that relate to the specific reading strategies around the room such as:
    • Developing relationships with your tutee/mentee
    • Reading goals
    • Reading aloud
    • Discussion questions
  • Divide the class into four groups, give each group a marker, and assign each group to one of the posters. Explain the overarching question, and what each of the poster topics is.
  • Allow groups to stand at each poster for three minutes to share, discuss, and write down their responses to the category.
  • When time is up, ask the groups to rotate clockwise so each group is in front of a new poster to continue the activity. Each group now reads the offerings of the previous authors, using sticky notes to add clarifying questions or comments/compliments. Rotate every three to five minutes, until every group has visited every poster.
  • Next, allow time for individuals to silently walk around the room and read the completed posters, noting ideas that they agree with or that seem like something they'd like to try.
  • Original group revisits their feedback and can add to their poster.
  • Use this information as a guide when implementing the lesson below.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ideas about reading and tutoring using the Gallery Walk strategy? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned during this Gallery Walk process? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Design four Google Docs with the headers mentioned above with a table with links to the Google Doc. Post the link to the table so that all of the students have access to it. Divide the class into four groups and send them to separate breakout rooms. Assign each group to begin at a different starting point and assign a time in which they will change to the next Google Doc topic. All students will access the doc and add comments at the same time. The teacher alerts each breakout room when to rotate. Return to the large meeting and post each Google Doc for all to see.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Activating students’ prior knowledge and sharing reading memories we have as children. Teacher can share a fond reading memory (optional).
    • What is your favorite book?
    • Did you have a favorite author?
    • Who read to you when you were young?
    • What’s your favorite book now?
    • Do you read to your younger siblings, cousins, nephews & nieces?
  • Explain that the purpose of this lesson is to understand what we like about reading so that we can share that with younger students, what is the purpose of reading, and how we break down reading strategies.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Teacher Preparation

  • Prior to teaching this lesson, watch the lesson walkthrough video 13.01 LIA Tutoring Video (11 minutes) to familiarize yourself with the tutoring process.

Activity

  • Present the PowerPoint: Latinos in Action Tutor Training. Explain that an element of professionalism is going to presentations and learning to take notes. Optional: give students a printed or virtual copy of the PowerPoint as a reference while they take notes.

Slide 1: Reading Buddies

  • The number one goal as mentors/reading tutors is building relationships with our mentees/tutees.

Slide 2: Reading – What’s involved?

  • Ask students the following questions:
    • What memories do you have of reading?
    • What is the purpose of reading?
    • What are the necessary skills for reading?

Slide 3: Reading Goals

  • Relationship building. (Emphasize that the goal is to build connections with our reading buddies.)
  • Comprehension (Understanding what you read)
  • Enjoyment (Reading should be fun! Tutors make reading fun!)

Slide 4: Elements of Reading

  • Vocabulary: the words that they need to understand to comprehend the story
  • Language structure: grammar and punctuation/sentences have a subject and a verb
  • Phonics: letters and sounds
  • Cadence: tone or rhythm of voice
  • Prior knowledge: what words and ideas do the students already know about the book?

Slide 5: Book Selection

  • Level: the book needs to be age-level and proficiency-level appropriate. If your mentee/tutee is struggling immensely, then the book may not be level appropriate.
  • Topic: Try to find books that meet the mentee’s interests. We focus more and are more interested if the book is about something we find interesting. If your mentee likes dinosaurs, try to find a book about dinosaurs.
  • Cover: Is the cover interesting? Are there pictures? Is there an appropriate title?
  • Illustrations: Are there many illustrations? Are they interesting and fun? Do they help tell a story?
  • Structure/organization: A straightforward plot is best for young students. For example, you would not read Harry Potter novels with a first grader because the books are not always chronological, they skip between different time periods and places, and don’t have many illustrations.

Slide 6: Before Reading

  • Go over the cover, author, and illustrator.
  • Take the student through a picture walk – either demonstrate a picture walk or show 13.01 Video Picture Walk. A picture walk is when you have students talk about what they think will happen in the book and activate their prior knowledge by walking through each picture and not reading any of the words.
  • Introduce vocabulary that you predict the student does not know and explain it.
  • Have students make predictions and brainstorm what will happen in the story.

Slide 7: Reading Format

  • Tutor reads to mentee- can be used in the beginning when mentee is shy and nervous.
  • Shared reading- mentee read a page, tutor read a page.
  • Mentee reads to the tutor- this happens when the mentee becomes more comfortable.
  • Modeled reading/Echo reading- this is when both the tutor and mentee read at the same time.
  • *NOTE: These formats should be varied and mixed. Use different formats on different days. Try them all!

Slide 8: Modeled Reading/Echo Reading

  • Step one: Tutor reads while the mentee/tutee follows along
  • Step two: Tutee reads silently, tells tutor when they are done
  • Step three: Repeat two-part process at least 2-3 times, until the tutee is ready to read aloud

Slide 9: Reading Aloud

  • As tutors, we model the process of reading first:
    • We introduce the book, the title, and front cover, and take the tutee through a picture walk.
    • We read aloud to the tutee and stop for thinking and predicting.
    • We discuss what’s happening in the book as we read aloud.
    • We may also demonstrate a reading strategy at this point.

Slide 10: Why We Read Aloud

  • Discuss the reasons why we read aloud and its importance.

Slide 11: During Reading

  • Comprehension checks- ask questions about characters’ names and attributes, location/setting, and major plotline questions.
  • Think aloud- “I wonder if…” “I think that…”
  • Predict and verify- “I predict that Clifford will befriend the grouchy neighbors…” then check at the end of the book to see if the predictions were correct.
  • Relate text to self/text/world- Bring the book back to their lives and their interests, so they feel invested in the story.
  • Visualization- Have tutees create a mental image in their minds to represent the ideas that they read in the text: “Close your eyes and imagine Clifford, his friends, their house, etc…”
  • Praise- Be genuine with compliments. Tell the tutees that they are trying very hard, or focusing really well, or that you have seen great improvement (if you have). They need to feel encouraged!

Slide 12: Self-Correct Strategies

  • Discuss the examples listed for teaching tutees to self-correct when reading.

Slide 13: Discussion Questions

  • Depending on the grade level that you are tutoring with, discussion questions will vary.
  • Be sure to insert the word “you” or “your” when possible in each question.
  • If they are young students (K-2), focus on easier questions, like:
    • What was your favorite part of the story?
    • Which character did you like?
    • What characters do you remember?
    • Where did the story take place?
  • If they are more advanced or older students (grades 3-5), you can dive into more difficult questions:
    • How would you compare (a character) to (another character)?
    • If you were in the situation, how would you have acted?
    • If you could change the ending, how would it end?
    • Were any of the characters like people you know? (Again, relating back to self/real world!)
    • What did you learn about the world?

Slide 14: Tutors in Action (An Overview)

  • Choose a book or text that’s appropriate for the student’s interests and reading level.
  • Introduce the book- title, cover, author, illustrator, picture walk.
  • Read aloud- use varied methods, stop for discussion/questions.
  • Wrap-up- ask comprehension questions to clarify that the tutee understood the story; ask what the tutee enjoyed about the book.

Slide 15: Correcting Negative Behaviors and Discipline

  • Some techniques to help when your tutee is not paying attention:
    • Point out another student who is on task and say, “Wow, look how well Victor is reading with his buddy. I think you could read like that too.”
    • Use incentives such as stickers. “I don’t think you are going to be earning your sticker today.”
  • If the tutee can really not focus after multiple attempts to get them back on track, try offering to take them back to class:
    • “I think I should take you back to class and maybe I can work with one of our classmates who wants to read with me. We will try again next time.”
  • If the tutee seems really off and unfocused, try asking what’s wrong:
    • “What’s going on with you today, Camila? Usually you are very focused, and today you seem off.”
  • Emphasize the following to your LIA students: If ever the problem is too large for the tutor to handle, always go seek the help of your LIA teacher or the elementary school student’s teacher.

Slide 16: Celebrate Reading!

  • Remind your LIA students to celebrate reading and make it fun for their mentees!
  • Remind students that the number one goal as mentors/reading tutors is building relationships with our mentees/tutees.

Guided Practice

  • Direct students to practice one or more parts of these components with a partner, using different books.

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Review

  • Remind your LIA students to celebrate reading and make it fun for their mentees!
  • Remind students that the number one goal as mentors/reading tutors is building relationships with our mentees/tutees.
  • Review the PowerPoint: Latinos in Action Tutor Training as needed. Ask students which parts they would like to review or have questions about.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Adaptation/Extension Activity

  • Have students break into their committees and come up with ten scenarios that could happen while tutoring and a solution for each scenario. For example:
    • Scenario: If my tutee starts crying in the middle of our reading session.
    • Possible solution: Try to calm my tutee down by taking a break from reading and getting some water, and if that doesn’t work, go find my LIA teacher or the elementary school teacher.

Adaptation for Virtual Tutoring

  • There are still plenty of unknowns about the impact of school closures during the pandemic and the effect it would have on schools in the long term. Many schools have implemented in-person, virtual, and hybrid instructional models that involve daily synchronous instruction. For this reason, it is important to establish and maintain a virtual tutoring model that can present content in multiple ways to help students retain information and address the need to reinforce vocabulary development, reading comprehension, and background knowledge. The benefits of using digital media resources in virtual tutoring provide students a multisensory experience while introducing new concepts and ideas remotely.
  • To begin a virtual tutoring model, the LIA class and the elementary school must utilize a common virtual learning platform with a built-in video conferencing tool to deliver instruction. Some examples of virtual platforms include Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, BigBlueButton on Canvas, Google Classroom, Schoology, etc. Once you decide on a platform, you and the elementary school teacher will need to familiarize yourselves with the ins and outs of this platform. If you need additional assistance, contact your school or district IT staff for support. 
  • It is also important for students to have one-to-one devices. Once the virtual platform is established, all tutors and tutees will either join one shared virtual classroom, or individual virtual spaces, with a code or link.
  • The LIA and elementary school teachers manage and maintain shared folders and provide materials for the tutors and tutees to use during the online tutoring sessions.
  • The LIA students and the elementary students will use a video-chatting tool through the chosen tutoring platform to provide live instruction during the tutoring session. Virtual tutoring sessions must be monitored and maintained, by at least one of the teachers.
  • If your chosen platform includes a breakout room option, it is imperative that you take time to familiarize yourself with how to utilize this tool. The following resources will provide you with a brief introduction of how breakout rooms work on the following platforms:
    • Article: Zoom Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Google Meet Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Microsoft Teams Breakout Rooms
  • The teachers create online breakout rooms by dividing the students into pairings or groupings. All breakout rooms are listed on a hyperlinked document in the virtual classroom for students to find. Use 13.01 LIA Virtual Tutoring Breakout Room Sample Sheet as a reference point. The functionality and practicality of online breakout rooms work similarly to physical groups in offline settings. In addition, breakout rooms offer online classroom tools, such as a virtual whiteboard to jot down notes and the ability for students to interact and speak to each other. Teachers can walk around to observe in-person tutoring sessions or virtually monitor remote students. It is recommended that an additional breakout room is created to serve as a virtual “help desk.” The teacher should monitor this breakout room for any concerns or questions that students may have while tutoring remotely.

Journal Entry Questions

  • Teacher or students will choose 1-2 questions below. These questions will be the same for all 3 lessons in this unit:
    • What is your fondest memory about reading?
    • What sorts of materials and topics do you enjoy reading?
    • What is your favorite book and why do you like that book?
    • What is the most challenging part of reading? What don’t you like about it?
    • What are some potential outcomes of a child who is read to versus a child who is not read to?
    • Agree/Disagree with the statement and explain your answer: Children don’t like to read because they are not good at it.

Students will: 

  • demonstrate knowledge of reading tutoring strategies and effective book selection by practicing with another student
  • develop understanding of how social interdependence affects trust (Self-Awareness)
  • understand impacts of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • deepen understanding about power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

Materials needed for this lesson:

  • Elementary school-level books for students to practice tutoring. You will need at least 1 book per pair of students. 
  • Print copies or provide the link to Unit 13 - Tutoring Timesheet and Daily Log. If printing copies, make sure there is 1 per student.

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use Partner Reading as a strategy to facilitate student interaction so that tutors have more patience, empathy, and compassion with their tutees. (Literacy Strategies for English Learners, Calderon 2016).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Partner Reading activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students – lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas).
  • Explain to students that they will participate in a Partner Reading simulation between a tutor and tutee. Use a grouping activity such as Academic Vocabulary Buddies (see HS Lesson 5.06) or Clock Buddies (see HS Lesson 1.05) to create pairs for this reading activity. In the case where there are ELs or struggling readers, intentionally pair these students with more proficient English speakers.
  • Remind the students of the qualities of patience, empathy, and compassion when reading with their tutees.
  • In the case where you have newcomers (NC), have the NC read or whisper-read the same sentence that the tutor reads.

Virtual Adaptation: Use Breakout rooms to work with your tutee on Partner Reading. Emphasize the use of patience, empathy, and compassion.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Show the students 13.02 Picture Walk Video (2:27 minutes). This will demonstrate an effective picture walk for students.
  • Explain the purpose of this lesson is for students to get a chance to practice the tutoring process that they will use with their tutees at the elementary school.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

Teacher will review the steps of tutoring with the students. Ask for volunteers to see if someone can recite the steps from slide 14 of the Powerpoint in the previous lesson.

Model these steps for the students:

  • Choose an appropriate text.
  • Introduce the book- title, cover, author, illustrator, picture walk!
  • Read aloud- use varied methods, stop for discussion/questions.
  • Wrap-up- ask comprehension questions to clarify that the tutee understood the story; ask what the tutee enjoyed about the book.
  • Complete the Unit 13 - Tutoring Timesheet and Daily Log and explain to students that this will need to be done at least once a week to keep track of each tutee's progress.

Guided Practice

  • Choose a sample elementary school book. Teacher will review and model different reading formats. If there is an experienced reading tutor, have the experienced tutor model the formats:
    • Tutor reads to the mentee.
    • Shared reading.
    • Child reads to the tutor.
    • Echo/Modeled reading.
  • Put students into pairs. Select one student to be the first tutor, and the other to be the tutee. Assign them the grade level that they will likely be working with at the elementary school. So, if you’re working with second grade, have their classmate playing the role of tutee be in second grade. Give the students 15-20 minutes to go through the reading tutoring process at each stage until they switch roles:
    • Choose an appropriate text (for the grade level you are working with).
    • Introduce the book- title, cover, author, illustrator, picture walk!
    • Read aloud- use varied methods, stop for discussion/questions.
    • Wrap-up- ask comprehension questions to clarify that tutee understood story; ask what tutee enjoyed about the book.
    • The tutor will practice filling out the Unit 13 - Tutoring Timesheet and Daily Log to keep track of their tutee's progress.

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in Partner Reading? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to learn about patience while reading with your tutee? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about being patient, empathetic and compassionate and the Partner Reading activity with your tutees? (Responsible Decision Making)

  • As a potential service project, the LIA service committee can speak to their local library about getting elementary school books donated to their LIA class that they can take with them to tutoring.

Adaptation for Virtual Tutoring

  • There are still plenty of unknowns about the impact of school closures during the pandemic and the effect it would have on schools in the long term. Many schools have implemented in-person, virtual, and hybrid instructional models that involve daily synchronous instruction. For this reason, it is important to establish and maintain a virtual tutoring model that can present content in multiple ways to help students retain information and address the need to reinforce vocabulary development, reading comprehension, and background knowledge. The benefits of using digital media resources in virtual tutoring provide students a multisensory experience while introducing new concepts and ideas remotely.
  • To begin a virtual tutoring model, the LIA class and the elementary school must utilize a common virtual learning platform with a built-in video conferencing tool to deliver instruction. Some examples of virtual platforms include Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, BigBlueButton on Canvas, Google Classroom, Schoology, etc. Once you decide on a platform, you and the elementary school teacher will need to familiarize yourselves with the ins and outs of this platform. If you need additional assistance, contact your school or district IT staff for support. 
  • It is also important for students to have one-to-one devices. Once the virtual platform is established, all tutors and tutees will either join one shared virtual classroom, or individual virtual spaces, with a code or link.
  • The LIA and elementary school teachers manage and maintain shared folders and provide materials for the tutors and tutees to use during the online tutoring sessions.
  • The LIA students and the elementary students will use a video-chatting tool through the chosen tutoring platform to provide live instruction during the tutoring session. Virtual tutoring sessions must be monitored and maintained, by at least one of the teachers.
  • If your chosen platform includes a breakout room option, it is imperative that you take time to familiarize yourself with how to utilize this tool. The following resources will provide you with a brief introduction of how breakout rooms work on the following platforms:
    • Article: Zoom Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Google Meet Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Microsoft Teams Breakout Rooms
  • The teachers create online breakout rooms by dividing the students into pairings or groupings. All breakout rooms are listed on a hyperlinked document in the virtual classroom for students to find. Use 13.01 LIA Virtual Tutoring Breakout Room Sample Sheet as a reference point. The functionality and practicality of online breakout rooms work similarly to physical groups in offline settings. In addition, breakout rooms offer online classroom tools, such as a virtual whiteboard to jot down notes and the ability for students to interact and speak to each other. Teachers can walk around to observe in-person tutoring sessions or virtually monitor remote students. It is recommended that an additional breakout room is created to serve as a virtual “help desk.” The teacher should monitor this breakout room for any concerns or questions that students may have while tutoring remotely.

Journal Entry Questions

  • Teacher or students will choose 1-2 questions below. These questions will be the same for all 3 lessons in this unit:
    • What is your fondest memory about reading?
    • What sorts of materials and topics do you enjoy reading?
    • What is your favorite book and why do you like that book?
    • What is the most challenging part of reading? What don’t you like about it?
    • What are some potential outcomes of a child who is read to versus a child who is not read to?
    • Agree/Disagree with the statement and explain your answer: Children don’t like to read because they are not good at it.

Watch a meaningful TED Talk about building relationships and relate it back to their tutoring at the elementary school.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • explore the impacts of perspective-taking and empathy (Social Awareness)
  • develop the ability to establish and maintain healthy and rewarding relationships (Relationship Skills)
  • recognize one’s ethical responsibility to treat others fairly and with respect (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To explore characteristics of mentoring in order to provide support, advice, friendship, reinforcement, and constructive role-modeling to mentees. This activity will help students understand the concept of mentoring and its positive impact on the elementary students involved. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This mentoring activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (5 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Explain to the class that a mentor helps their mentee by being a positive influence, giving their time, and being a role model. 
  • Print copies of 13.03 HO Characteristics of an Effective Mentor and hand out to students. Ask students to select four key words from the list that answer the question, "How should a mentor act?" Encourage students to think of words that describe individuals who may have been mentors to them. 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • Use an inclusive and equitable grouping strategy to divide the class into groups of three. Strategy Grouping Example–Partner high-skilled students with mid-level skilled students and/or partner mid-level skilled students with lower-skilled students.
  • Remind students of the class Shared Agreements and SEL competencies on everyone gets equal time, empathic listening and valuing diverse opinions and perspectives.
  • Use a Round Robin strategy to allow them to share the first word and explain its meaning to them and give one example when they may have practiced this characteristic or that may describe their experience with a mentor.
  • Share out a few examples with the class. 
  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore characteristics of an effective mentor? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about the characteristics of an effective mentor? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Design Google Docs with the list of the characteristics of a mentor and post the link to the list so that all of the students have access to it. Have students work on their list of four characteristics. Assign students to breakout rooms of three. The teacher reminds students in each breakout room to give each other equal time to share. After the designated time, bring all students back to the main meeting room and post the Google Doc for all to see and share out examples.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain that our main goal with our reading tutoring is to build relationships and provide mentorship to young students. We know that students do better when they have at least one role model or person to share things within their lives. LIA tutors are the role models the elementary school students need, and we hope that our work with them throughout the year allows them to see Latinos as leaders, and inspire them to also want to lead, and to read, as they grow up. But in order for us to have effective reading gains, we have to build a relationship first.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Activity

  • Watch the following video (8 minutes):                                                                             
    • Ted Talk - Rita Pierson "Every Kid Needs a Champion"
    • Ask the students to write down at least one quote while they are watching that they can identify with.
  • Partner Discussion.                                                                                      
  • Students will share with a partner which quote they wrote down and why that quote is meaningful to them.

Guided Practice

Reflection Questions: Ask students to reflect on what they learned from the TED Talk and how they can relate it back to LIA tutoring. Have students unpack the following quotes from the video and answer the following discussion questions in their committees:

  • “And we know why kids drop out. We know why kids don’t learn.”
    • Do we know why students drop out? Brainstorm 3-5 reasons why you think that students drop out of our high school.
    • How does Latinos In Action prevent students from dropping out of high school?
  • “James Comer says that no significant learning can occur without a significant relationship.”
    • How will you develop a significant relationship with your reading tutee?
    • Why is regular attendance in an LIA class important?
  • “How do I raise the self-esteem of a child and their academic achievement at the same time?”
    • What ways can LIA tutors raise the self-esteem of their tutees?
    • What ways are we as a class going to track our tutee’s progress?
  • “I gave a quiz, 20 questions. A student missed 18. I put a “+2” on his paper and a big smiley face.”
    • What does this quote say about the importance of perspective?
    • How can you as a reading tutor encourage tutees even when they are discouraged?
  • “Every child deserves a champion, an adult who will never give up on them, who understands the power of connection, and insists that they become the best that they can possibly be.”
    • Who was or is your “champion” as you are growing up?
    • Use one word to explain how you feel about becoming a champion for a young child.

Have each student share their one word response to the last question, "Use one word to explain how you feel about becoming a champion for a young child," with the entire class to gain excitement and momentum for tutoring.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="padding-5-percent" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color="#3a3a3a" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" font_color="#ffffff" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Adaptation/Extension Activity

  • The service committee can find a fun “getting-to-know-you” activity online and print/copy them for the class for the first day of tutoring so that students can begin the relationship building on the first day, and help elementary school tutees to become comfortable with LIA tutors.
  • Committees can set goals for reading tutoring this school year. Examples:
    • We want to see at least one reading level gain in each of our elementary school students.
    • We want to teach the student 10 new vocabulary words a week.
    • We want to get books donated to distribute for the Holidays.
    • We want to fundraise so that we can buy our tutees LIA reading shirts.

Adaptation for Virtual Tutoring

  • There are still plenty of unknowns about the impact of school closures during the pandemic and the effect it would have on schools in the long term. Many schools have implemented in-person, virtual, and hybrid instructional models that involve daily synchronous instruction. For this reason, it is important to establish and maintain a virtual tutoring model that can present content in multiple ways to help students retain information and address the need to reinforce vocabulary development, reading comprehension, and background knowledge. The benefits of using digital media resources in virtual tutoring provide students a multisensory experience while introducing new concepts and ideas remotely.
  • To begin a virtual tutoring model, the LIA class and the elementary school must utilize a common virtual learning platform with a built-in video conferencing tool to deliver instruction. Some examples of virtual platforms include Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, BigBlueButton on Canvas, Google Classroom, Schoology, etc. Once you decide on a platform, you and the elementary school teacher will need to familiarize yourselves with the ins and outs of this platform. If you need additional assistance, contact your school or district IT staff for support. 
  • It is also important for students to have one-to-one devices. Once the virtual platform is established, all tutors and tutees will either join one shared virtual classroom, or individual virtual spaces, with a code or link.
  • The LIA and elementary school teachers manage and maintain shared folders and provide materials for the tutors and tutees to use during the online tutoring sessions.
  • The LIA students and the elementary students will use a video-chatting tool through the chosen tutoring platform to provide live instruction during the tutoring session. Virtual tutoring sessions must be monitored and maintained, by at least one of the teachers.
  • If your chosen platform includes a breakout room option, it is imperative that you take time to familiarize yourself with how to utilize this tool. The following resources will provide you with a brief introduction of how breakout rooms work on the following platforms:
    • Article: Zoom Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Google Meet Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Microsoft Teams Breakout Rooms
  • The teachers create online breakout rooms by dividing the students into pairings or groupings. All breakout rooms are listed on a hyperlinked document in the virtual classroom for students to find. Use 13.01 LIA Virtual Tutoring Breakout Room Sample Sheet as a reference point. The functionality and practicality of online breakout rooms work similarly to physical groups in offline settings. In addition, breakout rooms offer online classroom tools, such as a virtual whiteboard to jot down notes and the ability for students to interact and speak to each other. Teachers can walk around to observe in-person tutoring sessions or virtually monitor remote students. It is recommended that an additional breakout room is created to serve as a virtual “help desk.” The teacher should monitor this breakout room for any concerns or questions that students may have while tutoring remotely.

Journal Entry Questions

  • Teacher or students will choose 1-2 questions below. These questions will be the same for all 3 lessons in this unit:
    • What is your fondest memory about reading?
    • What sorts of materials and topics do you enjoy reading?
    • What is your favorite book and why do you like that book?
    • What is the most challenging part of reading? What don’t you like about it?
    • What are some potential outcomes of a child who is read to versus a child who is not read to?
    • Agree/Disagree with the statement and explain your answer: Children don’t like to read because they are not good at it.

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY Purpose: To use Class Introductions, Developing Relationships, and Express Care with one another to further enhance relationships and support for one another.  Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Class Introductions and Developing Relationships activities will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making. Overview (4 min):
  • Welcome students – lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Introduce yourself to the students. Go over the purpose and objectives of the lesson.
  • Choose 1 – 2 ideas to facilitate from the Teacher Introduction Activities. (See Bright Ideas.)
    • Self-image and identity (Exploring your online versus your offline identity) 
    • Invite students to tell their personal stories (they may use digital tools to visually represent with images, recordings, etc.)
  • Introduce and lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices (3 minutes) (See Bright Ideas) 
  • Go over Class Norms of Collaboration and Shared Agreements (Virtual)
    • Be Present and visible (virtual)
    • Be Respectful
    • Empathic Listening
    • Equal Time
    • Give Me Five - Pause Activity, Eyes on Speaker
    • Digital footprint and reputation (How to protect your own privacy and respect others’ privacy and remind students to “self-reflect before they self-reveal” – in-person and online)
Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)
  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ways to build community? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about community building today? (Responsible Decision Making)
*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better. Include Hand Raise, Chat, Breakout Rooms, and Gallery conversations to engage students throughout the lesson.   Teacher Introduction
  • View the 10-minute video “What is LIA?”
  • Ask the students the following questions.
    • Why did you register for LIA? (Use pair-share or small groups in person; chat in virtual)
    • How has LIA made a difference for these students?
    • How do you think LIA can make a difference in your life?
    • How can your cultural and language background be of benefit to the LIA community?
