INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text text_direction="default"]INSTRUCTION  Activity
  • Use LIA Introduction to introduce LIA’s mission statement and purpose.
  • See examples and video clips embedded within the PPT.
Guided Practice
  • Divide class into groups of 3 to 4 students Review Norms of Collaboration, Group Roles (Leader, Reporter, Recorder, Timekeeper) 
  • Pass out LIA Reflection (English) to each group.
  • Instruct them to discuss the questions and record their answers and reflections.
Note
  • If the majority of students have taken LIA in previous years, teachers may want to forego this lesson, just watch the video clips as highlights, or concentrate on extension activities, or spend time debriefing on lessons learned from prior years, goals accomplished and new goals for the current year. (Create a K-W-L Chart for students to complete: Begin with students independently completing “What I Know” in the “K” column; students in pairs/small groups input “What I Want to Know” in the “W” column; prior students sharing  “What I Learned” in the “L” column) 
  • Spend additional time in building class community through journal writing and pair-share. 
  • May want to complete lessons 5.06 Leadership Committees Part 1: Committee Overview and 5.07 Leadership Committees Part 2: Election Day and First Committee Meeting (Leadership Unit) following this lesson or following the 1.02 Ice Breaker lesson to enable classes to create the LIA committees early in the year.

  • Conduct this lesson in Spanish or have a student translate each slide.
  • Use 1.01 HO LIA Reflection (Spanish) as an additional option.
Extension
  • Ask students who have taken LIA to prepare and present this lesson to the other class members.
  • Ask high school students or LIA Alumni to prepare and present this lesson.
  • If all students have already taken LIA in the past, ask students to organize/write a five-paragraph essay to demonstrate the benefits of LIA.  Use this template 1.01 HO Essay Outline Guide (English) or 1.01 HO Essay Outline Guide (Spanish) as a guide.
  • Read 1.01 Weblink Dr. Jose Enriquez Bio and discuss in small groups.  How do you think Dr. Enriquez’s years growing up influenced his current work?  Discuss some of his accomplishments.  How can LIA help you achieve your future goals?

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE
Class participation in ice breakers to build relationships and develop a class motto.

OBJECTIVES
Students will:

  • get to know their classmates by participating in Icebreaker and Team Building activities
  • develop an understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

PREPARATION

  • Digital Tools

MATERIALS
Main lesson
1.02 Video Icebreakers 1 – Teacher Materials
1.02 Weblink Icebreakers 2 – Teacher Materials
1.02 Icebreakers 3 – Teacher Materials
1.06 Team Building

Adaptations

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Social Interdependence and connections
  • Socio-cultural identities
  • Vision
  • Respect for diversity
  • Organizational Culture
  • Democratic Process
  • Empower
  • Linguistic
  • Proficiency

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY 

Purpose: To use the Ice-Breakers activity to build community; support self-awareness, social awareness, responsible decision-making

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Ice-Breaker activities will further enhance students’ competencies of Social Awareness and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Facilitate My Name, My Identity Activity  (see Greetings) - pair share, large group (Layered and process)
    • Share the story about how you were given your name and the meaning behind it.
    • Has anyone ever made assumptions based on your name? What was that like for you? What was that like for you? 
    • Is your name easy or difficult for other people at school to pronounce? Do other students in your school have the same name? What is that like? 
    • What can you do if someone’s name is difficult to pronounce?  If you have a name that is challenging for other students to pronounce, what can you do to help them learn your name?
    • Native Americans often had names that described something about the person or compared the person to something in nature. Examples are White Elk, Thunder Cloud, and Spotted Deer. If you could make up a name for yourself, what would it be? Share your reasoning. 
  • Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.”

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore our names and how people respond to them? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about names today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better. Include Hand Raise, Chat, Breakout Rooms, and Gallery conversations to engage students throughout the lesson.  

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement: “Empowering youth to lead and strengthen their communities.”
  • Explain to students that today’s lesson will help us to get to know each other better.  
    • If we know each other better, we are more likely to be respectful of others’ challenges, work better as a team, and more effectively create common goals that we can help each other achieve.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Introduce one of the icebreaker activities described in 1.02 Video Icebreakers 1-Teacher Materials or 1.02 Weblink Icebreakers 2 Teacher Materials or 1.02 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials.
  • Students complete the activity.
  • Debrief activity using questions noted in each icebreaker.  See 1.02 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials.  This document has 4 pre-selected icebreakers that may work well for the LIA classroom setting with debriefing questions identified in a simpler format.
  • Select another icebreaker activity as time allows and then debrief.

Guided Practice

  • Create a class motto by asking students for ideas and listing them on the board.
    • Now that we know each other better and have identified our strengths and weaknesses, we can develop a class motto that encompasses these strengths & our goals.
    • Let’s brainstorm some ideas.
    • Choose our best 3 ideas.  Can we reduce these phrases to 5 words or less?
  • Ask students to vote on their favorite motto.
  • Assign a student to write the motto on the banner.
  • Note: May choose a class motto during this class period or during the 1.06 Team Building lesson.

Class members/teachers name one fact about each class member.

  • Create a classroom website and blog (For examples - Google Sites, Weebly for Education, Blogger, Wordpress, Edublog, etc.)
  • Post the class motto on the website. Have each student respond to a blog post: “What does the motto mean to you?”

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiation Ideas

  • Create small groups and rotate groups through 3-4 stations with different ice breaker activities at each station. Especially effective for students that have anxiety participating in large groups.

Extension

  • Create a class poster/collage that represents each individual in the class.  (Each class member will find a picture in a magazine or newspaper that represents something about themselves.  Class members will create a collage using these pictures.)  This can be displayed in the classroom alongside the class motto.
  • Students create their own personal mottos with images and voice recordings. Students submit their mottos electronically using a whiteboard app. (For example - Educreations, Explain Everything Whiteboard, Jamboard, Doceri Interactive Whiteboard, etc. )

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why is it important to know each other well in a class like LIA?
  • Write down a few activities or thoughts about how you can get to know and build a strong, healthy relationship with the students you tutor.

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE

Connect the curriculum to current events by focusing on timely topics from pop culture to political controversies through articles, videos, social media, and podcasts.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • be able to research current events that have a direct impact on their school, local, student body and administration
  • analyze beliefs, mindsets and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)
  • explore the impacts of cultural awareness on effective team building (Relationship Skills)

PREPARATION

  •  Posters/Slides of images, numbers, words, quotes, or pictures

MATERIALS

Main lesson

1.03 Weblink Ignorance 1

1.03 Weblink Ignorance 2 LIA

1.03 HO Current Events GO (English)

1.03 Weblink Article 1

1.03 MS Current Events Graphic Organizer Teacher Model

1.03 HO Current Event Resources

1.03 HO Current Events GO (English)

1.03 HO Current Events GO (Spanish)

1.03 HO Five Minute Fact or Fiction Outline (English)

1.03 Weblink Article 2

1.03 Five Minute Fact or Fiction Teacher Model

 1.03 Calendar Template

Adaptations

1.03 HO Current Event Resources

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Beliefs
  • Mindsets
  • Social Norms
  • Cultural Characteristics
  • Calamity
  • Stereotype
  • Plagiarize
  • Subjective

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

 Purpose: To reflect on a statement, image, or prompt that relates to a characteristic, quality, or preference of their culture, language, history, or personal interest and move to a "corner" that matches their choice so they can share their rationale for choosing that corner. “Corners” is helpful in promoting the importance of divergent perspectives and the value of having all voices heard. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Reflection on a statement, image, or prompt will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (3 min): 

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Before the activity, mark four to five areas in the room with a large image, number, or word that corresponds to the choices from cultural characteristics that you will be giving in the areas of music, food, art, history, or language.
  • Ask participants to silently reflect on a statement or question prompt that is aligned with the content of the current event.
  • Share 4-5 choices with the group on a poster/slide (quotes, pictures, etc.).
  • Instruct participants to choose one of the responses, then ask them to move to that designated "corner" of the room, find a partner or trio within the group that forms in that area, and share what drew them to that choice.
  • NOTE: If you end up with a solo participant in a “corner,” join that person to hear their thoughts, using a timer to keep on track.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings about language, history, and other characteristics as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore each other's thoughts or ideas regarding personal preferences and interests? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do to continue building your relationship with others who were in your corner? (Relationship Skills)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing their interest in a certain response or topic in their own areas of interest. Send students to Breakout Rooms for the Corners activity to discuss their reasons for selecting their response.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “Empowering youth to lead and strengthen their communities.”
  • The purpose of this current event lesson is to establish the routine of the current event bell starter activity which is the first activity in the Introduction of every lesson.
    • The importance of knowing the current events occurring locally, in the U.S., and in the world, will help students meet the LIA mission to become more knowledgeable of culture to serve more effectively and broaden their education.
    • Write “ignorance is bliss” and “knowledge is power” on the board. Ask students to express their thoughts on each quote.
  • Ask the students if they agree or disagree with these quotes. Encourage students to support their argument with examples.

Weblink

  • View 1.03 Weblink Ignorance 1 and 1.03 Weblink Ignorance 2, or other similar examples of your choosing.
  • Ask the students to consider the following questions:
    • In what ways can parents improve their knowledge and understanding?
    • In what ways can you improve your knowledge and understanding?
    • List ways to increase your knowledge and build understanding.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Teachers may choose either current event bell ringer option 1 or option 2 or alternate between the two options (hybrid) throughout the year. If teachers choose to do a hybrid option, please use two class periods to complete this lesson. Daily, current event bell ringers are highly encouraged.

Option 1 Model – demonstrate a current event graphic organizer bell ringer

  • Display 1.03 HO Current Events GO (English).
  • Hand out 1.03 Weblink Article 1. 
  • Display 1.03 MS Current Events Graphic Organizer Teacher Model.
  • Demonstrate how to complete sections 1, 2, & 3.  Ask students the following questions.  Record students’ responses on the handout.
    • Based on the title, what will this article be about?
    • Who’s face is currently on the $20 bill?
    • What is your opinion?  Does this topic matter to you?
  • Read the article as a class.
  • Identify challenging vocabulary and discuss student-friendly definitions. List the vocabulary words and definitions in section 4.
  • Answer the questions (5 Ws and an H) in section 5 as a class.
  • Model writing a sentence describing a summary of the main point of the article in section 6.

Option 1 Guided Practice

  • Divide students into groups.
  • Choose an article, video, social media, or podcast (chosen by the teacher), to share with each group.
  • See 1.03 HO Current Event Resources.
  • Guide students in completing 1.03 HO Current Events GO (English) or 1.03 HO Current Events GO (Spanish) in their groups.

Option 2 Model – demonstrate a five-minute fact or fiction bell ringer

  • Display 1.03 HO Five Minute Fact or Fiction Outline (English)
  • Distribute 1.03 Weblink Article 2 to students.
  • Use 1.03 Five Minute Fact or Fiction Teacher Model.
  • Demonstrate how to complete the “Article Description” section. Ask students the following question and emphasize the following.        
  • What is this article about?
  • As we read the article, think about the main points the author makes.  We will be writing a summary, so you may want to highlight important facts.
  • Read the article as a class.
  • Identify challenging vocabulary and discuss student-friendly definitions. List the vocabulary words and definitions on the outline.
  • Ask students what they learned from the article, any thoughts, and how the subject relates to LIA.
  • Record student responses on the outline.
  • Model writing a summary paragraph for the article.
  • Model forming questions and fact and fiction statements for student discussion.

Activity

  • Students choose a historical event for their “What if?” history project
    • Students research an actual historical event, describe and explain the point of divergence, and create a timeline of newly imagined events in history leading to a new current event.
    • Students use an online tool for creating a Timeline to show their project (For example - Enwoven, Time.Graphics, estory, Knightlab Timeline, etc.)
  • Students conduct research on a topic and create a virtual public service announcement to educate others about recent trends in their communities or society in general.

  • Use easy to intermediate reading level resources from 1.03 HO Current Event Resources.

Extension

  • Have each student group translate the chosen article from English to Spanish.
  • Pair groups and see how their translations differ, check for correct grammar and word usage.
  • Instruct student groups to present the information from their article (Option 1).

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why should I be knowledgeable about current events?

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]PURPOSE

  •  Explore cultural backgrounds and family to learn more about yourselves and others.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • gather information about ancestors, family and self and prepare a presentation on their personal history and background to develop a better understanding of self
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • build an understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)

PREPARATION

  • Cards, paper
  • Digital tools  

MATERIALS

Main lesson

1.04 Video Yesika Salgado - Brown Girl

1.04 Personal History Part 1 of 2

11.02 Mi Herencia Project Requirements

1.04 Presentation Rubric

Adaptations

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Social norms
  • Personal and collective agency
  • Socio-cultural identities
  • Personal Story
  • Ancestors
  • Inherit
  • Trait
  • Culture

Purpose: To use the Mix and Mingle activity to have students move around the room and share ideas with a partner or small group. This is designed to build community by encouraging participants to interact with each other with the expectation that everyone's personal history, language, culture, and voice are valued. Skills for Life and Learning Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Mix and Mingle activity will further enhance students’  competencies of Self-Awareness and Social Awareness.

Overview (3 min): 

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Life and Learning Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • On a card or half-sheet of paper, ask participants to write down a response to a prompt you give related to their own personal history. (Begin with a low-vulnerability prompt such as, “Where were you born?” or “How would you describe the family and culture you were born into?” or something connected to upcoming work like “What’s one thing you like most about [insert LIA topics such as tutoring, leadership, bootcamp, LIA class, etc.]?”
  • When you announce, "Mix and mingle!" and turn on music (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, Norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc.) participants move around.
  • When the music stops, participants find a partner near them. Help with pairing if needed.
  • Partners share their responses, listen actively to each other, and ask follow-up questions.
  • Start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as your time permits.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own personal history with other people? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people’s personal history? (Self Management)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better. Include Hand Raise, Chat, Breakout Rooms, and Gallery conversations to engage students throughout the lesson. “Mix and Mingle” also works as an Optimistic Closure activity. Provide a prompt that draws from the content, experience, or process of your activity.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • In order to more fully understand yourself, each of you are going to explore your background by learning more about your family.
  • Watch 1.04 Video Yesika Salgado - Brown Girl (2 min) and discuss the following questions.
    • How can personal history make you a stronger individual?
    • How can knowledge of family history make you a “doer” not just a “dreamer”?

You will use your completed handout as a model for the students during this lesson. 

Model

  • Distribute Personal History Part 1 of 2 to each student.
  • Explain to students that they will complete the handout and then decide how they want to present this information to the class.  Some ideas include creating a poster, PowerPoint, or collage.
    • Display teacher completed version of Personal History Part 1 of 2.
    • Discuss each requirement and share out teacher responses.

Guided Practice

  • Allow students time to complete Personal History Part 1 of 2.  
  • Instruct them to choose a presentation format.
  • Ask students to take the assignment home in order for family members to assist them in completing it.  
  • Note:  May want to save this assignment to add to students' (11.02 Mi Herencia Project Requirements) portfolios.

Activities

  • Students will create a digital storytelling presentation about their personal history by interviewing and recording their own family history. Empower students to create and publish multimedia resources such as videos, podcasts, and e-books to help them organize and communicate their ideas more clearly and effectively.  Students can use tech devices to record images, audio, and video to provide a multisensory experience for the learner. Here are sample interview questions and prompts:
    • Tell me about your childhood home/country.
    • What is your first memory of your childhood?
    • Do you share a name with someone else in the family?
    • What was your school like?
    • What was your favorite subject and why?
    • What did you want to be when you grew up?
    • Tell me a funny story about our family.
    • Did you move around much?
    • Why did you move and to where?
    • How did you feel about moving to another place?
    • What haven’t we talked about that you’d like to mention in the time we have left?

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE

Explore personal cultural background to develop a better understanding of self.

OBJECTIVE:

Students will: 

  • present the personal history assignment to peers to explore personal cultural background to develop a better understanding of self
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • build an understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts
  • Download 1.05 Powerpoint Presentation Template– Teacher Model and complete

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer
  • Large index cards
  • 1.04 HO Presentation Rubric or
  • 1.04 HO (Spanish) Presentation Rubric
  • 1.09 Vocabulary Template Example
  • 1.09 Blank Vocabulary Template
  • 1.04 HO Personal History Part 1 of 2 -Teacher Model (completed by classroom teacher & student completed HOs)
  • 1.05 Powerpoint Presentation Template – Teacher Model

Adaptations

  • 1.05 HO “I Am Poem…”
  • 4.02 Personal and Family Life Sketch

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Clock Buddy
  • Collaboration
  • Empathic listening 
  • Valuing Diversity
  • Ancestors
  • Inherit
  • Trait
  • Culture

Purpose: To use the Clock Buddies activity to facilitate student interaction so that students will have specific partners for various activities throughout the period or week. is a quick and easy way to create pairs for future partnered activities that offers a break from continually turning to an elbow partner. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Clock Buddies activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Relationship Skills, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Make copies of a Clock Buddy handout.
  • Distribute a handout to each participant and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  • Instruct participants to stand up with their papers and a pencil and move quietly around the room until you use your attention signal, at which point they should stop and find a partner. Make sure that they select someone who they are not familiar with or from a different country of origin.
  • When everyone has a partner, ask them to make sure that they can pronounce each other’s first and last names properly. Sign each other’s paper on the 3 o’clock line. It is very important that they all start on the same line.
  • Give the signals to mix, stop, and find a new partner, making sure that they pronounce each other’s first and last name properly. Check to be sure everyone has a new partner before you ask participants to sign each other’s papers on the 6 o’clock line.
  • To complete the activity, have partners mingle and pair up two more times. They’ll sign next on the 9 o’clock line and finally on the 12 o’clock line.
  • After all lines are signed, invite participants to return to their seats.
  • Each time you need participants to form pairs during the engagement, have them take out their appointment clocks and announce one of the times to designate their partner for this activity. For example, “Now meet up with the person who is your 9 o’clock appointment to reflect and discuss..."
  • You will use the Clock Buddies for the Current Event Bell Starter, Guided Practice, Google My Maps Activity, Review and Assessment, and Adaptations.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you signed up your Clock Buddies? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to get to know other students who you do not know very well or from a different country of origin? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about different names, histories, and origins? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer to access the Clock Buddies and facilitate a virtual Clock Buddie list. Manually place Clock Buddies in Breakout Rooms to get to know each other and their histories. Emphasize Norms of Virtual Collaboration and Shared Agreements.

Current Event Bell Starter

  • Pair students up with their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy.
  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Display the 1.04 HO Presentation Rubric.  
  • Have students work with Clock Buddies to fill out the HO Presentation forms. Remind students of each area they need to include in the presentation.
  • Have students practice their presentations with each other before they present to the whole class.
  • Hand out index cards.
    • Say: Today we are going to listen to each class member’s presentation.  As we listen to each presentation, write down one new thing you learned about each peer’s background or family.

Vocabulary

Review vocabulary and their definitions. Guided Practice

  • Give them time to work on their presentations in class with their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy.  
  • Ask students to volunteer to give their presentations.
  • May need to continue presentations during the following class period as well.

Activity

Google My Maps Activity – Personal Student Stories

  • Google My Maps is an online mapping tool that allows students to create and share their own maps or collaborate simultaneously on the same map. Students are going to use the multimedia environment to tell their stories and present their research to the rest of the class. Have students work in pairs with their 6:00 O’Clock Buddies.
  • Teachers and students log in or create an account on Google My Maps. Begin by preparing a completely new Google My Maps with the share setting editable by anyone with the link. You can create and store My Maps directly in Google Drive. It is recommended that collaborative groups working on the same map have between 4-5 students. 
  • Students will use My Maps to write a story about their personal history. They will map the route of their personal journey by adding a pin for each location and including pictures, images, and videos. The final product will serve as a resource for others in the class to find out where everyone is from and to identify the diversity among the class members. Below are some sample steps to follow:
    • Build prior knowledge - Ask if anyone has ever used My Maps or GPS
    • Students will begin to explore the map and search for a location
    • Edit the My Map title and description
    • Add a pin on their hometown or native country
    • Students complete a description of the pin location
    • Students can add an image or a video to the pin location
    • Students can use the measurement tool to show the distance from their hometown to their school’s location
  • Encourage students to share what they’ve discovered about My Maps and the tools available. Students will share with their 6:00 O’Clock Buddies about their hometown or native country and their school community demographics (making connections between the two). Students will explain the differences between the communities.

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE

Assist students in identifying their strengths & weaknesses to promote team building within the classroom.

OBJECTIVE:

Students will:

  • build trust, communication, and skills related to teamwork through evaluation of self-esteem and team-building activities
  • explore elements of self-confidence and self-efficacy (Self-Awareness)
  • build an understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • understand the powerful nature of co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision Making)

PREPARATION

  • Copy Student Handouts
  • Read 1.06 Understanding Self-Esteem & Body Image Teacher Materials
  • Prepare 2-inch strips of colored paper (3 per student)
  • Purchase marshmallows and spaghetti noodles if using 1.06 Marshmallow & Spaghetti Teambuilding Exercise

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer
  • 2-inch strips of colored paper (3 per student)
  • Stapler
  • Markers
  • Butcher paper for class motto
  • 1.06 Understanding Self-Esteem & Body Image Teacher Materials
  • 1.09 Vocabulary Template Example
  • 1.09 Blank Vocabulary Template
  • 1.06 HO Personal Inventory

Adaptations

  • 1.06 Weblink Marshmallow & Spaghetti Teambuilding Exercise
  • 1.06 Weblink Self Esteem Activities
  • 2.01 Setting a SMARTE Goal

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Self-esteem
  • Self-confidence
  • Inventory
  • Personal preferences
  • Assets
  • Talents

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the SELFie activity to allow students to be reflective of their emotional response to challenges and identify personal strengths and assets through the use of a SELFie. A SELFie is a picture of a person taken by that person (selfie), to show a facial expression representing the social and emotional state at any given time.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The SELFie activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Make copies of a Clock Buddy handout and ask students to fill it out and find Clock Buddies (see Lesson 1.05)
  • Ask for the meaning of an emoticon - the little emotional faces that some people attach to emails. 
  • Then asked for the definition of a "selfie." Give examples on the board/screen and ask students to take a selfie with their own devices and share it with their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy.
  • Define the meaning of a SELFie as a picture of a person taken by that person (selfie), to show a facial expression representing the social and emotional state at any given time.
  • Have the students take out their cellphones/devices and take two SELFies, one representing happiness and the other representing anger or sadness. With their 3:00 O’Clock Buddy, have them share each SELFie, describing the things that make them happy and the things that make them sad or angry.
  • Have them take another SELFie representing feelings of self-confidence and self-esteem. With their 3:00 O’clock Buddy, have students describe their personal strengths and assets associated with their own feelings of self-confidence and self-esteem.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore your own feelings and thoughts about yourself? (Self-Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about yourself today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Have students work with their Clock Buddies or in groups of 4 in Breakout rooms to complete the activity.  

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Read the two paragraphs for students from 1.06 Understanding Self-Esteem and Body Image Teacher Materials.
  • Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement: “Empowering youth to lead and strengthen their communities.”
    • Today, we are going to take a personal inventory to help us each evaluate our strengths and weaknesses.  Knowing our talents will help us work more effectively as a team.
  • Ask students the following questions and have them discuss with their 6:00 O’clock Buddy.
    • What strengths or talents do you bring to our class?
    • How has your background helped you develop these talents?

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Model

  • Display 1.06 HO Personal Inventory on a projector screen or smartboard.
  • Read several examples aloud for students and explain how to complete each section of the handout.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute 1.06 HO Personal Inventory.
  • Allow students time to complete the task with their 9:00 O’Clock Buddy.
  • Once completed, divide the class into same-gender groups of 2-3 students.
  • Ask them to discuss each item on the handout in their groups. (May want to ask each student to share one item from each section to encourage participation from every class member).
  • Bring the class back together and have volunteers share any final thoughts.

Activity 1 (Choose between Activity 1 or Activity 2)

  • Pass out colored strips of paper (3 to each student).
  • Ask students to write one positive thing about themselves on each strip of paper.
  • Instruct students to make a paper chain out of their strips and then join them with all other students’ chains.

Activity 2 (Choose between Activity 1 or Activity 2)

  • Create a class motto by asking students for ideas and listing them on the board.
    • Now that we know each other better and have identified our strengths and weaknesses, we can develop a class motto that encompasses these strengths & our goals.
    • Let’s brainstorm some ideas.
    • Choose our best 3 ideas.  Can we reduce these phrases to 5 words or less?
  • Note:  May choose a class motto during this class period or during the 1.02 Icebreaker lesson.

Activity 3 - Agree/Disagree Virtual Activity: 

  • In the Agree/Disagree Virtual Activity, the teacher prepares 12 statements that show various levels of agreement or disagreement. Students prepare 4 pieces of paper in 4 different colors:
    • Blue = Agree
    • Green = Strongly Agree
    • Orange = Disagree
    • Red = Strongly Disagree
  • The teacher virtually shares one-by-one the 12 statements with the students. Students start by identifying the level of agreement or disagreement by showing on their camera the colored paper that represents agree, strongly agree, disagree, or strongly disagree after each statement. Next, students write in the chat box whether they agree, strongly agree, disagree, or strongly disagree with the statements by writing a sentence about their opinions. In a breakout room, students are paired or work in small groups to discuss their opinions.

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Review

  • Debrief the activity.
    • Our individual talents can be a strength, but collectively, our talents are limitless.  Together, we can make greater strides than on our own.  It’s important to know what our talents are so we can combine them with others to make differences in our community.  Teamwork is power and its fuel comes from our individual talents.

  • Instead of asking students to create a written personal inventory, have students work with their 12:00 O’Clock Buddy to interview each other using 1.06 HO Personal Inventory.

Extension

  • Use 1.06 Weblink Marshmallow & Spaghetti Teambuilding Exercise for a follow-up teambuilding activity.
  • Contact the school counselor for help using 1.06 Weblink Self Esteem Activities to create lessons focused on improving self-esteem.
  • Consider following this lesson with 2.01 Setting a SMARTE Goal to help students set goals in areas they have identified as their weaknesses.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Write about an example where individual talents were used to create benefits for a community as a whole.

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE

Educate students about bullying.

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • identify types of relational bullying and how to protect themselves against it
  • understand the linkage between thoughts and feelings (Self-Awareness)
  • develop stress management and coping skills (Self-Management)
  • examine elements of self-discipline and impulse control (Self-Management)
  • continue developing effective communication skills (Relationship Skills)

PREPARATION

  • Copy Student Handouts
  • Read 1.07 Understanding Relational Bullying Teacher Materials

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer
  • 1.07 Video Mean Girls
  • 1.09 Vocabulary Template Example
  • 1.09 Blank Vocabulary Template
  • 1.07 Understanding Relational Bullying Teacher Materials
  • 1.07 HO I Was Bullied
  • 1.07 HO Dealing With Bullies
  • 1.07 Anti-Bullying Outline Teacher Materials (Blank)

Adaptations

  • Poster paper
  • Markers
  • 2.01 Setting a SMARTE Goal 
  • 1.07 Unexpected Intelligence
  • 1.07 HS Healthy Relationships

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Bully and Bullying
  • Belittle
  • Intelligent
  • Humiliate
  • Intimidate
  • Taunt
  • Exclude
  • Stonewall

Purpose: To use the Fishbowl activity to strengthen listening skills and encourage everyone to participate in a class discussion. It can be used during a session to discuss content or at the end of an engagement to give everyone airtime to share about what they learned or found useful. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Fishbowl activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (10 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • In this Fishbowl activity, participants are divided into two groups that are seated in concentric circles, all facing the center. The outside circle listens while the inside group has a discussion about a topic. Then the groups switch places so the listeners become the speakers, and vice versa. 
  • Make sure the audience knows you will hold them accountable for sharing their observations. Use equity sticks (a cup of sticks with each student’s name on one) to increase audience participation and accountability.
  • Provide the question prompt or discussion topic. These would vary depending on the theme of the lesson. The prompts for this activity would be: 
    • What are some characteristics of a bully and of bullying?
    • What are some ways to respond to a bully that would stop this negative behavior?
  • Only the inside group members may speak during this time (4 minutes). Instruct the outside group to quietly listen and notice their own ideas that surface during the discussion. Note-taking on a graphic organizer may be helpful.
  • When the time is up, ask the groups to trade places so that the outside group is sitting on the inner circle chairs and vice versa. Set the timer again for four minutes and let the new inside group discuss the topic.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to understand the characteristics of a bully? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about what a bully is and how to respond to bullying? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Divide students into two groups on paper, Group 1 and Group 2. Either assign students a number or ask them to choose and number. Have them write their number on a card as assigned by the teacher. Those with the number “1” will hold up their cards to the screen, and they will symbolically be in the inner circle. Call their names using the equity sticks for them to share thoughts on the prompts. Switch numbers for the next group.

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 1.07 Video Mean Girls (4 min).
  • Ask the students the following questions and have them write their feelings and responses to the questions.  Reassure them that they do not need to share these responses.
    • Have you ever been bullied?  
    • Have you bullied someone else?
    • How did you feel?
    • Have you witnessed someone else being bullied?
    • Did you do anything about it?  Why or why not?

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • Reference 1.07 Understanding Relational Bullying Teacher Materials.
  • Explain the different types of relational bullying.  You may want to combine this with the vocabulary instruction.

Guided Practice

  • Divide the class into groups of 3-4.  You may want to consider same-gender groups.
  • Distribute 1.07 HO I Was Bullied.
  • Ask students to read the HO together.
  • Groups write their top 5 ways to deal with a bully on 1.07 HO Dealing With Bullies.

Activities

  • Adapted from Above the Line / Below the Line

Teachers create a digital handout for students to complete a list of healthy behaviors above the line and not healthy behaviors below the line. Students will brainstorm ideas to answer the following questions: What happens at our school when students engage in Above the Line behaviors? What happens when they engage in Below the Line behaviors? Have students share their answers and create a final, class version with selected responses to share with the entire class or post in your distance learning platform.

  • Adapted from Break the Cycle

#6: PSA Making (Public Service Announcement Making)
The teacher selects and shows some examples of what healthy friendships look like in the media. This can include popular TV shows, social media apps, or celebrities. Students find other examples and create their own examples of healthy friendships. [/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Review

  • Bring the class back together.
  • Display 1.07 Anti-Bullying Outline Teacher Materials (Blank).
  • Complete the outline as a class by asking students to share the information they have learned today.
  • Debrief the activity.
    • You are a Latinos In Action student.  You already know that you are a strong, intelligent person who has a bright future ahead of you. Bullying is a serious problem that needs serious action.  Thank you for all of your input and thought into today’s lesson.  Being more aware of the problem and specific actions on how to deal with it can improve our school environment.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Differentiation Ideas

  • Ask students to complete 1.07 Anti-Bullying Outline Teacher Materials (Blank) in their groups instead of completing it as a class.  Each group presents information for one area (I. Definition, II. Prevention, & III. Recovery).

Extension

  • Students create posters in their groups containing the information from the outline (I. Definition, II. Prevention, & III Recovery).  Display throughout the school.
  • Ask student committees to design and execute an anti-bullying campaign in the school.
  • You may want to consider following this lesson with 2.01 Setting a SMARTE Goal to help students set goals in promoting anti-bullying within the school.
  • Watch 1.07 Unexpected Intelligence and discuss how stereotypes are not always true and how everyone has different talents.
  • See 1.07 HS Healthy Relationships to help students learn how to set boundaries and identify healthy relationships.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Do you think our school has a bullying problem? Why or why not?  
  • Do you think bullying becomes better or worse as students get older?  
  • How can you make a difference in preventing bullying?

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE

Improve students’ communication skills.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • describe two parts of effective communication by naming strategies and demonstrating important body language for communicating effectively in a classroom
  • explore elements of self-confidence and self-efficacy (Self-Awareness)
  • build an understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-management)
  • deepen understanding about the power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • continue developing effective communication skills (Relationship Skills)

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer
  • Blank sheets of paper
  • 1.08 Video Spoken Word Poet Smego  (View minutes 5-7)
  • 1.09 Vocabulary Template Example
  • 1.09 Blank Vocabulary Template
  • 1.08 Video 60-Second Strategy: SLANT Listening
  • 1.08 Communication Activity Teacher Materials
  • 1.08 HO SLANT Strategy

Adaptations

  • 1.08 Video “Look Up”
  • 1.08 HO Making a Good First Impression

KEY VOCABULARY

    1. Diction
    2. Simile
    3. Metaphor
    4. Alliteration
    5. Clarify
    6. Proximity
    7. Facilitator
    8. Investigators
    9. Responders
    10. Think Tank
    11. Recorders
    12. Relevancy

WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Save the Last Word activity to help students to further develop their communication skills by following an established protocol to share and discuss their responses to a text, quote, image, or video clip. By creating a clear structure for discussion, this strategy encourages everyone to be both an active speaker and an active listener and supports equity of voice by ensuring that frequent speakers give space for others to share. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Save the Last Word activity will further expand students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Identify a relevant reading passage, quote, image, or video clip that will serve as the catalyst for this activity.
  • Have participants read/view the selected text/quote/image or video and highlight three sentences or make note of three ideas that particularly stand out for them.
  • Ask participants to write each sentence/idea on the front of an index card. On the back of the card, ask them to write a few sentences explaining why they chose that quote (what it meant to them, reminded them of, how it connects to their own experience, background, language, history, etc.).
  • Divide the participants into groups of three, identifying one person as A, one person as B, and one person as C.
  • Invite the A participants to read one of their chosen quotations or ideas to their group. Then persons B and C discuss the offering while person A listens. (For example, What do they think it means? Why do they think these words/ideas might be important? To whom?)
  • After several minutes, ask Participant A to read the back of their card (or to explain why they picked the quotation or idea), thus having “the last word.”
  • This process repeats with B sharing and others reflecting before B gets “the last word,” and then is repeated again with C sharing.

 Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to be able to communicate ideas and opinions effectively and to be able to listen effectively? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about communication skills today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Divide students into groups of three on paper, Groups 1, 2...etc. Either assign students a number or ask them to self-select by choosing two other students they want to work with. Have them write their number on a card. Those with the number “1” will hold up their cards to the screen and they will be assigned to a Breakout room

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch 1.08 Video Spoken Word Poet Smego (View minutes 5-7).
  • Introduce vocabulary before watching the clip if the students aren’t familiar with these terms (Smego uses several of these terms in the clip.).
  • Ask the students the following questions and have them write their responses.  You may want to post and read these questions ahead of watching the clip to enable students to listen to the phrases.
  • Smego uses words to communicate his feelings and experiences.  What do you think he means when he says “words come out to play”?
  • What did Smego say is like finding a “needle in the haystack”?
  • Smego wants us to elevate our __________.
  • How can words be powerful?
  • What is the overall message?
  • How does knowledge of vocabulary influence communication at school, home, work, and in the community?
  • Ask students to share their written responses.

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Model

  • Introduce the key parts of communication.
    • Communication involves two parts, speaking and listening, or in other words, sending and receiving a message.  Sometimes we can “send” a message, but the other person does not “receive” it in the same that it was sent.  Why might that be?  We are going to complete an exercise to demonstrate how this works.

Activities

  • Distribute blank pieces of paper.  Explain that you are going to read instructions to draw an animal.  See 1.08 Communication Activity: Teacher Materials.
    • As we saw in the previous activity, listening is a critical part of communication, but it was missing an important part, so most of you were unable to draw the chicken.  Asking questions (speaking) is an important part of communication that would have made this activity much easier.  Speaking and listening are both critical for communicating effectively.
  • MYSTERY SKYPE/ZOOM/GOOGLE MEET
    • Create a virtual mystery game with another LIA class in an unknown location. Your students' goal is to guess the other school and their location (country, state, city, school name) before they guess yours. (Students are provided a list of the 12 states and over 200 school names participating in LIA). The mystery guessing game helps build cultural awareness, critical thinking skills, and listening and speaking skills by challenging students to guess the location of the other classroom through a series of yes/no questions. This is a student-led activity.
    • It's important to prepare the students at least a few days in advance so they can gather materials, such as maps, or ask questions about their responsibilities.
    • Assigning roles or jobs prior to the virtual mystery game spreads out the responsibility and gives all students a sense of involvement and purpose. Below are some sample roles for students:
      • Facilitator – This student introduces the class to the other class and shares some cool facts about their own class without giving away the location.
      • Investigators – These students ask questions that were prepared before the event.
      • Responders – These students respond yes or no to the questions. These students need to know their state/geography facts.
      • Think Tank – These students work on figuring out the clues based on the yes/no answers from the other LIA class.
      • Recorders – They record all of the answers to the questions asked by their class.
  • Encourage students to collaborate before guessing, and set ground rules for how quickly they can guess the school and location. Watch the excitement build as they eliminate schools as they make their guesses. At the end of the game, give students time to reflect on what worked and what didn’t. This activity can lead to other virtual collaborations for future projects. 

Model

  • Show the video 1.08 Video 60-Second Strategy: SLANT Listening
  • Display 1.08 HO SLANT Strategy and review the acronym SLANT.  
    • Body language also plays an important part in communication.  This strategy helps us communicate to teachers that we are interested and ready to learn.
  • Discuss and model each action.

Guided Practice

  • Cover the descriptions in 1.08 HO SLANT Strategy.
  • Ask students to describe and model each letter’s (SLANT) description.
  • Practice with a partner (naming and modeling each description).
    •  Debrief: How can we use this strategy when communicating with family, friends, co-workers, or in professional settings?

  • Emphasize the following points:
    • Effective communication requires two parts: listening and speaking.
    • Word choice and gaining a greater knowledge of vocabulary, as Smego demonstrated in the video, can help us become better communicators.  
    • Even when we don’t say anything, our body language communicates with others.

  • Divide the 4 questions in the Relevancy / Linkage section of the lesson among 4 different groups in the classroom.  Watch 1.08 Video Spoken Word Poet Smego (min. 5-7). Ask students in each group to discuss their questions and share their group’s thoughts.

Extension

  • Select student partnerships.  Distribute 1.08 HO Making a Good First Impression to one student in each partnership.  Instruct students with the HO to physically demonstrate or act out each point listed on the HO.  Partners write down what steps are being acted out in order to make a good first impression.
  • Watch 1.08 Video “Look Up” (5 min). Ask students to discuss these questions:
    • How have we become a society without spoken word?  
    • What are the disadvantages of relying only on technology to communicate?
    • What do you think he means by the phrase, “Smart phones and dumb people?” 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What are the critical parts of effective communication?  Why do you need to think about your word choice when you are communicating with others?  (Think about the video clip 1.08 Video Spoken Word Poet Smego from the beginning of the lesson). 
  • Are there certain body language signals that are interpreted differently in Latino culture (i.e. eye contact, proximity to the speaker, handshake, etc.)?  How do meanings differ?
  • Why are good communication skills important when tutoring students?

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE

Identify problem-solving strategies to aid students in resolving conflict.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • demonstrate the ability to deal with conflict through brainstorming and journaling their problems
  • examine elements of self-discipline and impulse control (Self-Management)
  • explore the impacts of perspective-taking and empathy on patience (Social Awareness)
  • deepen understanding of collaborative problem-solving approaches (Relationship Skills)
  • make a realistic evaluation of the consequences of various actions and consideration of the well-being of oneself and others. (Relationship Skills)

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts
  • Print & cut 1.09 HO Case Studies

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro 
  • 1.09 Video Bullying Conflict Resolution 1
  • 1.09 Video Bullying Conflict Resolution 2
  • 1.09 Vocabulary Template Example
  • 1.09 Blank Vocabulary Template
  • 1.09 Case Study & Problem Solving Steps: Student Worksheet
  • 1.09 Case Study & Problem Solving Steps: Teacher Materials
  • 1.09 HO Case Studies

Adaptations

  • 1.09 Weblink Conflict Resolution Activities
  • 1.09 HO Resolving a Conflict
  • 1.09 Case Study & Problem Solving Steps: Student Worksheet

KEY VOCABULARY

  1. Paraphrasing
  2. Anger
  3. Frustration
  4. Brainstorm
  5. Compromise
  6. Conflict
  7. Solutions
  8. Consequence
  9. Mature

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Resolve Differences Quickly to help students learn how to participate in discussions and activities to learn how to initiate a compromise or a mutual agreement that is mutually beneficial when a conflict arises with another individual or group.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Resolve Differences Quickly activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Engage students in a discussion on the meaning of “compromise” as a way to settle differences by coming to a mutual agreement that benefits all parties in some way. Explain that reaching a compromise requires a degree of cooperation in order to “meet in the middle” especially when you feel that you are right. It is necessary if they want to move past the conflict. It is a skill that needs to be practiced and it is also one of the most mature actions that they can take to show that they can make adult decisions. 
  • Ask students to discuss with two other partners the following questions:
    • What are some of the potential benefits of reaching a compromise in resolving conflicts and differences respectfully and swiftly? 
    • Give an example of a disagreement you have been involved with personally such as differences of opinion, beliefs, or even conflicts between groups of different backgrounds.
    • Visualize a time when you helped dissolve a disagreement between friends or family members. What was the cause of the disagreement and what did you say or do to help resolve the conflict? What were the terms of the compromise? 
    • What were the long-term benefits of resolving this conflict? Did it eliminate the conflict and restore the relationship? What were the long-term benefits in terms of eliminating stress, anxiety, fear, and anger?
  • Ask students to write out the most important steps in resolving a conflict and reaching a compromise. Have them share with their partners and then with the larger class.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ways to resolve a conflict or disagreement? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about reaching a compromise today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Give students several scenarios of conflict and divide the class into groups of four. Make sure that each team is representative of the class diversity, cultures, and languages. Manually assign students to Breakout rooms to respond to the questions. Have students take on roles as Timekeeper, Recorder, Facilitator and Reporter. This should take them about 8 minutes. The Recorder enters the summary in the Chatbox while the Reporter gives a verbal summary when called on by the teacher. 

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch Day 1 and Day 2 of  1.09 Video Bullying Conflict Resolution 1  ( 0-1:10 m) or watch 1.09 Video Bullying Conflict Resolution 2 (2:02-6:52 m).
  • Ask students to write down responses to the following questions.
    • What would you do in this situation if this was you or a friend?
    • What types of conflicts are frequent in your life?
  • Watch the remainder of 1.09 Video Bullying Conflict Resolution 1.
    • Do you think this boy’s choice in resolving the conflict was a wise one?  Why or why not?

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • Display 1.09 Case Study & Problem Solving Steps: Teacher Materials.
  • Read aloud to students or ask a student to read the scenario.
  • Discuss each point listed in the problem-solving steps.
  • Brainstorm ideas.

Guided Practice

  • Divide the class into groups of 3-4 students.
  • Distribute 1.09 HO Case Study & Problem Solving Steps: Student Worksheet to each group.
  • Assign a case study to each group.
  • Ask students to read the case study and follow the steps to come up with the best solution to the problem.

Activity

  • Students will work in small groups to role-play and record a skit demonstrating a conflict and resolution. The videos will be posted in the digital classroom for all students to watch. Students will resolve the conflict using 1.09 HO Resolving a Conflict.
  • Students discuss reasons why people address conflict via social media rather than in person and discuss the pros/cons of doing so. Students complete and share a pros and cons list on a digital handout.

  • Ask groups to role-play their assigned scenario and solution.  Can the observing class members come up with better or other solutions to the problem?

Extension

  • Ask students to create problem-solving steps for elementary-age students.  Create a worksheet with simple language and pictures.  Share with the local elementary school where students tutor.
  • Extend the case studies further by using the specific suggestions/language in the corresponding high school lesson 1.09 HO Resolving a Conflict.
  • Use 1.09 Weblink Conflict Resolution Activities to find classroom activities/games that focus on conflict resolution.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Write a case study that demonstrates a frequent conflict among middle school or junior high students.  Use the steps presented in 1.09 HO Case Study & Problem Solving Steps: Student Worksheet to solve the conflict or ask a classmate to find a resolution to the problem.
