OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • create at least 2 SMARTE goals centered on LIA standards.
  • identify and explore ways to develop skills and talents (Self-Awareness)
  • develop skills in planning and organizational skills (Self-Management)
  • work collaboratively with others (i.e., listens, encourages, acknowledges opinions, compromises, reaches consensus) (Relationship Skills)

Purpose: To use the Mix and Mingle activity to have students move around the room and share ideas about personal and professional strengths and goals with a partner or small group. This is designed to build community by encouraging participants to interact with each other with the expectation that everyone's personal history, language, culture, and voice are valued.  See an example of the Mix and Mingle activity in the Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook.(optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Mix and Mingle activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Prepare index cards with one question per card from the list below (feel free to modify or add additional questions as needed). Randomly hand them out to the students while they are sitting in their community circle. Give them a minute to read their card and think about their response. Index Cards:
    1. What are your personal strengths?
    2. If one of your personal strengths was a superpower, what would it be?
    3. If you had to describe one of your strengths as a body of water (stream, a waterfall, a river, a tidal wave, etc) what would you be and why?
    4. How does your mood affect how you learn?
    5. Describe your mood as an outfit.
    6. What is a dish/food you like to eat on a special occasion?
    7. If you could serve one dish that would represent who you are, what would you serve? 
    8. If you were a flavor of ice cream, what flavor would you be?
    9. What are some examples of your personal goals? 
    10. What are you personally responsible for?
    11. What is great about being in charge?
    12. What are some skills you will need to develop in order to reach your personal goals?
    13. What are some examples of professional goals you have considered?
    14. What are some skills you will need to develop in order to reach your professional goals? 
    15. What is something you were blamed for that you did not feel responsible for?
    16. When was the last time you needed help?
    17. What do you need help with in your life today?
    18. Who do you turn to for help? Why?
    19. Who can you ask for help at home?
    20. What is one time you asked for help at school?
    21. Who can you ask for help in the community?
  2. When you announce, "Mix and Mingle!", turn on the music and have students move around the room greeting each other (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc).  When the music stops, students should find a partner near them. Help with pairing if needed. This activity also can be done without music by ringing a chime when it is time for students to stop walking around.
  3. Partners share their responses to the question on the cards.
  4. Have them exchange cards when you start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as time permits.
  5. Reconvene a community circle. Ask for volunteers to share out one thing that surprised them or one thing that they learned from this activity.
  6. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your personal and professional strengths and goals? (Self-Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ personal and professional goals? (Relationship Skills)

Relevancy/Linkage

  • View Latinos In Action Video (3 min) and ask the following questions:
  • Why did you decide to take LIA?
  • Why do you think LIA is offered at your school?
  • What is LIA’s purpose?
  • View LIA Standards – Student as a class, go over LIA’s purpose and standards.
  • LIA class materials were created to help you reach these goals; however, you all have individual talents and dreams. Today you will have time to set individual LIA goals.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • identify multiple bilingual career options of interest
  • recognize qualities of positive role models (Self-Awareness)
  • identify personal, cultural, and linguistic assets (Self-Awareness)
  • recognize various jobs and the responsibilities the jobs hold (Self-Management)
  • identify future careers that are aligned with personal interests, skills, and goals (Self-Management)
  • Identify and value similarities and differences among different social and cultural groups (Social Awareness)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To help further develop communication skills by following an established protocol that engages students to share and discuss their responses to a text, quote, image, or video clip through the Save the Last Word activity. This strategy encourages everyone to be an active speaker, an active listener and supports equity of voice by ensuring that frequent speakers give space for others to share. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Save the Last Word activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Identify culturally relevant reading passages, quotes, images, or video clips that will serve as the catalyst for students to discuss multiple bilingual career options.
  2. Have participants read/view the selected text/quote/image or video and highlight three sentences or make note of three ideas that particularly stand out for them.
  3. Ask participants to write each sentence/idea on the front of a sheet of paper or a 5x8 index card. On the back of the card, ask them to write 3-5 sentences explaining why they chose that quote or idea (what it meant to them, reminded them of, how it connects to their own experience, culture, language, history, etc.).
  4. Divide the students into groups of three, identifying one person as A, one person as B, and one person as C.
  5. Invite the A students to read one of their chosen quotations or ideas to their group. Then students B and C discuss the offering while student A listens. (For example, What do they think it means? Why do they think these words/ideas might be important in helping them identify multiple bilingual career options of interest? For whom?)
  6. After 1.5 minutes, ask student A to read the back of their card (or to explain why they picked the quotation or idea), thus having “the last word.”
  7. This process repeats with B sharing and others reflecting before B gets “the last word,” and then is repeated again with C sharing.
  8. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth to lead and strengthen their communities” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

 Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to be able to communicate ideas and opinions effectively and to be able to listen effectively? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about multiple bilingual career options? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch Video Bilingual Advantage
  • Discuss the following questions
  • How does speaking Spanish and/or English give you more opportunities in the future?
  • How can speaking Spanish be a benefit to you in your future career?

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Model

  • Explain: Some students know exactly what they want to do for a career while others have not thought about it. Regardless of your situation, today we are going to explore additional options by researching bilingual career opportunities.
  • Model the activity by using the Bilingual Career Exploration Teacher Model.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute Bilingual Career Exploration to each student.
  • Go to Career Options or another bilingual job search weblink.
  • Invite the class to choose an additional career option and complete the corresponding questions as a class.

Independent Practice

  • Allow students time to explore additional bilingual career options.
  • Invite students to choose their top career choice and set a short-term career goal using SMARTE Goal Template – Word.
  • Example: A student wants to be a veterinarian. Set a goal to learn more details by researching veterinarian school requirements on the internet, job shadowing at a local clinic, taking a vet science class next trimester, etc.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Differentiation Ideas

  • Work with your Professional Committee to organize a Virtual Career Day where students can interact with local professionals to practice authentic academic conversations and experience extracurricular learning. Assign students to contact/recruit local experts to participate in a wide variety of careers by utilizing a Google Form to register and to receive instructions on how to virtually participate and/or record and submit their videos. Utilize Google Meet or Zoom to engage students in a live interactive session or have professionals create pre-recorded videos using Padlet to introduce themselves and share details about their jobs. The interviews should ensure ethnic and linguistic diversity in connecting students with professionals that they can personally identify with.
  • Watch the Video Bilingual Benefits and ask students to listen for the following words and possible definitions by using context clues. Discuss the results of the study.
  • Bi and bilingualism
  • Mono and monolingual
  • Favor
  • Heightened
  • Neuroscientist
  • Introduce students to higher-paying technical career paths or career paths that accentuate their natural abilities. Encourage students to dream and assist them in finding an affordable, realistic way of reaching their career path.

Extension

  • Invite each student to pick their top career choice and research a Latino in the field.
  • Example: Lawyer – look up Marco Rubio's biography.
  • Watch career exploration videos at https://roadtripnation.com/ and https://www.careeronestop.org/ExploreCareers/Assessments/interests.aspx

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Students can add to their journals what they've learned about themselves, discuss the occupations they explored and found interesting, and ask any questions they still have about career planning.
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.
  • Do you think bilingual skills increase your ability to be an effective elementary school tutor? Why or why not?

Purpose: To strengthen listening skills and encourage everyone to participate in a discussion through the Fishbowl activity. This activity can be used during a lesson to discuss content, or at the end of an engagement activity to give airtime to everyone about what they learned or found useful. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Fishbowl activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. In this Fishbowl activity, students are divided into two groups that are arranged in concentric circles, facing the center. The outside circle listens while the inside group has a discussion about career exploration. Then the groups switch places so the listeners become the speakers and vice versa. 
  2. Make sure the students know you will hold them accountable for sharing their observations. Use equity sticks (a cup of sticks with each student’s name on one) to increase participation and accountability.)
  3. Provide one question prompt related to career exploration. Here are a few examples (feel free to consider other questions): 
  • Name a few examples of personal goals.
  • What are some skills you will need to develop in order to reach your personal goals?
  • Name a few examples of professional/career goals you have considered.
  • What are some skills you will need to develop in order to reach your professional/career goals?
  1. Only the inside group members may speak during this time (4 minutes). Instruct the outside group to quietly listen and notice their own ideas that surface during the discussion. Note-taking on a graphic organizer may be helpful.
  2. When the time is up, ask the groups to trade places so that the outside group is sitting on the inner circle chairs and vice versa. Set the timer again for four minutes and let the new inside group discuss the topic.
  3. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth to lead and strengthen their communities.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore your feelings about personal and professional/career goals? (Self-Management) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned today about exploring personal and professional/career goals? (Responsible Decision Making)

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
  • Last time we explored bilingual career options.  Today we are going to explore what majors are offered and which major best fits your career interests.
  • Complete Tupperware Activity Description and then ask the students the following questions:
  • Did all the lids fit all of the Tupperware?
  • Did some lids fit more than one Tupperware?
  • How does this relate to choosing a major and a career?

  • Explain: Many students choose a major they are interested in, then discover they dislike the career path.
  •  For Example, let's say a student enjoys studying and learning about anatomy so the student chooses to study nursing. They later find out they do not like the sight of real blood and do not like working with people.
  • Today we are going to explore what college majors are offered and what jobs those majors qualify you to do.

 

  • Display and use 2.03 Weblink Majors and 2.03 Career and Major Options Teacher Model to explain the first two education examples.
  • Choose an additional specific major under education to fill out as a class.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute 2.03 HO Career and Major Options to each student.
  • Divide students into groups of 3 or 4 and allow each group to choose a major category of interest to research.  Groups preferably should choose a different category/major than other groups.
  • Allow student groups time to research their chosen categories.

    • Broaden the major search to include certificate and technical schools.
  • Students work in pairs to identify and share personal strengths and interests and correlate how these qualities might impact their career paths. Students will pose the question: “What is Your Dream Job?” Students can interview their partner and share their partner’s information with the class. Provide a conversation sentence starter such as “My partner’s dream job is _______ because _________.”

Note: This practice will foster oral language development and support ELs by re-envisioning pair and group work to support speaking and listening skills in English and their home language. When you hold students accountable, they know they must partner share, and listen to what their partner is saying. Students can record their partner’s responses on a voice recording app, such as Audacity, to support learning and remembering before presenting.

Extension

  • Have each group create a visual to display their results (e.g., poster or PowerPoint).
  • Add the following additional columns to the 2.03 HO Career and Major Options :
  • What classes would be beneficial to take now to help prepare for this major?
  • What classes would be beneficial to take in High School to help prepare for this major?

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What have I learned about myself from tutoring elementary students that could help me choose a major/career path?
  • Do I like to work with people?
  • Do I like solving problems?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

Purpose: To facilitate student interaction through the use of the Clock Buddies (Part 1) tool so that students will have specific partners for various activities throughout the period or week. This is a quick and easy way to create pairs for future partnered activities that offers a break from continually turning to an elbow partner. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Interacting with Clock Buddies will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Self-Management.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Dedicate time in your Community Circles/ Class Meetings to establish norms of collaboration on:
    1. how to greet each other once they meet their new Clock Buddy, 
    2. have them practice pronouncing each other's first and last names properly, 
    3. how they will ensure that each partner has equal time, and 
    4. how to thank each other once they have completed their activity instead of just walking away once the time is up. 
  2. Make copies of the Clock Buddy handout and distribute to each student and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  3. Model how students should proceed in finding Clock Buddy partners by adding their names on the same time slot. Check to see if students understand the procedure. Make sure that they select someone who they are not familiar with or from a different country of origin.
  4. Have them continue finding Clock Buddies at a common time until all four time slots are filled. Invite students to return to their seats when the form is completed.
  5. Each time you need students to form pairs during the activity, have them take out their Clock Buddies sheet and announce one of the times for them to meet up with their Clock Buddy for this activity. For example, “Now meet up with your 9:00 Buddy to reflect and discuss..." Do this as a practice exercise.
  6. Use the Clock Buddies for the following activity: Write each of the following questions or activities on a separate 5x8 index card and spread them face down on a table or on the floor in the center of the Community Circle/Class Meeting. Have a student select a card and read it to the rest of the class (post on a whiteboard or PPT if possible). If it’s a question, give the students 1 minute to write a response in their journals before calling out which Clock Buddy they will meet with. Otherwise, they can engage immediately in the activity. The prompts for this activity could be (feel free to consider other questions or activities as well):
    1. Sit with your back against your buddy’s back on the floor and try to stand up together without using your hands.
    2. Make up a silly handshake with your buddy.
    3. Choose a classroom object with your buddy and write a short poem or rhyme about it.
    4. If one of your personal strengths was a superpower, what would it be? Explain what you would do with it to benefit others.
    5. Describe three skills or areas that you would like to improve. Why are they important to you?
    6. What does being successful mean to you? What do you use to measure progress? Success?
  7. Call out which Clock Buddy they will meet with to either share their response to the first question or begin the activity, i.e., meet with your 3:00 Buddy, etc. Repeat the process with a different question or activity for a few more Clock Buddy times (no more than 2 minutes for each Clock Buddy round). If time allows, select a few participants to share out after each round. 
  8. You can also use Clock Buddies for the Current Event Bell Starter, Guided Practice, Google My Maps Activity, Review and Assessment, and Adaptations.
  9. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth to lead and strengthen their communities.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you signed up with your Clock Buddies? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to get to know other students who you do not know very well or are from a different country of origin? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about working with others, your own superpowers and personal strengths? (Relationship Skills and Self-Awareness)

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
  • Last time we explored different major options available in groups and as a class.  Today you will have time to research your top three major and career choices individually.

  • Invite recent alumni to speak with students about their experiences in college, career training, or current employment. Utilize Google Meet or Zoom to engage students in a live interactive session. The interviews should ensure ethnic and linguistic diversity in connecting students with alumni that they can personally identify with. Students can prepare questions prior to the session. Some sample questions are:
  • What was the biggest transition from high school to college or work?
  • How did your time in high school help to prepare/impact you for your current career or college?
  • Why did you choose the college you are attending?
  • Did you know what you wanted to study in college?
  • Strategy grouping–Partner higher skilled students with students with mid-level skills and/or partner mid-level skilled students with students with lower skills to complete the activity.
  • Use the high school translated Top 3 Major and Career Options HS (Spanish) version.

Extension

  • Invite the students to take one or two career interest assessments from Assessments or another website.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • explore the concept of culture and valuing differences in others.
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrates how to work effectively with those who are different from oneself (Social Awareness)
  • develop the skills and mindsets to become culturally competent (Relationship Skills)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose:  To build community by having students move around the room and share experiences, emotions, and relationships with a partner or small group through the use of My Name, My Identity activity. Students will interact with each other with the expectation that everyone's personal history, language, culture, and voice are valued.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This My Name, My Identity activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Facilitate My Name, My Identity Activity (pair share, Clock Buddies, Mix & Mingle, large group, layered and process) in your community circle using the suggested prompts:
    1. Share the story about how you were given your name and the meaning behind it.
    2. Have you ever experienced stereotypes or assumptions based on your name? What was that like for you? (Name calling, stereotyping, etc.)
    3. Is your name easy or difficult for other people at school to pronounce? Do other students in your school have the same name? What is that like? 
    4. What can you do if someone’s name is difficult to pronounce?  If you have a name that is challenging for other students to pronounce, what can you do to help them learn your name?
    5. Native Americans often had names that described something about the person or compared the person to something in nature. Does your name or your partner’s name have meaning or history? 
  2. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore our names and how people respond to them? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about names today? (Responsible Decision Making)

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin this lesson by introducing a series of YouTube videos by Matt Harding. He is an American traveler, video game designer, and Internet celebrity who is known as Dancing Matt for his viral videos that show him dancing in front of landmarks and street scenes in various international locations. In these videos, Matt films himself dancing at different locations around the world. His 2005 and 2006 works are not as refined, but show how his idea started. His 2008 video is worth showing. In 2012, he released an even more polished version (it may need to be edited for school viewing). Note that one of YouTube’s founders said Matt’s 2008 video was his favorite video on YouTube.
  • Ask students to share moments that stood out and were interesting or entertaining. Ask students why those things stood out. 
  • Explain that today’s lesson is meant to inspire curiosity and to learn something new.

  • Ask students to raise their hands if they have culture. There might be confusion with the question which will create an opportunity to define it and ask the question again.
  • Direct students to describe the culture of their school/district/state. Write the responses on the board.
  • Explain to students the difference between the seen and unseen aspects of culture. Use the following blog entry for ideas and pictures.
  • Consider how we define our American culture. Is there consensus?

Guided Practice

Option 1

  • The following activity will help students think about their own culture and how it relates to those around them. This activity is borrowed from this site, but will be condensed for this lesson.
  • Class Activity: Hand out List of Various Groups (found on the last 2 pages of the PDF).
  • Direct each student to circle the groups on this list to which they belong.
  • Group Activity:
  • Tell students to take their list with them, and to move into groups of 4 students (or less.) Their job is to compare their individual lists with other people in their group. Then, they are to identify three things that everyone in their group has in common on their individual lists.
  • At the bottom of each paper, students will write down the name of the 3 groups they have in common, formatted as follows: 
  • a) Name of the group
  • b) Purposes of the group (why it exists)
  • c) The beliefs of the group
  • d) The rules of the group
  • e) Is membership voluntary or involuntary?
  • Give them some time. Then, ask each group to share one of the three things they had in common with the class, and have them state the answer(s) they chose for a-e above. It is okay if another small group presents the same selection (family, school, etc.)
  • As groups present, start throwing in monkey wrenches. School, for example: Your students may say school is involuntary and that they have to go to school. Throw in a monkey wrench. Say: What about college? What if you’re 17 years old? Family, for example: Throw in a monkey wrench. Ask: Does every family believe that? Do not challenge everything they say, but occasionally throw in a monkey wrench to keep them thinking.
  • Once every group has presented one thing they had in common, have them turn in their individual work and return to their desks.

Option 2

  • Create a Padlet Video connection using the Educator Dashboard in Padlet. Have students prepare a story or folktale that is tied to their own culture and share it with students from a different part of the world in a synchronous activity. Students learn from diverse perspectives and see what life is like from a different point of view. An alternate asynchronous activity can be to create a Flip topic and post their video responses for other students to reply to and share their own stories.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Review

  • Have students think about the unique diversity in the United States. Should this be considered a good or bad characteristic? Point out places like New York City (or any other place you have visited where there was a distinct cultural shift that you enjoyed). Reference the videos from the lesson’s introduction by noting that differences don’t have to be seen as a negative- as they will explore in upcoming lessons.

  • Complete the activity “My Multicultural Self.”

Extension

  • Have students choose another location, either in the US or abroad, that has a melting pot of cultures. Ask students to list the Main Culture, Sub-Culture(s), and how they came to be. 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What did you think about diversity before this lesson? What do you think about it now?
  • Share some cultural differences that you have seen. What value do differences play in culture?

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • examine the historical and present relationship between race and society.
  • notice how personal beliefs, mindsets, and stereotypes integrate personal and social-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  •  describe what happens in their brains and bodies when they experience strong emotions (Self-Management)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)
  • recognize that social cues may be different among various families, and social/cultural groups (Social Awareness)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To build community by using the Mix and Mingle activity so that students share and value each other’s personal history, language, culture, and voice. See an example of the Mix and Mingle activity in the Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook. (optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Mix and Mingle activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness and Social Awareness.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meeting activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. On a 5x8 card or half-sheet of paper, ask participants to write down a response to two prompts you give related to their experiences. Begin with a low-vulnerability prompt such as:
    1. What are some words you would use to describe yourself? 
    2. What are some words you think society would use to describe you?
  2. Begin the "Mix and Mingle!" activity by turning on music so that the students can begin to move around the room (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, Norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc). 
  3. When the music stops, students need to find a partner near them. Help with pairing if needed.
  4. Partners share their responses to the questions, listen actively to each other, and ask follow-up questions.
  5. Start the music again and repeat the sequence a few more times with another partner, as your time permits.
  6. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.”

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your views about our society? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people’s experiences in our society? (Self Management)

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Show students one of the following social experiments (associated videos on the YouTube sidebar may also provide more options) and allow time for their reaction. Prompt students to discuss what they saw in the video. Ask them to share discomfort, questions, or other thoughts.  
    • 3.02 Racism, Black vs White (Social Experiment)
    • 3.02 Racism is alive (Social Experiment)
  • Explain that today’s lesson will focus on how our society has and continues to struggle with treating people differently based on different factors.
  • Be sure to prepare students to talk about societal hierarchies and how they can be cautious with their words and actions so that they are considerate and respectful of others.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Activity

  • Show students your choice of “What Would You Do?” episodes found on YouTube that focus on race and discrimination. Allow students the opportunity to give their reaction and discuss whether or not race in the United States is a real issue. Some examples are:
    • 3.02  Shopping while Black (social experiment) 
    • 3.02 Stealing a Bike (social experiment) 
    • 3.02 Car Vandalism (social experiment) 
  • Introduce and define the word “Stereotype.” The dictionary defines the term this way: noun: An overly simple picture or opinion of a person, group, or thing.

Guided Practice

  • Use the following guided practice ideas from 3.02 Bursting Stereotypes for a balloon activity with the students.
  • Give examples of stereotypes using the following phrases:
    • All old people are forgetful.
    • Men are better at math than women.
    • African-American men are the best basketball players.
  • Give students a few moments to consider those phrases. Then ask them to share their reactions. Lead students to the conclusion that the statements are too general to be true; encourage them to recognize that it is unfair to make such sweeping statements. Help students make the connection between the phrases and the term stereotype.
  • Have students return to their small brainstorming groups and ask them to come up with additional stereotypes they might have heard or thought about. Tell them to keep a written record of the stereotypes they think of. When the flow of stereotype statements seems to be slowing down, ask students in each group to take a final look at their lists and mark with an asterisk 6-10 of the most interesting stereotypes. Bring the class back together so they can share their ideas. Each time a student shares a stereotype, hand that student a sentence strip so s/he can write the stereotype on a sentence strip. Instruct students to write large and bold; markers or crayons work best.
  • Some stereotypes that students might have thought of include:
    • Kids who are into computers are geeky.
    • Young kids are noisy.
    • People who wear glasses are smart.
    • Women are better cooks than men.
    • Girls are more mature than boys.
    • All politicians are crooks.
    • Everyone believes in God.
    • Native Americans live on reservations.
    • All doctors are rich.
    • All Americans like to watch baseball.
    • All tall people are good basketball players.

Bursting Stereotypes- balloon activity

Now it’s time to grab from the closet the bag of inflated balloons (see the Guided Practice portion of the lesson, 3.02 Bursting Stereotypes ) or to stand near the bulletin board you have prepared.

  • If you have created a bulletin board for this activity, ask students to read each sentence strip aloud and staple it next to a balloon on the bulletin board. When all sentence strips are stapled to the board, lead a class discussion about each stereotype. [Have a common pin concealed in your hand for the next part of the activity.] Ask students if the stereotype statements are fair statements. When you are satisfied that students have refuted the stereotype, swipe the balloon with the common pin. Pop! — that stereotype has been burst.
  • If you choose not to create the bulletin board, call students holding sentence strips to come one at a time to the front of the classroom. Have each student read aloud the statement on his or her strip and hold the strip up for classmates to see. Hold up a balloon as the strip holder calls on classmates to refute the stereotype on the strip. Once satisfied that the stereotype has been blasted, pop the balloon.

  • Ask students to share how they felt about the lesson. What did they learn? Were there times during the lesson when they felt angry or sad?

  • Differentiation
    • For additional activities related to this topic, see the following links:

    3.02 Understanding Stereotypes-Discovery Edu.

     

    Extension

    • Invite students to work in small groups to act out scenarios where stereotyping is evident. The small groups select a scene and are given time to practice and then present their scene to the whole group. After each group performs, the class discusses how the scene shows stereotyping, what they have learned, and how they might act in the same situation. The scenarios can include cultural stereotypes, racial stereotypes, gender stereotypes, religious stereotypes, age stereotypes, and social stereotypes. Include opportunities for students to record their group presentations in order to decrease students’ anxiety, increase engagement using technological tools, gain skills talking and presenting on camera, and promote autonomy and self-evaluation skills. By engaging with presentation tools, such as VoiceThread and Screencastify, they learn to communicate their ideas in English or their home language and they learn to collaborate in physical and virtual spaces.

     

Journal Entry Suggestions

    • What are your thoughts on stereotypes?
    • How do stereotypes affect society?
    • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • examine the historical and present relationship between wealth, poverty, status, and society.
  • analyze personal beliefs, mindsets and preconceptions (Self-Awareness)
  • practice acknowledging diverse social norms (Social Awareness)
  • recognize that others may experience situations differently from one’s own experience (Social Awareness)
  • define stereotyping, discrimination, and prejudice (Social Awareness)
  • foster ethical responsibility by creating spaces for voice (Responsible Decision-Making)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To facilitate student interaction through the use of the Clock Buddies (Part 1) tool so that students will have specific partners for various activities throughout the period or week. This is a quick and easy way to create pairs for future partnered activities that offers a break from continually turning to an elbow partner. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Interacting with Clock Buddies will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Self-Management.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meeting activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Dedicate time in your Community Circles/ Class Meetings to establish norms of collaboration on:
    1. how to greet each other once they meet their new Clock Buddy, 
    2. have them practice pronouncing each other's first and last names properly, 
    3. how they will ensure that each partner has equal time, and 
    4. how to thank each other once they have completed their activity instead of just walking away once the time is up. 
  2. Make copies of the Clock Buddy handout and distribute it to each student and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  3. Model how students should proceed in finding Clock Buddy partners by adding their names on the same time slot. Check to see if students understand the procedure. Make sure that they select someone who they are not familiar with or from a different country of origin.
  4. Have them continue finding Clock Buddies at a common time until all four time slots are filled. Invite students to return to their seats when form is completed.
  5. Use the Clock Buddies sheet each time you need participants to form pairs during an activity. For example, “Now meet up with your 9:00 Buddy to reflect and discuss..." Do this as a practice exercise.
  6. On a card or half-sheet of paper, ask participants to write down a response to a prompt you give related to their own personal experience with society’s view of class and socioeconomic differences. Begin with a low-vulnerability prompt such as:
    1. What is socioeconomic class? What examples can you think of?
    2. How does our society view class or people from various socioeconomic levels in terms of how people are treated and represented in various roles and positions?
  7. Call out which Clock Buddy they will meet with to share their response to the questions, i.e., meet with your 3:00 Buddy, etc. Repeat the process with a different question with a new Clock Buddy (no more than 2 minutes for each Clock Buddy round). If time allows, select a few participants to share out after each round. 
  8. Have students turn in their Clock Buddies sheets before the end of the period and redistribute them the following day so they can use them for subsequent partner activities.
  9. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

  

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you signed up with your Clock Buddies? (Self-Awareness)
  1. So What? Why do you think it’s important to get to know other students who you do not know very well? (Social Awareness)
  2. Now What? What can you learn from working with others from different socioeconomic classes? (Relationship Skills and Self-Awareness)

 

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin class by telling the class you have a significant announcement to make about the next test they will have in class (or some other class). Advise them the new policy will be that you will take the class average of all the scores and give that grade to everyone. Give the rationale that this is in the interest of equality and making sure no one feels bad or falls behind. This will help those who struggle and allow those “gifted” students to share their wealth and be of service to their fellow students.
  • Allow students to give their feedback, but continue to promote your cause.
  • After the discussion, let students know this will NOT be your new policy, but that many people/countries want to operate under these types of policies. Introduce this lesson by telling students the way the United States perceives money and wealth is unique and just like race, tends to separate people. Money has its advantages and disadvantages.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Consider showing the following video clip of a game show in Britain. (Preview it once to understand the scene and prep the class before viewing). Explain that although this is British, it can represent how we view obtaining wealth in America.
    • Ask the students what they would do if they were one of the players on the show. Would they split or steal? Do they agree or disagree with the outcome in the video?
  • Display a list of the richest people in America and explain that our society values people trying to get ahead and gain wealth. We want people to make money- perhaps even be greedy.
    • Ask students how they feel about people being allowed to have so much money. What are the positives and negatives to this?
    • Positives: People fulfill their dreams, we enjoy their services/products (Disneyland, Amazon, Apple), they can do good things with their money (Bill Gates Foundation, Ronald McDonald House)
    • Negatives: Debt (JibJab Video), Materialistic, Debt, Black Friday, Risky behaviors such as gambling and the lottery.

Guided Practice

  • Students will be divided into three groups based on an economic social class: Poor, Middle Class, or Rich. Students will be given a budget to plan a family healthy dinner by taking them to an online grocery site, such as Instacart or Walmart, where they can learn how much it costs to put dinner on the table. Students begin by creating a grocery list of healthy items for the online grocery shopping trip. They will calculate how much they are spending based on their given budget.
    • The group representing the poor will be given $50 to provide dinner to a family of four.
    • The group representing the middle class will be given $75 to provide dinner to a family of four.
    • The group representing the rich will be given $100 to provide dinner to a family of four.

Tough decisions on purchases will be negotiated among the members of each group. All of the groups will compare their purchases and differences in their food choices. After they have completed their discussions, each group can share their scenario based on the questions below:

  • How did the budget affect what we chose for dinner?
  • What cost-cutting decisions were made within the poor, middle class, and rich groups?
  • What was the quality of food purchased for each group’s healthy dinner? 
  • Which group was able to provide the healthiest dinner and why?
  • Explain that since the United States uses a system of rich and poor, sometimes that translates into winners and losers. We tend to judge people’s value on how much they have. Is this fair?
    • Show students the following videos or ones like them:
    • 3.03 Would you stop if you saw this little girl on the street?
    • 3.03 Rich vs Poor Free Money (social experiment )
    • Ask students for their reactions. Do you think these represent how all people in both situations act?
  • Ask students to brainstorm ways we can eliminate this negative perception of wealth and poverty.

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • research and present on a person or group who demonstrated pivotal lessons or progress in overcoming barriers within our society
  • recognize qualities of positive role models (Self-Awareness)
  • recognize the importance of effort in goal attainment (Self-Management)
  • develop teamwork and leadership skills (Relationship Skills)
  • analyze individual and institutional impacts (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To facilitate the discussion of quotes from important people and groups through the use of Clock Buddies (Part 2)  

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Interacting with Clock Buddies will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Self-Management.

Overview:

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meeting activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Dedicate time in your Community Circles/ Class Meetings to establish norms of collaboration on:
    1. how to greet each other once they meet their new Clock Buddy, 
    2. have them practice pronouncing each other's first and last name properly, 
    3. how they will ensure that each partner has equal time, and 
    4. how to thank each other once they have completed their activity instead of just walking away once the time is up. 
  2. Make copies of the Clock Buddy handout and distribute to each student and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  3. Select a number of sayings or quotes of famous people or groups who reflect the backgrounds and cultures of the students, combined with international personalities as well. Put a different quote on separate cards, small sheets of paper, etc. and hand them out to the students. 
  4. Have students meet with their first Clock Buddy (ex. 3:00 Buddy, etc) and read their quote to each other and reflect on what it means to them. Explain that each student will have 1.5 minutes to talk about what the quote means to them. You can use a chime after 1.5 minutes so that the next person shares. 
  5. After the first round, have them thank their partners for sharing and then exchange their quotes and proceed to the next Clock Buddy (ex. 6:00 Buddy) to reflect and share as with the first round. Continue for a total of 3-4 rounds. 
  6. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.”

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own thoughts or opinions of other students’ quotes? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ quotes and opinions? (Self Management)

Relevancy/Linkage

  • This lesson will require some initial prep work by the teacher. A list of important people/groups will need to be generated for students to either choose or to be assigned. There are many ways this list could be constructed and teachers will want to make adjustments and additions as they see fit. A sample list is included here.  
  • Announce to the class they will begin a new project today that will explore some of the people or groups who demonstrated progress in our society by their innovation or perseverance. Also, hint that this may turn competitive as well!
  • The purpose of this project is to learn from the experiences of people who faced challenging circumstances in their time and successfully made it through.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • The first part of this project will be to form groups of 3-5 students and explain that they will be holding a “draft” where they will be choosing the people/groups that they will be representing. Review the following outline of the project with the students:
  • Explain that after choosing their people, each student will choose to be one of these people. They will need to research their person and create a 30-60 second pitch about their accomplishments. Their objective is to convince the rest of the class that they demonstrated the most courage, innovation, change, etc.
  • The groups can be formed into playoff brackets or some other way of being pitted against another. On presentation day, the students will deliver these statements as a team and the class will vote on which team presented a more powerful group.  
  • Also explain that when it comes time for students to present their person, they need to include some form of dress or prop that makes them in character with that person.

Guided Practice

  • The “draft.” Post the names available to students and allow each team to select one in whatever order that is established. When it’s over, allow students to trade if two teams agree.
  • Allow students time to research and compose their statements. Remind students that in a quick pitch, certain details like birth-year or death date are not necessary compared to highlighting the stories or experiences that made them great. Note this research process can take place over a number of class periods to give students time to think and prepare.

Independent Practice

  • Include opportunities for students to record their presentations in order to decrease students’ anxiety, increase engagement using technological tools, gain skills in talking and presenting on camera, and promote autonomy and self-evaluation skills. By engaging with presentation tools, such as VoiceThread and Screencastify, they learn to communicate their ideas and collaborate in physical and virtual spaces. Create a space for ELs where languages and cultures are valued and invite students to record their presentation in English or their home language.

  • Ask students to turn in a paper that lists which student is assigned to which person. Assign the research and prop as homework if needed.
  • Allow students to have a voice in the assessment process and develop an understanding of the expectations of the assignment. Create a rubric with the students to assess the performance of the presentations. Determine the criteria, ratings, and score to be used with the students.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • research and present on a person or group who demonstrated pivotal lessons or progress in overcoming barriers within our society
  • recognize common qualities of positive role models (Self-Awareness)
  • understand impacts of developing self-discipline and self-motivation (Self-Management)
  • describe the steps in setting in getting to know one another at a deeper level (Relationship Skills)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To have students identify a personal challenge that they have had and the steps they used to overcome it through the use of a Card activity. This is designed to build self confidence by encouraging students to interact with each other with the expectation that everyone has had personal challenges and steps they have taken to overcome them.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Card activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Give out a 5x8 card to each student and ask students to write about a personal challenge that they don’t mind sharing and the steps they used to overcome it.
  2. Collect the index cards, mix them up, and return them to the students so that everyone has a new card.
  3. Ask students to question each other to find the original author. When a student finds the original author, the author signs the card and gives it to the teacher.
  4. Post all of the index cards on a bulletin board in the classroom.
  5. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings about sharing a personal challenge that you have had and the steps you used to overcome it? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own personal history with other students? What was something interesting you learned about other members of the class? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ personal challenges? (Self Management)

 

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Announce to the class that today is presentation day where teams will compete to prove their assigned people demonstrated more courage, innovation, and progress than the other.
  • Determine the order and teams competing against each other, and remind students of their behavior while others are presenting. Most importantly their job will be to determine which team shows a stronger presentation of the people.

Option 1

  • Begin the presentations and voting. Teachers may opt for a bracket to organize how teams “advance” or may just call for a final vote at the end of class.

Option 2

  • Students will independently watch the recorded bilingual presentations and use the class created rubric to score the criteria included in the rubric. Students involved in the creation of a rubric have a more concrete understanding of what is expected, and how to reach certain ratings and scores.
  • Transcribing a video’s audio to text allows ELs to read a transcript of the video presentation and not miss any of the information shared while listening to the video. Students can follow along at their own pace and review the material later for scoring. Combining a video lecture with readable text is a powerful form of multi-sensory learning.

Activity

  • Provide a prize for the winning team. The classes may also vote for the strongest presentation and best dress/props. Also, consider a class picture while everyone is dressed up.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • be able to identify the differences and appropriateness between argumentative and opinion writing
  • explore elements of self-confidence and self-efficacy (Self-Awareness)
  • define perspective and point of view (Social Awareness)
  • distinguish between disrespectful and respectful disagreement (Social Awareness)
  • continue developing effective communication skills (Relationship Skills) 
  • Identify solutions for personal and social problems (Responsible Decision-Making)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To build a positive class community by encouraging students to identify areas of needed school improvement and to discuss and debate possible changes. Using the Imagine (Part 1) activity, students will think about any changes or improvements that they would like to see in their school that would make it a better place for them to learn and to make new friends.  

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Imagine activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. While still in the Community Circle, have students close their eyes and envision approaching a school, opening the front door, and what they would want to see in the perfect school environment. It could be their school or an imaginary school. 
  2. As you read the four questions, take 30 seconds to have them reflect on each. Post the prompts in a visible location (white board, Smart board or anchor chart) or have them printed out on a handout. As you entered the school:
    • What did it look like?
    • What did it sound like?
    • What did it feel like?
    • What interactions did you see? 
  3. Ask students to write down a short response to each of the four prompts on a sheet of paper.
  4. Have them Turn and Talk to an elbow partner and share each response. 
  5. Now have them write a response to this 5th question: 
    • List any changes or improvements that you would make to your school to make it a better place for you to learn and make new friends. 
  1. Once completed use the "Mix and Mingle!" activity with music (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, Norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc) to have students find a different partner to compare their responses to the 5th prompt.
  2. Partners share their responses, listen actively to each other, ask follow-up questions and debate any differences of opinion that they may have.
  3. Start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as time permits.
  4. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own ideas  with other students on how to improve the school climate? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ ideas on school improvement? (Self Management)

 

  • Relevancy/Linkage
    • Announce to the class that they will be taking on a new role today – a detective! Explain that a serious accident has taken place and they are tasked with finding out exactly what happened. You may read or have the students read Part A of 3.06 Article – Driver Plows into Illinois Wendy’s.
    • Ask students for their initial reaction. What do they think happened?
    • Next, reveal to the class that a photo was taken right as the event happened and display the image found in Part B of 3.06 Article – Driver Plows into Illinois Wendy’s. Ask students to share their instant reactions to what they see, thoughts on what could have happened in this situation, and what they think about the driver.

    Stop the conversation after a few minutes and explain to the class that they are delivering their opinions at this point. There’s nothing wrong with having opinions and we value people’s opinions all the time. Opinions don’t require any work and can be formed very quickly. As students, it is critical to go beyond just opinions and develop argumentative writing skills. Argumentative writing “requires the student to investigate a topic; collect, generate, and evaluate evidence; and establish a position on the topic in a concise manner” (Reference: Purdue University).
