INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Display and have a student read Part C of 3.06 Article – Driver Plows into Illinois Wendy’s out loud.
  • Ask students to silently analyze all of the evidence they have seen in Parts A, B and C. Have them make a list of any objects or aspects of the report and photo that they believe are significant in telling us what happened.
  • When they are ready, allow students to share what they found. Encourage other students to respond and debate.
  • Be sure to deliberately point out when a fact is being stated and when an opinion is being shared.

Guided Practice

  • Now have the students pretend that they are before a judge or supervisor who wants their assessment of whether or not the driver should be arrested. This person wants an account of what happened with evidence to support it. Ask students to write an argumentative paragraph that explains what happened after hearing and seeing all the evidence and arguments. Stress that this means their statements must include opinion + facts.
  • When students are finished, direct them to re-read their paragraph and underline the parts that are facts or evidence. If they aren’t underlining anything, then they are still stuck on delivering opinions only.
  • Allow a few students to share their final statement and as a class, determine whether or not they wrote an opinion or argumentative piece.
  • Explain to the class that this upcoming project will ask them to develop an argumentative piece or presentation around a controversial topic that will be chosen next lesson.

  • Explain to students that to finish class you will provide a sample of what they will be researching for this project. Read Article – The Sky’s the Limit or a different article of your choosing. Ask students to read it and again identify the facts or evidence. This activity may also be done as a class. 
    • Use the following resources to locate a writing sample:
      • Student Models of Writing (Note the samples are called “Persuasive Writing” here).
      • Writing Work Samples
  • Utilize Google Slides or a PowerPoint template to identify the facts or evidence of the selected writing sample. Students take opposing positions to create balanced and informed arguments by using supporting evidence to explain their position. The slideshow will support their findings and include visual cues that support the opposing viewpoints. ELs benefit from additional time to express their perspective in writing. This activity encourages an appreciation and acceptance of multiple perspectives. Manage your lessons and student presentations with free Google Slides themes and PowerPoint templates on slidesgo.

  • Explain in your own words the difference between argumentative and opinion writing.
  • Which form of writing do you think is harder, argumentative or opinion? Explain your reasons.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • research a current social issue and write an argumentative statement that describes and defends their position
  • identify passive, aggressive, and assertive responses (Self-Awareness)
  • recognize words and actions that hurt others (Social Awareness)
  • identify differing perspectives in given situations (Social Awareness)
  • continue developing effective communication skills (Relationship Skills)
  • analyze individual and institutional impacts (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To build a positive class community by encouraging students to identify areas of needed school improvement and to discuss and debate possible changes. Using the Imagine (Part 1) activity, Students will think about any changes or improvements that they would like to see in their community that would make it a better place for them to live and be happy through the use of the Imagine (Part 2) activity. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Imagine activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. While still in the Community Circle, have students close their eyes and envision their own community where they live and imagine what they would want to see in an ideal living environment. It could be their own community or an imaginary city. 
  2. As you read the four questions, take 30 seconds to have them reflect on each. Post the prompts in a visible location (white board, Smart board or anchor chart) or have them printed out on a handout. As you thought about the ideal living community: 
    1. What did it look like?
    2. What did it sound like?
    3. What did it feel like?
    4. What type of interactions did you see? 
  3. Ask students to write down a short response to each of the four prompts on a sheet of paper.
  4. Have them Turn and Talk to an elbow partner and share each response. 
  5. Now have them write a response to this 5th question: 

e.  List any changes or improvements that you would make to your current community where you live that would make it a better place for you and your family. 

  1. Once completed use the "Mix and Mingle!" activity with music (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, Norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc) to have students find a different partner to compare their responses to the 5th prompt.
  2. Partners share their responses, listen actively to each other, ask follow-up questions and debate any differences of opinion that they may have.
  3. Start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as time permits.
  4. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own ideas  with other students on how to improve your immediate community where you live? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ ideas on an ideal community? (Self Management)

 

Relevancy/Linkage

  • In order to complete this project, some preparation will be needed before class begins. Teachers will need to:
  • Determine the topics. These will depend on how many students you want per debate team (4-8 is a good number). For example, a class of 25 may need two topics, which makes four teams, as each topic has a “for” and “against.” The topics themselves can be any social issue. Most effective are those topics relevant to the students’ interests, but not something they hear a lot about already. They should also be topics they can research fully using the school’s technology.
  • Teachers may prefer to assign the topics and teams or allow them to happen at random through drawing straws or some other method.
  • Announce to the class that today’s lesson will consist of planning for a formal debate, which will happen next lesson. 
  • Before making topic and team assignments, review with the class the components of each part.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Explain that students will be assigned a topic, team, and research paper. You may allow the class to vote on the topics or reveal your choices instead.
  • Once received, students will be asked to research and write a short argumentative paper or statement about their topic (Teachers should specify their requirements depending on their class’s specific circumstances).
  • It is vital that students understand the purpose and skills developed during this project:
    • Write an argument for a topic that you don’t necessarily believe in.
    • Diligently research and strategize to convince others of your position on the topic, regardless of your personal beliefs.
    • Put your argumentative skills to the test.
  • Teachers will likely need to review the above points throughout the project.
  • Teachers may now assign the topics and teams. It may be helpful to ask students to sit with their teams.

Guided Practice

  • With their teams, explain to students the following steps:
  • Teams should engage in an initial discussion of their topic (consider letting them use their phones to gather some quick information).
  • Within their teams, students should identify subtopics that relate to the main topic. For example: if the topic was for animals in captivity, subtopics for each student may include zoos to educate the public, sanctuaries to rescue injured animals, conservation projects for endangered species, research to cure diseases, etc.
  • Once the subtopics are identified, students should decide which team member will research which subtopic. The goal is that each student will become an expert in their assigned subtopic.
  • Teams should designate a scribe to write down each student’s assignment and deliver it to the teacher.
  • Teachers should visit each group as they work to help generate ideas and feedback.
  • Allow students time as needed to research and write their statements. Ensure that students understand that during the debate, they will need both their written statement as well as additional evidence to refer to and support their side. They should collect these additional facts as they do their research. 
  • After the papers are written, the teacher will share the debate procedures and rules so that students can begin planning and strategizing: 
    • Debate Procedure
    • Team A will start the debate with an opening statement.
    • Team B will have one member deliver a rebuttal and the back and forth exchanges will commence.
    • The teacher may call a half-time to allow each team to talk and strategize.  
    • Team A presents their closing statement.
    • Team B will end the segment with their closing statement.
  • Some additional rules to consider:
  • Teams must designate who will deliver the opening and closing statements before the debate begins.
  • All other speakers can be chosen and changed during the debate.
  • Members are limited to a maximum 30 seconds of speaking time.
  • Teams may only discuss strategy in-between members speaking, and not while someone else is speaking. 
  • Teams and members may use their notes while speaking or preparing during the debate.
  • Each member can only speak twice during a debate.
  • The student teams not presenting will make up the audience for the debate. The audience should remain completely silent during the debate.
  • Make sure to give enough time to the teams so that they can strategize together before beginning the debate.
  • These rules should be reviewed right before the debate and can be modified by the teacher to fit the needs of the class.

  • The teacher should determine which aspects need to be reviewed during the lesson and debate preparations. Examples could include:
    • Review relevant subtopics and the student assignments.
    • Review each student’s progress as they prepare for the debate.
    • Review students’ written research papers, argumentative statements, and supporting evidence.
    • Review the debate rules with all teams and students to make sure they understand how the debate will work.
    • The teacher should touch base with each team to ensure they are ready prior to initiating the debate class period.
  • Utilize Google Slides or a PowerPoint template to host the debate. Students take opposing positions on an issue to create balanced and informed arguments by using supporting evidence to develop effective communication skills. The slide show will support their findings and include visual cues that support the opposing viewpoints. ELs benefit from additional time to express their perspective in writing as well as sentence starters to model standard debate language. Students can participate in the debate by posing questions in the commenting features of their online presentation.
  • Engage students to ask questions to the presenters with interactive presentation tools such as Google Slides Q & A, Mentimeter, and Padlet.

  • How do you think being able to form clear, evidence-based arguments will benefit you in the future?

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • participate in a formal class debate on the current social issue.
  • identify passive, aggressive, and assertive responses (Self-Awareness) 
  • demonstrate the ability to interrupt escalating emotions (Self-Management)
  • demonstrate positive behaviors and self-regulation, i.e., listening, paying attention, following directions, ignoring distraction. (Self-Management)
  • share examples of demonstrating respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • distinguish between disrespectful and respectful disagreement (Social Awareness)

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To build a better society by encouraging students to identify areas of needed improvement and to discuss and debate possible social changes. Students will think about any changes or improvements that they would like to see in their society that would make it a better place for everyone to be successful and prosperous through the use of the Imagine (Part 3) activity.  

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Imagine activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. While still in the Community Circle, have students close their eyes and envision current social issues and imagine what they would want to see in an ideal society. 
  2. As you read the four questions, take 30 seconds to have them reflect on each. Post the prompts in a visible location (whiteboard, Smart board, or anchor chart) or have them printed out on a handout. As you think about social issues in general: 
    1. What are the main issues people are struggling with?
    2. Select one that stands out in your mind.
    3. How does it make you feel?
    4. What are the main causes of this social issue? 
  3. Ask students to write down a short response to each of the four questions on a sheet of paper.
  4. Have them Turn and Talk to an elbow partner and share each response. 
  5. Now have them write a response to this 5th question:

e.  List any changes or improvements that you would make to society that would make it a better place for everyone to be successful and prosperous. 

  1. Once completed, use the "Mix and Mingle!" activity with music (use samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, Norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc) to have students find a different partner to compare their responses to the 5th prompt.
  2. Partners share their responses, listen actively to each other, ask follow-up questions, and debate any differences of opinion that they may have.
  3. Start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as time permits.
  4. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower Latino youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own ideas with other students on how to improve society? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ ideas about an ideal society? (Self Management)

 

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin with an in-depth review of the rules and format for the debate. Make sure to cover all of the following elements of the debate procedure:
    • Team A will start the debate with an opening statement.
    • Team B will have one member deliver a rebuttal, and the back and forth exchanges will commence.
    • The teacher may call a half-time to allow each team to talk and strategize.  
    • Team B will end the segment with a closing statement.
  • Some additional rules to consider:
    • Teams must designate who will deliver the opening and closing statements before the debate begins.
    • All other speakers can be chosen and changed during the debate.
    • Members are limited to a maximum of 30 seconds of speaking time.
    • Teams may only discuss strategy in-between members speaking, and not while someone else is speaking. 
    • Teams and members may use their notes while speaking or preparing during the debate.
    • Each member can only speak twice during a debate.
    • The student teams not presenting will make up the audience for the debate. The audience should remain completely silent during the debate.
  • Teachers should make modifications as needed.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Teachers may instruct the audience to keep a score or note the most powerful moments or statements.
  • Start the debate by allowing Team A to deliver the opening statement, followed by Team B.
  • Allow for back and forth exchanges.
  • Teachers may find it necessary to “pause” the debate to make clarifications or provide guidance to the teams. Find a good stopping point to call a time-out. The time-out will allow teams to regroup and strategize and the audience a chance to discuss the debate’s progress.
  • Allow the debate to continue until the material or time is used up before calling for the closing statements.
  • Have Team A deliver their closing statement, followed by Team B.

Guided Practice

  • Allow the audience time to give feedback on the debate and discuss which team made the stronger argument. Teachers should also use this time to give feedback on the performance of each team.
  • For classes with a second topic, they will simply repeat the debate process with the new teams.

  • Ask for debate participants to turn in their papers, notes and/or statements and review that their work contains both opinion and facts. 
  • Utilize Google Slides or a PowerPoint template to host the debate. Students take opposing positions on an issue to create balanced and informed arguments by using supporting evidence to develop effective communication skills. The slide show will support their findings and include visual cues that support the opposing viewpoints. ELs benefit from additional time to express their perspective in writing as well as sentence starters to model standard debate language. Students can participate in the debate by posing questions in the commenting features of their online presentation.
  • Engage students to ask questions to the presenters with interactive presentation tools such as Google Slides Q & A, Mentimeter, and Padlet.

  • How do you think your team did during the debate? What would you do differently in the future?
  • Do you feel like you were able to make a strong argument for your side? Why or why not?
  • Did you enjoy participating in the debate? Why or why not?
  • Students can create video journals to document their personal growth, self-reflect, and share their thoughts and experiences. All major Learning Management Systems (LMS) support student recordings within the interface such as Screencastify Submit with Google Classroom or Canvas.

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain that students will be starting a new unit focused on learning more about themselves. Today’s lesson will focus on the students’ unique characteristics and later lessons will look at family and cultural qualities.
  • Begin the class by having the students take the following warm-up personality test:
    • Short Personality Test 1
  • Ask students their reaction and whether or not they believe these tests do show real differences between people. Why do we have differences? Are there advantages to knowing your personality?
  •  Explain that today’s lesson will explore one universally recognized (Myers Briggs or MBTI) test that may show some insight into the characteristics of a student’s personality. Be careful to note that such tests can’t capture all or even most parts of one’s personality, nor can they tell you how you will be in the future or what type of job you must get. However, they can be interesting and perhaps reveal or explain parts of one’s personality that may be insightful and helpful.

Activity

  • For a free Myers-Briggs Personality Test online, use the option from this website or one of your choice. Teachers may want to preview any chosen test links to ensure they work with their school's internet and devices. They may also take one of the tests to share some of the results with their students.

Guided Practice

  • When finished, show students some graphics of the Myers-Briggs personality types explained (be sure to scroll down after clicking on the link) or applied to pop culture.
    • Star Wars
    • Harry Potter
    • Disney
    • Historical People
  • Ask students to review their results and, in pairs, discuss whether or not they believe they are accurate. Can students identify the strengths and weaknesses of their personality?

    • 16 Personalities

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Do you think your personality test results were helpful? Why or why not?
  • Did any of the tests help you learn anything about yourself?

OBJECTIVE:

Students will create an autobiographical sketch of their lives and family history.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="padding-5-percent" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color="#3a3a3a" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" font_color="#ffffff" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Note that it may be helpful to share the prompts for this writing assignment before the lesson so students can ask their parents for more information.
  • One critical theme for this lesson and unit is family. For teachers wanting to understand more about how family and Latino culture related, consider reading this short description.  As an extension activity, ask students if they agree or disagree, or share their thoughts on this description. 
  • Prompt students to share what they believe are differences between how family is viewed in Latino culture compared to the United States. Ask students about respect, individual family member roles, support/aid, and time spent together.
  • Explain to students that family is recognized as a significant part of Latino culture. It’s no surprise that when Pixar creates Coco, a movie based in Mexico, the central theme is family. Explain that the assignment for this lesson focuses on helping students share their story in relation to their family. This first lesson will ask students to look at themselves and what they know about their recent family history.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Activity

  • Demonstrate for students how often they will be asked to describe “their story.” This is likely to happen in job interviews, school assignments, college entrance essays, scholarship opportunities, admissions to certain programs, etc. Note in all these cases the audience is not just looking for the facts behind your history, but the experiences of what you have accomplished, your goals, what you have learned, and the kind of person you are. People who have refined their message will have an advantage in these situations. Teachers may want to share an example of their own experience or an example of how they would respond to one of the prompts below.

Guided Practice

  • Allow students time to write about the following prompts and instructions. These should be modified according to the teacher’s preferences.
    • Personal Narrative
      For this assignment, you will write a short paper about yourself. There are three required parts:
    1. Describe who in your family was the first to come to the United States and under what circumstances. If you do not know this information, describe what you know about your grandparents, great-grandparents, and where your family came from.  
    2. Look up the meaning and history of your first and last names. Do you think they fit you? Were you named after anyone?
    3. In another paragraph write about:
      • Your strengths and weaknesses
      • Your biggest accomplishments so far
      • What are your goals?
      • Where do you want to be in 10 years? What job do you want to have?
      • Who has impacted you the most? Who do you admire most?
      • What experience in your life changed you?
      • How do you want to fit in the world?

Review

  • Ask students if they would be willing to share certain parts of the essay with the class. Also, ensure that it is saved or printed in a place that students will be able to reference later. Teachers may also request students to share through social media some part of their essay experience like a shout-out to a certain person, goal, or event.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Differentiation

  • Allow students to write their Personal Narrative in their native language if desired.
  • Provide a Sample Personal Narrative answering the questions in the Guided Practice section based on your own experience students can refer to as a model.
  • Provide a fill-in-the-blank template that includes a word bank for support.

Extension

  • Pair students up and encourage them to compare and contrast the information written in their Personal Narrative.
  • Have pairs of students think of and ask each other additional questions that were not mentioned in the Personal Narrative assignment in the Guided Practice section.

 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How did you feel sharing "your story" in relation to your family?
  • Do you now feel ready to share your story with others who might not know you? Why or why not?

  • Greetings
  • Discussion and Sharing
  • Energizers and Community Building

  • Watch Video “My Dad’s Story”. (3.5 min)
  • Ask the students the following questions.  May want to have students write their responses or do a combination of discussion and journaling.
  • What was the overall message of the clip?
  • What are the “lies” the daughter references?
  • What does the dad sacrifice for his daughter?
  • What have your parents/grandparents/guardians sacrificed for you?
  • Make a connection between the video clip and the importance of family stories.
  • Think about the video clip we watched at the beginning of class.  Family stories are powerful and help us to appreciate our parents’, grandparents’, or guardians’ sacrifices from a more personal perspective.  Over the next two class periods, we are going to use descriptive writing and also write narratives to tell about our families.

Practice

  • Distribute Family Narrative Graphic Organizer.
  • Ask students to complete the organizer at home with the family and return the following class period.

Proofread

  • Display and distribute Editing & Proofreading Rubric.
  • Use a student’s draft to model how to complete at least 2 items (i.e. topic sentence & figurative language) on the rubric.

Teacher Note

  • May want to divide this lesson across two class periods depending on student progress to give students time to write and edit the family story in class using 11.03 HO Family Narrative Graphic Organizer (student completed).

PURPOSE

Understand cultural capital by researching heritage, country, and modern-day culture through the creation of a personal heritage portfolio.

OBJECTIVES

Students will complete a portfolio representing themselves and their culture during this unit. Students will identify their definition of “culture” by using the anticipation guide and creating a group poster displaying their definition.

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts
  • Print student cards from 11.01 HO Cultural Anticipation Cards for students to cut apart
  • Prepare a set of anticipation cards for teacher use (Ideally, print each card on a separate piece of paper so they are large enough to read on the board)
  • Read 11.01 Weblink Definitions of Culture

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

Poster board or butcher paper

  • Crayons/markers/scissors
  • 11.01 Weblink Definitions of Culture
  • 11.01 HO Cultural Anticipation Cards

Extension

  • 11.01 HO Culture Comparison Chart

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Culture
  • Values
  • Rituals
  • Symbol
  • Collective

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Write the word “culture” on the board.
  • Ask students to think of the definition and write it down.
  • Distribute 11.01 HO Cultural Anticipation Cards.
  • Give students time to cut & sort them into three piles (“I agree”, “I disagree”, “I am not sure”).

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary words and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or  Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

Model

  • Explain that culture has many definitions and some are more complicated than others.  
  • Display 11.01 Weblink Definitions of Culture and highlight some of the definitions.
  • Write the three phrases on the board “I agree”, “I disagree”, and “I am not sure” in three different columns.
  • Ask a student to come up to the board and demonstrate how they sorted the 11.01 HO Cultural Anticipation Cards.  
  • Lead a discussion about why each card was placed in the different categories.  
  • Allow students to debate and come up with different reasons why they placed cards in different categories.

Guided Practice

  • Divide students into groups of 3-4.
  • Ask student groups to come up with their “best definition of culture” using their own definitions they wrote at the beginning of class, the 11.01 HO Cultural Anticipation Cards, and/or the class discussion.
  • Student groups create a poster with their culture definition.
  • Encourage students to use a limited number of words (i.e. less than 10 or less than 5) and draw pictures to represent their definitions as well.

  • Display “Culture Definitions” throughout the classroom.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Complete the activity using the 11.01 HO Cultural Anticipation Cards in student groups or as a class.

Extension

  • Extend the lesson and give student groups an opportunity to present their definition.  Each group will present their poster and explain why their group thought their definition was the best and most concise.  Ask students to use personal examples to explain their definitions as well.
  • Complete the 11.01 HO Culture Comparison Chart as a class, individual student activity, or group activity.  Debrief following the activity.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can understanding my native culture and my American culture help me to know what strengths/talents I can use to help my family, my class, my school, and my community?

Relevancy/Linkage

  • To review the last lesson about culture, introduce a slightly modified concept of the “culture tree.” You may choose to illustrate this by drawing, using paper cutouts, or graphics on the computer. Explain that each of us may be considered a tree with ourselves being considered the trunk. We also desire to produce great leaves; we want to look good! Leaves for us may be material possessions, how we physically look, talents we develop, accomplishments, education, hobbies, what we wear, etc.
    • Prompt students about what parts of the tree are missing (the roots) and why they are needed (they provide water and support for the tree). In other words, they help the tree survive the elements. In a similar way, Latinos In Action and the following project asks students to strengthen their roots. At times when minorities continue to face struggles and barriers, strong roots will help students withstand and navigate their way through society.
    • Explain this project will consist of two parts. First is an exploration of a civilization related to the students’ background. Second is a display of a student’s current culture and values.

Activity

  • Ask students if they believe our schools, society, and/or country help all youth understand, learn, and strengthen their heritage and roots. 
    • In early social studies classes, students learn about Greek mythology, Egyptian culture and pyramids, The Great Wall of China. Ask if/what they have learned about African or Latino cultures, religions, and histories. 
    • Ask students if the selection of readings found in secondary English classrooms and school libraries have enough representation from Latin American authors. Consider referencing this article on AP Literature.
    • Ask students to consider how people from their culture or background are represented in tv and movies. 
  • Prompt students to reflect on ways their roots have been enhanced or weakened as a result of our society. Where do they look for role models? Note that the discovery of your roots has a powerful effect on people.

Guided Practice

  • Using maps like 4.04 Pre-Columbian Map 1 and 4.04 Pre-Columbian Map 2, students should locate a civilization closely related to their ancestral background. For some students, their background may be associated with other parts of the world and other students may not know what area applies to them. In any case, students should choose whichever they feel most comfortable with. For Latin America, these are generally referred to as “pre-Columbian civilizations.”
  • Using the internet students should research information about their culture in the present day, using the following handout as a guide. This guide will be useful as they research and plan their presentations and complete their Heritage Portfolios.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Ask students if they are familiar with the concept of “branding.” As an example, show students an image of well-recognized brands and ask what they picture or think about when they see their logo. The reason those thoughts come into our heads is because of a process called branding. Companies want you to see the best in their products and constantly try and deliver that message to you.
    • Ask students to consider how they would brand themselves. What colors, logo, mission statement, motto, and values would they promote? Teachers may consider building out this assignment as an option for the activity or guided activity in this lesson.
  • Explain that this lesson and project will look at students branding themselves by combining the learning from the last three lessons. While there is power in knowing who you are, there’s even more when you take on, display, and proclaim who you are!  We want students to create their own brand about who they are.

Purpose: To use this Leadership Shout Out activity for Identifying positive leadership characteristics of a specific person who is personally admired. Students will discuss perspectives about what constitutes admirable qualities in a leader.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Leadership Shout Out activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (5 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Before students arrive, write directions on the board or screen. As they arrive, greet them warmly at the door by preferred name and correct pronunciation. Point them toward the posted Welcoming Activity.
  • Use a pairing activity to group students intentionally ensuring that English-dominant students are paired with ELs. 
  • Welcome! In the next five minutes:
    • THINK ABOUT a leader in your family, community, or the world, who you admire. What qualities does that leader (show?) (demonstrate?)
    • CHAT with at least two other people and share your thoughts about the leader and their admirable qualities.
    • PREPARE to share with the whole group.
    • Chart their responses on the board, looking for similarities and differences. 
    • Ask students to reflect on the leadership qualities they would like to develop. Share with a partner.
    • When the time is up use an attention signal to bring the group to quiet focused attention. Invite volunteers to share their own thinking (not their partner’s—although they may want to encourage their partner to share!).  

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore the characteristics of a leader? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about leadership today? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Use breakout rooms for partner/trio conversations. NOTE: This takes away the important element of open choice of partners.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Pass out index cards to students.
  • Ask the following question and state the directions.
  • What is leadership?
  • On the index card, write your own definition of leadership.  You may use words, examples, or a story to demonstrate your definition.
  • Share out definitions.

Video

  • Watch 5.01 Video Everyday Leadership (6 min).
  • As you watch Drew Dudley’s TED talk on leadership, write/describe, on the back of your index card, what he defines as leadership.
  • Ask students to share their own definitions and highlights of Drew Dudley’s definition.
  • Summarize the main points.

  • Watch 5.01 Video Martin Luther King, Jr. (2 min).
  • Display 5.01 HO Leadership Traits.
  • Ask students the following questions.
  • What leadership traits does King demonstrate?
  • How did these traits help him to be a successful leader?
  • Which traits do you have?
  • Write student responses on 5.01 HO Leadership Traits.

Guided Practice

  • Watch 5.01 Video Cesar Chavez (4 min).
  • Instruct students to list Chavez’s leadership traits on 5.01 HO Leadership Traits.
  • Watch 5.01 Video Nelson Mandela (7 min).
  • Instruct students to list Mandela’s leadership traits on 5.01 HO Leadership Traits.

Activity

  • Students will work in pairs or small groups to identify other influential leaders/activists and list their leadership traits on 5.01 HO Leadership Traits. The teacher provides a list of contemporary influential leaders as a sample for students to choose from:
    • Jose Antonio Vargas, immigration and citizenship
    • John Lewis, civil rights leader
    • Sonia Sotomayor, Supreme Court Justice
    • Malala Yousafzai, Pakistani activist
    • Greta Thunberg, Environmental Activist
    • Yara Shahidi, Actress and Activist
  • Students will record a 90-second Padlet video about what leadership means to them. After viewing each video, students must add a comment by recording a video response to their classmates' message.

  • Divide students into three groups and provide computer access to each group.
  • Invite each group to watch one video clip (Martin Luther King, Jr., Cesar Chavez, or Nelson Mandela) and identify leadership qualities in that leader.
  • Groups share with classmates the qualities they identified.
  • Classmates record all leadership traits on 5.01 HO Leadership Traits.

Extension

  • Have students find their own video on Martin Luther King, Jr., Cesar Chavez, Nelson Mandela, or any other impactful leader.  
  • Ask students to create a timeline based on events they see in the video.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Does anyone have the ability to be a leader?  Why or why not?
  • How do leadership qualities differ and stay the same between cultures?

Identify the leadership traits and qualities that you would like to develop to become better leaders.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • reflect on the purpose and objectives of the LIA course in developing leadership
  • explore integrating personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • analyze beliefs, mindsets, and preconceptions (Self-Awareness)
  • develop an understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-Management) 

PREPARATION

  • Poster
  • Magazines, pictures
  • Digital Tools

MATERIALS

Main lesson
5.02 HO Leadership Traits
5.02 Life Size Leader Model 1
5.02 Life Size Leader Model 2
5.02 Life Size Leader Model 3

Adaptations
5.02 SMARTE Goal Template

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Biography
  • Social Justice
  • Civil rights
  • Non-violent

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use this Stand Up / Hand Up activity to help students get to know one another better, visually see how others are similar to and different from themselves, and build confidence within the community to share who we are and to interact with growing ease.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Stand Up / Hand Up activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Management, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (5 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • The teacher reads a series of statements aloud. Students stand up or raise their hands to indicate that the statement applies to them. 
    • When explaining the activity to students, explicitly encourage them to ‘boldly look around, don’t just sneak a peek!’ to see how others are responding, since our goal is to learn about each other.
    • Keep the pace lively and fun—read each statement with an equally upbeat expression so students can feel positive about any they respond to; do a quick look around, acknowledging the responders by nodding, smiling, eye contact; zip on to the next statement.
    • Some students enjoy the option for more movement (stand up) while others prefer less (hand up). Teachers know best about their comfort level and about their class, so might choose to offer only one response option.
  • First round of Statements (Stand up, hand up if you…)
    • Did something fun outdoors in the past two days
    • Listened to music that helped you feel good
    • Read for pleasure, not an assignment
    • Laughed out loud about something
    • Wrote in a journal
    • Played any kind of game (inside, outside, or online)
    • Prepared some food for yourself and/or others
  • Second round of Statements (Stand up, hand up if you…)
    • Belong, use to belong, to any kind of organization, club, committee, or group that meets regularly 
    • Held a position in a club or organization such as president, VP, captain, secretary, reporter, etc.
    • Lead a meeting or activity where others follow your direction
    • Were responsible for organizing materials, supplies, and resources of a club or organization
    • Know what an agenda is and why it is important to have one
    • Were responsible for resolving a misunderstanding, conflict, or disagreement where you were able to reach a compromise
  • Have students form a trio and tell them the name of the club, committee, or organization that they belong to now or have in the past, or one that they would like to belong to someday. After each partner names their club or organization, explain why they want to belong to it.
  • Have them share with the larger class.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ways to be a leader of a club, committee, or organization? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about leadership today? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Return completed Leadership Traits to students.
  • We identified many leadership traits demonstrated by famous world leaders.  Today you are each going to identify the qualities that you would like to develop to become better leaders.

  • Display and discuss one or more of these examples: Life Size Leader Model 1, Life Size Leader Model 2, Life Size Leader Model 3. Tell the students they will be making their own "Life Size Leader Model" poster. 
  • Display the 5.01 HO Leadership Traits that you and your class completed in the previous lesson 5.01.
  • Model for students how to choose 5-10 leadership traits they would like to display/develop on their poster and how to represent each trait. Reference Life Size Leader Models 1, 2, and 3 (linked above) as needed. 

Guided Practice

  • Students find (in magazines or online) or sketch pictures that demonstrate the qualities they want to develop. (i.e. “hands”-service, “mouth”-public speaking, “brain”-academics)
  • Students create their individual posters.

  • The class will use a multimedia poster tool to support the creation of digital content to help students develop their critical thinking skills, research skills, and visual design skills. Extension

  • Assign students to present their posters to classmates.  
  • Ask students to select one or two of their identified leadership traits.  Use SMARTE Goal Template to write goals to develop these specific qualities.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why is it important to develop leadership qualities?  Do you think it will benefit you in the future?  Why or why not?
  • What cultural traditions have been passed down in your family that could help you develop leadership qualities?

Research the contributions of three leaders and complete a graphic organizer.

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • summarize the life of three leaders and recognize how the leaders have influenced the students’ lives
  • notice how they integrate personal and social-cultural identities (Self-awareness)
  • practice acknowledging diverse norms (Social Awareness)
  • develop teamwork and leadership skills (Relationship Skills)

PREPARATION

  • Graphic organizer
  • Digital Tools/Devices/Internet

MATERIALS

Main lesson
5.03 Video Roberto Clemente Athlete Mini Bio
5.03 Leaders Graphic Organizer
5.03 R. Clemente/J. Perez Teacher Model

Adaptations
5.03 Alternative Biography Options
5.03 Video El Chavo Del Ocho

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Public Policy
  • Journalism

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY  

Purpose: To use this 1-2-3 CLAP! skill-building activity to help a group quickly bond in preparation for collaboration, cooperation, and team building that would encourage innovation and creativity in building leadership skills. It demonstrates how making mistakes together can be a fast track to greater cooperation, creative collaboration, and leadership development. (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This 1-2-3 CLAP! activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (7 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Use one of a number of pairing strategies to assign students in pairs that are inclusive, equitable, and diverse. 
  • Once students have been paired, the same partners face each other during each of the three rounds of this activity. When modeling with a student partner, it’s always the teacher who ‘makes the mistake.’

Round 1:

  • Explain that pairs will count to three over and over again, with each player saying the next number in the sequence.
  • Model slowly with a partner.
  • Once everyone has had a minute or two to play, call the game to a close with your agreed-upon attention signal. Ask, "How many of you made a mistake?" "What did you do when you made a mistake?" (Common answers: “Laughed” or "Said sorry" or “Pulled back.”)
  • Explain that these are all ways that people give cues to the group that say, "I've got this. I'll laugh at myself or apologize as my way of handling making a mistake."
  • Tell the group that during the next round, whenever they make a mistake, they should raise their hands in the air and say, "Tah-dah!"

Round 2:

  • Explain that for this round, pairs should replace the number “1” with a clap and then continue the number sequence “2-3" counted out loud (Clap-2-3, Clap-2-3, etc.).
  • Model slowly with a partner. During the modeling purposefully make a mistake, such as saying “1” instead of clapping after “3.” Raise your hands in the air and say, "Tah-dah!"
  • Once everyone has had a minute or two to play, use your attention signal to call the round to a close. Ask, "Was anyone glad that they weren't the one making a mistake?"
  • Tell the group that in the next round when one person makes a mistake, both partners will raise their hands in the air, give each other a double high-five, and both say, "Tah-dah!"

Round 3:

  • Explain that in this round, participants should clap for “1,” replace the number “2” with a foot stomp, and say “3.” (Clap, stomp, 3; Clap, stomp, 3; etc.).
  • Model this with a partner while YOU purposefully make a mistake, such as saying “two” instead of stomping. You and your partner now give each other double high-fives and shout, “Tah-dah!” together, and start over again.
  • Once everyone has had a minute or two to play, call the round to a close with your usual attention signal.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to participate in team-building activities that require cooperation as a part of leadership skills? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about cooperation and leadership when working with another person or group? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: This activity does not lend itself well to a virtual environment.

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous lesson.

  • So far, we have learned about leadership and what qualities make an effective leader.  We talked about Cesar Chavez, Martin Luther King, and Nelson Mandela.  Today we will explore different leaders and their contributions to the world around them.
  • What leadership qualities did these leaders demonstrate?

Video

  • Introduce the Roberto Clemente video.
  • Watch Roberto Clemente Athlete Mini Bio (4 min).
  • Ask students to think about the following questions:
    • How did he demonstrate leadership qualities?
    • How did he contribute to the world around them?
  • Summarize the video, highlighting the questions above by using a few responses from the students.

  • Display 5.03 HO Leaders Graphic Organizer.
  • Model completing the HO by using the information provided in 5.03. Clemente/J. Perez Teacher Model. Students assist with information from the clip.

Guided Practice

  • Divide students into pairs at individual computers.
  • Invite pairs to select 3 leaders from the list (ideally, all pairs choose different leaders) or select other Latino/a leaders.
  • Ask the following questions:
    • What leaders did you select to research?
    • What information is needed to fill out the graphic organizer? (i.e. birthplace and date, immigration story, leadership qualities/contributions, & how the leader has influenced me).

Independent Practice

  • The teacher will assist students in preparing for their research by: 
    • enlisting the help of the school librarian for appropriate resources
    • avoiding internet wandering by reviewing student’s topic, their keywords, and their plan
    • providing articles and online databases 
    • providing a list of hyperlinks to websites
  • Allow pairs time to use the internet to research the three leaders and fill out the information required.

  • If computers are unavailable, choose three leaders from 5.03 HO Leaders Graphic Organizer and print out biographies.  Divide students into three groups and have them rotate to stations to find out about each leader and record the facts they learn on the organizer.
  • Use Strategy Grouping: Partner high-skilled students with mid-level skilled students and/or partner mid-level skilled students with the students that have lower skills.

Extension

  • Instruct students who complete initial research quickly to choose additional leaders to research.
  • Give students additional time to research information or pictures of their three selected leaders.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can LIA help you develop leadership qualities like the leaders you researched?  Give specific examples.  

Language Enhancement

  • Watch 5.03 Video El Chavo Del Ocho in Spanish with English subtitles and have the students answer the following questions:
    • What does the teacher do well and how could the teacher improve as a leader and role model? (e.g., yells at the students, uses examples/demonstrations the students can understand, etc.)
    • Identify at least 2 phrases that were mistranslated in the English subtitles. Share the correct English translation.

Identify a leader and write a 5 paragraph essay using an essay outline guide for your research project.

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • complete an essay outline and a one-page informative paper on a leader of their choice.
  • analyze personal beliefs, mindsets, and stereotypes that are foundational for leadership (Self-Awareness)
  • develop stress management and coping skills (Self-Management)
  • increase understanding of ethical responsibility (Responsible Decision Making)

PREPARATION

  •  Digital Tools

MATERIALS

Main lesson
5.04 Essay Outline Guide 
5.04 R. Clemente/J. Perez Teacher Model

Adaptations
5.04 Editing & Proofreading Rubric 

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Courage
  • Sacrifice
  • Bravery
  • Commitment
  • Beliefs
  • Biography
  • Social Justice
  • Public Policy
  • Journalism

Purpose: To use this Five Corners skill-building activity to help a group continue building community through self-reflection and interpersonal dialogue (conversations) and build a foundation for courageous decision-making.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Five Corners activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview (7 min):  

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Before students arrive, post a set of quotes of courage around the room in areas where groups can gather for conversation. Quotes should be bilingual and from diverse international leaders who represent the population of the class. Share quotes about courage using the slide deck. 
  • After reading each quote aloud, pause for students to make their private choice of where they are going to go when you give the signal. Remind them to break into groups of no more than four, so everyone has a chance to speak, and ask that everyone be mindful that there is equity in sharing time. (Tell them groups of three are the limit if time necessitates.) When the sharing time is up, use your attention signal to bring the room to quiet, focused attention.
  • Sample Quotes:
    • “I am convinced that the truest act of courage...is to sacrifice ourselves for others in a totally non-violent struggle for justice.” — Cesar Chavez
    • "The original definition of courage is to tell the story of who you are with your whole heart.” ― Brené Brown
    • “Life shrinks or expands in proportion to one's courage.”   — Anais Nin
    • “Being deeply loved by someone gives you strength while loving someone deeply gives you courage.” - Lao Tzu
    • “If one has courage, nothing can dim the light that shines from within.” — Maya Angelou
  • Encourage one volunteer from each quote group to speak for themself about why they chose that quote.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to read and understand the thoughts of leaders from throughout the world? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about the beliefs and thoughts of leaders when working with other people? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Create trios in breakout rooms and each person says what their quote was and why they chose it.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson:
    • So far, in pairs, we have learned about many different Latino/Latina leaders and their contributions to the world around them.
  • Ask students the following questions:
    • What was the most interesting fact you learned about one of your chosen leaders?
    • What is one leadership quality they possess?
  • Explain to students:
    • This lesson will help you and your partner focus your research on one influential leader.  We will learn how to complete an outline and write an essay on the leader you have chosen.

  • Display the Essay Outline Guide on the electronic whiteboard.  
  • Model developing an Introduction and filling out the information for Paragraph I using complete sentences. Be sure to include the Topic Sentence and details A-D, which include information about birthplace, birthdate, & growing up years. Guided Practice

  • Guide the class to develop a Topic Sentence for Paragraph II and details A-D. Use complete sentences.

  • Instruct student pairs to identify the leader they want to write about.
  • Ask students to work together to complete an Essay Outline Guide.
  • Students may need to access the computer again to find more information on their chosen leader.

    • Demonstrate how to use the outline to create five paragraphs.
    • Assign students to write a five-paragraph essay at home using their outline.  Each student will do their essay independently and return it the next day.
    • Students will identify the Latino/Latina Leader for their research project and create a multimedia presentation by:
      • using their essay outline to create storyboards of the content 
      • determining the number of slides and plan the content for each slide
      • organize the content in order of events

  • Assign students to complete the essay in partnership in class. Use an additional day of instruction to offer more guided practice for the composition.  Follow-up with editing and proofreading activities for the essays.  See 5.05 HO Editing & Proofreading Rubric.
  • Students may write their essays in Spanish.

Extension

  • Assign students to create posters/visual aids/Powerpoint for their presentations.  Present leader presentations in Spanish to Spanish classes during Hispanic Heritage month (September 15-October 15).
  • Create student-friendly presentations and present to elementary schools where students attend tutoring sessions.
  • Ask student pairs to complete the five-paragraph essay in both Spanish and English.

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]PURPOSE

Present your research project and evaluate peer presentations utilizing the Presentation & Peer Evaluation Rubric.

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • present the life of one leader to a peer and the class
  • demonstrate self-confidence (Self-Awareness)
  • practice effective communication skills (Relationship Skills)
  • incorporate identification of social problems and ethical responsibilities (Responsible Decision-Making)

PREPARATION

  • Digital Tools 

MATERIALS

Main lesson
5.05 Essay Outline Guide 
5.05 R. Clemente/J. Perez Teacher Model
5.05 Presentation & Peer Evaluation Rubric

Adaptations
5.05 Oral Language Development
5.05 Editing & Proofreading Rubric  

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Rubric
  • Critical
  • Concise
  • Generalizations
  • Various
  • Enunciation
  • Originality

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Academic Vocabulary Buddies (AVB) tool to facilitate student interaction so that students will have specific partners for various activities throughout the period or week. This is a quick and easy way to create pairs for future partnered activities that offers a break from continually turning to an elbow partner.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Interacting with Academic Vocabulary Buddies (AVB) will further enhance students’ competencies of Relationship Skills, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Access the Academic Vocabulary Buddy handout and add 3-4 vocabulary words in the left-hand column that relate to characteristics that Latino/a/x leaders should possess when leading. These are more common words that have surfaced in Lessons 3 & 4. 
  • Distribute the AVB handout with the 3-4 words to each participant and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  • Instruct participants to stand up with their AVB papers and a pencil and move quietly around the room until you use your attention signal (could be music, chime, or bell), at which point they should stop and find a partner. Make sure that they select someone who they are not familiar with or from a different country of origin.
  • When everyone has a partner, ask them to make sure that they can pronounce each other’s first and last names properly. Sign each other’s paper on the vocabulary word in the space to the right. It is very important that they start with the same word. 
  • Give the signals to mix, stop, and find a new partner, making sure that they select someone whom they are not familiar with or from a different country of origin and that they pronounce each other’s first and last name properly. Check to be sure everyone has a new partner before you ask participants to sign each other’s papers on the second vocabulary line. Have partners mingle and pair up two more times until they have completed the activity.
  • After all lines are signed, invite participants to return to their seats.
  • Each time you need participants to form pairs during the lesson, have them take out their AVB and announce one of the vocabulary words to designate their partner for this activity. For example, if the first word is “Courage” then you would say “Now get together with your “Courage” AVB to reflect and discuss..." Do this as a practice exercise. 
  • You will use the AVB in the sections below in addition to any other LIA Lessons.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you signed up for your Academic Vocabulary Buddies? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to get to know other students who you do not know well or from a different country of origin? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about leadership? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer to access the Academic Vocabulary Buddies and facilitate a virtual AVB list. Manually place AVBs in Breakout Rooms to get to know each other and even practice reading their essays. Emphasize Norms of Virtual Collaboration and Shared Agreements.

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous week’s lesson.

  • Now that you have successfully researched and written about your chosen leader, today we are going to present our information to the class.
  • Ask students to practice reading their completed essay with their Academic Vocabulary Buddy for the first word.
  • Teacher Note: May need to forgo Current Event Bell Starter and Vocabulary on presentation days.  Links are provided as time permits.  The vocabulary provided for this lesson improves student understanding of the grading rubric, 5.05 HO Presentation & Peer Evaluation Rubric.

INSTRUCTION
