  • Display the Essay Outline Guide on an overhead projector or smartboard.  
  • Model presenting information about Clemente or Perez using R. Clemente/J. Perez Teacher Model.  
  • Instruct students to follow the outline guide as they present their information (i.e. introduction, birth & growing up years, immigration, contributions to society, and close the presentation by sharing a leadership quality and how this leader influences me).
  • Display and read Presentation & Peer Evaluation Rubric together.
  • Summarize grading procedures and demonstrate how to calculate points.
  • Explain that students will be evaluating their peers during the presentations.

Guided Practice

  • Distribute Presentation & Peer Evaluation Rubric.
  • Partner with students and have Student 1 present their leader to Student 2.  Student 2 will grade Student 1 using the rubric.  These should be different partnerships than before.
  • Give students time to share feedback with each other and fill out the rubric.
  • Instruct students to switch roles.
  • Collect the completed Presentation & Peer Evaluation Rubrics.  

Independent Practice

  • Select students will present their outline to the class.  (One student from each partnership will present since initial partnerships developed the outline together).

  • Review
    • Students finalize the multimedia presentation for their Latino/Latina Leader research project by:
      • using their essay outline to create storyboards of the content 
      • determining the number of slides and plan the content for each slide
      • organize the content in order of events
      • select a design for each slide
      • enter the content on each slide
      • add and format graphics, audio, video, animations, transitions
      • record a narration of information in English or Spanish
    • Wrap up by highlighting leadership qualities that were identified during student presentations.

  • Provide opportunities for students to present in English or Spanish.  Give students translating opportunities as well.
  • Invite students to act out their outlines or use the Think-Pair-Share model to highlight sections of their essay or chosen leader. View Oral Language Development for a more detailed description and additional ideas.

Extension

  • Extend this lesson an additional day and ask student partnerships to edit and proofread each other’s essay using Editing & Proofreading Rubric.
  • Students locate or make visual aids for their presentation.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Was it difficult to read your essay to your peer? Did sharing help you improve?
  • How did you and your partner decide who would present to the class?
  • Did you feel prepared to speak in front of your class? What made it difficult or easy?
  • Do you enjoy public speaking? Would more practice make it easier?  Why or why not?

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]PURPOSE

Discuss each of the LIA committee’s organization, responsibilities, and purpose, and use the LIA Leadership Selection Guidelines to elect leadership positions.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • learn about leadership styles  
  • learn the purpose and responsibilities of LIA leadership committees 
  • build an understanding of personal and collective agency (Self-management)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
  • determine common social goals and interests related to LIA leadership committees (Responsible Decision-Making)

PREPARATION

  • Digital Tools

5.06 Service

5.06 LIA Leadership Selection Guidelines

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Belonging
  • Qualities (personal)
  • Leader
  • Organization

  • Dependability
  • Reliability
  • Responsibility
  • Commitment

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To facilitate student interaction so that students will better understand the qualities of leadership and related behaviors such as dependability, responsibility, reliability, and commitment. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Understanding the meaning of dependability and associated behaviors will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Access the Academic Vocabulary Buddy handout and add the following seven vocabulary words in the left-hand column that relate to characteristics of dependability:
    • Dependable
    • Responsible
    • Reliable
    • Committed
  • Distribute the AVB handout with the 4 words to each participant and ask them to write their own name at the top of their paper.
  • Instruct participants to stand up with their AVB papers and a pencil/pen and move quietly around the room until you use your attention signal (could be music, chime, or bell), indicating that they should stop and find a partner. When everyone has a partner, ask them to make sure that they can pronounce each other’s first and last names properly. Sign each other’s paper on the vocabulary word in the space to the right. It is very important that they start with the same word.  
  • Give the signals to mix, stop, and find a new partner again until everyone has a partner for the 4 vocabulary words. 
  • After all lines are signed, invite participants to return to their seats and make sure that all the spaces have been filled out. They can repeat partners if it is a small group.
  • For the next five minutes call out the four of the words one by one and allow them 1 minute to discuss the meaning of each word. For example, if the first word is “Dependable” then you would say “Now get together with your “Dependable” AVB to reflect and discuss the meaning for one minute" Do this until you have covered all four words.
  • Use the AVB in the sections below in addition to any other LIA Lesson.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you signed up your Academic Vocabulary Buddies? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to get to know the meaning of “dependability” and other related words? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about being a leader? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer to access the Academic Vocabulary Buddies and facilitate a virtual AVB list. Manually place AVBs in Breakout Rooms to get to know each other and even practice the use of the vocabulary. Emphasize Norms of Virtual Collaboration and Shared Agreements.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Discuss the need for organization and leadership by discussing the following questions. Have students work with their Academic Vocabulary Buddy (first word):
    • What do you think would happen if the school did away with teachers, principals, and other leadership?
    • What if the president decided he no longer wanted to attend any of his meetings?
    • Why are organization and leadership important? 

Video

  • Watch Video Leadership (3.5 min)
  • Ask students to think about the following questions. Have students work with their Academic Vocabulary Buddy (second word):
    • What poor leadership decisions were made?
    • If you were assigned to lead this small group of birds, what changes would you make to help them be more successful?
    • In what ways does LIA place you in leadership positions and allow you to influence people in the school and community?

  • Display and discuss each committee’s purpose, responsibilities, and resources/ideas:
  • 5.06 LIA Leadership Committee Overview
    • Professionalism
    • Service
    • Social Activities
    • President, Historian, and Secretary
    • Explain that students will elect leadership positions and be placed on committees during the next class period. Reference LIA Leadership Selection Guidelines. Depending upon how the teacher chooses to run the election, it may extend into 2 or 3 class periods.

Model

  • Explain that each LIA student will participate in regular committee meetings.  
  • Ask the students what they picture an LIA Leadership Meeting to be like.
  • Demonstrate a model LIA meeting by using LIA Meeting Agenda Teacher Model.

Guided Practice

  • Students will use the LIA Meeting Agenda Outline for this activity.
  • Brainstorm and discuss as a class possible activities or events they can plan and execute within the school, community, and country.
  • Choose an activity then split into groups of 5-7 and hold a pretend LIA meeting using the above example handout as an agenda guide.

Independent Practice

  • Give the students time to try to plan an activity and then ask the students the following questions. Have students work with their Academic Vocabulary Buddy (third word).
    • Did anything unexpected happen?
    • Was it difficult to stay on topic?
    • How can good leaders make meetings more effective?

Activity

  • Challenge small groups of students to simulate a campaign for an assigned LIA leadership role by building arguments to support issues that are relevant to the specific role. Students research sample slogans to create a campaign slogan and digital poster.
  • Host a mock election based on the simulated campaign developed by the small groups of students. Students choose the electronic resource to be used for the voting process.

Discuss each of the LIA committee’s organization, responsibilities, and purpose, and use the LIA Leadership Selection Guidelines to elect leadership positions.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • hold individual leadership committee meetings
  • analyze beliefs, mindsets, and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  • understanding the impacts of developing self-discipline and self-motivation (Self-Management)
  • identify common social goals and interests (Social Awareness)

Purpose: To use Partner Reading as a strategy to facilitate student interaction so that students will learn more about leadership roles and responsibilities while reading together (Literacy Strategies for English Learners, Calderon 2016).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Understanding the meaning of Leadership while Partner Reading will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Social Awareness.

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas).
  • Use a grouping activity, such as Academic Vocabulary Buddies or Clock Buddies, to create pairs for this reading activity. In the case where there are ELs or struggling readers, intentionally pair these students with more proficient English speakers.  
  • Select a text or passage that is relevant to the topic of leadership. The text could also be a narrative, story, case study, or biography that is culturally representative of the students in the class. Make copies for each student.
  • Have students get together with their partner, face to face, with the reading passage. Decide which partner will be A and which will be B.
  • Explain the steps to Partner Reading. Model with a student  “reading by alternating sentences.” Remind them of their Shared Class Agreements regarding respect and patience. 
    • Partner A reads the first sentence
    • Partner B reads the next sentence
    • After each paragraph, partners verbally summarize what they read
    • Partners continue until they finish reading the section assigned
  • In the case where you have newcomers (NC), group the NC together with two higher-level ELs or native English speakers A & B. When A reads a sentence, the NC whisper-reads the sentence. When B reads a sentence, the NC reads along. The pattern is: A-NC-B-NC-A-NC-B-NC. This gives the NC double turns during each cycle.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in Partner Reading? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to learn about leadership while reading with a partner? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about leadership and the Partner Reading activity? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Manually place As, Bs, and NCs in Breakout Rooms to get to know each other and practice Partner Reading. Emphasize Norms of Virtual Collaboration and Shared Agreements.

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous lesson.

Yesterday, we discussed LIA committee organization, responsibilities, and purpose. Toda,y we will be electing leaders and forming committees. How are leaders elected or come to power in different nations?

Display Mexico, Philippines, and America’s presidential qualifications from Presidential Requirements. Ask the students the following questions:

  • How do the presidential qualifications differ between the countries?
  • How are they similar?
  • Why do you think countries have presidential requirements?
  • Why do you think LIA has leadership guidelines?

Leadership Committees

  • Review your chosen class election process and the LIA Leadership Selection Guideline.
  • Elect and announce the leaders and committee members.
  • As each class election process is different, the time needed may vary; please adjust the lesson accordingly.

Independent Practice

Students split into their committees. Pass out the corresponding LIA Leadership Overview handout to each committee (Professionalism, Service, Social Activities, and President/Historian/Secretary).

  • The committees do not have to use any of the ideas, but it gives them a bank of ideas to help them brainstorm.
  • Students may use the LIA Meeting Agenda Outline or create their own agenda.
  • Students have the remainder of class time to hold their first committee meeting.

  • Strategy Grouping: Partner high-skilled students with mid-level skills students and/or partner mid-level skilled students with lower skills students.
  • New committees and new LIA students may need more support in running a committee meeting. The teacher should sit in and guide the meeting as needed.

Extension

  • Explain to the class that some social platforms are designed specifically for professional networking. Colleges and employers look for individuals who stand out from other applicants. In order to set themselves up for college and career success, students will create a LinkedIn profile to post their skills, interests, LIA leadership roles, and accomplishments. Provide students with the LinkedIn Profile Checklist.
  • Go to the computer lab and invite the students to select additional countries and research the presidential qualifications. Have the students share with the class the presidential qualifications for their chosen country.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why do you think the United States has presidential qualifications?
  • If you could change the U.S. presidential qualifications, what changes would you make and why?

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]PURPOSE

Relate the videos within the lesson to those traits and characteristics needed to build trust and relationships within teams and classmates.  

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • develop trust within their groups through relationship-building strategies
  • develop understanding of social interdependence affects trust (Self-Awareness)
  • understand impacts of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • deepen understanding of collaborative problem-solving approaches (Relationship Skills)
  • explore the impacts of cultural competency on effective team building (Relationship Skills)

PREPARATION

  • Digital tools 

MATERIALS

Main lesson
5.08 First Follower Video
5.08 Dale Carnegie Quote
5.08 Vulnerability Quote
5.08 Dr. Brené Brown Video
5.08 Article: Why Vulnerability Can Be Your Biggest Strength
5.08 Article: The 13 Essential Traits of Good Friends

Adaptations

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Traits
  • Vulnerability
  • Trust
  • Respect
  • Influence

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use components of Developmental Relationships to help guide students to build trust within a team, establish close connections with their peers, cultivate abilities to shape their own lives, and learn how to engage with and contribute to the world around them (The Developmental Relationships Framework).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Understanding components of the Developmental Relationships Framework will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (3 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas).
  • Use a grouping activity such as Academic Vocabulary Buddies or Clock Buddies to create pairs for this engaging activity. In the case where there are ELs or struggling readers, intentionally pair these students with more proficient English speakers. 
  • Prepare five cards or sheets of paper with one of the five Elements on each paper from The Developmental Relationships Framework. Make sure that there is a different element with its Actions and Definitions on each page. Divide the number of students you have by 5 and make enough copies so that one student gets one card listing only one of the Elements. 
    • Express Care
    • Challenge Growth
    • Provide Support
    • Share Power
    • Expand Possibilities
  • Have pairs of students select (or handout) one of the Elements that differs from their partner’s Element.
  • Give them two minutes each to discuss the contents of their Element with their partner. Have students switch partners based on your pairing strategy and repeat the process as time permits. 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in sharing your feelings about the Elements of the Developmental Relationships activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to learn about building trust while sharing your thoughts with a partner? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about building trust through this activity? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Manually place pairs in Breakout Rooms to share their thoughts on the Elements. Emphasize Norms of Virtual Collaboration and Shared Agreements.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Show 5.08 First Follower Leadership Lessons Video. 
  • Note that the narration in this video is very good as it focuses on the idea of being a “first follower.” However,  teachers could mute this video and analyze it by providing their own narrative out loud:
    • How does the first dancing man react to the first person who tries to join him?
    • How did the dancing group get so large?
    • What conditions had to be in place for people to follow the leader?
    • Why do students follow or copy other students?
  • Explain to the class that building trust is essentially about creating friends and followers, and this is a critical skill leaders need to develop within their teams.

INSTRUCTION

Activity

(This activity can be structured for one class period or extended through multiple periods.)

  • Display and discuss this quote related to trust from Dale Carnegie, a well-known author on leadership principles. 
  • Plan the following “All About Me Bag” activity for one or more class periods as needed: 
    • Students choose a few objects which reveal things about themselves or are special in some way and bring them in to share with the class.
    • The teacher models this first by bringing in items special in his/her life and describing what the object is and what it represents, or why it is important. Items could include a photograph, a piece of sports equipment, a paintbrush, etc.
    • At this point, the activity may need to be continued in the following class period(s) to allow students to gather their own items.
    • Students can share their items in various ways — a few students can share each day, or students can share in small groups or with a partner, taking turns to ask each other questions. Question frames can be helpful for lower-level students. (For example, “Why did you pick _____?”) It may also be helpful for the teacher to remind students that very valuable items should be left at home, and students could instead draw or take a picture of the item to share.
  • Display this quote on vulnerability and building connections.
  • Ask students how they would define vulnerability and if they have any examples of this concept.
  • Explain that while we often look for ways to understand each other, we cannot forget that understanding ourselves is an important tool to building trust in a team.
  • Show this video by Brene Brown to start a discussion about vulnerability. You can also choose an alternate video from Brene Brown to show.
  • Use the exercises on this page to learn about and practice vulnerability. Make a list with students of examples of how we can be vulnerable.
  • Give students examples from your own experiences or model each of the principles.  

Guided Practice

  • Brainstorm the types of traits a leader or friend should have and encourage students to debate them. For example, if you want your friend to be honest, how honest should they be? Should they be honest enough to tell you:
    • That you have something in your teeth?
    • That your new outfit isn’t flattering?
    • That you did something wrong?
  • Consider this post, The 13 Essential Traits of Good Friends, to generate some ideas about what makes a good friend. 
  • Brainstorm and create a way to display these traits and their examples within the classroom.

  • Review
    • Assign each student, pair, or small group, to take one of the characteristics the class identified and to either discuss or research one way they could develop that skill. For example, for the idea of “ being caring” a student might say that leaders could make it a point to ask how each team member is each day and if there is anything they need.
    • Ask students to try one of the building trust principles (making friends, building unity)with another student or class outside LIA. After a set time period, ask that students be prepared to report their experiences.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiation Ideas/Extension

  • Follow the Leader (In-person/Google Meet/Zoom)
  • Brief the group. Explain that they will be playing the game Follow the Leader. The class is divided into two breakout groups. The teacher selects a leader for each group in this pattern-themed game/activity. This 1-2-minute activity can be conducted in a live virtual session or as a pre-recorded activity to avoid internet issues. Within the breakout rooms, the leader will perform gestures and patterns for the members of their group to practice and copy as quickly as possible (recorded). The two groups come back together in the main session to watch the game/activity. The objective of the game is for a guesser in the other breakout group to attempt to identify who is the originator or leader of the gestures and patterns. Repeat the activity to allow students to participate in the role of guesser, leader or follower.
  • Discussion:
    • What role was most challenging (guesser, leader, or follower)?
    • What effective team building skills did the leaders demonstrate?
    • How well did your group work as a team?
    • How could the activity have been improved?

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • In the video, The Biggest Myth About Vulnerability, why does Brené Brown explain that the first ASL symbol “weak in the knees” is not how she talks about vulnerability? How does the second ASL symbol embody her views about vulnerability?
  • Why is being trustworthy an important quality?
  • How does vulnerability benefit you as a leader?
  • How can being trustworthy and vulnerable help you build relationships?

Recognize servant leadership as leaders that impact the lives of others by giving of themselves.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • explore the concept of Servant Leadership and identify which characteristics accompany a true servant leader.

PREPARATION

  • Paper, pencil
  • Digital tools

MATERIALS

Main lesson

5:09 Image: Leaders Eat Last
5:09 Video: Simon Sinek US Marines Leadership Lesson
5:09 Servant Leadership Activity 1
5.09 Article: Karambir Kang
5.09 Article: Heroes of the Taj Hotel

Adaptations

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Selfless
  • Being
  • Empathy
  • Healing
  • Awareness
  • Persuasion

  • Stewardship

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Card Sorts activity to help develop a better understanding of servant leadership by having them share their thoughts with peers, establish close connections on the meaning of servant leadership, and cultivate abilities that would shape their own lives in becoming a servant leader (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook-optional).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: Exploring their thoughts about servant leadership with other students will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (5 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas).
  • Each student has four cards or sticky notes to write down their ideas about servant leadership.
  • Post the prompt “List four different characteristics of a servant leader, one characteristic per card. Provide an example of each.”  Students legibly write one idea per index card or sticky note (2 minutes).
  • Either assign or allow students to form groups of four and have them lay their cards out together on a table so that all group members can see them. Let them know they’ll be working as a team to group the ideas by listening respectfully to each person’s contributions. 
  • Groups read all the cards and then decide together how they want to sort them into categories that emerge from their conversation. Remind the groups to work toward equity of voice and take turns moving the cards into a variety of categories. The goal is to hear and understand a variety of ideas; there are no “wrong answers.” 
  • Have students share what patterns and meaningful categories they found, the challenges of the process, and the strategies they used to accomplish the task.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in sharing your opinions about servant leadership? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to learn about becoming a servant leader? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about servant leadership through this activity? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Manually place pairs in Breakout Rooms to share their thoughts about servant leadership. Emphasize Norms of Virtual Collaboration and Shared Agreements.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin the class by showing students image one 5.09 Image: Management Hierarchy and image two 5.09 Image: Leaders Eat Last. Ask them if they can explain what these images are saying about leadership.
  • Share the following clip from 5.09 Video: Simon Sinek US Marines Leadership Lesson and their practice of “officers eat last.”
  • Use the short activity found on page three of the 5.09 HO Servant Leadership Activity material to further introduce this topic. You may modify some of the questions for your specific class.
  • Explain to the class that the purpose of today’s lesson is to understand what it means to be a “servant” while being a leader. It may be different than what they typically think of when they think about leadership.

  • Use the following articles to read about Karambir Kang, the general manager of the Taj Hotel during a terrorist attack:
    • 5.09 Article: Karambir Kang has kept away from his family suite on Taj’s sixth floor
    • 5.09 Article: Heroes Of The Taj Hotel: Why They Risked Their Lives
  • Share Karambir’s actions with the students and discuss how the employees’ actions reflect a servant leadership attitude.

Guided Practice

  • Post or hand out the following terms with their definitions. You may want to review them as a class before continuing. Divide your class into groups and have them rank these characteristics of a servant leader in order of importance. Allow a spokesperson from each group to share and defend their top three choices.
  • Characteristics of a Servant Leader:
    • Selfless (puts the group or organization before the needs of self)
    • Being a good listener
    • Empathy (putting themselves in someone else’s shoes)
    • Healing (trying to make things better in the group)
    • Awareness (knowing what is needed by others)
    • Persuasion (using skill to bring others to agreement on what is best)
    • Vision (what is the long-term goal for the group?)
    • Stewardship (being ethical to keep the trust of the group to be able to pass on knowledge, resources, etc.)
    • Commitment to the growth of others (empowerment—helping others to grow by not keeping information, etc.)

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

  • Review
    • This review involves an ongoing activity. Review with students the goal to become servant leaders. Explain that to do this, we must know what servant leadership is, identify servant leadership in others, and make it a part of our own behavior. Challenge students to begin looking for examples of servant leadership wherever they are- at school, home, church groups, the store, the news, etc. They should look for people who:
      • Listen
      • Include everyone
      • Create a community
      • Dream great dreams
      • See the best in everyone
      • Try to understand others
      • Put others before themselves
      • Help to change things for the better
    • Allow for or designate opportunities to share these examples with the class. You may also want to share examples in your life to model this process for your students.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Extension

  • Instagram – Servant Leadership
    • Discuss with students the characteristics of a servant leader. Have students analyze their personal Instagram accounts and discuss what theme/purpose they are trying to communicate to their followers through images and videos. Explain to students how to use social media in professional ways. Create a class Instagram account for the theme of Servant Leadership. 
  • Students will use Instagram to record their tutoring experiences with the elementary school. (Review with student’s school privacy policies when sharing photos or images of other students). Students will use images and short videos to document their experiences in service learning/tutoring. Students will engage their followers by describing who, what, when, where, why, and how. Students will share their tutoring strategies when working with the elementary school children and create a virtual learning community among LIA students in other schools and other states.

Journal Entry Suggestions:

  • What do you think is the hardest part about being a good leader?
  • Can leaders ever follow other people—or do they always need to lead?  Why or why not?
  • Does a good leader take risks, or does a good leader play it safe in order to protect his or her team?  Why?

Differentiate between the three types of communication tools: Verbal, Written, and Body Language.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • develop strategies to communicate while in leadership roles
  • explore perspective-taking (Social Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision Making)

PREPARATION

  • Digital tools

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Fishbowl activity to strengthen listening skills and encourage everyone to participate in a class discussion. It can be used during a session to discuss content, or at the end of an engagement to give airtime to everyone about what they learned or found useful. Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The Fishbowl activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview (10 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • In this Fishbowl activity, participants are divided into two groups that are seated in concentric circles, all facing the center. The outside circle listens while the inside group has a discussion about a topic. Then the groups switch places so the listeners become the speakers, and vice versa. 
  • Make sure the audience knows you will hold them accountable for sharing their observations. Use equity sticks (a cup of sticks with each student’s name on one) to increase audience participation and accountability.
  • Provide the question prompt or discussion topic. These would vary depending on the theme of the lesson. The prompts for this activity would be: 
    • What are the characteristics of good communication skills?
    • What are some of the negative consequences of poor communication skills?
  • Only the inside group members may speak during this time (4 minutes). Instruct the outside group to quietly listen and notice their own ideas that surface during the discussion. Note-taking on a graphic organizer may be helpful.
  • When the time is up, ask the groups to trade places so that the outside group is sitting on the inner circle chairs and vice versa. Set the timer again for four minutes and let the new inside group discuss the topic.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore communication skills? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about communication skills? (Responsible Decision Making)

*Virtual Adaptation: Divide students into two groups on paper, Group 1 and Group 2. Either assign students a number or ask them to choose a group to belong to. Have them write their number on a card. Those with the number “1” will hold up their cards to the screen and they will symbolically be in the inner circle. Call their names using the equity sticks for them to share thoughts on the prompts. Switch numbers for the next group.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin the class by showing students examples of communication gone wrong from Communication Pictures.
  • Share with students an example in your life where something was miscommunicated and what the consequences were.  Ask students if they have any examples to share.
  • Explain to the class that leaders must be experts at communication and that this lesson will focus on three types of powerful (for good or bad) communication tools. The three types are: Verbal (Conflict Resolution), Written (Text and Email), and Body Language.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity and Guided Practice

  • Review examples of passive-aggressive text messages from Jimmy Kimmel Explains Passive Aggressive Texts or Here’s What 12 Passive Aggressive Texts Really Mean. Ask students to decipher the text message responses.
  • Explain the term “passive-aggressive” as a trait where someone avoids direct confrontation or exhibits indirect resistance. This is a classic example of poor communication skills.
  • Explain the opposite of passive-aggressive is being assertive or being able to state your opinion and needs in a calm and positive way.
  • Use the following sites to discuss how students should respond to the scenarios. Try to identify patterns or keywords to write on the board that best describe assertive behavior:
    • Assertiveness: Role Plays and Sample Situations
    • Assertiveness Role-Plays for Adolescents 12 to 14 Years Old
    • Negotiation and Conflict Resolution Activities 
  • Body language is an important way we communicate messages. Scientists say that approximately 70% of our communication is actually non-verbal.
  • Check out lists of positive vs negative body language. Assign different terms to students or as a class review each term, demonstrate it, and determine if it is a positive or negative signal.
  • Have students demonstrate the following body language characteristics of a leader: How Your Body Language Can Tell People You’re a Leader—or Not

  • End class acting as if you are an administrator/staff member and you are wrapping up a meeting you have had with an LIA student regarding an activity or service project.
    • “Well thank you for meeting with me this morning about your parent night activity you are planning. Even though this will take place after school in the evening, I trust that you will take the necessary steps to make sure it runs smoothly and that the room you are using will be well taken care of. Of course let me know if there is anything else I can help with.”
  • Have students send you a thank you or follow-up email that demonstrates professionalism (Thank you, review of what was discussed, what commitments were made, and a plan for follow-up)

  • Podcast Activities – Perspective Writing and Storytelling Whole Class. Podcast should be no longer than 7-10 minutes long.
  • Discuss with students the idiomatic expression to “walk a mile in someone else's shoes.” Explain what it means to have empathy and the ability to take another person’s point of view. Describe how a person’s upbringing, culture, and environment impact their personality, behavior, and perspectives. Students will learn to better understand what they do, how they think, and what they believe.
  • Storytelling: The teacher and students will work together to write about a past event or circumstance that has changed how they see their school, community, or the world.
  • One or more student volunteers will read the final story out loud for a class audio podcast.

Extension

  • Podcast Activities – Perspective Talking by Interviewing in Student Pairs. Podcast should be no longer than 7-10 minutes long.
    • Discuss with students the idiomatic expression to “walk a mile in someone else's shoes.” Explain what it means to have empathy and the ability to take another person’s point of view. Describe how a person’s upbringing, culture, and environment impact their personality, behavior, and perspectives. Students will learn to better understand what they do, how they think, and what they believe.
    • Interviewing: Students will choose a prompt/discussion topic for their audio podcast. Students work in pairs to develop and practice questions and answers for the interview. Students will identify an issue they feel strongly about (e.g., culture, discrimination, politics, immigration, education, etc.).
    • Students will interview each other and share how their own experiences have impacted their perspectives in some situations.
    • The pairs will contribute their recorded story to a class audio podcast. 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How would you describe your communication style? 
  • Why is it important for a leader to be assertive rather than passive-aggressive?

Recognize the difference between professionalism and unprofessionalism.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • understand four concepts of professionalism and how they can be applied to their work.

PREPARATION

  • Digital tools

MATERIALS

Main lesson
5:11 Image: Tattooed Doctor
5:11 Video: Professional Behavior
5:11 Video: Front Desk First Impressions
 

Adaptations

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Professionalism
  • Ethics
  • Perception
  • Responsibility
  • Team oriented
  • Interpersonal Skills
  • Problem-Solving Skills

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use this professionalism activity to strengthen students’ skills in being more responsible, team-oriented, and to possess strong communication, interpersonal, and problem-solving skills. Students will rate themselves and their own professional actions which will give them the opportunity to reflect on the positive behaviors they demonstrate, and to how these behaviors impact others.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The professionalism activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview (10 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Make a copy of the list of professional skills and personal ratings below on a sheet of paper and hand it out to students.
    • I get to school on time. If I am going to be late, I try to let a friend or someone in the school know.
      [Always • Sometimes • Never]
    • I rarely miss my homework. If I am going to miss my homework, I try to ask for help or let the teacher know.
      [Always • Sometimes • Never]
    • I work as hard as I can.
      [Always • Sometimes • Never]
    • I am friendly to students in the school.
      [Always • Sometimes • Never]
    • I try to solve problems with other students rather than ignoring them or getting angry.
      [Always • Sometimes • Never]
    • I follow safety and school rules.
      [Always • Sometimes • Never]
  • Ask students to rate themselves on behaviors that are typically thought of as “professional” in the workplace but that they would need to practice while still in school. Encourage students to be honest.
  • Either assign or allow students to form groups of two or three. 
  • Taking one skill at a time, ask the group to share in a round-robin style how they rated their skills and why.
  • Ask students to select one area that they would want to improve on and share with the group.
  • Ask for volunteers to share one example with the rest of the class and how would they improve on this skill. 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore professional skills while still in school? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about professional skills today? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Assign students to a Breakout room in groups of two or three to complete the activity on professionalism. They can share in the larger group.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Open by asking students to imagine visiting a doctor/surgeon and to describe what type of person they would expect to walk in as the doctor. How would they be dressed?
  • Show students the image on the right side of Tattooed Doctor. Ask how they would feel if the tattooed man was their doctor or teacher.
  • Now show the class the full image, with both photos side by side. Explain that this man is actually a real doctor in New York, and it is not that tattoos are bad, but that appearance matters depending on the time and place. This is a concept called professionalism.
  • Explain to the class that the level of respect they receive at work or school is connected to the level of professionalism they choose to display. LIA believes in a professionalism model called L.E.A.D. or Language, Ethics/Example, Appearance, and Dependability.

INSTRUCTION

  • Show examples of poor professionalism and discuss how the people involved could have reacted differently. You can use the video below or pull your own. YouTube is unfortunately full of videos of professionals behaving badly. While the example below focuses on an office setting, there are many other examples depending on the age level of your class and your overall discretion that you can use.
  • Use part or all of the video Professional Behavior for your class discussion.
  • Be sure to point out why unprofessional behavior can be damaging for business or perception. Do you have any stories to relate about experiences you have had? Also note, that many times people are not naturally unprofessional, but every moment counts when working with others as they will form impressions of you within the first few seconds.
  • Explain that doctors, soldiers, police officers, lawyers, teachers, etc. can lose their jobs for “unprofessional behavior.”

Guided Practice

  • Divide your class into four groups and assign each group one of the L.E.A.D. terms. This project could be extended for more than one class period. Working together each group should:
  • Research and then write their own definition for the term
  • Create some way of demonstrating this term for the rest of the class. This could be a skit, poster, PowerPoint, PSA, etc. It could be examples of poor professionalism related to their term but should focus on how it applies to their work as LIA students. *This activity could be framed around LIA students and tutoring.
  • Students will present their work to the class

  • Review
    • Show the video Front Desk First Impressions and ask students to try and identify as many unprofessional behaviors as they can (At the 4:15 mark the video reviews all the unprofessional behavior examples).

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Differentiated Ideas/Extension

  • Quizlet/Kahoot Review: The teacher will create and use terms, definitions, images, and videos in a digital game format to review the four concepts of professionalism: L.E.A.D. - Language, Ethics/Example, Appearance, and Dependability.  
  • Students will answer questions related to professionalism in an exciting digital environment. The games can include examples of whether or not it represents one of the four concepts of professionalism. (e.g., a person poorly dressed during a virtual interview ≠ appearance). The digital game format is a shared experience where students respond at the same time. Results from the game allow teachers to assess whether or not students understand the concepts. 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What type of professional behavior is expected during the LIA tutoring?
  • Write down your thoughts about the phrase “You never get a second chance at a first impression.”
  • What are some professional behaviors that you would like to improve in yourself? How will you become better in these aspects?
  • How can you and your LIA classmates support each other to be professionals in your class, school, and community?

Purpose: To use this delegation activity to strengthen students’ understanding of the importance of delegating tasks, and to get others to participate in accomplishing goals. Students will evaluate a scenario and explore ways they can be more involved in assisting others in completing tasks.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: The delegation activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview (10 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Copy the parable below and hand it out to students. 

DELEGATION: A Parable

Once upon a time, there was a little red hen who owned a wheat field. “Who will help me harvest the wheat?” she asked.

“Not I,” said the pig. “I don’t know how.” 

“Not I,” said the cow. “I’m too clumsy.” 

“Not I,” said the dog. “I’m busy with some other things.” 

So the little red hen did it herself.“Who will help me grind the wheat into flour?” she asked. 

“Not I,” said the pig. “That is another vocation in which I am untrained.” 

“Not I,” said the cow. “You can do it much more efficiently.” 

“Not I, “ said the dog. “I’d love to, but I’m involved in some matters of greater urgency. Some other time, perhaps.”

So she did it herself.“Who will help me make some bread?” asked the little red hen. Again all declined... so she did it herself.

That evening when guests arrived for her big dinner party, she had nothing to serve except bread. She had been so busy doing work that could have been done by others that she had forgotten to plan a main course, prepare a dessert, or even set the table.

Moral: A good leader will find a way to involve others to the extent of their ability. To do the whole thing yourself is to “chicken out!”

  • Use a pairing strategy such as Clock Buddies or Academic Vocabulary Buddies to have students work with a partner. 
  • Have them partner read the Parable, where one student reads the part of the little red hen and the other student reads the part for the other animals. Discuss the meaning of the moral of the story as it relates to the Parable.
  • Questions for students to answer:
    • Why didn’t the other animals want to help the little red hen?
    • What could have the little red hen said or done differently to get the other animals involved? 
    • If the other animals had assisted with the tasks, what more could she have done to prepare for the dinner?
    • What lessons can be learned about delegation from this Parable?
    • Which classroom routines can the teacher delegate to the students in order to get them more involved? 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore delegating tasks in order to accomplish more? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about delegating? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Assign students to a Breakout room to complete the activity on delegation. They can share in the larger group.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Apollo 13: Give the class a quick summary of the Apollo 13 mission. Note to students that these scenes are at a point where things are going wrong and strong leadership and delegation were needed to see the mission through. After viewing, ask students to point out specific moments of strong leadership examples.
    • Apollo 13 (1995) clip: Failure is not an option.
    • Apollo 13 (1995) clip: Square peg in a round hole
  • Explain to the class that today’s lesson is on a specific leadership function called “delegating.” Define the term and note that the best leaders in today’s world have mastered this skill.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Activity

  • Consider the following video from a Steve Jobs interview.
    • It might be effective to demonstrate how powerful Apple became under Jobs’ leadership. His style of working with people has been extremely effective.
  • Display the following image and ask students why people choose not to delegate. 
  • Discuss examples of how to delegate.

Guided Practice

  • Use the following activity to demonstrate the idea of delegation and working as a leadership team. Modify this activity according to your class’s resources.
  • You will need a designated separate area so that people can’t see or overhear one another, and 1 multi-page comic/children’s book with words and illustrations.
  • Divide students into groups of at least 5. Each group will consist of 1 leader and 2 mid-level managers with at least 1 junior employee per manager. Each manager and his or her employees constitute a department. One department handles pictures; the other handles text.
  • The leader can communicate only with the 2 mid-level managers.
  • Junior employees can communicate only with their assigned manager.
  • Managers aren’t allowed to overhear or look at the work done by the other manager or their junior employees. In other words, the “Pictures” and “Text” departments are completely segregated.
  • Only the leader can view the comic/children’s book – and only when alone. While communicating intentions to the managers, the leader must depend on a remembered idea. Between questions from the managers, the leader can review the original document, which he’s trying to get the junior employees to reproduce.
  • The leader is not allowed to make notes or communicate except aloud. Managers are not allowed to take notes – only listen to orders and ask for clarification. The leader is not allowed to view the work of junior employees.
  • The leader’s job is to describe the comic book separately to the “Picture” manager and the “Text” manager. They can each return to ask questions as many times as necessary. But at the end of the process, when time runs out, the book that resides in the leader’s head should be reconstituted by the separate work of these 2 subgroups.
  • At the end, debrief with students by allowing each role (leader, manager, employee) to discuss their challenges with the activity. As a class, develop key lessons learned in relation to how delegation and communication happen between members.

    • Note with students that the “secret sauce” to delegation is the follow-up with praise, if the task is performed appropriately. Use the following article to review five ways to give effective praise. Demonstrate examples for your students, i.e., if you have recently completed a project, ask students to give their own.   • Delegation is an ethical responsibility leaders owe to themselves, those with whom they work, and their organization. Briefly review the roles of each member within the LIA Leadership Committees (Professionalism, Service, Social Activities, President, Historian, and Secretary). Allow each committee to meet in breakout rooms or in-person to discuss ideas to support the goals of each committee. Each member of the hierarchy will openly share ideas to promote college and career readiness, social activities, community-building activities, and a positive social media presence. Committees will brainstorm how to delegate these activities to volunteers or appointees to ensure that all members can grow and benefit from the responsibility. Create a project outline with deadlines to post on the digital classroom page and calendar.  

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Do you find it difficult to delegate tasks to others? Why?
  • Do you trust others to complete key tasks?
  • What key tasks are delegated to you for the LIA tutoring?

Purpose: To use this Gallery Walk activity to help students brainstorm a topic that would be a goal of a student-run committee. Like viewers at an art gallery, small groups of students will rotate from poster to poster, stopping to view, discuss, and add ideas at each station (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Gallery Walk activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Relationship Skills.

Overview (15 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Establish a specific goal that would be a topic of discussion of a student-run committee, such as, "How can we make our school environment safer for students?"
  • Hang four posters with headings that relate to the specific topic of discussion around the room such as “In the Classroom,” "Between Classes," "At Dismissal" and "During Lunch."
  • Divide the class into four groups, give each group a marker, and assign each group to one of the posters. Explain the overarching question, and what each of the poster topics is.
  • Allow groups to stand at each poster for three minutes to share, discuss, and write down their responses to the category.
  • When time is up, ask the groups to rotate clockwise so each group is in front of a new poster to continue the activity. Each group now reads the offerings of the previous authors, using sticky notes to add clarifying questions or comments/compliments. Rotate every three to five minutes, until every group has visited every poster.
  • Next, allow time for individuals to silently walk around the room and read the completed posters, noting ideas that they agree with or that seem like something they'd like to try.
  • The original group revisits their feedback and can add to their poster.
  • Use this information as the first project once a student-run committee is formed.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ideas using the Gallery Walk strategy? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about the Gallery Walk process? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

Virtual Adaptation: Design four Google Docs with the headers mentioned above with a table with links to the Google Doc. Post the link to the table so that all of the students have access to it. Divide the class into four groups and send them to separate breakout rooms. Assign each group to begin at a different starting point and assign a time in which they will change to the next Google Doc topic. All students will access the doc and add comments at the same time. The teacher alerts each Breakout room when to rotate. Return to the large meeting and post each Google Doc for all to see.

  • Show one of the following videos: Example of a Dysfunctional Meeting or Why Everyone Hates Bad Meetings.
  • Ask students if they can relate to the personalities in this video with experiences they have had working in groups. Can they identify additional challenges?
  • As a teacher can you point out examples from a group you have? A club, team, faculty meeting, and even your own class? (Who is the social medialite, always late, the class clown, then fervent note-taker, etc.?)
  • Review the strategies your committees can use that encourage all students to participate. Choose one that you would like to use/practice in your LIA committees.
    • Think-Pair-Share
    • Last Word
    • My Two Cents

Guided Practice

  • Review and agree upon the possible roles students can have in a committee. Some options are:
    • Secretary- A person who keeps copies of all documents and submissions
    • Scribe/Recorder- The person who writes the minutes and/or completes the agenda.
    • Spokesperson- A person who reports to the teacher or class if needed
    • Time Keeper- Makes sure the group is aware of the time and pacing of the meeting
    • Runner- A person who runs to ask questions or gather materials
    • Explorer- A person who speaks with or asks questions of others outside the LIA classroom
    • Facilitator- The person who opens the meeting and guides the discussion
  • Allow students to create a poster or display that defines these roles and makes them visible to the class:
    • Weblink: group roles

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use the Attention Signal skill-building activity to bring the group’s attention back to the facilitator or team leader during a meeting. A well-practiced and consistently implemented attention signal is essential in group learning, interactive team meetings, and special project situations. Whether adults or students, any gathering of engaged participants is going to be deeply immersed in meaningful, task-oriented conversations during which you will need to get their attention. (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional)

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Attention Signal activity will further enhance the students’ competencies of Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (8 min):

  1. Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  2. There are many versions of attention signals (flashing the lights, clapping, raising or lowering your voice) but one that has been most consistently effective is to raise your hand in the air and wait for everyone else in the room to raise their own hand and be silent before you proceed with directions, information or the next agenda item.
  3. The teacher explains: When you see me raise my hand, you’ll have two jobs. One is to raise your hand too. That gives others around you a visual cue that they should quietly look my way. The other is to bring your conversation to a close. That will help the room quickly become silent so you can hear the next direction or announcement.
  4. Allow students to self-select into teams of three. Once they cluster in a group, have them come up with topics or themes that are of greatest interest to them at the time. Select up to five themes and post them on the board or screen. Another option is to post a teacher-made list.
  5. Have students select one of the topics they will discuss with their group of three. Each one selects a different topic. 
  6. To determine the order in which students will discuss their topic, have them arrange their first names alphabetically. They will proceed in alphabetical order. 
  7. Begin the activity by holding your hand up and dropping it as if signaling the beginning of a race. Each student will have 60 seconds to talk about the topic of choice. After the first 60 seconds raise your hand and wait until all students give you their full attention. Drop your hand down to begin the second round of sharing. Repeat the activity for the third round. 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore attention-getting signals? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about attention-getting signals? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: This activity does not lend itself well to a virtual environment.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Link the idea behind an agenda by introducing students to a map of a theme park and ask students why the park provides these to their guests. Ask students who have been to large parks to describe their experience walking around and trying to find attractions. Is there an advantage at Disneyland if you know where you are going and what you are doing? Use this Disneyland Map as an example. 
  • Share any experiences where you did not have clear directions or a destination point.
  • Explain to students that today’s lesson will focus on using an agenda as a tool to know where they are going in their classroom activities.

  • Show the video Effective Meetings that highlights how agendas are meant to avoid the very reasons people often don’t like meetings.
  • Use one or both of the following sample agendas: Trevor Beck's Meeting Agenda Sample; 5.06 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Teacher Model.    
  • Explain to the students that an agenda is their map for their committee meetings.
  • Explain the parts of an agenda and what each space should be used for.

Guided Practice

  • Demonstrate to students that they have likely interacted with agendas in other activities outside of school. Programs handed out for performances, funerals, and church are all types of agendas. 
  • Show students a few different examples of agendas:
    • Summer Day Camp Agenda Example
    • Music Recital Program Example
    • Funeral Program Example
  • As a class or in smaller groups, have the students analyze the differences between the 3 Examples above. Use the following questions to help guide the discussion:
    • Is the speaker identified?
    • Are time limits identified?
    • Do they specify people’s roles?
    • Are topics written out?
    • Which agenda do they like best?
  • Display 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline.
  • Lead students in filling out 5.01 HO LIA Meeting Agenda Outline to plan a service project or activity as a class. A great starting point could be your upcoming parent night activity.

  1. All committees should agree on the format of an electronic shared agenda that will be used for all meetings (Google Docs, OneDrive, etc.). Students can add items, comments, and notes before, during, and after each meeting. At the end of the meeting, students can rate how they felt the meeting went using an electronic survey. 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can using an agenda helps to guide committee meetings?
  • Why is it important for everyone's voice to be heard in a meeting?
  • Why do you think it is important to prepare and follow an agenda during a meeting?
