INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch Video Literacy is Like Velcro (4 min).
  • Ask the following questions:
    • What does the figurative language imply about the relationship between literacy and Velcro? (“The more that you have, the more learning sticks to you.”)
    • Do you agree with this?  Why or why not?  
    • Can you think of an example where this applies?
  • Explain: Literacy affects all aspects of our lives.  You have the opportunity to make a difference in the lives of the students you tutor by helping them develop stronger literacy skills.  In order to do that, you need to have a strong understanding of literacy and the skills students need to become better readers.
  • Teacher Note: You may want to only introduce literacy, imply, and tutoring during the vocabulary instruction.  Students will take an in-depth look at phonemes, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, and comprehension during the application section of the lesson.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Model

  • Introduce the “Big Five” components of reading instruction by explaining the following:
    • The most basic definition of literacy is the ability to read and write.  In order for students to be successful in school and life, they need to be strong readers.  Students require instruction in five main areas to learn to read.  Because you will be tutoring students, you need a good understanding of each of these areas.  
    • The “Big Five” areas of reading instruction include phonemic awareness, phonics, fluency, vocabulary, & comprehension.
    • Today we are going to do a jigsaw activity.  We will have five groups within our classroom and each group will research one of the “Big Five” components/areas of reading instruction.  Each group will then share with the class the meaning and importance of their assigned component.
  • Display Literacy Definition.  
  • Divide students into five groups and assign each one a reading component/area.
  • Assign a group leader in each group and ask the group leader to read their group’s definition aloud from Literacy Definition.
  • Distribute “Big Five” Reading Components to each student.

Guided Practice

  • Each student group needs access to at least one computer or electronic device.
  • Instruct student groups to use the web link associated with their topic to fill out the information needed on “Big Five” Reading Components.
  • Remind students to briefly summarize information and not copy the text directly from the weblink.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Instead of watching the video clip in the relevancy/background section students will participate in a writing response activity.  Write the word “Literacy” on the board.  Ask students to brainstorm words that define literacy.  Record student responses.  Display Literacy Quotes 1 or Literacy Quotes 2.
    • Choose a quote to write about. Address the following in your quick write: 1) describe what you think the quote means 2) state whether you agree or disagree with the quote 3) give examples from your life, society, or current events as evidence for your statement.
    • You will have five minutes.
  • Ask students to share their responses.  Add other phrases to the definition of literacy.
  • If teachers wish to conduct the application/engagement activity in smaller groups or if the class has a large number of students, assign two groups to each reading component.

Extension

  • Follow this lesson with explicit instructions on how to tutor elementary students.  Many districts/schools have developed their own cross-age tutoring program.  Follow your district’s recommendation.  Districts may provide training for your students.  If a tutoring program is not available, refer to the LIA Elementary Partnership Booklet, 2017

 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Write and describe two things you learned about reading during this lesson that you didn’t know before.  Include real-life examples in your descriptions.

  • Watch Video Service Learning Definition (1 min).
    • What is service learning?
    • Have any of you participated in service learning activities before?  What were they?
    • What do you think you learned from these activities?
    • How did you benefit the school or community?
  • Today we are going to learn more about service learning and brainstorm ideas for service learning projects we can do in our school or community.

Model: Brainstorm

  • Display 6.02 Weblink “Learning by Doing” (p. 2) Environmental Topics.
  • Discuss the five points emphasized in “What is Service Learning”? 
  • Discuss the points emphasized in 6.02 Video Service Learning Definition and how they relate to the  6.02 Weblink “Learning by Doing”. Use the environmental topics listed to generate ideas for possible service activities. 
  • Explain that students will have the opportunity to propose a service learning project in groups.
  • Display Service Learning Brainstorm.
  • Introduce the four different types of service learning projects.
  • Share the teacher model examples.

Guided Practice: Brainstorm

  • Divide students into groups of four.
  • Distribute  Service Learning Brainstorm.
  • Give students 5-10 minutes to produce as many ideas as possible.

Model: Proposal Form

  • Stop brainstorming activity.
  • Instruct groups to choose their favorite service learning project.
  • Display Service Learning Proposal Form Template.
  • Discuss each section of the Project Proposal Template.  Teacher Note:  Ideally, this activity/process has been previously modeled during the formation of leadership committees.

Guided Practice: Proposal Form

  • Instruct student groups to fill out the template with their groups.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Watch Video Youth Making a Difference (4 min).
  • Ask students:
    • If you had no limitations in what you could do to make an impact in this country or your native country, what would it be?
  • Introduce service learning by discussing what changes students would want to see to make improvements in the state or country. Ask the following questions: 
    • What are some problems you see?
    • Do you know of an issue where you want to make your voice heard?
  • Explain: Today we are going to research different topics or issues that are relevant to you and identify what you can do to make a difference.

Model: Brainstorm

  • Display Service Learning Brainstorm (Country)
  • Introduce the three different areas to help students brainstorm ideas.
  • Share the teacher model examples.

Guided Practice: Brainstorm

  • Divide students into groups of three to four.
  • Distribute Service Learning Brainstorm (Country).
  • Allow student groups computer access to research issues.
  • Give students 5-10 minutes to produce as many ideas as possible.

Model: Project Proposal

  • Stop brainstorming activity.
  • Instruct groups to choose their activity.
  • Display Service Learning Proposal Form Template (Country).
  • Discuss each section of the Project Proposal Template.  Encourage letter or email contact.  Teacher Note:  Ideally, this activity/process has been previously modeled during the formation of leadership committees and/or 6.02 Impacting Your Community.

Guided Practice: Project Proposal

  • Distribute Service Learning Proposal Form Template (Country).
  • Instruct student groups to fill out the template with their groups.

Review

  • Ask student groups to share aloud their chosen service learning project or activity.
  • Collect or ask students to submit their Service Learning Proposal Form Template (Country)  for teacher review and approval.
  • Explain to students that during the next class period, the class will vote on the group proposal.  The class will combine their efforts and be given time to write letters or contact leaders of organizations about their cause.

INTRODUCTION

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain: Yesterday all of you found worthy issues or causes to pursue in areas that you want to make a difference.  Today we are going to vote on the cause that we will pursue together.  With our combined efforts, we can make more of a difference than pursuing our causes on our own.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Activity

  • Instruct students to sit with their groups.
  • Each group should appoint a group leader to share their issue or cause.
  • Use the Service Learning Proposal Form Template (Country) (completed) to share all main points of the proposal (Roman Numerals I-V).  Students should explain if this proposal is to contact state or national leaders regarding an issue, or if they have chosen to raise money for an organization.  All groups should present.
  • Instruct students to write on a piece of paper which group’s proposal they would like to pursue for the class project.
  • Read the votes to determine the proposal with the highest votes.

Model

  • Ask the group leader of the winning proposal to write the contact information for all students to include in their individual letters.
  • Model letter writing using Sample Letter to Your Senator (click on the link & it downloads a Word document that can be edited) and/or Letter Template depending on the issue/cause.
  • Discuss what information should be included in each paragraph.

Teacher Note:  Students may need additional time to research the issue to enable them to write knowledgeable letters.  Teachers may need to provide additional resources depending on the topic.

Guided Practice

  • Instruct students to begin writing a letter using the Letter Template.

Independent Practice

  • Students may complete their individual letters as a homework assignment.
  • Remind students to edit and proofread their letters as well.

Review

  • Debrief by asking the students the following questions:
    • Why do you feel _______________ (the issue/cause students are addressing) is important enough to contact ____________________________?
    • What should be our next steps in following up with our letters?
    • Did you learn anything new today about _____________________?

Differentiation Ideas

  • If the class chose an organization where they wish to sponsor a fundraising activity, it may be more appropriate to write a class Action Plan using the Action Plan Template.  One class letter could be written to the development officer of the organization.

Extension

  • Read Effective Letters to Congress as a class.  Discuss the steps to write effective letters to our state and national leaders.  
  • Ask students to find a current event article (online or in a newspaper or magazine) that discusses the issue/cause students are interested in pursuing.  Instruct student groups to prepare and then present these articles to the class before voting on the class proposal.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Do you think writing to state leaders makes a difference?  Why or why not?
  •  What about writing a letter to the President of the United States?

OBJECTIVE:

Students will explore the positive and negative effects of technology usage for adolescents in our society.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin class by introducing the unit topic- technology. Tell students that technology has had such a positive impact on society and their lives that we felt we need to take time and appreciate it more.
    • Mention things like the wheel, the printing press, and electricity. Acknowledge to students that those are great, but they are all in the past and there are more current examples of technology that has brought so much positive into their lives (Consider some of the following examples to try and generate a reaction from students that not all technology inventions have only positive effects): The internet, guns, nuclear bombs, self-driving cars, social media, smartphones, video games, Snapchat, Netflix, etc.
  • After allowing students to engage in this discussion mention that although technology has its positives, clearly it has its negatives as well, which is the purpose of this unit. Technology moves so quickly, we sometimes do not know how much harm or good it is doing. In particular, we are not sure our youth are being prepared enough to deal with technology today.

INSTRUCTION

Activity

  • For skeptical students, give them the example of smartphones. We all know the benefits, like being able to keep in touch with parents, the news, and the convenience of being able to handle many of our daily tasks using one device (banking, pictures, entertainment). But has it all been good?
    • Show any one of the following videos:
    • 7.01 video-How Is Your Phone Changing You?
    • 7.01 video Do You Smart Phones Cause Sleep Problems- pbs.org Note that the additional information on this page may be useful material for expanding this section.
    • 7.01 video Mother On Mission To Stop Driving And Texting
    • Allow students to give their reactions to the videos.

Guided Practice

  • Tell students that one focus of this unit will be social media, and that it is important to establish how positive or negative it really is for us. Direct students to 7.01 pdf- Are Social Networks Good For Society, or print out copies of this page.
    • Arrange students to take a side or specific argument, allow them to read it, put it into their own words, and share it with the class. This can be done in groups, as a class, or individually.
    • Ask students if they have any experiences with the points mentioned or if there should be more points than the ones that were listed.

  • Ask students for an exit card where they report one new piece of information they learned today or to give their overall reaction to how they would parent their own kids with smartphone usage in the future.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Strategy Grouping for the Guided Practice portion of the lesson–Partner highly skilled students with mid-level skilled and/or partner mid-level skilled students with lower-skilled ones.
  • Require only select portions of the assignment/reading for students that are unable to complete the entire assignment within the time allotted or reduce the length of the assignments.

Extension

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Share with students the following news story: 7.02 pdf- Police Solves Two Crimes By Tracking Footprints
    • Ask students why the footprints were so important in this case.
    • Explain that today’s lesson is also about footprints- not ones left in the snow, but ones that are left online. Ask students whether they have filled out a form, created a profile or post, or sent a picture, message, or email. Explain that everything a person does on the internet, even just visiting a website creates a trail that someone else may follow (ad companies already do this constantly to tailor ads to what you have recently searched online). The question for students is whether their digital footprint is one they want others to see and how they create a trail that is positive for future employers.
  • Share with students examples of where even one post could cost a person his/her job.
    • Share with students any positive or negative examples from your experience of digital footprints.

Guided Practice

  • This activity will ask students to study the profiles of two different people who are competing for a position on a game show. Working in groups, students will need to study, choose, and defend their decision.
  • Follow the “Analyze: Search for a Host” activity from the lesson plan. The handouts are included in the lesson plan. Note: Teachers will need to distribute a copy of the Truth Be Told Student Handout. (Note: This is a lengthy handout, so you could also print just a couple of copies per group. OBJECTIVE:

Students will learn the importance of creative credit and how to avoid plagiarism or copyright infringement.

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Introduce the lesson topic by citing this article about Frozen’s “Let it Go” song having been accused of being copied from someone else’s work. Play samples of each song and see if the students agree with the allegation.
    • Students may also be interested in a similar allegation involving Coldplay and their hit song “Viva la Vida.”
  • Write the word “Plagiarism” for students to see, ask them to define it, and clarify its meaning. Tell students that plagiarism can involve both small (like a simple school assignment) or big (see examples above) consequences, but with today’s technology, it is a growing and often misunderstood problem.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="padding-5-percent" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color="#3a3a3a" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" font_color="#ffffff" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Activity

  • Show students this article and give them a summary of what happened. Highlight the importance of a Senator and his Master’s Thesis. Explain to students that most schools have access (and most colleges automatically route their assignments) to plagiarism programs that will detect whether or not something has been copied. They can see how easy it was to spot the plagiarism of Senator Walsh, and it ultimately cost him his degree.

Guided Practice

  • Have students watch the following video clip that explains how to avoid plagiarism, and then have them complete the activity below.
    • Locate a short article or set of articles from a site dedicated to teen news and ask students to practice using one of the two ways (quote or paraphrase) to write about this article as if doing a school paper. Ask for examples and ask the class to give feedback on whether or not plagiarism was avoided. You may secretly ask some students to provide poor examples to see if they are spotted by the rest of the class.
    • Be sure to demonstrate how you would prefer something cited in your class. Even though there are formal citation methods for academic writing, there are less formal ways a student could cite material that you may find acceptable.

REVIEW/ASSESSMENT

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Review

  • Ask students to consider what would have happened if someone’s ideas would have been stolen. What about Facebook? What would the consequences have been in money or charity if the idea had been stolen? Sometimes companies like other ideas so much that they purchase them outright instead of copying them (Facebook bought Instagram). Show how many programs and tools Google has purchased from third parties.

  • Allow students to practice writing without plagiarizing using a teen-friendly article in Spanish from Hola Qué Pasa.

Extension

  • Students can search for additional examples of accusations or allegations of copying ideas in the media, movies, songs, etc., and note the outcomes and consequences in each case.

 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • What are some common reasons students might have for plagiarizing when writing a paper or doing an assignment?
  • How does plagiarism affect the learning process?
  • What tips can we give students to prevent them from plagiarizing?

OBJECTIVE:

Students will learn how to define cyberbullying, understand its prevalence, and develop prevention strategies.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin class by explaining to students the seriousness of this topic. While Cyberbullying is something they have likely heard a lot about, it’s a growing problem and has serious consequences.
  • Share the following article about a girl who took her own life as a result of cyberbullying. Let students share their thoughts about the article.
  • Ask students to share their experiences with cyberbullying. Have students had it happen to them or someone they know?

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Activity

  • Explain that in order to understand cyberbullying, there are two areas that need to be explored: Defining cyberbullying and knowing what its effects are.
  • Explain that there is overall confusion among youth about what cyberbullying actually is. Prompt your students for their ideas.
    • Note that generally cyberbullying is defined as 1) There is an intention to hurt by the perpetrator 2) There perception of hurt by the victim 3) It is repetitive 4) There is a power imbalance. However, point out that there are problems with these points. For example, many perpetrators and their friends believe something is a joke or tease there may not have been an “intention to harm.” Or sometimes victims may feel hurt, but it may not be validated by their parents, school staff, friends, or society, which tells them to “tough it out.” Finally, does cyberbullying need to be repetitive?
  • After coming up with a definition, show students this video that describes 10 forms of cyberbullying.
  • Prompt students to see if they can describe any of the effects of cyberbullying. Show this short video and ask students for their reactions.

UNIT ASSESSMENT:

Guided Practice

  • Note that this project can be used within this lesson only, or in conjunction with other Digital Citizenship lesson plans by giving students options for which topic they want to highlight.
  • Ask students to create a Public Service Announcement (PSA) to help their peers with this (or one of the other) Digital Citizenship topics. This is important because research consistently shows youth are unprepared to handle the technology they use. Stress that PSA’s are meant to convince or teach people something about a topic. Your students will want others to take note of what they have to say, so it’s not just relaying facts, but doing so in a way that attracts people’s attention. It is very much an art and persuasion assignment.  
  • Because of the wide range of PSA projects, it will be important to clarify your parameters and expectations. At a minimum, do a Google search of “Public Service Announcements”  and choose examples of what PSA’s look like. Be sure to clarify what mediums students can use (poster, paper, video, printed picture, or hand drawn).
  • Specify what should be included in the PSA (An image, a statistic/fact statement, a catchy title).
  • Note that these could be displayed in class or even throughout the school, which means neatness and accuracy are essential.

Review

  • Show this short clip about cyberbullying from What Would You Do?
  • Ask students to think about what they would say if they saw cyberbullying taking place or if they had a friend confide in them they were being cyberbullied. What would their advice be?
  • Mention that students often advise others to “turn off” the technology where the bullying is taking place, just ignore it, or even fight back. Are these the best responses? Could they be improved?

  • Encourage students to write a script and allow for rehearsal time if creating a video for their PSA project.
  • Allow students to choose their PSA format. Acceptable PSA's might be written, spoken in Spanish/English, or expressed with pictures.

Extension

  • Have students write and perform a skit for the class about cyberbullying and its effects.

 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How is cyberbullying different from other types of bullying?
  • How can you prevent cyberbullying among your peers?

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin the lesson by showing one or more of the following videos about teens and internet scams.
  • Discuss with students of the major pitfalls of the digital age, which is the ability for people to take advantage of others’ money and privacy. Consider displaying the following article that puts into context how the younger generation is targeted and how much money is lost through internet scams.
  • Explain that today’s lesson will look at different ways teens are targeted today and how they can stay safe online.

Activity

  • For an overview, review the following article that discusses what types of internet scams are targeted toward teens. Prepare thoughts from personal experience or from people you know to share with the class. Depending on your students’ needs and class time, you may choose to focus on the following areas:
    • Scams targeted to get money: Reference our government's publication on scams in the United States in 2017. Google “Funny Email Scams” for examples of what students could receive in their emails. Common sense is the best form of protection against these scams.
    • Password security: Discuss the most common passwords using this article. Review this article for ways to protect passwords.
    • Show students this video on avoiding online Phishing and Scams.
    • Privacy- It might be helpful to give students some background knowledge when it comes to how the United States has historically viewed privacy. The Fourth Amendment was created specifically to protect a person’s privacy, long before the issues we have today. There are many videos that demonstrate how people can gather data from your phones/computers.
  • Relationships- The following video shares some tips that include being careful about sharing personal information, reporting anyone who makes you feel uncomfortable online, getting familiar with privacy settings, and meeting up in person with people they meet online. Preview the video to determine its fit for your class.

Guided Practice

  • Note that this project can be used within this lesson only, or in conjunction with other Digital Citizenship lesson plans by giving students options for which topic they want to highlight.
  • Ask students to create a Public Service Announcement (PSA) to help their peers with this (or one of the other) Digital Citizenship topics. This is important because research consistently shows youth are unprepared to handle the technology they use. Stress that PSA’s are meant to convince or teach people something about a topic. Your students will want others to take note of what they have to say, so it’s not just relaying facts, but doing so in a way that attracts people’s attention. It is very much an art and persuasion assignment.
  • Because of the wide range of PSA projects, it will be important to clarify your parameters and expectations. At a minimum, do a Google search of “Public Service Announcements”  and choose examples of what PSA’s look like. Be sure to clarify what mediums students can use (poster, paper, video, printed picture, or hand-drawn).
  • Specify what should be included in the PSA (An image, a statistic/fact statement, a catchy title).
  • Note that these could be displayed in class or even throughout the school, which means neatness and accuracy are essential.

  • Allow students to work in pairs to complete this handout Don't Feed the Phish - How to Catch A Phish Student Handout from commonsense.org. for additional practice with analyzing examples of messages that use tricks to phish for your information.

Extension

  • For an expanded discussion about privacy, students might consider how this man’s DNA test ultimately got him caught.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How confident do you feel that you can use message clues to avoid internet scams?
  • What would you say to a friend who is unsure if a message they received is a scam or not?

Activity

  • The Impact of Fake News is sometimes hard to quantify, but videos like this demonstrate why people choose to spread fake news and its potential consequences.
  • As a class or individually, read the following article about what tech companies are doing to stop fake news. Afterward, ask students if they believe enough is being done.
  • This short video provides tips for spotting fake news.
  • Demonstrate websites like Snopes that fact-check popular stories.

Guided Practice

  • Consider this resource from Shady Side Academy that helps students analyze the reliability of a website. Use this list or one like it to evaluate news stories and their websites with students. Possible websites to examine are:  
    • 7.06 weblink- Not The Whitehouse
    • 7.06 weblink- Dihydrogen Monoxide FAQ
    • This site provides additional links: 7.06 weblink- Fake Fact Websites
  • Alternatively, this guided practice may be used in conjunction with the Public Service Announcement activity found in the preceding Digital Citizenship lesson plans.

  • Ask students to respond to the following scenario: While talking with a group of friends, one says that fake news doesn’t matter and it’s impossible to tell the difference between real and fake news anyway. Relevancy/Linkage

Instruct the students to take out a piece of paper. Allow students 30 seconds to answer each question below.

  • Question 1: What qualities do you think one must possess in order to become a successful professional?
  • Question 2: List as many successful professionals as you can.

Discuss student answers to Question 1.

Discuss student answers to Question 2 and ask the following follow-up questions:

  • How many professionals were listed that look or speak like you?
  • Why do you think this number is high or low?

Differentiation Ideas

  • Allow students to use 8.01 Weblink Influential Latinos – Spanish Version as a reference for the 2 or 3 individuals that the teacher reviews from the English list in the Modeling portion of the lesson. 
  • Invite a professional guest speaker to discuss the professional skills necessary to be successful in the workforce. You may need to use this option if computers/internet are not available.

Extension

  • Invite students to choose an individual from 8.01 Weblink Influential Latinos to research. Give each student 10-15 minutes to briefly research their chosen individual’s story, interesting facts, and what the individual did to become a successful professional. Place students in groups of four and have each student present their chosen individual to their group.
  • View 8.01 Video – Professionalism in Soccer 1 (15 sec) or 8.01 Video – Professionalism in Soccer 2 (4 min) and discuss how a soccer player’s unprofessional behavior may change a teammate or opposing team member’s view of that player. How does this relate to professionalism in the workplace?

Journal Entry Suggestions

Answer the following questions in relation to LIA Tutoring, your LIA Class, and in general:

  • How do your behaviors reflect positively or negatively? What does that say about you?
  • Is your attitude professional?  
  • What could you change or do differently to improve your professionalism?

Language Enhancement

  • Invite the students to complete Spanish/English Question Guide individually or as pairs. If you choose not to show 8.01 Weblink - Influential Latinos you may need to adjust the questions.

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous lesson:

  • Last time we learned about a few Latino professionals. What parts stood out to you?
  • One of the first steps of joining the professional field is finding a job. In order to find a job of interest, you need to submit a competitive, standout resume.

Display 8.02 Middle School Resume Example Teacher Model and 8.02 Middle School Resume Non-Example Teacher Model.

  • Let’s pretend you are an employer and these two resumes come across your desk.
  • Ask the students which candidate they would hire and why.
  • Discuss the importance of submitting a clean, concise resume.

Model

  • View the resume tips from 8.02 Weblink Resume Tips, or another similar website, as a class.
  • Use Middle School Resume Template to create one sample resume as a class, choosing the name and other details together. Use Middle School Resume Example Teacher Model, if needed.

Guided Practice

*Teacher Note 1: You may have some students who already have a resume, have participated in volunteer opportunities, or even have an introductory job. However, this resume assignment will be used as the unit assessment so everyone will need to participate. 

  • Instruct each student to choose a job they would like to apply for. This can be a job they would like to have in the future, a volunteer position they would like to apply for, or another similar option. 
  • Have students begin to draft their own resumes, using the resume example as a reference. Remind students that their resume isn't just composed of work experience, and can include household duties, skills, awards, and volunteer experiences. Encourage students to list activities that they have done in their LIA class, including tutoring, service projects, planning events, and college/career learning opportunities. 
  • Encourage students to use specific, powerful language.
  • Invite the students to share their resumes with a peer and ask for feedback.

**Teacher Note 2: You may invite students to use 8.02 Weblink – Canva Resume Templates as a guide to create a final draft of their resume if they would prefer to have a modern finish. Students would need to create a free account in order to use this service. 

Independent Practice

  • Go to the computer lab and allow students sufficient time to complete their resume. There is no one size fits all resume, encourage the students to tailor the resume to accentuate their strengths.
  • If students do not finish, invite them to complete it at home.

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous lesson:

  • Last time we learned how to make a more competitive resume. Today we are going to hold mock job interviews.

View Video - Interview with a 7-Year-Old.

  • What did the man being interviewed do wrong?
    • (Possible answers: Changed the subject, didn't answer the questions, asked the interviewer to skip a question, didn't speak in complete sentences.)
  • Did the man being interviewed do anything right?
    • (Possible answers: Dressed professionally, made eye contact, spoke clearly, was well-groomed.)

View Video Interview Tips (5 min) and ask the following questions:

  • What tips stood out to you?
  • Has anyone had an interview experience they would like to share with the class?
  • Any additional tips?
  • How can being bilingual give you an advantage in a job interview?

Model

  • Display Mock Interview Questions and Middle School Resume Example Teacher Model for students to view.
  • Using 8.03 Teacher Model Mock Interview Questions as a guide, model a job interview by reading through these common interview questions and responding to them. 

Independent Practice

  • Instruct students to gather their thoughts and write down notes, examples, and ideas under each question in the 8.03 HO Mock Interview Questions to prepare for mock interviews.
  • Invite students to use their completed 8.02 HO High School Resume Template to assist them. You may need to pull up and display 8.02 Middle School Resume Example Teacher Model as a reference for students.  

Activity 

  • Pair students up to conduct mock interviews, using the notes they prepared with 8.03 HO Mock Interview Questions and their resumes from the previous lesson.   
  • Remind the students that this is a professional interview and a great opportunity to practice the interview tips that were discussed at the beginning of class.  
  • Allow 5-7 minutes for each interview before having students switch roles. 
  • The teacher may walk around offering support as needed.

Relevancy/Linkage

Review the previous lesson.

  • So far we have discussed professional qualities, resumes, and interviews.  Today we are going to explore alternative ways to find job openings besides the traditional online job search.

Ask students what they think about the phrase, “Be nice to the nerds in high school because they will be your future boss."

View 8.04 Weblink Networking in High School as a class, focusing on the five takeaways:

  1. Eat lunch at a different table each day.
  2. Connect with the “untouchables.”
  3. Stop thinking that everything is about you.
  4. Interact with people who are not just like you.
  5. Have a life outside of high school.

After reviewing the list above, ask the following questions:

  • Which of the five tips stood out to you?
  • Do you agree or disagree with these suggestions? Why or why not?
  • How could these tips potentially benefit you?

Activity

  • Give each student a copy of Networking Activity (English).
  • Instruct the students that they will complete this activity twice. 
  • Point out that there is a column for Round 1, and a second column for Round 2.
  • Give the students two minutes to complete Round 1 of the handout without speaking.
  • After students have completed Round 1, give them two more minutes to complete Round 2, allowing speaking and interactions.
  • Once the activity has been completed, discuss the following questions:
    • Which activity was more successful and why?
    • Were you able to complete either activity? Why or why not? What other tools or contacts would have been helpful?
    • How does the first activity relate to finding a job through the newspaper or advertisement? How does the second relate to networking?
    • Do you think networking is simple or difficult? Please share any networking experiences you may have.

Model Practice

  • Share the following with the students:
    • Face-to-face talking, using social media, texting, etc. are all very effective networking tools. We are now going to begin a brief networking project to test out these tools.
  • Display 8.04 Teacher Model Networking Project and discuss the first three examples together.

Guided Practice

  • Give each student a copy of Networking Project.
  • Allow students to network with a “good friend” and/or an “acquaintance”.
  • Discuss what went well or what aspects of the conversation were awkward. Brainstorm ways to improve.

Independent Practice

  • Allow students time to contact individuals as class time allows and invite the students to complete the remainder of the project at home.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Note that the content for the lesson plan has been adapted from Empowering Education.
  • Begin by asking students to think about being in a field of tall grass or a thick forest and they are the first people to be passing through. There is no trail.
    • Have students describe what it would be like to get through to the other side. Why would it be hard?
    • Next, ask students to talk about what the experience would be like if they were asked to pass through that same field/forest the next day. What would it be like if they were asked to pass through every day for a long period of time?
    • Also ask students what would happen if they stopped passing through the field/forest for a long period of time. What would happen to their trail?
  • Explain to the class that what is happening with you and the field is very much like what happens with you and your brain, whenever you do...anything! Whether it's learning how to walk, brushing your teeth, or a new sport, it is initially hard at first because your brain is forging new pathways. This lesson will demonstrate how those pathways function and why it’s an important concept to understand for our learning.

Activity

  • Guide students through a short presentation about how your brain works:
  • New research tells us that our brains are literally forming new pathways, and this concept is called neuroplasticity.
    • Neuro = anything involving the brain.
    • Plastic = something that can be changed.
    • Highlight the importance of this discovery. Up until about 20 years ago, scientists believed our brains could not change after our childhood years. In other words, you were stuck with whatever you had!
  • Another term: neurons. Neurons are tiny electrical wires in your brain. They transfer signals through complicated networks that form the basis of all of our thoughts, emotions, and behaviors. Some fun facts about neurons:
    • There are about 100 billion neurons in your brain.
    • Each neuron has anywhere between 1,000 to 10,000 connections to other neurons (known as synapses).
    • This means there are trillions of connections in one human brain. To put that in perspective, there are 1,000 times more connections in one human brain than there are stars in the Milky Way galaxy!
    • Neurons develop at a rate of over 250,000 per minute during pregnancy.
    • Neurons continue to develop and form new connections throughout your life. This is neuroplasticity.
    • 50% of neural connections do not survive into adulthood, due to a process called synaptic pruning that happens during adolescence. Your brain gets rid of connections that aren’t being used.
  • Consider using a short video to supplement this presentation:
    • Neuroplasticity (2 min)
    • How the Brain Works (1 min)
    • Growing Your Brain (3 mins)
    • Your Brain is Plastic (4 mins)

Guided Practice

  • Use the Guided Practice Activity starting on page four of the Empowering Education lesson plan.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin the class by introducing the story of the man with the red paperclip who eventually was able to trade it for a house. 
    • How did the paperclip (and subsequent objects) get their value and grow? Nothing about it changed and there were likely a lot of people who did not want to trade for the paperclip (and the subsequent objects). What gave it value?
    • Direct the class to focus on the man trading the paper clip. His belief that the paperclip could grow into something greater is what gave it value. Had he not believed it and accepted its “fixed” attributes, it would have likely amounted to nothing.
  • Explain to the class that you will transfer this idea to people. Can people grow, despite the initial limitations they might have? Do beliefs in one’s self make a difference? Display the following image showing the early setbacks of people who eventually became famous and influential.
    • Discuss with the class the mindset these people have had to experience challenges, but not give up. If we could learn more about how they were thinking, maybe it could help us learn to deal with our own challenges today. Researchers have started calling this a growth vs fixed mindset.

Activity

  • Use the following video to introduce Growth vs Fixed Mindsets
    • After watching the video, ask students to discuss why having a growth mindset can be difficult. What factors contribute to us developing a fixed mindset?
  • Consider the following trailer from Frozen. What mindset is being modeled here?
    • Have students think about how hard they work to overcome setbacks. Is it as hard as the characters in the trailer worked? Are there some setbacks they are more willing to put forth effort on than others?

Guided Practice

  • Distribute or direct students to the following list of 10 ways a person can develop a growth mindset. Teachers may consider using small groups or pairs and ask students to do the following:
    • Assign or distribute each group a number from the list.
    • Read and discuss the description so all members understand their concept.
    • Rewrite the concept into 1-3 sentences in a way that the rest of the class can understand. A person in the group will read this out loud.
    • Another group member will provide a real-life or personal example of the concept to the class.
    • After a sufficient amount of time, call on each group to share their definition and example with the class.

OBJECTIVE:

Students will learn the power of “Yet” and strategies to develop optimism in their perspectives.[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="padding-5-percent" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color="#3a3a3a" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" font_color="#ffffff" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Teachers may find Carol Dweck’s explanation (10 minutes) of the power of yet informative before teaching this lesson.
  • Explain to the class that you are going to share a short story from a well-known children’s book called, Giraffes Can’t Dance. A number of YouTube videos read this story aloud, with pictures, and sometimes animations. See this video as one example.
    • Halfway through the book where the giraffe walks away from the party, alone and disappointed, pause the reading and introduce a poster or writing on the board with the title, “Things We Can’t Do Yet.” Ask students to think about and write at least one response on the posters. You may ask each student to share theirs with the class.
    • Finish the rest of the book and as a class, identify what the giraffe needed to discover his own dance. Note how the giraffe was given an inspiration, but it was still up to him to re-frame his mind to accept that he could dance if he was willing to jump in and try.
    • Explain that today’s lesson introduces the “Power of Yet,” which is an essential characteristic of developing a growth mindset.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="padding-5-percent" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color="#3a3a3a" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" font_color="#ffffff" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Activity

  • Allow the class an opportunity to see a growth mindset in action with this scene (stop at 3 min) from the movie Pursuit of Happiness. Note to stop the clip at 3 minutes or the elevator scene due to language. It is not necessary to know the background of the movie except to understand the main character needs a job desperately. Before watching the clip, have students create a simple T-chart and ask them to look for any cues (both verbal and non-verbal) from anyone in the scene that demonstrates growth or fixed mindsets. Explain that this activity is only an introduction. It is not meant for students to have perfect answers but to simply explore how behavior and words have power.  Have students note any examples and afterward direct them to share with a partner or group.
  • Discuss as a class these cues what some of the most significant cues were and what they said about the person’s mindset.

Guided Practice

  • Explain again that the “Power of Yet” can only be unlocked through a mind that is willing to adapt and problem-solve. A person must accept that they aren’t there but can get there eventually. While future lessons will continue to address this message, the following activity is designed to help students adapt constantly and hopefully have a little fun. The activity comes from the Khan Academy and is demonstrated through their video here.
    • Debrief with students the struggles they had as their partners put something unexpected in the process. Ask students to think about their thinking as that happened. Were they frustrated and ready to quit? Were they frustrated but ready to continue? Did they enjoy the challenge?
    • Explain that this mind exercise highlights the “Yet” mindset. Very little of something valuable comes easy, but a thought process that emphasizes a willingness to see it through is the heart of this unit.

Review

  • Ask students to share any “Yet” examples from their own experiences. Note that there is often a middle ground when students think about their larger "Yet" goals. For example, a student might say, “I’m not passing science class- yet, but I can turn in the missing assignment.” Have students consider not only the yet, but what they can do now.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin class by showing the following video that highlights the power of positivity. Teachers may want to preview the video first to be able to explain beforehand how the experiment works.  
    • After the video, discuss with the class what factors were changed and the difference they made in relation to the performance of the participants. This phenomenon is actually seen throughout sports with the concept of “home field advantage.” Ask students if they are familiar with the phrase and understand what it means. Evidence throughout the sports world confirms there is an advantage to playing where fans are cheering for you instead of against you.
    • Introduce to the class the “power of positivity,” and not that these examples reflected external positivity- a good thing, but today’s lesson wants to focus on a more internal positivity. This is where you can give yourself that extra boost.

Activity

  • Demonstrate for students the problems with judging ourselves. Using the following video from Dove.
  • Highlight the phrase “we are our harshest critics,” and note that this is not just a saying but also backed up by research.  Consider sharing any personal examples related to some of the relevant terms, like self-fulfilling prophecy, stereotypes, self-criticism, etc.
  • This video may be helpful in emphasizing the importance of positive self-talk.

Guided Practice

  • Google “positive self-talk statements” and locate a list that you feel is appropriate for your class. Whether in groups or individually, ask your students to review the list and choose a statement they find more relevant or impactful for themselves.
  • Ask students to create a poster or advertisement that highlights the quote they chose that will serve to inspire others. Use the following images as examples.
    • Note that teachers will want to structure this assignment according to the available resources. For example, how will students create the images in their advertisements- drawing, computer, magazines, etc?
    • Students may prefer to think of this as creating a meme instead of an ad.

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Begin class by relating the following story (You may want to preface with an explanation of what Southwest is and perhaps the food/trash experience that one might have in a typical plane flight for students who have flown before):
    • When Southwest Airlines flight attendant Rhonda Holley was helping to clean up the plane by collecting all the empty cups from the cabin of the Southwest Boeing 737, she discovered that the Southwest logo was being printed on the trash bags. When she saw this, she had two quick epiphanies. 1 – Passengers knew what plane they were on, whether they saw the logo on the trash bag or not. 2 – Trash bags are always immediately thrown away after use, and no passengers see them again. She wrote to the Southwest leadership team, headed up by Colleen Barrett, to see how much money it was costing the company on an annual basis to print the logos on the trash bags. Colleen Barrett called her and famously said, “You’ve just saved us $300,000 a year. We’re not going to be printing logos on the trash bags anymore.” 
    • Point out that in order for Southwest Airlines to save money, a few critical items needed to take place: 1) The employee had to feel safe giving feedback, and then give it in the right way. 2)The supervisor had to be willing to receive it and then do something about it.
    • Explain that today’s lesson is about giving and receiving feedback, one of the vital components of developing a growth mindset.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Activity

  • Use the following activity idea to highlight the importance of valuable feedback. Note that the activity can be modified to use something other than clapping, like asking students to draw an object instead.
    • Be sure to debrief with students by identifying what were the characteristics of improved feedback.
    • Ask students if they have examples of coaches or teachers who demonstrated positive or negative feedback qualities.

Guided Practice

  • Explain that feedback can also be influenced by culture. For example, in American Idol, judge Simon Cowell was often criticized for his feedback methods. Ask students for their reactions to the video. Note that at times, Simon’s comments were unquestionably too personal, although they also reflected cultural differences, as British criticism is often considered too direct and rude by American standards. Teachers may consider this article for reference.
  • Either as a class or in groups, ask students to develop a “Code of Conduct” when it comes to feedback. This code will be displayed in class to serve as a reminder about how the class will focus their criticism.
    • Ask students to decide on their three most important guidelines when it comes to appropriate feedback.
    • Students should then create an infographic or visual model of their three steps. Teachers can determine the guidelines for this assignment, as it can be completed in a variety of ways, from the computer to a poster board. Use the following ideas as potential examples for your students:
      • 21 Components of Effective Feedback Infographic
      • Sandwich Feedback Examples
      • The Everyday Feedback Model

Relevancy/Linkage

  • For background on the idea of learning from mistakes, Watch Carol Dweck explain the problem with easy work (1 min).
  • Take a trip down memory lane and ask students if they recognize Ms. Frizzle from The Magic School Bus series- and her famous catchphrase,  “Take chances, make mistakes, and get messy!”
  • Also, explain to students that there is an opposite side to this type of thinking and introduce them to the term "Helicopter Parents."Note that many believe our society seems to be trending toward (over)protecting our kids. Give students a chance to think about the advantages and disadvantages of this trend. They will have an opportunity to discuss this more in the activity portion of the lesson.
  • End this section by noting that mistakes are a part of our lives and society. We often choose to be critical and make fun of mistakes wherever we see them. The purpose of the lesson is to explore what a growth mindset teaches us about how we should be thinking about mistakes.

Activity

  • Explain that you want to highlight more real-life examples of how we think about mistakes in things that all kids do (sports and schools).  Use the following examples:
    • Youth sports and not keeping score.
    • Students who can’t get a “zero” on an assignment.
    • After viewing and sharing out both examples, allow students to discuss and then share the pros and cons of these types of policies.
    • Ask students if they were parents of a child, would they prefer that he/she participate in this type of league or school? Students could vote on which policies they would be in favor of.
    • Eventually, the discussion should be guided toward how students perceive the idea of losing or making mistakes- and perhaps if those are connected.

Guided Practice

  • Explain that learning from mistakes is an essential characteristic of successful business and people. Using articles like the example below, assign students as groups or individuals a person or business to read about. Students should identify the mistake that was made and the response to that mistake:

  5 spectacular examples of turning failures into success

  • Give students time to share about the person or business they learned about.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson about learning from mistakes. Explain that part of learning from mistakes is being willing to take risks. (Note that several ideas from this lesson were adapted from the Lesson plan are you a risk taker
  • Do a quick survey asking students: Do you enjoy taking risks?
    • Play only the first 55 seconds of the following video and pause it. Ask students in pairs to discuss what they would do in this situation. Get feedback. Ask the class as a whole to predict what might happen to the people who decide to run the risk and take the two empty seats.
    • Play the video until the end.
  • Explain that today’s lesson will focus on taking risks and students will learn more about their own risk-taking behaviors.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Activity

  • Class as a whole. Ask students: What’s the most dangerous thing you’ve ever done?
  • Put students in pairs. Tell them you are going to show them different activities that involve taking risks. Ask students to discuss whether they would be willing to try them or not, giving reasons for their choice.
  • Share any or all the following videos with the students:
    • Bike Parkour
    • Driving on Mountaintop
    • GoPro Wingsuit

Ask students to list the potential benefits of taking risks. Then ask students to list the potential negatives of taking risks.

Consider preparing positive and negative examples of taking risks. Ideas could include:

      • Gambling/Lottery
      • Risks in business 
      • Steve Irwin "The Crocodile Hunter"
      • Game shows: An excellent example comes from a British game show. Preview the Split or Steal video (5 minutes) before showing students so that you can explain what’s happening. Afterward, ask: Does playing it safe always work?

Guided Practice

  • This activity is a chance for students to model risk/reward-type decision-making processes. The trick for the teacher is to find a valuable commodity that the students are willing to “gamble” with. That being said, several options exist for the students to hoard, such as candy, hall passes, lunch privileges, extra credit points, daily grade points, or even money. We believe the “commodity” should be able to be held in the students' hands, something tangible so the students can be tied to it kinesthetically.
    • 1. Explain to the students that they will be engaged in a game in which they will attempt to gain as much of their “commodity” (coins, candy, daily points, etc.) as possible. Everyone will be starting with the same amount of that “commodity,” and it is in their best interest to gain as much as possible to be used as a starting point for the second variation of the game.
    • 2. Distribute the same amount of the commodity to all students. Make this amount enough to get them started, yet not enough for a kid to not want to play the game. It should be approximately 25 to 30% of the total maximum amount possible.
    • 3. Have each student visit the teacher a total of three times to play a game of chance that has these options:
      • Choose to flip the coin with positive or negative consequences, or
      • Choose not to participate in the game of chance and receive a set amount of the commodity. This set amount of the commodity should be a bit conservative yet a safe and rewarding gain for those who choose not to gamble. We believe it should essentially be half of what a student would gain if they won on the gamble.
      • Here are the options: ○
  • Gamble: Heads will get you the same amount of what you have in your cache, thus doubling your total amount in the coffers. Tails will get you nothing for your coffers
  •  Not Gamble: Receive a guaranteed payoff of half of your coffers
    • 4. Have them play this game a total of three times.

Activity Outline

  • Instead of learning about hard work, we are going to do hard work! Today we are going to . . . (see Work Suggestion List), choose an activity and make arrangements prior to class.

Model

  • Explain attitude and work expectations. Give instructions or pre-teach any skills that the student may not be familiar with.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Review the previous lesson.
    • Last time we learned to not sit and dream, but to go and out and work hard! Today we are going to discuss relevant life issues that require perseverance and self-discipline.
    • Give each student an ice cube with a chocolate chip frozen in the middle and follow the Ice Cube Activity Instructions. As this activity may take a few minutes, teach the vocabulary while waiting for the ice cubes to melt.

Model

  • Teach the students about the Inner Circle/Outer Circle Debate Strategy using Weblink Debate Tips.
  • View Video Bullying (6 min) as a class.

Guided Practice

  • Invite students to choose one of two sides.
    • Persevering through criticism or bullying builds character and is the best option.
    • Changing your situation to prevent criticism or bullying is the best option.
  • Instruct students to pair up with someone who has the same view as them. Give each pair 5 minutes to brainstorm and write down points, examples, stories, etc., to back up their chosen side.

Inner Circle/Outer Circle Class Debate

  • Place students in their positions and hold a class debate.

Differentiation Ideas

  • During the guided practice section, use any response protocol to assist students in forming ideas and helping them verbalize information correctly. Use the Response Protocol Article for more details.

Extension

  • Instruct students to write a one to two paragraph editorial opinion summarizing the debate topic.
  • Skim over or view the short video clip Story of Perseverance 1, Story of Perseverance 2, or Story of Perseverance 3. Discuss as a class how these people displayed perseverance.
