Purpose: To help students explore their identity by responding to critical questions related to the factors that shaped their values, ideas, and actions. By having students examine and share their own talents, interests, and experiences, students are able to build positive relationships that are more accepting, patient, understanding, and value diversity among themselves. Students will use the Identity and Community (Part 1) Little-known Fact activity to ask themselves the questions “Who am I” and ”What are my interests?” 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 1) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. On a card (or half-sheet of paper), ask students to write one little-known fact about themselves. It could be something in the areas of type of music they like the most, favorite foods, subject areas of interest such as art, sports, or movies, a personal experience, or something about their family history or traditions. Their names should not appear on the cards. Collect the cards/papers.
  2. Randomly select and read a card and ask the class to guess who the fact describes. Once the person is identified, then the person is given 30 seconds to explain why they wrote the fact about themselves. 
  3. The person who wrote the card now randomly selects the next card from the teacher and reads the description. The person reading the card gets the first opportunity to identify who the mystery person is. If that person is not identified, the rest of the class can now try to identify the author of the card. Repeat the process as with the first person in selecting a card, guess who that person might be, and then give the author 30 seconds to explain their entry. 
  4. Depending on the size of the class, select only 5-10 cards per session and continue the process the next day. Through this activity, students often learn that they have something in common with a classmate or they learn something interesting about someone that might not have known otherwise.
  5. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share an interesting fact about yourself with the rest of the students in your class? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other students’ personal stories? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

Today we are going to begin a project centered around your identity through art. The purpose of this project is to explore your identity, cultural background, belief system, etc., and express it through different forms of art and word.

Explain 11.08 Four Corners Discussion Activity Teacher Materials and allow students time to complete the activity.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art.
  • explore how their cultural background influences their beliefs through written word and collage.
  • identify family, peer, school, community strengths and supports (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • explore the impacts of perspective-taking and empathy on patience (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrate expressing concern or showing compassion for someone (Relationship Skills)

Purpose: To help students explore their identity by responding to critical questions related to the factors that shaped their values, ideas, and actions. Students will use the Identity and Community (Part 2) Index Card activity to ask themselves the questions “Who am I” and ”How is my identity formed?”  By having students examine and share their own identities students are able to build positive relationships that are more accepting, patient, understanding, and value diversity among themselves. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 2) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Life and Learning Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Prepare index cards with the questions listed below (feel free to modify or add additional questions as needed):
    1. To what extent are you defined by your talents and interests? 
    2. To what extent are you defined by your language/multilingual abilities?
    3. To what extent are you defined by your family or community background?
    4. To what extent are you defined by your social and financial background? 
    5. To what extent are you defined by your beliefs? 
    6. To what extent does your nationality define you? 
    7. How do you label yourself and how are we labeled by others? 
    8. How are your decisions and actions influenced by how you think others see you? 
    9. How do your experiences shape your values, ideas, and actions? 
    10. In what ways might you assume a different identity in a different context or environment? 
    11. How do you adapt when interacting with people from various language backgrounds?
  2. Randomly distribute the cards to the students as they are sitting in their community circle. Give them a minute to read their card and think about their response. 
  3. Explain to students that when you announce, “Mix and mingle!”, you will turn on music to cue when participants are to move aimlessly around the room and then stop when the music stops. (recommend using samples of culturally familiar music such as cumbias, salsa, merengue, bachata, norteños, mariachi, reggaeton, etc). 
  4. When the music stops, have participants find a partner near them. Help with pairing if needed. *Note that this activity also can be done without music by ringing a chime when it is time for students to stop walking around the room and find a partner.
  5. Partners share their responses to the question on the cards.
  6. After partners have shared, have them exchange cards and give another minute to read their new card and think about their response. Start the music again and repeat the sequence with another partner or two, as your time permits.
  7. In the end, ask for volunteers to share one thing that surprised them or one thing that they learned about themselves.
  8. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own personal story, identities and values with other people? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people’s personal history? (Responsible Decision Making)

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts

 

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • Magazines and newspaper
  • White poster (1 per student)
  • Glue and scissors
  • 11.09 Weblink Word Collage
  • 11.09 Weblink Pictures and Words 1
  • 11.09 Weblink Pictures and Words 2
  • 11.09 HO My 30 Beliefs
  • 11.08 HO Project Overview (for reference)
  • 11.08 HO Project Rubric (for reference)

Differentiation11.08 HO Project Rubric

  • 11.09 Weblink Common Phrases

 

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro Demo for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Last time we discussed different aspects of our identity and today we will focus on our beliefs and how our cultural background can influence those beliefs.
  • Invite everyone to write down 30 beliefs on 11.09 HO My 30 Beliefs.
  • Instruct students to choose their top 5 beliefs and star them.
  • Pair students and ask them to swap papers. The students will then ask the owner of the list why they chose these 5 and the partner writes the response on the back of the list.

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • We are now going to take most, if not all,  of your beliefs and express them through an art collage.
  • Explain that the collage can include pictures and/or words. Display a few examples, 11.09 Weblink Word Collage, 11.09 Weblink Pictures and Words 1, and 11.09 Weblink Pictures and Words 2.
  • Review the Arty Creation expectation on 11.08 Project Rubric.

Guided Practice

  • Give each student poster board, markers, scissors, magazines, etc.
  • Assist the students in finding or creating pictures and/or words that fit their beliefs.

Independent Practice

    • Allow students the remaining time to individually find and arrange needed materials.
    • Inform students that they will have about 20 minutes tomorrow to finish their collage. Each student will present their collage (1 min each) at the end of class.
  • Include opportunities to create a digital collage using technology to piece and layer together a variety of virtual images and textures from different sources. Combining art and technology allows students to explore creativity in different ways. Here are some resources for creating digital collages:
    • https://www.canva.com/create/photo-collages/
    • https://picsart.com/collage-maker
    • https://piccollage.com/
  • Print and display the student work in the classroom. Allowing students to display their work makes the classroom an engaging and welcoming environment for ELs.
  • Create QR (Quick Response) codes to display students’ digital work in the classroom. A QR Code is very similar to a bar code. QR Codes can contain digital text, recordings, links, and much more. The free tool, QR Code Generator, also has a guide with suggestions for how teachers can use QR Codes in the classroom.

    • 1→ I have not learned anything today

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art
  • create a collage to demonstrate beliefs and how cultural background has influenced them
  • analyze beliefs, mindsets and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural factors that shape their identities (Self-Awareness)
  • take others’ perspectives (Social Awareness)
  • develop the skills and mindsets to become culturally competent (Relationship Skills)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To read Sandra Cisneros’ book, The House on Mango Street, and use the Identity and Community (Part 3) to analyze how she reflects on her name, and explore information about her identity, self-perception, her family history, and values. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 3) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Use a grouping activity such as Academic Vocabulary Buddies or Clock Buddies to create pairs for this activity which will include partner reading. In the case where there are ELs or struggling readers, intentionally pair these students with more proficient English speakers (see additional details for partner reading with newcomers in Unit 5, Lesson 7). 
  2. Distribute copies of “My Name,” a chapter from the book The House on Mango Street.
  3. Have students sit together with their partner, face to face, and with the reading passage. Decide which partner will be A and which will be B. Explain the steps to Partner Reading. Model with a student  “reading out loud alternating sentences.” Remind them of their Shared Class Agreements regarding respect and patience. 
    1. Partner A reads the first sentence or paragraph
    2. Partner B reads the next sentence or paragraph
  4. After each paragraph, partners verbally summarize what they read. As the text is read aloud, students can underline any words or phrases that give them information about how Esperanza would answer the question, “Who am I?” Partners continue until they finish reading the assigned chapter.
  5. Together with their partners, have students create an identity chart for Esperanza. Here is the link to examples of identity maps/wheels/charts. 
  6. Before filling in the chart, ask students to brainstorm a list of categories people use to help define themselves such as gender, age, physical characteristics, language as well as ties to a particular religion, ethnic group, neighborhood, and nation. Students can begin with the words or phrases they underlined in the passage that represent how Esperanza defines her identity.
  7. Where are some questions that can also be used as a guide:
    1. Who is in Esperanza’s family? 
    2. Where is her family from?
    3. What languages does she speak? 
    4. What does she hope for her future?
    5. What does she think about her name? 
    6. What does this reveal about her personality? 
  8. Finally, create Esperanza’s identity chart as a whole class activity. 
  9. This activity helps students think about the various factors that shape their identities.This text also introduces other interesting themes such as the concepts of stereotypes and prejudice and questions such as, “How do we perceive and judge others?” and “How does it feel to be labeled?” 
  10. Students can also create identity charts for historical figures as well as for their native countries, civilizations and nation-states.
  11. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore, map out and discuss how Esperanza feels about her own identity and answering the question “Who am I?” (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about Esperanza’s personal identity? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts

 

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • Magazines and newspaper
  • White poster (1 per student)
  • Glue and scissors
  • 11.10 Video Oral Presentation Tips
  • 11.08 HO Project Overview (for reference)
  • 11.08 HO Project Rubric (for reference)

Journal Entry

  • 2.01 HO LIA Standards – Student

 

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Last time we focused on our beliefs and how our cultural background can influence those beliefs by identifying your top beliefs and putting them into collage form. Today we will be completing and presenting your collages.
  • View 11.10 Video Oral Presentation Tips (2 min) as a class and ask the following questions.
  • Why do you think some students are more nervous than others when giving a presentation?
  • Which tips did you find useful, difficult, easy or new?
  • Please share any additional presentation tips.

Vocabulary

Introduce vocabulary and their definitions.   • Allow students about 20 minutes to complete their collages.
  • Encourage students to gather their thoughts for their 1-minute presentation.

Presentations

    • Invite each student to present their collage.
    • Instruct the students to display their collage in the classroom after presenting.
  • Invite each student to present their digital collage using the classroom technology available. Include opportunities to create and modify their digital collage using technology to piece and layer together a variety of virtual images and textures from different sources. Combining art and technology allows students to explore creativity in different ways. Here are some resources for creating digital collages:
    • https://www.canva.com/create/photo-collages/
    • https://picsart.com/collage-maker
    • https://piccollage.com/
  • Print and display the students’ work in the classroom. Allowing students to display their work makes the classroom an engaging and welcoming environment for ELs.
  • Create QR (Quick Response) codes to display students’ digital work in the classroom. A QR Code is very similar to a bar code. QR Codes can contain digital text, recordings, links, and much more. The free tool, QR Code Generator, also has a guide with suggestions for how teachers can use QR Codes in the classroom.

  • Discuss any overall themes or interesting topics that the students noticed.
  • Ask the students to vote by raising their hand. If needed, discuss suggestions on how to get more out of the next class period.
    • 5→ I have learned a lot today
    • 1→ I have not learned anything today
  • Using digital tools like Gimkit, Quizziz, Kahoot, Socrative, or Quizlet, students can quickly and easily demonstrate what they’ve retained at the end of a lesson. These tools allow teachers to design their own ungraded assessments to determine how well ELs are retaining information in class.

  • Invite students to present their collage in groups of 4-5 students.
  • Invite students to write down their thoughts on an index card and practice with a peer before presenting to the class.

Extension

  • Invite the class, as a whole, to do this activity. As a class, choose 5 beliefs and make a wall-sized collage to display in the school or present at a school assembly.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Which of my beliefs align or do not align with LIA standards? Use 2.01 HO LIA Standards – Student as a quick reference. How do your beliefs influence those around you (e.g., school, community, tutees, etc.)?

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art
  • create a mind map showing their identity, cultural background, belief system and personality
  • analyze beliefs, mindsets and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural factors that shape their identities (Self-Awareness)
  • take others’ perspectives (Social Awareness)
  • develop the skills and mindsets to become culturally competent (Relationship Skills)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To have students examine and share their own identities as a way to build relationships within the classroom community. Students will use the Identity and Community (Part 4) Identity Map/Chart activity to learn that many of the same factors that influence their identities, factors such as religion, gender, and geography, also shaped the identities of their peers and ancient civilizations around the world such as the Greeks, the Mayans, and the Chinese. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 4) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Students often feel they are in the company of strangers; they may feel that nobody really knows them and that they don’t really know their classmates. To help students push beyond judging their peers based on simple stereotypes, have them participate in creating their own personal identity map, wheel, or chart. 
  2. Before beginning this activity, ask students to brainstorm a list of categories people use to help define themselves such as gender, age, physical characteristics, and hobbies as well as ties to a particular religion, ethnic group, neighborhood, and nation. Explain to students that they will be sharing their identity maps/charts with the class (they should be cautious about including information that they want to remain private). 
  3. As they gain a deeper understanding of identity, they will add to their personal identity maps/charts over time. Their identity charts will also serve as useful prewriting tools for future assignments such as students’ biopoems.
  4. In preparation for this activity, you may want to create your own identity chart. Not only will this model the assignment for your students but it also provides a way for students to get to know you to reinforce the idea that you are a member of their classroom community too.

*One option is to have students complete their personal identity charts as homework and be ready to share them with the class the next day.

  1. Depending on the size of the class, have up to 10 students share the highlights of their personal identity maps/charts during the opening community circle. Once they have shared their maps/charts, they should be posted on a bulletin board or located where all students would be able to review each other's maps/charts.
  2. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

 

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore, map out and share your own identities with other people? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people’s personal identities? (Responsible Decision Making)

 

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts

 

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • White poster (1 per student)
  • Crayons, markers, etc.
  • 11.09 HO My 30 Beliefs  (completed)
  • 11.08 HO My Identity (completed)
  • 11.11 Mind Map Activity Teacher Materials
  • 11.08 HO Project Overview (for reference)
  • 11.08 HO Project Rubric (for reference)

Extension

  • Personal Values Assessment

 

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Today we are going to combine the previous lessons together and explore identity, cultural background, belief system, and personality by creating your own mind map.
  • Lead and invite students to participate in an introduction to mind maps using 11.11 Mind Map Activity Teacher Materials.

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • Display an example from 11.11 Mind Map Activity Teacher Materials and discuss the chosen guidelines for creating a mind map using 11.08 HO Project Rubric as a reference.
  • Invite the students to use 11.09 HO My 30 Beliefs  (completed) and 11.08 HO My Identity (completed) to help spark ideas for their mind map.
  • Review the Art Creation expectations on 11.08 HO Project Rubric.

Guided Practice

  • Pair the student and allow them a few minutes to brainstorm different ways to create a mind map.

Independent Practice

    • Allow the students time to work on their mind maps.
  • Working with virtual collaboration boards, such as Padlet and Jamboard, and mind mapping tools, such as Prezi and Mindmeister, students receive immediate feedback on their progress and allows them to easily share their thoughts or ideas with the class. Students can post text, images, links, or videos on the virtual wall to answer open-ended questions, extend discussions, and share their viewpoints. Mind mapping activities help ELs connect concepts in different contexts through visual representations.

  • Inform the students that they will have until the end of next class period to complete their mind map.
  • Ask the students to vote by raising their hand. If needed, discuss suggestions on how to get more out of the next class period.
    • 5→ I have learned a lot today
    • 1→ I have not learned anything today
  • Using digital tools like Gimkit, Quizziz, Kahoot, Socrative, or Quizlet, students can quickly and easily demonstrate what they’ve retained at the end of a lesson. These tools allow teachers to design their own ungraded assessments to determine how well ELs are retaining information in class.

  • How has your belief system changed or been added to over the past few years? What has been a major influence of change?

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art
  • complete a mind map showing their identity, cultural background, belief system and personality
  • analyze beliefs, mindsets and stereotypes (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural factors that shape their identities (Self-Awareness)
  • take others’ perspectives (Social Awareness)
  • develop the skills and mindsets to become culturally competent (Relationship Skills)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To have students use poetic language to express their deepened understanding of how experiences can shape their own identities in the Identity and Community (Part 5) Bio-poem activity.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 5) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, and Relationship Skills.

Overview: 

  1. Have students review their identity charts from the previous lesson as a way to reflect on their own identities. To further develop their relationships with their classmates, use a pairing activity such as Mix and Mingle with music, Clock Buddies, or Academic Vocabulary Buddies, and have students share their identity charts with their partners. Have them do this activity twice with different partners. 
  2. Sharing identity charts can help students recognize similarities and differences within the classroom community. Through the sharing process, students often discover factors included in others’ charts that they may not have considered. For example, some students may have included information about their families’ histories that other students have not. Encourage students to add to their identity charts after they have viewed the work of their classmates.
  3. To further explore the question “Who am I?”, students will now write a bio poem about themselves to help them clarify important elements of their identities. Bio-poems help students get beyond the aspects of identity that are often more obvious and familiar (such as ethnicity, gender, and age) by asking them to focus on factors that shape identity, such as experiences, relationships, hopes, and interests. By providing a structure for students to think more critically about an individual’s traits, experiences, and character, bio poems are a way for students to demonstrate what they understand about their own identity. 
  4. A poem typically includes the following information (Adopted from Facing History and Ourselves):
    1. Adjectives that you would use to describe yourself
    2. Relationships in your life (e.g., friend, brother, daughter)
    3. Things you love
    4. Important memories
    5. Fears
    6. Accomplishments
    7. Hopes or wishes
    8. Home (location)
    9. important moments, heroes, beliefs, and special sayings or words.
  5. Explain the format of a bio-poem to your students. Share with them several examples of bio-poems, including one that the teacher has written.
  6. Using the same pairing strategy at the beginning of the activity, have students share their bio poems with their partner. Each pair will have a reader and a “responder.” After the bio-poem is read aloud, the responder has to comment about something he or she heard that was particularly interesting or surprising, or offer suggestions to improve on the poem. Switch roles after each reading. Having students share their bio-poems is a great way to build peer relationships and foster a cohesive classroom community.
  7. Post the bio-poems around the room as part of a gallery walk activity.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own bio-poem with other people? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people’s personal history through their bio-poems? (Responsible Decision Making)

  • Copy student handouts

Main Lesson

  • White poster (1 per student)
  • Crayons, markers, etc.
  • 11.12 Video 19 Mexicans
  • 11.09 HO My 30 Beliefs  (completed)
  • 11.08 HO My Identity (completed)
  • 11.08 HO Project Overview (for reference)
  • 11.08 HO Project Rubric (for reference)

Extension

  • 11.12 Weblink Fishbowl Activity

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Today we are going to continue to explore identity, cultural background, belief system, and personality by completing your own mind map.
  • (Optional) View 11.12 Video 19 Mexicans (3 min) and discuss the following questions.
  • How do cultural events influence your beliefs?
  • What cultural events are you passionate about, or have an opinion about, right now? Why are you passionate about them?

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

Independent Practice

    • Allow the students time to work on their mind maps.

  • Ask the students to vote by raising their hands. If needed, discuss suggestions on how to get more out of the next class period.

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art
  • conduct research on an artist/painter from their country of origin
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • demonstrate an awareness of clues in faces, bodies, and situations to help understand how others are feeling (Social Awareness)
  •  identify similarities and differences among different social and cultural groups (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrate cultural competency (Relationship Skills)
  • deepen their understanding of the structures for co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: Throughout their exploration of their identity, students will learn how to visually represent an answer to the question, “Who am I?” through artistic expression. In the Identity and Community (Part 6) Identity Mask activity students will begin to synthesize their understanding of identity through the creation of a mask. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 6) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. Have students review their bio poems from the previous lesson as a way to continue reflecting on their own identities. To further develop their relationships with their classmates use a pairing activity such as “Mix and Mingle” with music, “Clock Buddies”, or “Academic Vocabulary Buddies” and have students share their bio poems with their partners. Have them repeat this activity with different partners. Sharing bio poems can help students recognize similarities and differences within the classroom community and further develop their language and literacy skills and abilities for verbal expression. Encourage students to make any modifications to their bio poems after they have shared with their classmates.
  2. To further explore the question “Who am I?” students will now make a mask that reflects a part of their identity that they would like their peers and the rest of the class to know about. Begin the activity with a discussion around why people wear masks, literally and figuratively. Sometimes people wear masks to hide their feelings or to pretend to be something they are not. At other times people wear masks to emphasize a particular facet of their personalities. 
  3. To make their masks, have students decide how they want to present themselves to the class. Which aspects of their identities do they want to emphasize? Which aspects of their identities do they wish to conceal? Students can also refer to their identity charts and bio poems for ideas about what to include on their masks. Here are a few ideas for identity masks which should also include descriptors to further explain who they are. 
  4. Have students write the aspects of their identities that they want to illustrate on their masks in their journals and sketch out a design. 
  5. Using the same pairing strategy at the beginning of the activity, have students share with their partner which characteristics they want to include on their identity masks. Each pair will have a presenter and a “responder.” After the first person discusses the list of traits and rough sketch of their identity mask, the responder has to comment about something he or she heard that was particularly interesting or surprising or offer suggestions to improve to better communicate their identities on their masks. Switch roles after each presentation. 
  6. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share the traits that you want to add to your identity mask? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people’s identity through their list of items to be added to their identity masks? (Responsible Decision Making)

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts
  • Sign up for computer lab

 

MATERIALS

Main Lesson

  • 11.13 Weblink Claude Monet – The Rue Montorgueil
  • 11.13 Weblink Diego Rivera Painting
  • 11.13 Weblink Latin American Artists
  • 11.13 HO Research Paper Overview
  • 11.08 HO Project Overview (for reference)
  • 11.08 HO Project Rubric (for reference)

Extension

  • 11.13 Weblink Tissue Paper Art
  • 11.13 Weblink Multicultural Art Projects

 

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Last time we completed our personal mind maps. Today you are going to explore an artist from your country.  One can develop a deeper understanding of his/her own culture through the understanding of art.
  • View 11.13 Weblink Claude Monet – The Rue Montorgueil and/or 11.13 Weblink Diego Rivera Painting (choose one or multiple) as a class and ask the following questions. Please invite the students to view the picture before reading the descriptions.
  • What do you think is going on in this picture?
  • What emotions are evoked from or weaved within the painting?
  • From viewing the picture and reading the description, what did you learn about French and/or Mexican culture?

Vocabulary

Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • https://www.weareteachers.com/virtual-museum-tours/

Independent Practice

  • Go to the computer lab and allow the students time to begin to collect the needed information.
  • Inform the students that they will also have the next class period to work on their research papers.

  • Ask the students to vote by raising their hand. If needed, discuss suggestions on how to get more out of the next class period.

  • 1→ I have not learned anything today

  • Encourage students to use Spanish resources to collect information and then summarize the information in English or Spanish.
  • Invite students from the same or nearby country to work together.
  • Allow the students to put together a powerpoint display of their chosen artist’s work and discuss each piece’s relevance to culture and/or history.

Extension

  • Read the article: “Lesson of the Day: Art Without Borders” https://www.nytimes.com/2021/04/14/learning/lesson-of-the-day-art-without-borders.html

Explain to students that a mural is usually a painting that is large in scale and commonly found in public areas. Ask groups of students to create drawings for a class mural that depicts an artist or a form of art from their country. The mural should include objects, words, people, places, symbols, themes and messages to represent their artist or culture. Decide on whether the mural will be painted on a classroom or school wall or on a heavy duty paper or canvas to be mounted to a wall. The mural is a reminder to the LIA students that they come from a place of greatness, history and tradition.

  • Invite the students to make their own art that depicts something from their culture. For ideas, check out 11.13 Weblink Tissue Paper Art or 11.13 Weblink Multicultural Art Projects.

 

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why should I conduct research on an artist from my own culture?

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art
  • conduct research on an artist/painter from their country of origin
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Self-Awareness)
  • demonstrate an awareness of clues in faces, bodies, and situations to help understand how others are feeling (Social Awareness)
  • identify similarities and differences among different social and cultural groups (Social Awareness)
  • demonstrate cultural competency (Relationship Skills)
  • deepen their understanding of the structures for co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: Throughout their exploration of their identity, students can learn how to visually represent an answer to the question, “Who am I?” through artistic expression. Students will use the Identity and Community (Part 7) Identity Mask activity to begin synthesizing their understanding of identity through the creation of an identity mask. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 7) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview: 

  1. To further explore the question “Who am I?” students will now make a mask that reflects a part of their identity that they would like their peers and the rest of the class to know about, based on their discussions from the prior lesson. 
  2. Materials needed for mask making: paper plates, large pieces of paper, glue, scissors, markers, magazines to cut out words and images, and large ice cream sticks. Inform students that they can decorate both the outside and the inside of the masks. They can use the outside to represent the aspects of their identities they openly show to the outside world, and the inside to represent the more private aspects of their identities.
  3. This activity can be extended over several days. You can also ask students to finish their masks for homework. 
  4. By providing a structure for students to think more critically about an individual’s identity, traits, experiences, and character, this mask activity is a way for students to demonstrate what they understand about their own identity and what they want to reveal to others. Here are a few ideas for identity masks, which should also include descriptors to further explain who they are. 
  5. Using a creative pairing strategy, have students share their identity masks with their partner. Each pair will have a presenter and a “responder.” After their identity mask is shared, the responder has to comment about something they heard that was particularly interesting or surprising or offer suggestions to improve on the mask to better communicate their identities. Switch roles after each presentation. Having students share their identity masks is a great way to build peer relationships and foster a cohesive classroom community.
  6. Post the identity masks around the room as part of a gallery walk activity.
  7. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own identity masks with other people? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about other people’s identity through their masks? (Responsible Decision Making)

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts
  • Sign up for the computer lab

Vocabulary

Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • Encourage students to use Spanish resources to collect information and then summarize the information in English or Spanish. Invite students from the same or a nearby country to work together. Allow the students to put together a PowerPoint display of their chosen artist's work and discuss each piece's relevance to culture and/or history.

Extension

  • Read the article: “Lesson of the Day: Art Without Borders”

Explain to students that a mural is usually a painting that is large in scale and commonly found in public areas. Ask groups of students to create drawings for a class mural that depicts an artist or a form of art from their country. The mural should include objects, words, people, places, symbols, themes, and messages to represent their artist or culture. Decide on whether the mural will be painted on a classroom or school wall, or on a heavy duty paper or canvas paper to be mounted to a wall. The mural is a reminder to the LIA students that they come from a place of greatness, history, and tradition.

  • Invite the students to make their own art that depicts something from their culture. Use 11.13 Weblink Latin American Crafts, or ask the students to give ideas.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How do modern day artists (musicians, poets, artists, etc.) display America’s, or your own country’s, culture?

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art
  • start a poem, in the form of spoken word, that encompasses the importance of their cultural background
  • identify family, peer, school, community strengths and supports (Self-Awareness)
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • demonstrate personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • understand the powerful nature of co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision Making)
  • learn about building and participating in a class community (Responsible Decision Making)

  • 11.15 Video Spoken Word Example 1
  • 11.15 Video Spoken Word Example 2
  • 11.15 Weblink What is Spoken Word
  • 11.08 HO Project Overview (for reference)
  • 11.08 HO Project Rubric (for reference)

Differentiation

  • 11.15 Weblink Glossary of Key Terms

Extension

  • 11.13 Weblink Latin American Crafts

Language Enhancement

  • 11.15 Weblink Code Switching
  • 11.15 Weblink Diamante
  • 11.15 Weblink Poema en Dos Voces

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for the template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Last time you explored an artist from your country to help deepen your cultural knowledge through art. Today we are going to begin to express your individual cultural background through spoken word, a poem spoken aloud.
  • Watch 11.15 Spoken Word Example 1 (2 min) and ask the students the following questions:
  • How does this poet feel about her culture? Give examples.
  • How is spoken word different and similar to a traditional poem?

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

  • Display 11.15 Weblink What is Spoken Word and go over things students should consider when writing spoken word. 
  • Discuss previously viewed 11.15 Video Spoken Word Example 1 and watch an additional example, 11.15 Video Spoken Word Example 2 (3 min).
  • Discuss how these spoken word examples are similar and different. Note the artist’s bilingual usage.
  • Review the Spoken Word expectations on 11.08 HO Project Rubric.

Guided Practice

  • Invite students to write ideas in an outline they want to include in their own spoken word poetry.
  • Pair students to brainstorm ideas together.

Independent Practice

  • Give the students the remaining amount of classroom time to begin creating their own spoken word poem.

  • Generate a class portfolio of the spoken word poems using Book Creator for students to create their spoken word poems and include images, text, and audio. 
  • Encourage students to insert their native language into their spoken word poem.
  • Introduce  and discuss 11.15 Weblink Glossary of Key Terms in Spanish and English.
  • Group students of varying English and/or Spanish proficiency levels together.

Extension

  • Students will record their spoken word poems on a video or voice recording app, such as Seesaw or Explain Everything, to create a virtual anthology of poems for the classroom that will represent the cultures of all students in the LIA class. Students will utilize the language enhancement resources at the bottom of this lesson and the project rubric to identify one major theme or event in their lives and vocalize their feelings in an original spoken word poem. Invite students to record their poems in their home language. The anthology of poems can be posted on the school’s website or student volunteers can recite their spoken word poems over the school’s public address (PA) system.

Language Enhancement

  • Introduce students to 11.15 Weblink Code Switching, 11.15 Weblink Diamante and/or 11.15 Weblink Poema en Dos Voces  in poem form. Encourage them to incorporate this into the spoken word poem.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can you share your cultural heritage with those that you tutor?

Purpose: To  have students think about their class as a community and transition from the question “Who am I?” to the next step of exploring the question “Who are we?” Students will use the Identity and Community (Part 9) My Community activity.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 9) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook 
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. In addition to addressing the question “Who am I?” the next step would be for students to now explore the question “Who are we?” While in a community circle. Begin this activity with a discussion using the following prompts:
    1. Write your own definition of a community. 
    2. Based on your experience with identity charts, bio poems and identity masks, what do you have in common with other members of your class? 
    3. As a member of a class community, what roles, responsibilities or obligations do you now have to further build a positive learning environment? 
    4. What is your commitment to make your classroom more inclusive, enjoyable and positive?
  2. Have students respond to the prompts in their journals. If time does not permit, have them complete their responses as homework. All students need to complete this assignment in preparation for the following lesson. 
  3. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own definition of a community? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about building and participating in a class community? (Responsible Decision Making)

  • Generate a class portfolio of the spoken word poems using Book Creator for students to create their spoken word poems and include images, text, and audio. 
  • Allow students to combine and write a pair or team poem like the example watched in the relevancy/linkage section, 11.16 Video Spoken Word Example 1. 

Extension

  • Students will record their spoken word poems on a video or voice recording app, such as Seesaw or Explain Everything, to create a virtual anthology of poems for the classroom that will represent the cultures of all students in the LIA class. Students will utilize the language enhancement resources at the bottom of this lesson and the project rubric to identify one major theme or event in their lives and vocalize their feelings in an original spoken word poem. Invite students to record their poems in their home language. The anthology of poems can be posted on the school’s website, or student volunteers can recite their spoken word poems over the school’s public address (PA) system.
  • Host an in-person or virtual poetry festival that showcases the students’ final spoken word poems. Consider inviting parents to the festival or post the videos on a secure website such as SchoolTube or your district/school webpage.
  • Invite the students to practice and receive peer feedback by using 11.16 Weblink Bilingual Poem Evaluation.

OBJECTIVES

Students will: 

  • explore their cultural background through the expression and knowledge of word and art.
  • make any modifications desired to complete their projects and set-up for tomorrow’s presentations
  • identify family, peer, school, community strengths and supports (Self-Awareness)
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • demonstrate personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • understand the powerful nature of co-creating a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision Making)

Purpose: To have students further build their sense of community and to appreciate their differences and commonalities. Students will use the Identity and Community (Part 10) Our Community activity as a way to reflect on how their class is a community and leave with a better understanding that all students are responsible not only for their own learning but for supporting the learning of their classmates as well.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 10) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview: 

  1. Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity, see (Optional)
    • Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook
    • Introduction to Welcoming Rituals
    • Greetings
  1. Have students count off 1, 2, 1, 2, etc around the community circle. The 1s are now partners with the 2s to their left (form a triad if the last student doesn’t have a partner). Have them share out their journal entries to the prompts from the prior lesson ping pong style:
  • What is your definition of a community? 
  • Based on your experience with identity charts, bio poems, and identity masks, what do you have in common with other members of your class? 
  • As a member of a class community, what roles, responsibilities, or obligations do you now have to further build a positive learning environment for all? 
  • What is your commitment to making your classroom more inclusive, enjoyable, and positive?
  1. Using a talking stick or object, have students take turns around the circle to share one or two personal commitments to make their classroom a more inclusive, enjoyable, and positive learning environment that will further develop their sense of community and belonging. 
  2. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own definition of a community and your roles and responsibilities to make their classroom a more inclusive, enjoyable, and positive learning environment? (Responsible Decision Making 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about building and participating in a class community? (Responsible Decision Making)

  • Invite others to attend the presentation (optional).

OBJECTIVES

Purpose: To have students consolidate their prior work on personal identity and a sense of community by valuing, respecting, and honoring each other's diverse backgrounds and lived experiences. Students will use the Identity and Community (Part 11) Diversity is Our Strength activity and then create a “Who We Are” display of identity charts, bio poems, and identity masks. 

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Identity and Community (Part 11) activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, and Responsible Decision Making.

Overview: 

  1. Divide students into teams of three by first labeling three corners in the room. Randomly select students' names written on a sheet of paper from a bowl, hat, or bag and assign them to one of the corners in numerical order. Another option is to pre-select the teams by intentionally diversifying each group by English language ability (evenly mixing ability levels in each group), gender, national origin, etc.
  2. In the 1st corner place all the identity charts, in the 2nd corner are all the bio poems, and in the 3rd corner are all the identity masks. Each team will be responsible for securing the artifacts on chart paper using blue tape. These charts will be displayed on the walls either in the classroom or hallway. Each chart should have a two-lined header: 

Who We Are

Diversity is Our Strength 

  1. To ensure collective responsibility, each student will be responsible for placing one artifact on the chart paper.
  2. Once completed, take a group photo of students from each corner holding up their final chart(s) with the artifacts. 
  3. Conclude the activity by having students do a gallery walk to review, discuss and reflect on their final displays and the meaning of Diversity is Our Strength.
  4. Remind the students of LIA’s mission statement, “To empower our amazing youth through culture, service, leadership, and excellent education with the sole purpose of graduating from college.” Make sure that it is posted in a visible location.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  1. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  2. So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore and share your own definition of Diversity is Our Strength? (Social Awareness) 
  3. Now What? What will you do with what you learned about the saying that Diversity is Our Strength? (Responsible Decision Making)

PURPOSE

Gain an understanding of the importance of academic achievement in relation to high school graduation and postsecondary education.

OBJECTIVES

Students will identify their individual strengths & weaknesses within academic achievement and set goals to improve.

  • Obtain grade printouts for individual students or progress towards graduation (credit accrual for entering 9th graders).

Model

  • Ask students to go to 12.01 Weblink Online Questionnaire.  Note:  Each student will need a computer for this activity.
  • Instruct students to carefully read each question and rate themselves from 1-5 (1 = “doesn’t describe you at all” and 5 = “describes you exactly”).
  • Submit the questionnaire. Note:  Students may want to print the results to take back to class to complete the remainder of the lesson.
  • Display 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses.  Ideally, teachers will model filling out the HO based on their own questionnaire results.
  • Distribute 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses & Individual Grade Printouts (for this school year) or Progress Towards Graduation (entering 9th graders).
  • Ask students to highlight grades/subjects where they excelled and highlight (using a different color) grades/subjects they need to work to improve.

Guided Practice

  • Instruct students to complete the 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses using the information they received from 12.01 Weblink Online Questionnaire.

Independent Practice

  • Ask students to finish the remainder of the HO independently.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Use 12.01 Weblink Questionnaire PDF instead of the online questionnaire.  Print & distribute.  Students will identify their strengths by looking at all items that were answered “No” and identify their weaknesses by looking at all items that were answered “Yes”.

Extension

  • Ask students to pair up with someone in the class they know well.  Students can help each other identify additional educational strengths for 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses.
  • Research ways to improve specific educational weaknesses.  Write a paragraph describing the specific suggestions discovered.
  • At the end of each term, ask students to complete 12.01 HO Strengths & Weaknesses based on their performance for the term. Save this information for the year in order to allow students to compare every term/semester’s performance.
  • Ask students to identify what school supports can help them improve their academic achievement. Write a paragraph describing these supports.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • How can I help those I tutor identify their educational strengths?  
  • How can I help my peers to recognize their strengths?

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]

Activity #1

  • Distribute 12.02 Weblink Study Habits Questionnaire
  • Ask students to read and carefully evaluate each statement, then circle the corresponding answer. (A= Always, B= Generally, C= Sometimes, & D= Rarely)
    • Say: Once you have completed the questionnaire, record your scores on 12.02 HO Study Skills.
    • Do you have an area that needs improvement?
    • Reflect, brainstorm, and write ideas on what you can do to make a change in the area you identified.
    • Share some of your ideas with a partner.

Model #1

  • Explain that one thing that can help improve study skills and make students more aware of their learning is to use a learning log.
  • Distribute 12.02 HO Learning Log. 
    • Say: Look at the learning log. This log is designed to help you identify content and skills you learn daily and help you keep track of homework assignments.
  • Read the example aloud.
    • Say: Sometimes it is most effective to only record subjects/courses that are the most challenging for you.  Other times, students may want to record all subjects.  Today, for practice, we will record all subjects.

Guided Practice #1

  • Complete the learning log for all subjects (with yesterday's or today’s lessons).
    • Say: Once you are comfortable with the format, feel free to use a regular notebook for your learning log.

Independent Practice #1

  • This week, as a homework assignment, I want you to keep a learning log.  This assignment will be due next _________________.

Model #2

Share the following with the students:

  • Say: Good note-taking is also critical in developing effective study skills. One popular and effective method for note-taking is called Cornell Notes.
  • Has anyone used Cornell Notes?
  • What is your opinion about this note-taking system?
  • This video clip gives a good introduction on how to take notes using the Cornell method:
    • Watch 12.02 Video Cornell Notes (2 min).

Guided Practice #2

  • Distribute 12.02 HO Note Taking.
    • Say: Now we are going to watch the clip again (12.02 Video Cornell Notes). This time, I want you to take notes on the handout using this method.  
  • Ask students if they have questions or need clarification.
  • Review student work to make sure they have grasped the concept.

Teacher Note

*You may want to review the learning log and note-taking skills once a term, and ask students to show them to you for a grade/feedback. Differentiation Ideas

  • Divide students into groups of 3-4. Ask student groups to research online and locate a Spanish news story. Show the different groups’ news clips in class. Require students to take notes on these news stories using the Cornell method.

Extension

  • Check ahead of time to see if some students are familiar with Cornell notes. Ask these students to plan a lesson to present the how-to portion of note-taking.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Describe the purpose of learning logs and note-taking systems.  
  • Why are learning logs and note-taking systems beneficial to students?  
  • Do you think either of these note-taking methods (Logs or Cornell Notes) will help you to improve your study skills?  Why or why not?  
  • What other methods of note-taking work for you?

PURPOSE

Gain an understanding of the importance of academic achievement in relation to high school graduation and postsecondary education.

OBJECTIVES

Students will learn test-taking strategies to help reduce test anxiety and to improve test scores.

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts.
  • Print & copy 12.03 Weblink PPT Test Taking Questionnaire, or plan to distribute the link during class.

Current Event Bell Starter

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Distribute an index card to each student.
  • Ask them to label the top “Test Taking Strategies”.
    • Say: As you watch the video, write at least three test taking tips or strategies you hear in the song on your index card.
  • Watch 12.03 Video Taking Tests Song (3 min).
  • Ask the following questions:
    • What were some of the strategies you heard?
    • Why would these strategies help you to do better on a test?
    • Today we are going to discuss test anxiety and how we can manage that by using different test taking strategies.

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions. Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

Model

  • Display and distribute 12.03 Weblink PPT Test Taking Questionnaire.
  • Ask students to complete the questionnaire.
  • Ask the students the following question:
    • Are you a good test-taker? Why or why not?
  • Ask students to add up their total scores from all the questions. 
  • Once all students have completed the questionnaire, read the last slide aloud and have them self-evaluate their test-taking anxiety levels. 
  • Ask the students the following questions:
    • What does it take to improve in the areas that you need to work on?
    • Are they easy fixes?
    • Do you have anxiety before and during a test?  Some anxiety is good because it helps motivate us to prepare. Too much anxiety can prevent us from doing our best. However, preparing well and having strategies to successfully approach a test will help get rid of some of the unnecessary anxiety.
    • One way to improve your test taking is by using a mnemonic called PIRATES. This mnemonic will help you remember what to do when you begin a test.
  • Display and distribute 12.03 Weblink HO PIRATES Mnemonic.
  • Ask individual students to read the description for each letter.

Guided Practice

  • Partner students.
  • Ask them to take turns rehearsing the PIRATES strategy.
  • Practice writing the strategy.

Teacher Note

*It is important to remember that students need extensive practice when using a new mnemonic or other strategy.  Try to incorporate this strategy often.

  • Review key concepts of the lesson by asking students to complete an Exit Ticket addressing these questions:
    • On the back of your index card, write a paragraph describing your own level of test anxiety.
    • What you can do to reduce it and be better prepared for tests?

Differentiation Ideas

  • Watch 12.03 Video Flocabulary (3 min) before introducing the vocabulary. This clip uses “test taking” vocabulary words in a creative, fun way and helps students grasp the meaning in context.

Extension

  • Instruct students to complete a practice test using the PIRATES strategy.  
  • Complete a follow up lesson using the ANSWER strategy for essay tests found at 12.03 Weblink HO PIRATES Mnemonic (page 2).
  • Review the key vocabulary regularly since the test-taking vocabulary words are critical for students to understand when completing short answer and essay tests. You may want to post these words on the wall and ask students to create (visual and/or written) examples of each.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Do you think it is important to learn test taking strategies? Why or why not?  
  • How can you share the information you learned today with the students you tutor?

PURPOSE

Gain an understanding of the importance of academic achievement in relation to high school graduation and postsecondary education.

OBJECTIVES

Students will gain an understanding of why literacy is important and improve their ability to use comprehension strategies to access challenging text.

PREPARATION

  • Copy student handouts
  • Print & copy weblink articles
  • Pre-select student groups based on reading ability
  • Purchase small sticky note tabs
  • For more detailed instructions on the QAR strategy, see 12.04 Weblink QAR Teacher Resources.

  • See 1.03 Current Event Bell Ringer Intro for template and detailed instructions.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Display 12.04 Weblink Adol. Literacy Fact Sheet.
  • Select 1 to 2 paragraphs to read together. Ask: 
    • What does the term “literacy” mean?
    • Why is literacy so important for high school and middle school students?
  • Scroll down the fact sheet to display the graphs on page 2. Ask: 
    •  What do these graphs tell us?
  • Read points 4, 5, and 6 on page 3 of the fact sheet. Ask: 
    • What patterns do you notice?
    • What is the number one predictor of college success?
  • Explain to students that today we are going to learn some comprehension strategies that will help strengthen our reading skills.
    • Say: Throughout your middle, high school, and postsecondary education, good reading skills are critical for your success.

Vocabulary

  • Introduce vocabulary and their definitions.
  • Let the students know that in this lesson, they will identify and define key vocabulary in an article assigned to them.
  • Use Vocabulary Template Example and/or Blank Vocabulary Template as a suggested guide.

Teacher Note

  • You may want to divide students into groups based on the text they will read.  Students will create example sentences in their groups with the key vocabulary they choose.

Model

  • Display 12.04 Weblink QAR Question Types.
  • Using the weblink above, discuss the four types of Question-Answer Relationship Types:  1) Right There; 2) Think & Search; 3) Author & Me; 4) On My Own.  
  • Demonstrate creating each type of question using 12.04 Weblink Article QAR Teacher Model.  Use labeled sticky note tabs (1-4) to identify each area in the reading that will be used to write the question.
  • Write an example of each type of question using 12.04 Weblink Article QAR Teacher Model.  Fill out the 12.04 HO Article QAR (English) with these model questions.

Guided Practice

  • Divide students into leveled groups.
  • Distribute 12.04 Weblink Article 1-Easy, 12.04 Weblink Article 2-Intermediate, or 12.04 Weblink Article 3-Difficult to each group.
  • Instruct them as a group to identify key vocabulary, read the article, and then create the 4 types of questions and record them on 12.04 HO Article QAR.

Differentiation Ideas

  • Use 1.03 HO Current Event Resources to find other articles for student groups.
  • Use 12.04 Weblink ReadWorks to find leveled passages for up to grade 8. A few passages are available for 9-10 grade-level readers. Teachers can sign up for a free account.
  • For more detailed instructions on the QAR strategy, see 12.04 Weblink QAR Teacher Resources. 
  • Use 12.04 HO Article QAR (Spanish) to conduct this activity in Spanish.

Extension

  • This lesson can easily be expanded over 2-3 class periods.  Once student groups have written each type of QAR question, ask students to discuss each question in their groups.  Students may form opinions about the article and draw final conclusions.  Student groups can present their opinions and final conclusions to other groups.
  • Ask students to create a SMARTE goal using 2.01 SMARTE Goal Template - Word around improving reading comprehension.

Journal Entry Suggestions

  • Why do you think literacy is important for middle school students?  
  • Describe the QAR comprehension strategy you learned in class.  
  • Do you think the QAR comprehension strategy helped you understand your assigned article? Why or why not?

Understand the steps to becoming an effective tutor.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • understand the purpose of reading and the elements of reading so they can be effective reading tutors  
  • develop an understanding of how social interdependence affects trust (Self-Awareness)
  • understand the impacts of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • deepen understanding about the power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)

PREPARATION

  • Prior to teaching this lesson, watch the lesson walkthrough video 13.01 LIA Tutoring Video (11 minutes) to familiarize yourself with the tutoring process.
  • Printed copies of the PowerPoint (optional)
  • Digital tools

MATERIALS

Main lesson

13.01 PowerPoint: Latinos in Action Tutor Training
13.01 Video: Picture Walk

13.01 13.01 LIA Virtual Tutoring Breakout Room Sample Sheet

Adaptations

KEY VOCABULARY

Elements of Reading

  • Vocabulary
  • Language structure
  • Phonics
  • Cadence
  • Prior knowledge
