INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use this Gallery Walk activity to help students brainstorm about the role of a tutor and expectations on helping tutees with their reading skills. Like viewers at an art gallery, small groups of students will rotate from poster to poster, stopping to view, discuss, and add ideas at each station (Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook- optional).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Gallery Walk activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self Management, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (15 min):

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas) 
  • Establish the goal of developing clarity of the roles and responsibilities of effective tutors. A good prompt would be: "What skills do you need to become an effective tutor in helping your tutee further develop their reading skills?
  • Hang four posters with headings that relate to the specific reading strategies around the room such as:
    • Developing relationships with your tutee/mentee
    • Reading goals
    • Reading aloud
    • Discussion questions
  • Divide the class into four groups, give each group a marker, and assign each group to one of the posters. Explain the overarching question, and what each of the poster topics is.
  • Allow groups to stand at each poster for three minutes to share, discuss, and write down their responses to the category.
  • When time is up, ask the groups to rotate clockwise so each group is in front of a new poster to continue the activity. Each group now reads the offerings of the previous authors, using sticky notes to add clarifying questions or comments/compliments. Rotate every three to five minutes, until every group has visited every poster.
  • Next, allow time for individuals to silently walk around the room and read the completed posters, noting ideas that they agree with or that seem like something they'd like to try.
  • The original group revisits their feedback and can add to their poster.
  • Use this information as a guide when implementing the lesson below.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ideas about reading and tutoring using the Gallery Walk strategy? (Social Awareness) 
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned during this Gallery Walk process? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Design four Google Docs with the headers mentioned above with a table with links to the Google Doc. Post the link to the table so that all of the students have access to it. Divide the class into four groups and send them to separate breakout rooms. Assign each group to begin at a different starting point and assign a time in which they will change to the next Google Doc topic. All students will access the doc and add comments at the same time. The teacher alerts each breakout room when to rotate. Return to the large meeting and post each Google Doc for all to see.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Activating students’ prior knowledge and sharing reading memories we have as children. Teachers can share a fond reading memory (optional).
    • What is your favorite book?
    • Did you have a favorite author?
    • Who read to you when you were young?
    • What’s your favorite book now?
    • Do you read to your younger siblings, cousins, nephews & nieces?
  • Explain that the purpose of this lesson is to understand what we like about reading so that we can share that with younger students, what is the purpose of reading, and how we break down reading strategies.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Teacher Preparation

  • Prior to teaching this lesson, watch the lesson walkthrough video 13.01 LIA Tutoring Video (11 minutes) to familiarize yourself with the tutoring process.

Activity

  • Present the PowerPoint: Latinos in Action Tutor Training. Explain that an element of professionalism is going to presentations and learning to take notes. Optional: give students a printed or virtual copy of the PowerPoint as a reference while they take notes. 

Slide 1: Reading Buddies

  • The number one goal as mentors/reading tutors is building relationships with our mentees/tutees.

Slide 2: Reading – What’s involved?

  • Ask students the following questions:
    • What memories do you have of reading? 
    • What is the purpose of reading?
    • What are the necessary skills for reading? 

Slide 3: Reading Goals

  • Relationship building. (Emphasize that the goal is to build connections with our reading buddies.)
  • Comprehension (Understanding what you read)
  • Enjoyment (Reading should be fun! Tutors make reading fun!)

Slide 4: Elements of Reading

  • Vocabulary: the words that they need to understand to comprehend the story
  • Language structure: grammar and punctuation/sentences have a subject and a verb
  • Phonics: letters and sounds
  • Cadence: tone or rhythm of voice
  • Prior knowledge: what words and ideas do the students already know about the book?

Slide 5: Book Selection

  • Level: the book needs to be age-level and proficiency-level appropriate. If your mentee/tutee is struggling immensely, then the book may not be level-appropriate.
  • Topic: Try to find books that meet the mentee's interests. We focus more and are more interested if the book is about something we find interesting. If your mentee likes dinosaurs, try to find a book about dinosaurs.
  • Cover: Is the cover interesting? Are there pictures? Is there an appropriate title?
  • Illustrations: Are there many illustrations? Are they interesting and fun? Do they help tell a story?
  • Structure/organization: A straightforward plot is best for young students. For example, you would not read Harry Potter novels with a first grader because the books are not always chronological, they skip between different time periods and places and don't have many illustrations.

Slide 6: Before Reading

  • Go over the cover, author, and illustrator.
  • Take the student through a picture walk – either demonstrate a picture walk or show 13.01 Video Picture Walk. A picture walk is when you have students talk about what they think will happen in the book and activate their prior knowledge by walking through each picture and not reading any of the words.
  • Introduce vocabulary that you predict the student does not know and explain it.
  • Have students make predictions and brainstorm what will happen in the story.

Slide 7: Reading Format

  • The tutor reads to the mentee- this can be used in the beginning when the mentee is shy and nervous.
  • Shared reading- mentee read a page, tutor read a page.
  • The mentee reads to the tutor- this happens when the mentee becomes more comfortable.
  • Modeled reading/Echo reading- this is when both the tutor and mentee read at the same time.
  • *NOTE: These formats should be varied and mixed. Use different formats on different days. Try them all!

Slide 8: Modeled Reading/Echo Reading

  • Step one: Tutor reads while the mentee/tutee follows along
  • Step two: The Tutee reads silently, and tells tutor when they are done
  • Step three: Repeat the two-part process at least 2-3 times, until the tutee is ready to read aloud

Slide 9: Reading Aloud

  • As tutors, we model the process of reading first:
    • We introduce the book, the title, and the front cover, and take the tutee through a picture walk.
    • We read aloud to the tutee and stop to think and predict.
    • We discuss what’s happening in the book as we read aloud.
    • We may also demonstrate a reading strategy at this point.

Slide 10: Why We Read Aloud

  • Discuss the reasons why we read aloud and its importance.

Slide 11: During Reading

  • Comprehension checks- ask questions about characters' names and attributes, location/setting, and major plotline questions.
  • Think aloud- “I wonder if…” “I think that…”
  • Predict and verify- “I predict that Clifford will befriend the grouchy neighbors…” then check at the end of the book to see if the predictions were correct.
  • Relate text to self/text/world- Bring the book back to their lives and their interests, so they feel invested in the story.
  • Visualization- Have tutees create a mental image in their minds to represent the ideas that they read in the text: "Close your eyes and imagine Clifford, his friends, their house, etc..."
  • Praise- Be genuine with compliments. Tell the tutees that they are trying very hard, or focusing really well, or that you have seen great improvement (if you have). They need to feel encouraged!

Slide 12: Self-Correct Strategies

  • Discuss the examples listed for teaching tutees to self-correct when reading. 

Slide 13: Discussion Questions

  • Depending on the grade level that you are tutoring with, discussion questions will vary.
  • Be sure to insert the word “you” or “your” when possible in each question.
  • If they are young students (K-2), focus on easier questions, like:
    • What was your favorite part of the story?
    • Which character did you like?
    • What characters do you remember?
    • Where did the story take place?
  • If they are more advanced or older students (grades 3-5), you can dive into more difficult questions:
    • How would you compare (a character) to (another character)?
    • If you were in the situation, how would you have acted?
    • If you could change the ending, how would it end?
    • Were any of the characters like people you know? (Again, relating back to self/real world!)
    • What did you learn about the world?

Slide 14: Tutors in Action (An Overview)

  • Choose a book or text that's appropriate for the student's interests and reading level. 
  • Introduce the book- title, cover, author, illustrator, and picture walk.
  • Read aloud- use varied methods, stop for discussion/questions.
  • Wrap-up- ask comprehension questions to clarify that the tutee understood the story; ask what the tutee enjoyed about the book.

Slide 15: Correcting Negative Behaviors and Discipline

  • Some techniques to help when your tutee is not paying attention:
    • Point out another student who is on task and say, “Wow, look how well Victor is reading with his buddy. I think you could read like that too.”
    • Use incentives such as stickers. “I don’t think you are going to be earning your sticker today.”
  • If the tutee can really not focus after multiple attempts to get them back on track, try offering to take them back to class:
    • “I think I should take you back to class and maybe I can work with one of our classmates who wants to read with me. We will try again next time.”
  • If the tutee seems really off and unfocused, try asking what’s wrong:
    • “What’s going on with you today, Camila? Usually, you are very focused, and today you seem off.”
  • Emphasize the following to your LIA students: If ever the problem is too large for the tutor to handle, always go seek the help of your LIA teacher or the elementary school student’s teacher.

Slide 16: Celebrate Reading!

  • Remind your LIA students to celebrate reading and make it fun for their mentees!
  • Remind students that the number one goal as mentors/reading tutors is building relationships with our mentees/tutees.

Guided Practice

  • Direct students to practice one or more parts of these components with a partner, using different books.

  • Have students break into their committees and come up with ten scenarios that could happen while tutoring and a solution for each scenario. For example:
    • Scenario: If my tutee starts crying in the middle of our reading session.
    • Possible solution: Try to calm my tutee down by taking a break from reading and getting some water, and if that doesn’t work, go find my LIA teacher or the elementary school teacher.

Adaptation for Virtual Tutoring

  • There are still plenty of unknowns about the impact of school closures during the pandemic and the effect it would have on schools in the long term. Many schools have implemented in-person, virtual, and hybrid instructional models that involve daily synchronous instruction. For this reason, it is important to establish and maintain a virtual tutoring model that can present content in multiple ways to help students retain information and address the need to reinforce vocabulary development, reading comprehension, and background knowledge. The benefits of using digital media resources in virtual tutoring provide students a multisensory experience while introducing new concepts and ideas remotely. 
  • To begin a virtual tutoring model, the LIA class and the elementary school must utilize a common virtual learning platform with a built-in video conferencing tool to deliver instruction. Some examples of virtual platforms include Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, BigBlueButton on Canvas, Google Classroom, Schoology, etc. Once you decide on a platform, you and the elementary school teacher will need to familiarize yourselves with the ins and outs of this platform. If you need additional assistance, contact your school or district IT staff for support. 
  • It is also important for students to have one-to-one devices. Once the virtual platform is established, all tutors and tutees will either join one shared virtual classroom, or individual virtual spaces, with a code or link. 
  • The LIA and elementary school teachers manage and maintain shared folders and provide materials for the tutors and tutees to use during the online tutoring sessions.
  • The LIA students and the elementary students will use a video-chatting tool through the chosen tutoring platform to provide live instruction during the tutoring session. Virtual tutoring sessions must be monitored and maintained, by at least one of the teachers.
  • If your chosen platform includes a breakout room option, it is imperative that you take time to familiarize yourself with how to utilize this tool. The following resources will provide you with a brief introduction to how breakout rooms work on the following platforms:
    • Article: Zoom Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Google Meet Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Microsoft Teams Breakout Rooms
  • The teachers create online breakout rooms by dividing the students into pairings or groupings. All breakout rooms are listed on a hyperlinked document in the virtual classroom for students to find. Use 13.01 LIA Virtual Tutoring Breakout Room Sample Sheet as a reference point. The functionality and practicality of online breakout rooms work similarly to physical groups in offline settings. In addition, breakout rooms offer online classroom tools, such as a virtual whiteboard to jot down notes and the ability for students to interact and speak to each other. Teachers can walk around to observe in-person tutoring sessions or virtually monitor remote students. It is recommended that an additional breakout room is created to serve as a virtual "help desk." The teacher should monitor this breakout room for any concerns or questions that students may have while tutoring remotely. 

Journal Entry Questions

  • Teacher or students will choose 1-2 questions below. These questions will be the same for all 3 lessons in this unit:
    • What is your fondest memory about reading?
    • What sorts of materials and topics do you enjoy reading?
    • What is your favorite book and why do you like that book?
    • What is the most challenging part of reading? What don’t you like about it?
    • What are some potential outcomes of a child who is read to versus a child who is not read to?
    • Agree/Disagree with the statement and explain your answer: Children don’t like to read because they are not good at it.

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE

Practice the tutoring process with a classmate.

OBJECTIVES

Students will:

  • demonstrate knowledge of reading tutoring strategies and effective book selection by practicing with another student
  • develop an understanding of how social interdependence affects trust (Self-Awareness)
  • understand the impacts of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • deepen understanding about the power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)  

 PREPARATION

  • Elementary school-level books for students to practice tutoring. You will need at least 1 book per pair of students.
  • Print copies or provide the link to Unit 13 – Tutoring Timesheet and Daily Log. If printing copies, make sure there is 1 per student.

MATERIALS

Main lesson

13:01 Picture Walk Video

Adaptations 

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Read aloud
  • Shared reading
  • Echo reading
  • Vocabulary
  • Language structure
  • Phonics
  • Cadence
  • Prior knowledge

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To use Partner Reading as a strategy to facilitate student interaction so that tutors have more patience, empathy, and compassion with their tutees. (Literacy Strategies for English Learners, Calderon 2016).

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This Partner Reading activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (8 min):

  • Welcome students - lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) - see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas).
  • Explain to students that they will participate in a Partner Reading simulation between a tutor and a tutee. Use a grouping activity such as Academic Vocabulary Buddies (see MS Lesson 5.05) or Clock Buddies (see MS Lesson 1.05) to create pairs for this reading activity. In the case where there are ELs or struggling readers, intentionally pair these students with more proficient English speakers. 
  • Remind the students of the practice of patience, empathy, and compassion when reading with their tutees.
  • In the case where you have newcomers (NC), have the NC read or whisper-read the same sentence that the tutor reads.

Virtual Adaptation: Use Breakout rooms to work with your tutee on Partner Reading. Emphasize the use of patience, empathy, and compassion.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Show the students 13.02 Picture Walk Video (2:27 minutes). This will demonstrate an effective picture walk for students. 
  • Explain the purpose of this lesson is for students to get a chance to practice the tutoring process that they will use with their tutees at the elementary school.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Activity

  • Teacher will review the steps of tutoring with the students. Ask for a volunteer to refer to their notes and recite the steps from Slide 14 of the PowerPoint: Latinos in Action Tutor Training in the previous lesson:
    • Choose an appropriate book/text.
    • Introduce the book- title, cover, author, illustrator, picture walk.
    • Read aloud- use varied methods, stop for discussion/questions.
    • Wrap-up- ask comprehension questions to clarify that the tutee understood the story. Ask what the tutee enjoyed about the book.
    • Complete the Unit 13 – Tutoring Timesheet and Daily Log and explain to students that this will need to be done at least once a week to keep track of each tutee’s progress.

Guided Practice

  • The teacher chooses a sample elementary school book. The teacher will review and model different reading formats. If there is an experienced reading tutor, have the experienced tutor model the formats:
    • The tutor reads to the mentee (can be used in the beginning when the mentee is shy and nervous).
    • Shared reading (mentee read a page, tutor read a page).
    • The mentee reads to the tutor (this happens when the mentee becomes more comfortable).
    • Modeled reading/Echo reading (this is when both the tutor and mentee read at the same time).
  • Have students break into the pairs they chose in the Welcoming Ritual. In their pairs, students will decide who will be the tutor and tutee. 
  • Assign students the grade level that they will likely be working with at the elementary school. So, if you’re working with second grade, have their classmate playing the role of tutee be in second grade.
  • Tutors sit face to face with their tutee and explain to them the steps to Partner Reading. Practice modeling with the tutee what it is like to read alternating sentences. Remember the SEL competencies of patience, empathy, and compassion. Give the students 15-20 minutes to go through the reading tutoring process at each stage until they switch roles:
    • Choose an appropriate text (for the grade level you are working with).
    • Introduce the book- title, cover, author, illustrator, and picture walk.
    • Read aloud- use varied methods, stop for discussion/questions. For example, shared reading would use the following format: 
      • The tutor reads the first sentence
      • The tutee reads the next sentence
      • After each paragraph or page, verbally summarize what was read
      • Continue reading until done with the paragraph, page, or book
    • Wrap-up- ask comprehension questions to clarify that the tutee understood the story. Ask what the tutee enjoyed about the book.
    • The tutor will practice filling out the Unit 13 – Tutoring Timesheet and Daily Log to keep track of the tutee’s progress. Ask your partner for help if you run into any problems.

  • As a potential service project, the LIA service committee can speak to their local library about getting elementary school books donated to their LIA class that they can take with them to tutoring.

Adaptation for Virtual Tutoring

  • There are still plenty of unknowns about the impact of school closures during the pandemic and the effect it would have on schools in the long term. Many schools have implemented in-person, virtual, and hybrid instructional models that involve daily synchronous instruction. For this reason, it is important to establish and maintain a virtual tutoring model that can present content in multiple ways to help students retain information and address the need to reinforce vocabulary development, reading comprehension, and background knowledge. The benefits of using digital media resources in virtual tutoring provide students a multisensory experience while introducing new concepts and ideas remotely.
  • To begin a virtual tutoring model, the LIA class and the elementary school must utilize a common virtual learning platform with a built-in video conferencing tool to deliver instruction. Some examples of virtual platforms include Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, BigBlueButton on Canvas, Google Classroom, Schoology, etc. Once you decide on a platform, you and the elementary school teacher will need to familiarize yourselves with the ins and outs of this platform. If you need additional assistance, contact your school or district IT staff for support. 
  • It is also important for students to have one-to-one devices. Once the virtual platform is established, all tutors and tutees will either join one shared virtual classroom, or individual virtual spaces, with a code or link.
  • The LIA and elementary school teachers manage and maintain shared folders and provide materials for the tutors and tutees to use during the online tutoring sessions.
  • The LIA students and the elementary students will use a video-chatting tool through the chosen tutoring platform to provide live instruction during the tutoring session. Virtual tutoring sessions must be monitored and maintained, by at least one of the teachers.
  • If your chosen platform includes a breakout room option, it is imperative that you take time to familiarize yourself with how to utilize this tool. The following resources will provide you with a brief introduction to how breakout rooms work on the following platforms:
    • Article: Zoom Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Google Meet Breakout Rooms
    • Article: Microsoft Teams Breakout Rooms
  • The teachers create online breakout rooms by dividing the students into pairings or groupings. All breakout rooms are listed on a hyperlinked document in the virtual classroom for students to find. Use 13.01 LIA Virtual Tutoring Breakout Room Sample Sheet as a reference point. The functionality and practicality of online breakout rooms work similarly to physical groups in offline settings. In addition, breakout rooms offer online classroom tools, such as a virtual whiteboard to jot down notes and the ability for students to interact and speak to each other. Teachers can walk around to observe in-person tutoring sessions or virtually monitor remote students. It is recommended that an additional breakout room is created to serve as a virtual “help desk.” The teacher should monitor this breakout room for any concerns or questions that students may have while tutoring remotely.

Journal Entry Questions

  • The teacher or students will choose 1-2 questions below. These questions will be the same for all 3 lessons in this unit:
    • What is your fondest memory about reading?
    • What sorts of materials and topics do you enjoy reading?
    • What is your favorite book and why do you like that book?
    • What is the most challenging part of reading? What don’t you like about it?
    • What are some potential outcomes of a child who is read to versus a child who is not read to?
    • Agree/Disagree with the statement and explain your answer: Children don’t like to read because they are not good at it.

bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]PURPOSE:

Watch a meaningful TED Talk about building relationships and relate it back to their tutoring at the elementary school.

OBJECTIVES:

Students will: 

  • develop an understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • explore the impacts of perspective-taking and empathy (Social Awareness)
  • develop the ability to establish and maintain healthy and rewarding relationships (Relationship Skills)
  • recognize one’s ethical responsibility to treat others fairly and with respect (Responsible Decision-Making)

PREPARATION

  • Print copies of 13.03 HO Characteristics of an Effective Mentor

MATERIALS

Main lesson

13.03 HO Characteristics of an Effective Mentor

13.03 Image: Round Robin strategy

13.03 Video (8 min): Ted Talk - Rita Pierson "Every Kid Needs a Champion"

Adaptations 

KEY VOCABULARY

  • Mentorship
  • Role Model
  • Self-esteem
  • Champion
  • Accepting 
  • Approachable
  • Dependable
  • Empathetic 
  • Non-judgemental 
  • Trustworthy

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]WELCOMING ACTIVITY

Purpose: To explore characteristics of mentoring in order to provide support, advice, friendship, reinforcement, and constructive role modeling to mentees. This activity will help students understand the concept of mentoring and its positive impact on the elementary students involved.

Skills for Learning and Life Focus: This mentoring activity will further enhance students’ competencies of Self-Awareness, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, and Responsible Decision-Making.

Overview (5 min): 

  • Welcome students in a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning and Life Signature Practices Playbook (optional) and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals (Bright Ideas)
  • Explain to the class that a mentor helps their mentee by being a positive influence, giving their time, and being a role model.
  • Print copies of 13.03 HO Characteristics of an Effective Mentor and hand them out to students. Ask students to select four keywords from the list that answer the question, “How should a mentor act?” Encourage students to think of words that describe individuals who may have been mentors to them.

Debrief (3 min): (Reflection Model, Rolfe, 2001)

  • Use an inclusive and equitable grouping strategy to divide the class into groups of three. Strategy Grouping Example–Partner high-skilled students with mid-level skilled students and/or partner mid-level skilled students with lower-skilled students.
  • Remind students of the class Shared Agreements and life skills on everyone gets equal time, empathic listening, and valuing diverse opinions and perspectives.
  • Use a Round Robin strategy to allow them to share the first word and explain its meaning to them and give one example of when they may have practiced this characteristic or that may describe their experience with a mentor.
  • Share out a few examples with the class.
  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness)
  • So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore the characteristics of an effective mentor? (Social Awareness)
  • Now What? What will you do with what you learned about the characteristics of an effective mentor? (Responsible Decision Making)

Virtual Adaptation: Design Google Docs with the list of the characteristics of a mentor and post the link to the list so that all of the students have access to it. Have students work on their list of four characteristics. Assign students to breakout rooms of three. The teacher reminds students in each breakout room to give each other equal time to share. After the designated time, bring all students back to the main meeting room and post the Google Doc for all to see and share out examples.

Relevancy/Linkage

  • Explain that our main goal with our reading tutoring is to build relationships and provide mentorship to young students. We know that students do better when they have at least one role model or person to share things within their lives. LIA tutors are the role models the elementary school students need, and we hope that our work with them throughout the year allows them to see themselves as leaders, and inspire them to also want to lead, and to read, as they grow up. But in order for us to have effective reading gains, we have to build a relationship first.

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]Activity

  • Watch the following video (8 minutes):
    • Ted Talk – Rita Pierson “Every Kid Needs a Champion”
    • Ask the students to write down at least one quote while they are watching that they can identify with.
  • Partner Discussion.
  • Students will share with a partner which quote they wrote down and why that quote is meaningful to them.

Guided Practice

Reflection Questions: Ask students to reflect on what they learned from the TED Talk and how they can relate it back to LIA tutoring. Have students unpack the following quotes from the video and answer the following discussion questions in their committees:

  • “And we know why kids drop out. We know why kids don’t learn.”
    • Brainstorm FIVE reasons why you think that students drop out of high school.
    • How does Latinos In Action prevent students from dropping out of high school?
  • “James Comer says that no significant learning can occur without a significant relationship.”
    • How will you develop a significant relationship with your reading tutee?
    • Why is regular attendance in an LIA class important?
  • “How do I raise the self-esteem of a child and their academic achievement at the same time?”
    • In what ways can LIA tutors raise the self-esteem of their tutees?
    • In what ways are we as a class going to track our tutee’s progress?
  • “I gave a quiz, 20 questions. A student missed 18. I put a “+2” on his paper and a big smiley face.”
    • What does this quote say about the importance of perspective?
    • How can you as a reading tutor encourage tutees even when they are discouraged?
  • “Every child deserves a champion, an adult who will never give up on them, who understands the power of connection, and insists that they become the best that they can possibly be.”
    • Who was your “champion” when you were growing up?
    • Use one word to explain how you feel about becoming a champion for a young child.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Adaptation/Extension Activity

  • The service committee can find a fun “getting-to-know-you” activity online and print/copy them for the class on the first day of tutoring so that students can begin the relationship building on the first day, and help elementary school tutees to become comfortable with LIA tutors.
  • Committees can set goals for reading tutoring this school year. Examples:
    • We want to see at least one reading level gain in each of our elementary school students.
    • We want to teach the students 10 new vocabulary words a week.
    • We want to get books donated to distribute for the Holidays.
    • We want to fundraise so that we can buy our tutees LIA reading shirts.

Adaptation for Virtual Tutoring

    • There are still plenty of unknowns about the impact of school closures during the pandemic and the effect it would have on schools in the long term. Many schools have implemented in-person, virtual, and hybrid instructional models that involve daily synchronous instruction. For this reason, it is important to establish and maintain a virtual tutoring model that can present content in multiple ways to help students retain information and address the need to reinforce vocabulary development, reading comprehension, and background knowledge. The benefits of using digital media resources in virtual tutoring provide students with a multisensory experience while introducing new concepts and ideas remotely.
    • To begin a virtual tutoring model, the LIA class and the elementary school must utilize a common virtual learning platform with a built-in video conferencing tool to deliver instruction. Some examples of virtual platforms include Zoom, Google Meet, Microsoft Teams, BigBlueButton on Canvas, Google Classroom, Schoology, etc. Once you decide on a platform, you and the elementary school teacher will need to familiarize yourselves with the ins and outs of this platform. If you need additional assistance, contact your school or district IT staff for support. 
    • It is also important for students to have one-to-one devices. Once the virtual platform is established, all tutors and tutees will either join one shared virtual classroom, or individual virtual spaces, with a code or link.
    • The LIA and elementary school teachers manage and maintain shared folders and provide materials for the tutors and tutees to use during the online tutoring sessions.
    • The LIA students and the elementary students will use a video-chatting tool through the chosen tutoring platform to provide live instruction during the tutoring session. Virtual tutoring sessions must be monitored and maintained, by at least one of the teachers.
    • If your chosen platform includes a breakout room option, it is imperative that you take time to familiarize yourself with how to utilize this tool. The following resources will provide you with a brief introduction to how breakout rooms work on the following platforms:
      • Article: Zoom Breakout Rooms
      • Article: Google Meet Breakout Rooms
      • Article: Microsoft Teams Breakout Rooms
    • The teachers create online breakout rooms by dividing the students into pairings or groupings. All breakout rooms are listed on a hyperlinked document in the virtual classroom for students to find. Use 13.01 LIA Virtual Tutoring Breakout Room Sample Sheet as a reference point. The functionality and practicality of online breakout rooms work similarly to physical groups in offline settings. In addition, breakout rooms offer online classroom tools, such as a virtual whiteboard to jot down notes and the ability for students to interact and speak to each other. Teachers can walk around to observe in-person tutoring sessions or virtually monitor remote students. It is recommended that an additional breakout room be created to serve as a virtual “help desk.” The teacher should monitor this breakout room for any concerns or questions that students may have while tutoring remotely.

Journal Entry Questions

  • The teacher or students will choose 1-2 questions below. These questions will be the same for all 3 lessons in this unit:
    • What is your fondest memory about reading?
    • What sorts of materials and topics do you enjoy reading?
    • What is your favorite book and why do you like that book?
    • What is the most challenging part of reading? What don’t you like about it?
    • What are some potential outcomes of a child who is read to versus a child who is not read to?
    • Agree/Disagree with the statement and explain your answer: Children don’t like to read because they are not good at it.

Music wakes the schema and promotes history, memory, and recollections. Lead the students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources. 45-50 minute lesson Objectives Students will:
  • understand the purpose and objectives of the LIA course.
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness, Social Awareness). Refer to 1.01 slide deck to expand on highlighted vocabulary.
  • demonstrate effective communication skills (Self-Management, Relationship Skills).
  • co-create a sense of belonging and a respectful community (Responsible Decision-Making).
  • define Fundamentals lesson 1 vocabulary.
  • create visual representations of knowledge.
21st Century Competencies Skills for Learning & Life
Critical thinking, digital literacy, communication, collaboration, creativity, social skills Self-Awareness, Self Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills, Responsible Decision-Making

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Welcoming Routine (slide # 3) Students will refer to emojis to describe how they feel. Sentence stem: Today I feel ______ because ________.   
Building The LIA Classroom Community (10-15 minutes) F.01 Slide Deck Go over the objectives of this lesson. (slide #5)
Purpose: To use Class Introductions, Developing Relationships and Express Care with one another to further enhance relationships and support for one another.  Skills for Learning & Life Focus: The Class Introductions and Developing Relationships activities will further enhance students’ SEL competencies of Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Relationship Skills and Responsible Decision-Making. LIA Teacher Introduction: Introduce yourself. Choose 1 – 2 ideas to facilitate from the Teacher Introduction Activities. Go over the purpose and objectives of this lesson.
LIA Student Introductions Lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning & Life 3 Signature Practices Playbook and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals  Suggested Activities for in-person class:
  • Greeting Frenzy (3 minute activity, pg. 12 SEL 3 Signatures Playbook)
  • Name and Motion (5-7 minutes, pg.13 SEL 3 Signatures Playbook)
  • A Little Known Fact Greeting (5-7 minutes Greeting Slide Deck #11)
Suggested Activities for online class:
  • Roll a die or spin a wheel to select a question  (#4 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Play Guess Who with Flipgrid (#5 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Choose Your Favorite (#4 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)
  • What, Where, When? (#7 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)
Virtual Adaptation: Show students how to use their computer’s “thumbs up” response and practice once to see that all are showing that signal with a question such as “I am a part of this class right now.” or “I know what day of the week it is!” Give the same encouragement to students to boldly look around on their screen, to see who’s answering yes to each question, since the goal is to get to know one another even better. Include Hand Raise, Chat, Breakout Rooms, and Gallery conversations to engage students throughout the lesson.
Reflection (5-7 minutes) Emphasize the following:(slide #7)
  • Students have begun to build a strong LIA classroom community.
  • Students are developing RELATIONSHIPS (show relationships slide), have demonstrated RESPECT (show respect slide), COLLABORATED (show collaboration slide), and are learning positive SOCIAL INTERDEPENDENCE (show social interdependence slide)
Write the following on the board or display the slide (optional: print the slide for each student to fill out)(slide # 7) What? So What? Now What? Initiate a brief discussion using the questions below: What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness) So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore ways to build community? (Social Awareness)  Now What? What will you do with what you learned about community building today? (Responsible Decision Making) Activities to foster student engagement

Engagement Activity LIA Introduction: Show LIA logo (slide #10), or the acronym LIA (slide #11). Initiate a brief discussion of what students know about the logo, or acronym. Allow students to share thoughts. In-person class:
  • ball toss (toss a ball or bean bag to a student and they share, then the student tosses the ball to another student)
  • Turn and Talk (students turn to the student sitting to the left or right (teacher decides) of them and discuss the question).
Online class:
  • Wheel of Names or Random Name Picker
  Use LIA Student Introduction PPT to introduce LIA’s mission statement and purpose (click slide # 12 in instructional slide deck to open PPT). Go through each slide with the students. The following slides should follow this instructional format:  Encourage volunteers to take turns reading each bullet. After reading all the bullets allow the students to review the simplified explanation of community, personal, professional, multicultural development. 
  • Community Development(slide #6 )
  • Personal Development (slide #9)
  • Professional Development(slide #12)
  • Multicultural Development (slide #17)
See examples and video clips embedded within the PPT.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]
In- Person Class Assessment Options: 
  • Exit ticket. Students will respond to this question: What do you hope to gain from LIA? Students will write their response on a sticky note and turn it in as they exit the classroom, (Save the sticky notes. Students will put the exit ticket in their LIA journal) or turn and talk to discuss.
  • Bubble Map- students fill out a bubble map by writing LIA in the middle and writing ideas that represent LIA. See sample.
  • Create a video on Flipgrid or Canvas and answer the questions from the LIA Reflection sheet.
  • Fill out  LIA Reflection sheet and pair share or turn and talk to share answers.
Journal Entry Questions:
  • How can LIA make a difference in your life?
Online Class Assessment Options:
  • Exit Ticket. Create a discussion assignment in your Learning Management System (LMS). Students respond to this question: What do you hope to gain from LIA?
  • Digital Bubble Map- students fill out a digital bubble map by typing LIA in the middle and typing ideas that represent LIA.  Teachers will be required to make a copy of the digital bubble map, then See sample.
  • Create a video on Flip or Canvas and answer the questions from the LIA Reflection sheet.

Differentiation:
  • Conduct this lesson in Spanish or have a student translate each slide.
  • Use F.01 LIA Reflection (Spanish) as an additional option.
Extension:
  • Students create a visual representation of LIA using the shield handout.
  • Students choose a vocabulary word that has not been discussed and work in small groups or with a partner to discuss the meaning of the words. 
  • Frayer model- Students create a Frayer model for 3-5 vocabulary words. Encourage students to choose words that resonate with them or have more significance.
  • Students create a Wordart using the acronym LIA. See sample and Loom video.
  • Compare and contrast read aloud with Dr. Enriquez’s story. Choose a read-aloud story from the selected F.01 literature page to read to the class. Use a  Venn Diagram Lined/ Venn Diagram Unlined or a Double Bubble Map to compare and contrast the main character of the book and Dr. Enriquez.

Lead the students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources. 45-50 minute lesson Objectives Students will:
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness, Social Awareness) Refer to 1.02 slide deck to expand on highlighted vocabulary.
  • demonstrate effective communication skills (Self-Management, Relationship Skills)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and a respectful community (Responsible Decision-Making)
  • define Fundamentals lesson 2 vocabulary
  • produce class norms of collaboration
  • create visual representations of self
  • create an LIA journal

If I were a color I’d be ________ because __________.    
Building The LIA Classroom Community (10-15 minutes) F.02 Slide Deck
Go over the objectives of this lesson. (slide #3)
Community Building Activity Purpose: To use the Ice-Breakers activity to build community; support self-awareness, social awareness, responsible decision making Skills for Learning & Life Focus: The Ice-Breaker activities will further enhance students’ Social Awareness and Responsible Decision-Making. Lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning & Life Signature Practices Playbook and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals  Suggested Activities for in-person class:
  • Switching Sides Game (3-5 minutes)
  • Four Corners  (5-7 minute activity, pg. 12 SEL 3 Signatures Playbook)
Suggested Activities for online class:
  • Roll a die or spin a wheel to select a question  (#4 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Play Guess Who with Flip (#5 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Choose Your Favorite (#4 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)
  • What, Where, When? (#7 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)
Mini-Lesson: Surnames Engagement hook: Display “surname” slide (slide #7). Engage students in a brief discussion about surnames. Expected response: a last name, a family name, father’s last name/mother’s last name, name you share with other members of your family. Facilitate My Name, My Identity Activity- focus only on surnames  (see Greetings slide #3) – pair share, large group (Layered and process) Following the introduction of students’ surnames use slide # 8 to explain the following:
  • Many Spanish surnames consist of two surnames.
  • The first surname is paternal.
  • The second surname is maternal.
Importance of Pronunciation (slide #9) Questions for students to respond to: Students share responses by turning and talking or sharing with the group.
  • Have you ever been in a situation where people didn’t say your surnames correctly?
  • How did it make you feel?
  • What can you do to help people learn your name? 
Possible responses: clap it out into syllables, write it the way it sounds, practice saying it several times.
Reflection (5-7 minutes) Emphasize the following-What’s the Take-away?:(slide #10)
  • Surnames are an important part of identity.
  • Surnames are links to our culture, our heritage, our ancestors.
Write the following on the board or display the slide (optional: print What? So What? Now What?) WHAT? SO WHAT? NOW WHAT? Initiate a brief discussion using the questions below. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness) So What? Why do you think it’s important to explore our surnames? (Social Awareness)  Now What? What will you do with what you learned about surnames today? (Responsible Decision Making) Activities to foster student engagement

INSTRUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]
Engagement Activity Display the word ETHOS (slide # 12) Display the word. Ask students if they know how to say the word or what the word means. Prompt students by saying the word out loud: Does it sound like any other familiar words? Expected response: ethics. Ethics is derived from the Greek word “ethos” which means ‘character’. Ethos are distinguishing characteristics or guiding beliefs of a person or group. Introduce the Elementary Latinos In Action Ethos. The guiding beliefs of Elementary LIA are: Elementary LIA Ethos. Display the ES LIA Ethos (slide #13). Suggest printing out the page for students to keep in their LIA Journal. Classroom Culture:   Show the following linked video of a class in chaos. After viewing the video ask the following questions (slide #12): What was the problem? How would you feel if you were part of this class?  Display ‘organizational culture’ vocabulary slide (slide # 15). Ask the students what they think of when they see the word organizational. Expected response: organize, organization.  Discuss the meaning of organize/organization. Arrange, or order into a structured whole. Ask students what they think of when they see the word ‘culture’. Expected response: expected behaviors, customs, traditions, beliefs, codes of dress, language, religion. Discuss the meaning of culture. Invite the students to combine the meaning of the two words to define organizational culture. Guide the students to define as ‘expectations, beliefs, norms (rules), attitudes that members of an organization are a part of’. Ask students to give examples of where you might see organizational culture. Expected response: school, home, sports teams, church. Critical Thinking Prompt: How can organizational culture be helpful in our LIA class? Emphasize the following:
  • Our LIA class needs to be a positive place and a place where we feel safe, respected, and valued.
How do we create that? Expected responses: class expectations, class rules. Talking Points:
  1. In LIA we will be engaging in a lot of cooperative learning and there will be opportunities for collaboration. What is collaboration? (Show vocabulary slide or printed version).
  2. In our LIA class it is important for students to work together to develop class norms and expectations. What are norms?
  3. For the next few minutes you will be collaborating and using a democratic process to develop class norms. What is a democratic process?
  4. BUT FIRST . . . We will vote on a “Call and Response”.
Select 3-4  classroom call and response cards and demonstrate each one. Encourage students to vote for 2 classroom calls and responses. Practice a few times. Norms of Collaboration Activity Divide the students into two or three groups. Distribute F.02 Proposed Norms handout to each group.  Encourage each group to choose a spokesperson and a note taker. Display Norms of Collaboration Guidelines (slide # 21). Allow students to collaborate for an appropriate amount of time. Use a call and response to bring the students back to attention. Allow the spokesperson for each group to share the norms that they have created. As norms from each group are shared, direct the note taker of each group to cross out any norms that are the same. Once repeat norms have been discarded encourage the students to select 4, 6, or 8 norms that are of greatest importance for the LIA class.  Each group will use butcher/chart paper to create a display of the chosen norms (assign norms to each group). Journal Creation Activity Emphasize the following: Part of personal growth and learning is the ability to reflect on yourself and your learning. In this LIA class we will be using a journal to help boost our critical thinking and take charge of our learning and feelings.

In- Person Class Assessment Options: 
  • Exit ticket. Students will respond to this question: Why is it important to create norms in a classroom? Students can turn and talk to discuss the discussion question.
  • Journal personalization: Assign journal personalization as an assignment. Students can take the journal home and personalize it to reflect their personality, likes, passions, interest, etc. Emphasize that representations must be school appropriate.
Journal Entry Suggestions
  • Why is it important to create norms?
Online Class Assessment Options:
  • Exit Ticket. Create a discussion assignment in your Learning Management System (LMS). Students respond to this question: Why is it important to create norms in a classroom?
  • Create a video on Flipgrid or Canvas and answer the questions from the LIA Reflection sheet (English) LIA Reflection Sheet (Spanish)

Lead the students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources. 45-50 minute lesson Objectives Students will:
  • get to know their classmates by participating in Icebreaker and Team Building activities
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
  • develop understanding of self advocacy
  • recognize digital citizenship skills
  • demonstrate responsible use of digital tools
21st Century Competencies Skills for Learning & Life
Critical thinking, communication, collaboration, creativity, social skills, leadership, productivity, initiative, flexibility, technology literacy Social Awareness, Self-Awareness, Responsible Decision-Making, Self-Management

INTRODUCTION

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text]Welcoming Routine  Students can record responses in their LIA journals and share-out with the class.   “I Gotta Feeling” Activity. Display slide # 5. Show 4-5 different emoticons. Students will be given 60 seconds to list different words to describe the emoticons. Students will not be able to include the words that are shown below the emoticon in their list. The purpose of this activity is to help students identify emotions and develop higher level vocabulary of each emotion by searching for synonyms. (Teacher is encouraged to record the different responses on chart paper to reference during another lesson.)    
Building The LIA Classroom Community (10-15 minutes) F.03 slide deck
Go over the objectives of this lesson.
Community Building Activity Purpose: To use the Ice-Breakers activity to build community; support self-awareness, social awareness, responsible decision making Skills for Learning & Life Focus: The Ice-Breaker activities will further enhance students’ Social Awareness and Responsible Decision-Making skills. Lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning & Life 3 Signature Practices Playbook and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals 
  • Introduce one of the icebreaker activities described in F.03 Video Icebreakers 1-Teacher Materials or F.03 Weblink Icebreakers 2 Teacher Materials or F.03 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials.
  • Students complete the activity..
  • Debrief activity using questions noted in each icebreaker.  See F.03 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials.  This document has 4 pre-selected icebreakers that may work well for the LIA classroom setting with debriefing questions identified in a simpler format.
  • Select another icebreaker activity as time allows and then debrief.
  • Line Up (3-5 minutes)
  • One, Two, Three Clap!  (7 minute activity, pg. 15 Skills for Learning & Life Signatures Playbook)
Suggested Activities for online class:
  • Roll a die or spin a wheel to select a question  (#4 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Play Guess Who with Flip (#5 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Choose Your Favorite (#4 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)
  • What, Where, When? (#7 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)

INSTRUCTION

Mini-Lesson: My Name, My Identity/Your Name is a Song:  Engagement hook: Display slide that integrates words “given name” into music notes. (slide #7). Engage students in a brief discussion about the image. 
  • What is a “given name”? After a discussion, display the vocabulary slide (printed or digital).
  • Why do you think the names are woven into the music notes? Accept all answers.
Facilitate My Name, My Identity Activity- focus only on first names (given names) (see Greetings slide #3) – pair share, large group (Layered and process) Following the introduction of students’ first names discuss the following:
  • Share the story about how you were given your name and the meaning behind it.
  • Allow students 2 minutes to turn and talk and share how they were given their name and the meaning behind it.
Use slide #9 to lead a brief discussion.
  • Is your name easy or difficult for other people at school to pronounce? 
  • Do other students in your school have the same name? What is that like? 
Display slide #10. Read the book “Your Name is a Song” by Jamilah Thompkins-Bigelow.(the YouTube read aloud is about 9:32 minutes)
  • What can you do if someone’s name is difficult to pronounce?  
  • If you have a name that is challenging for other students to pronounce, what can you do to help them learn your name?
Possible responses: clap it out into syllables, write it the way it sounds, practice saying it several times.
Reflection (5-7 minutes) Emphasize the following:(slide #11)
  • Just like our surnames, our first name (given name) is an important part of our identity.
  • When you take action and AFFIRM your name you begin to ADVOCATE for yourself. Briefly discuss the meaning of affirm and advocate. Show printed vocabulary card or slide.
Write the following on the board or display the slide (optional: print the slide for each student to fill out) WHAT? SO WHAT? NOW WHAT? Initiate a brief discussion using the questions below. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness) So What? Why do you think it’s important to learn to say people’s first names correctly ? (Social Awareness)  Now What? What will you do with what you learned about “given names”  today? (Responsible Decision Making) Activities to foster student engagement. (click link for resource) Your Name is a Song Guided Practice
  • Distribute “My Name is a Song” blank template. Direct students to create a visual representation of their first name. Encourage students to include unique drawings, symbols, or words that are meaningful and part of their identity. (Save this template as it will be used in F.04 lesson)
  • Divide the class into groups. 
  • Tell the students they will be working together to create a MURAL (explain the meaning of “mural” by displaying printed vocabulary card or slide). Groups will work together to create a music MURAL on a 5-6 ft. white piece of butcher paper . Encourage students to use the following image as a guide or display slide # 15 so students will know which notes can be used. Teacher may want to consider drawing  the bar lines of the mural in pencil then dividing the butcher paper into sections for the groups to insert color and music notes (after each section is complete the mural will need to be pieced together).
The music mural will be used for the next lesson F.04 Icebreakers Part 2.

In- Person Class Assessment Options: 
  • Exit ticket. Distribute Family Interview document2. Instruct students to take the form home and work with a parent to fill out the questionnaire. Students should expect to return the completed document at the next class meeting. Note: The teacher should fill out the document to use as an engagement hook for F.04.
  • Distribute “Making Connections”2  worksheet. Students can fill it out and glue it into their journal. (Consider shrinking the document when it is copied so that it will fit into the students’ journals).
Online Class Assessment Options:
  • Exit Ticket. Create an assignment in your Learning Management System (LMS) and link the interview document. Suggest linking the document with a “force copy” option or assigning the document so that each student gets their own copy to edit.
Journal Entry Suggestions:
  • Why is it important to know each other’s first names?
  • Write down a few activities or thoughts about how you can get to know and build relationships with students in your LIA class.

Differentiation:
  • Create small groups and rotate groups through 3-4 stations with different ice breaker activities at each station. Especially effective for students that have anxiety participating in large groups.
Extension:
  • Create a class poster/collage that represents each individual in the class.  (Each class member will find a picture in a magazine or newspaper that represents something about themselves.  Class members will create a collage using these pictures.)

Lead the students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources. 45-50 minute lesson Objectives Students will:
  • get to know their classmates by participating in Icebreaker and Team Building activities
  • develop understanding of social interdependence (Self-Awareness)
  • integrate personal and socio-cultural identities (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
  • develop understanding of self advocacy
  • recognize digital citizenship skills
  • demonstrate responsible use of digital tools
21st Century Competencies Skills for Learning & Life
Critical thinking, communication, collaboration, creativity, social skills, leadership, productivity, initiative, flexibility, technology literacy Social Awareness, Self-Awareness, Responsible Decision-Making, Self-Management

Play the song “We Go Together”. Encourage students to stand up and clap to the beat, tap their foot to the beat, or snap their fingers.  Students will respond to the following prompt: We go together like ___________.  
Building The LIA Classroom Community (10-15 minutes) F.04 slide deck
Go over the objectives of this lesson.
Community Building Activity Purpose: To use the Ice-Breakers activity to build community; support self-awareness, social awareness, responsible decision making  Skills for Learning & Life Focus: The Ice-Breaker activities will further enhance students’ Social Awareness and Responsible Decision-Making skills. Lead a Community Circle/ Class Meetings activity (collaborative process) – see Skills for Learning & Life Signature Practices Playbook and Introduction to Welcoming Rituals 
  • Select icebreaker activities described in F.03 Video Icebreakers 1-Teacher Materials or F.03 Weblink Icebreakers 2 Teacher Materials or F.03 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials. Debrief activity using questions noted in each icebreaker.  See F.03 Icebreakers 3 Teacher Materials.  This document has 4 pre-selected icebreakers that may work well for the LIA classroom setting with debriefing questions identified in a simpler format.
Suggested Activities for online class:
  • Roll a die or spin a wheel to select a question  (#4 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Play Guess Who with Flip (#5 in 8 Virtual Icebreakers-Back to School)
  • Choose Your Favorite (#4 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)
  • What, Where, When? (#7 in 9 virtual icebreaker games for remote teams and meetings)
Class Coat of Arms/Elementary LIA logo Display slide # 6. Activate prior knowledge by showing the coat of arms images.  Ask the following questions:
  • What do these images represent?
  • Where have you seen these before?
  • Why do you think these are important?
Click the “Coat of Arms” text to watch a short video that explains a coat of arms.  Engage the students in a brief discussion about the similarities between a logo and a coat of arms. Divide the students into 4-5 groups. Task the students with creating a logo/coat of arms that will represent their Elementary LIA class. Encourage students to focus on the following:
  • Include school representation
  • Keep it simple
  • Make it relevant
  • Make it unique
  • Make it colorful
  • Make it timeless
Allow the students to vote on the class logo/coat of arms that will represent the LIA class. Suggest using a ballot so that students do not feel influenced by their peers. Consider asking one or two students to create a poster size of the LIA logo.
Reflection (5-7 minutes) Write the following on the board or display the slide (optional: print the slide for each student to fill out)(slide # 10) WHAT? SO WHAT? NOW WHAT? Initiate a brief discussion using the questions below. What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity? (Self-Awareness) So What? Why do you think a class coat of arms builds the LIA class community? (Social Awareness)  Now What? What will you do with what you learned about community building today? (Responsible Decision Making) Activities to foster student engagement

Mini-Lesson: Your Name is a Song Part 2 Engagement Hook: Display the teacher’s completed Family Interview document. (document camera, completed slide). Share details of the interview with the students. Display slide #13. Students will use the completed interview document to fill out the graphic organizer. Allow students 5-7 minutes to complete the organizer. After the organizers have been completed use the Mix and Mingle activity for students to share “All About My Name”1. (Skills for Learning & Life Signature Practices Playbook) Use My Name is a Song Chrome Music Activities (shared with permission from the author) to allow students to create a Name Song. 1 to 1 technology is recommended for this activity.  Students can create a song using Chrome Music Lab-Song Maker and will add it to their “My Name is a Song” visual representation from F.03 (see sample). Encourage students to infuse elements of Latin music. See Basics of Latin Music video or Introduction to Latin American Music for a short clip about Latin music. Options Include:
  • Students can save the link and email it to the teacher. The teacher can create QR codes for the students using the free QR Code generator.
  • Students can save the link and create their own QR code using the free QR Code Generator. A teacher tutorial is recommended prior to students working independently. 
Students will attach their decorated names and the QR code to the mural.

Lead the students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources. 45-50 minute lesson OBJECTIVES Students will:
  • understand the purpose of reading and the elements of reading so they can be effective reading tutors  
  • develop understanding of how social interdependence affects trust (Self-Awareness)
  • understand impacts of personal and collective agency (Self-Management)
  • deepen understanding about power of empathy and showing respect for others (Social Awareness)
  • co-create a sense of belonging and thriving (Responsible Decision-Making)
21st Century Competencies Skills for Learning & Life
Critical thinking, communication, collaboration,, social skills, leadership, productivity, initiative, flexibility Social Awareness, Self-Awareness, Responsible Decision-Making, Self-Management
