Lesson steps [Slides #6-#8 are the same in Lessons 7 and 8. If taught during this lesson, it does not need to be taught in the other lesson]
  • Ask students to define communication and brainstorm ways we communicate (slide #6). Once you have a definition and a few examples, move on to slide #7. ADAPTATION: print out the slide so students can brainstorm in writing ADAPTATION: use the definition from the Vocabulary Slide Deck 
  • Ask students to refer back to their brainstorms and sort the communication methods in verbal and written communication. (slide #7-#8). OPTIONAL: use the Venn Diagram on slide #8 to sort communication methods.  
  • Split students into 2-3 lines and explain that you will play a game of “telephone” where you will give the line leaders a short message that they will then whisper into the next person’s ear. The purpose of the game is to have the same message at the end as they did in the beginning (slide #9). Message options are provided in the slide notes. 
Reflection: WHAT? | SO WHAT? | NOW WHAT? (slide #10) Initiate reflection using the questions below. Students can reflect quietly or in writing before sharing out in pairs, as a group, or as a class. 
  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity?
  • So what? What strategies would have helped the message be clearer? Or - what strategies did you use that helped the message stay consistent?
  • Now what? What will you do with what you learned about verbalcommunication today?
Lesson closure 
  • Students will practice good verbal communication based on the reflections shared. (Slide #11) Students will be placed in groups of 3 and create short skits using the scenarios found on the Group Scenarios handout. 
  • Provide a timer to students so that they know how long they have to do the interview, and how long they have to provide feedback and discuss the scenarios. 
  • Students will rotate through their roles so that everybody has a chance to be the interviewer, interviewee, and feedback provider. 
Virtual Class Adaptations:  
  • Conduct the lesson on an established LMS or use tools such as FlipGrid, Canvas, Miro, Google Classroom, or other interactive platform. 
  • Create a padlet and allow students to type their reflections into the padlet. 
  • Invite students to use the chat option to share their responses.

Exit ticket: Students complete one of the following prompts
  1. What are your strengths when it comes to verbal communication?
  2. How can you strengthen your verbal communication?
In Person Class Assessment Options:
  • Write responses on a sticky note and place in a designated space in the classroom. 
  • Write in a journal / daily worksheet. 
  • Share out loud/with their groups

  • Discussion assignment on LMS.
  • Virtual board such as jamboard, miro, Zoom Whiteboard, etc.
  • Create a video on Flipgrid or Canvas.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" bottom_padding="7px" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]
DIFFERENTIATION: 
  • Use sentence stems to guide student conversations. 
  • Have students write their responses to each question in a journal or worksheet before sharing out loud. 
EXTENSION: 
  • Conduct research or read Dr. Mélida Anaya Montes’ history. 
  • Students engage in discussion on body language, eye contact, hand gestures, etc. 
  • Conduct a Socratic Seminar or small group discussions on the following prompts. There are no right or wrong answers, and it is important to provide a safe space for students to answer thoughtfully.  
    • What does strong verbal communication look like?
    • Describe how you can improve your communication skills. 
    • Discuss how culture and cultural differences can change what is considered “good” verbal communication.

Purpose: Students will learn about digital citizenship and develop skills to be good digital citizens. (self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, social management, social engagement, responsible decision-making). 

LIA Themes: Professionalism, Responsive Conflict Resolution, Leadership

 

Setting the Stage

Display the quote on the board and have students respond to one of the prompts as they get in their seats. 

 

OPTIONAL: Play culturally relevant music as students enter the class.

OPTIONAL: Lead students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources. 

 

45-90 minute lesson

 

OBJECTIVES:

Students will

  • Demonstrate effective and appropriate communication skills across different mediums (2.2.A.).
  • Demonstrate leadership skills (2.2.B). 
  • Demonstrate conflict resolution skills in relation to interpersonal relationships (2.2.C.).
  • Demonstrate an understanding of appropriate behavior and language across a variety of settings (3.1.A.).
  • Increase interpersonal skills through interactive games and situational practice (5.2.A.)
  • Act on feedback to revise understandings of how or why something is or works in particular ways (WIDA ELD-SI.4-12.Explain).
  • Evaluate the impact of key word choices in a text (WIDA ELD-LA.4-5.Inform.Interpretive).
  • Support opinions with reasons and information (WIDA ELD-LA.4-5.Argue.Expressive).

 

Vocabulary

Digital Citizenship Online Safety Privacy  
       

 

Competencies and Skills

21st Century Skills Skills for Learning and Life
Critical Thinking, Collaboration, Communication, Information Literacy, Media Literacy, Technology Literacy, Leadership, Productivity, Social Skills Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Social Awareness, Social Engagement, Responsible Decision-Making

Digital Citizenship

R.09 Slide Deck
Review objectives of the lesson with students (slide #5)

As students take their seats

Students will respond to the prompt in their journal / daily worksheet. Prompt suggestions:

  • Do you believe this quote? Why or why not. 
  • What are some of your dreams?

 

Provide 5-7 minutes for students to write their reflections. Display a timer on the board if able. 

OPTIONAL: Ask students to share reflections. They can pair-share, group-share in tables, or volunteer responses to the class. 

 

For virtual class: 

  • Allow students to use the chat, a discussion board, or unmute their microphones to share responses with the class.

Lesson steps

  • Pre Assessment: Ask students to reflect and then demonstrate with their fingers how much they think they know about digital citizenship. (slide #6)
  • Brainstorm & Reflect: ask students to reflect on the questions on the slide. Sample answers are provided in the slide notes. (slide #7)

ADAPTATION: have students write answers in their journals before sharing out to provide thinking time.
Kinesthetic ADAPTATION: Have students move to one corner or one side of the room depending on their responses for time spent on digital media. 

  • Brainstorm: Students will try to define digital citizenship. Sample answers provide in slide notes  (slide #8).
    ADAPTATION: print out this slide so students can write on it 

ADAPTATION: use the definition from the Vocabulary Slide Deck 

ADAPTATION: students work in small groups before sharing ideas out with the class

  • Brainstorm: Students will come up with descriptive words for good digital citizenship. (slide #9). Sample answers provided in slide notes.
    ADAPTATION: print out the slide so students can write on it 

ADAPTATION: students work in small groups before sharing ideas out with the class

  • On slide #10, provide an example of good citizenship and good digital citizenship, or ask students to provide examples. 

ADAPTATION: students can complete the Digital Citizenship worksheet. 

  • Practice. Slides #11-#15 contain different scenarios that students can discuss and work through.

 

Reflection: WHAT? | SO WHAT? | NOW WHAT? (slide #16)

Initiate reflection using the questions below. Students can reflect quietly or in writing before sharing out in pairs, as a group, or as a class. 

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity?
  • So what? Why do you think it’s important to know about good digital citizenship?
  • Now what? What will you do with what you learned about digital citizenship today?

 

Lesson closure 

  • Students will come up with a digital citizenship agreement. On slide #17, ask students to brainstorm keywords related to good digital citizenship. Based on the words provided by the class, students will write a sentence using those keywords. This could be an exit ticket, filled out individually.
    OPTIONAL:  students can work in small groups to come up with an agreement, then share out as a class. The class can vote on an agreement for the entire class. 
  • Post-Assessment: have students demonstrate with their fingers how much they know about good digital citizenship (slide #18). 

 

Virtual Class Adaptations:  

  • Conduct the lesson on an established LMS or use tools such as FlipGrid, Canvas, Miro, Google Classroom, or other interactive platform. 
  • Create a padlet and allow students to type their reflections into the padlet. 
  • Invite students to use the chat option to share their responses.

Exit ticket: Students complete one of the following prompts

  1. Why is it important to be a good digital citizen?
  2. List 3 ways to be a good digital citizen.

 

In Person Class Assessment Options:

  • Write responses on a sticky note and place in a designated space in the classroom. 
  • Write in a journal / daily worksheet. 
  • Share out loud/with their groups

 

Virtual Class Assessment Options:

  • Discussion assignment on LMS.
  • Virtual board such as jamboard, miro, Zoom Whiteboard, etc.
  • Create a video on Flipgrid or Canvas.

DIFFERENTIATION: 

  • Use sentence stems to guide student conversations. 
  • Have students write their responses to each question in a journal or worksheet before sharing out loud. 
  •  

 

EXTENSION: 

  • Conduct research or read Gabriel García Márquez’s history. https://www.britannica.com/biography/Gabriel-Garcia-Marquez 
  • Vocabulary support. Students enhance vocabulary by using a search engine or thesaurus to find synonyms for their descriptive words. 
  • Conduct a Socratic Seminar or small group discussions on the following prompts. There are no right or wrong answers, and it is important to provide a safe space for students to answer honestly.  
    • What does digital citizenship mean to you? 
    • Describe what good digital citizens are like. 
    • Describe what bad digital citizens are like.

(self-awareness, self-management, social awareness, social management, social engagement).  LIA Themes: Responsive Conflict Resolution, Leadership   Setting the Stage Display the quote on the board and have students respond to one of the prompts as they get in their seats.    OPTIONAL: Play culturally relevant music as students enter the class. OPTIONAL: Lead students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources.    45-90 minute lesson   OBJECTIVES: Students will
  • Demonstrate effective and appropriate communication skills across different mediums (2.2.A.).
  • Demonstrate leadership skills (2.2.B.).
  • Demonstrate conflict resolution skills in relation to interpersonal relationships (2.2.C.).
  • Practice and use action plans to define problems, brainstorm possible solutions, then form and implement plans to address them (2.3.A.).
  • Increase interpersonal skills through interactive games and situational practice (5.2.A.)
  • Establish perspective (WIDA ELD-SS.4-5.Argue.Expressive).

Conflict Resolution R.10 Slide Deck
Review objectives of the lesson with students (slide #5)
As students take their seats Students will respond to the prompt in their journal / daily worksheet. Prompt suggestions:
  • When have you learned from a mistake?
  • How can mistakes make you better? 
Provide 5-7 minutes for students to write their reflections. Display a timer on the board if able.  OPTIONAL: Ask students to share reflections. They can pair-share, group-share in tables, or volunteer responses to the class.  For virtual class: 
  • Allow students to use the chat, a discussion board, or unmute their microphones to share responses with the class.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]
Lesson steps
  • Step in the circle activity (slide #6). 
  • We all wear different hats. After displaying the hats, ask students to reflect on what types of “hats” they wear.  (slide #7). EXTENSION: have students create their own hats.  
  • Reflection (slide #8). Ask students to demonstrate with their fingers if they have experienced conflict before. 
  • Explain conflict types to students (slide #9) and ask them to share additional examples. 
  • Reflection (slide #10). Ask students if they believe conflict is good or bad. Once all students have responded, explain that conflict is part of life and completely normal. Conflict is not good or bad, but how we respond and learn from it is good or bad. 
  • Brainstorm (slide #11). Ask students how they would know there is a conflict or that a conflict is brewing? Sample answers provided in the slide notes.  
  • Explain the conflict escalator to students (slide #12). 
  • (We do). Have students provide ideas for how to escalate and de-escalate conflicts (slide #13). 
  • ABC’s of solving conflicts (slide #14). 
Reflection: WHAT? | SO WHAT? | NOW WHAT? (slide #15) Initiate reflection using the questions below. Students can reflect quietly or in writing before sharing out in pairs, as a group, or as a class. 
  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity?
  • So what? Why do you think it’s important to have conflict resolution strategies?
  • Now what? What will you do with what you learned about conflict resolution  today?
Lesson closure 
  • Work through scenarios on slides #16-19
Option 1: split students into groups and have them work on one scenario per group. Option 2: split students into groups and have them work on each of the scenarios.  Option 3: students work through each of the scenarios individually.  EXTENSION: students create skits.  Virtual Class Adaptations:  
  • Conduct the lesson on an established LMS or use tools such as FlipGrid, Canvas, Miro, Google Classroom, or other interactive platform. 
  • Create a padlet and allow students to type their reflections into the padlet. 
  • Invite students to use the chat option to share their responses.

Exit ticket: Students complete one of the following prompts
  1. What conflict resolution strategy will you use next time you find yourself in a conflict?
  2. How can conflict resolution skills help you in life?
In Person Class Assessment Options:
  • Write responses on a sticky note and place in a designated space in the classroom. 
  • Write in a journal / daily worksheet. 
  • Share out loud/with their groups

  • Discussion assignment on LMS.
  • Virtual board such as jamboard, miro, Zoom Whiteboard, etc.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" bottom_padding="7px" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]
DIFFERENTIATION: 
  • Use sentence stems to guide student conversations. 
  • Have students write their responses to each question in a journal or worksheet before sharing out loud. 
EXTENSION: 
  • Conduct research or read Lionel Messi’s history. https://www.britannica.com/biography/Lionel-Messi 
  • Vocabulary support. Students enhance vocabulary by using a search engine or thesaurus to find synonyms for their descriptive words. 
  • Conduct a Socratic Seminar or small group discussions on the following prompts. There are no right or wrong answers, and it is important to provide a safe space for students to answer honestly.  
    • What does conflict resolution mean to you? 
    • How does conflict differ from bullying? How is it the same? 
    • Who are the adults you trust most when it comes to helping resolve conflicts?
    • Have you ever felt scared to face a conflict? What did you do to change your situation?
    • Talk about a time you ignored a conflict. What was the outcome?
    • Talk about a time you faced a conflict. What was the outcome?

(self-awareness, self-management, responsible decision-making).

LIA Themes: Professionalism, Academic Excellence, Leadership

 

Setting the Stage

Display the quote on the board and have students respond to one of the prompts as they get in their seats. 

 

OPTIONAL: Play culturally relevant music as students enter the class.

OPTIONAL: Lead students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources. 

 

45-90 minute lesson

 

OBJECTIVES:

Students will

  • Demonstrate leadership skills (2.2.B). 
  • Begin a collection of service, academic, and professional artifacts (3.2.A.)
  • Develop the needed skills to be successful in honors, AP, and college-level courses in the future (3.2.B.).
  • Maintain or progress toward a high academic GPS and challenging classes that will prepare them for college and career readiness (3.2.C.).
  • Share ideas about one’s own and others’ lived experiences and previous learning (WIDA ELD-SI.4-12.Narrate). 
  • Create closure, recap, and offer next steps (WIDA ELD-SI.4-12.Narrate). 
  • Describe the parts and wholes of a system (WIDA ELD-SI.4-12.Inform).
  • Logistically  connect opinions to appropriate evidence, facts, and details; offer a concluding statement or action (WIDA ELD-LA.4-5.Argue.Expressive).
  • State reasoning used to generate solutions (WIDA ELD-MA.4-5.Explain.Expressive). 
  • Analyze sources for a series of contributing factors or causes (WIDA ELD-SS.4-5.Explain.Interpretive). 

 

Vocabulary

GPA Rights Responsibilities Resources

 

Competencies and Skills

21st Century Skills Skills for Learning and Life
Critical Thinking, Creativity, Information Literacy, Initiative, Productivity Self-Awareness, Self-Management, Responsible Decision-Making

Academic Excellence

R.11 Slide Deck
Review objectives of the lesson with students (slide #5)

As students take their seats

Students will respond to the prompt in their journal / daily worksheet. Prompt suggestions:

  • How does education help you stand out?
  • Do you believe this quote? Why or why not?

Provide 5-7 minutes for students to write their reflections. Display a timer on the board if able. 

OPTIONAL: Ask students to share reflections. They can pair-share, group-share in tables, or volunteer responses to the class. 

For virtual class: 

  • Allow students to use the chat, a discussion board, or unmute their microphones to share responses with the class.

  • Explain to students that they have rights, responsibilities, and resources (slide #6). Distribute Academic Excellence Handout and work through it with students. 

OPTION: Add your school or district’s mission statement to the worksheet under Your Educational Rights. EXTENSION:  Students reflect on and discuss the mission statement. 

EXTENSION: Students research other legal protections they have related to education. 

 

Reflection: WHAT? | SO WHAT? | NOW WHAT? (slide #7)

Initiate reflection using the questions below. Students can reflect quietly or in writing before sharing out in pairs, as a group, or as a class. 

  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity?
  • So what? Why do you think it’s important to know your rights, responsibilities, and resources in education?
  • Now what? What will you do with what you learned about educational rights and responsibilities today?

 

Lesson Steps

  • Students will reflect on what they know about GPA (slide #8). The definition is on slide #9. If your school does not use this GPA system, please modify the lesson. 
  • Based on what students have learned about their rights, responsibilities, resources, and their own academic state, they will fill out page 2 of the Academic Excellence Handout. They will use the information on this page to write an academic SMARTE goal. SMARTE GOAL template 

 

Virtual Class Adaptations:  

  • Conduct the lesson on an established LMS or use tools such as FlipGrid, Canvas, Miro, Google Classroom, or other interactive platform. 
  • Create a padlet and allow students to type their reflections into the padlet. 
  • Invite students to use the chat option to share their responses.

Exit ticket: Students complete one of the following prompts

  1. I can help my tutees recognize their academic strengths by…
  2. 1 of my academic strengths is… and 1 thing I would like to improve is…

In Person Class Assessment Options:

  • Write responses on a sticky note and place in a designated space in the classroom. 
  • Write in a journal / daily worksheet. 
  • Share out loud/with their groups

  • Discussion assignment on LMS.
  • Virtual board such as jamboard, miro, Zoom Whiteboard, etc.

DIFFERENTIATION: 

  • Use sentence stems to guide student conversations. 
  • Have students write their responses to each question in a journal or worksheet before sharing out loud. 
  • Allow students to partner with someone. 

EXTENSION: 

  • Conduct research or read Ellen Ochoa’s history. 
  • Vocabulary support. Students enhance vocabulary by using a search engine or thesaurus to find synonyms for their descriptive words. 
  • Students present their SMARTE goals to the class. They can create a song, skit, video, or something else.

(Self-Management, Responsible Decision-Making) LIA Themes: Leadership   Setting the Stage Display the quote on the board and have students respond to one of the prompts as they get in their seats.    OPTIONAL: Play culturally relevant music as students enter the class. OPTIONAL: Lead students in a midline crossing activity. Use Educational Kinesiology document to find useful resources.    45-90 minute lesson   OBJECTIVES: Students will
  • Read, write, and speak academically in both languages (2.1.A.). 
  • Demonstrate leadership skills (2.2.B.).
  • Practice and use action plans to define problems, brainstorm possible solutions, then form and implement plans to address them (2.3.A.).
  • Increase interpersonal skills through interactive games and situational practice (5.2.A.)
  • Compare changing variables, factors, and circumstances (WIDA ELD-SI.4-12.Explain).
  • Support opinions with reasons and information (WIDA ELD-LA.4-5.Argue.Expressive).
  • Analyze points of view about the same event or topic (WIDA ELD-LA.4-5.Argue.Interpretive).
  • State reasoning used to generate solutions (WIDA ELD-MA.4-5.Explain.Expressive).

Financial Literacy R.12 Slide Deck
Review objectives of the lesson with students (slide #5)
As students take their seats Students will respond to the prompt in their journal / daily worksheet. Prompt suggestions:
  • Have you ever been underestimated? 
  • Do you agree with the quote? Why or why not? 
Provide 5-7 minutes for students to write their reflections. Display a timer on the board if able.  OPTIONAL: Ask students to share reflections. They can pair-share, group-share in tables, or volunteer responses to the class.  For virtual class: 
  • Allow students to use the chat, a discussion board, or unmute their microphones to share responses with the class.

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]
Lesson steps
  • Begin the lesson by asking students what they know about income and expenses (slide #6). Use the Financial Literacy Handout if desired. ADAPTATION: print out this slide so students can write on it. ADAPTATION: use the definition from the Vocabulary Slide Deck to scaffold the activity. ADAPTATION: students work in small groups before sharing ideas out with the class.
  • Explain (or remind, if you already introduced the vocabulary) that Financial Literacy means knowing how to manage money and make smart financial decisions. (slide #7). EXTENSION: Ask students to share smart financial decisions. 
  • Knowledge check (slides #8 - 11). Each student shows 1, 2, or 3 fingers to show their answers.
Reflection: WHAT? | SO WHAT? | NOW WHAT? (slide #12) Initiate reflection using the questions below. Students can reflect quietly or in writing before sharing out in pairs, as a group, or as a class. 
  • What? What were your thoughts and feelings as you participated in this activity?
  • So what? Why do you think it’s important to have financial literacy?
  • Now what? What will you do with what you learned about financial literacy today?
Lesson steps
  • Next, you will teach students the difference between debit and credit. 
EXTENSION: ask students to share examples. 
  • Scenario practice (slides #14-16). Work through the scenarios with students. 
Lesson closure 
  • Assessment. Students will self assess what they have learned (slides #17-#18)
Virtual Class Adaptations:  
  • Conduct the lesson on an established LMS or use tools such as FlipGrid, Canvas, Miro, Google Classroom, or other interactive platform. 
  • Create a padlet and allow students to type their reflections into the padlet. 
  • Invite students to use the chat option to share their responses.

Exit ticket: Students complete one of the following prompts
  1. How can financial habits affect your life?
  2. What should you consider before making purchases?
In Person Class Assessment Options:
  • Write responses on a sticky note and place in a designated space in the classroom. 
  • Write in a journal / daily worksheet. 
  • Share out loud/with their groups
Virtual Class Assessment Options:
  • Discussion assignment on LMS.
  • Virtual board such as jamboard, miro, Zoom Whiteboard, etc.
  • Create a video on Flipgrid or Canvas.

ADAPTATIONS

[/vc_column_text][/vc_column_inner][/vc_row_inner][vc_row_inner column_margin="default" column_direction="default" column_direction_tablet="default" column_direction_phone="default" bottom_padding="7px" text_align="left" row_position="default" row_position_tablet="inherit" row_position_phone="inherit" overflow="visible" pointer_events="all"][vc_column_inner column_padding="no-extra-padding" column_padding_tablet="inherit" column_padding_phone="inherit" column_padding_position="all" column_element_direction_desktop="default" column_element_spacing="default" desktop_text_alignment="default" tablet_text_alignment="default" phone_text_alignment="default" background_color_opacity="1" background_hover_color_opacity="1" column_backdrop_filter="none" column_shadow="none" column_border_radius="none" column_link_target="_self" overflow="visible" gradient_direction="left_to_right" overlay_strength="0.3" width="1/1" tablet_width_inherit="default" animation_type="default" bg_image_animation="none" border_type="simple" column_border_width="none" column_border_style="solid"][vc_column_text css="" text_direction="default"]
DIFFERENTIATION: 
  • Use sentence stems to guide student conversations. 
  • Have students write their responses to each question in a journal or worksheet before sharing out loud. 
EXTENSION: 
  • Conduct research or read Rubén Bláde’s history. https://www.britannica.com/biography/Ruben-Blades 
  • Vocabulary support. Students enhance vocabulary by using a search engine or thesaurus to find synonyms for their descriptive words. 
  • Conduct a Socratic Seminar or small group discussions on the following prompts. There are no right or wrong answers, and it is important to provide a safe space for students to answer honestly.  
    • What does financial wellness mean to you? 
    • How can your circumstances change what financial wellness looks like? (think: socioeconomic status, wages, etc). 
    • What financial goals do you have for yourself? 
    • Describe a time you demonstrated financial literacy. 
    • Do you think you make financially sound decisions? Explain. 
    • How can you set yourself up to meet your financial goals?

title: 1.03 What LIA Does
content:
← Return to Module 1

1.03 What LIA Does

Learning Objective
Understand the purpose, mission, vision, and pillars of Latinos In Action.

What Exactly Does LIA Do?

What exactly does LIA do? How does our program take José's journey and apply it to the classroom?

Latinos In Action is a yearlong elective course designed to help Latino youth meet their potential by:

  1. Leveraging their personal assets,
  2. Excelling in education,
  3. Serving the community, and
  4. Being a leader.

While the core of our program is designed around the secondary student population, its reach extends into all levels of the education system.

Our Mission

Empowering Latino youth to lead and strengthen their communities through college and career readiness. We achieve this through culturally responsive social and emotional learning, college and career readiness, and leadership development.

Our Vision

We are the model of Latino Youth Engagement by leveraging four pillars: Personal Assets, Excellence in Education, Leadership, and Service.

The LIA Pillars

The LIA Pillars are the foundation of our program and are essential for empowering students in the classroom. LIA teachers use the pillars as the underlying motive for all lessons and initiatives.

Our four main pillars are:

  • Personal Assets
  • Excellence in Education
  • Service
  • Leadership

These pillars were the key aspects that helped the LIA founder find success, and they remain key to student success today. They are the stepping stones students need to bridge achievement and opportunity gaps and reach their social, educational, and professional goals.

Reflection Question

Which LIA pillar feels most connected to your role as an educator, and why? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

title: 1.04 LIA Students
content:
← Return to Module 1

1.04 Who are LIA Students?

Learning Objective
Understand who LIA students are and recognize the positive impact the program has on student achievement, graduation, and college readiness.

Latinos In Action serves students throughout the United States and is designed to help students develop leadership skills, strengthen academic achievement, and prepare for college and career success.

While approximately 90% of LIA students identify as Latino/Hispanic, students of all backgrounds are welcome and benefit from participation in the program.

LIA classrooms are encouraged to maintain at least 80% Latino enrollment in order to preserve the cultural focus and safe harbor of the classroom environment.

Student Demographic Data

  • Approximately 90% of students identify as Latino/Hispanic.
  • Students from all ethnic backgrounds participate in LIA.
  • Approximately 65% of participants are female.
  • Approximately 35% of participants are male.
  • LIA is actively working to increase participation among boys and young men.

Student Achievement Data

LIA students consistently outperform national averages in several key areas.

  • 95% of LIA students graduate high school on time.
  • 85% of LIA students enroll in college.

Research also shows that the longer students participate in LIA, the more likely they are to take college preparatory coursework and become involved in extracurricular activities that support long-term success.

Reflection Question

What stands out most to you about the demographic and achievement data of LIA students? How might this influence your approach as an LIA educator? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

title: 1.05 Elevator Pitch
content:
← Return to Module 1

1.05 What is an Elevator Pitch?

Learning Objective
Develop a concise and authentic explanation of Latinos In Action that can be shared with students, families, school staff, and community members.

One question LIA educators frequently receive is:

"What is Latinos In Action?"

Being able to answer this question clearly and confidently helps introduce the program to students, families, school staff, and community members.

An elevator pitch is a brief explanation that can typically be delivered in 20–30 seconds.

What Should Your Pitch Include?

Your elevator pitch may include:

  • The mission of Latinos In Action
  • Your role as an LIA educator
  • The impact LIA has on students and communities
  • What makes the program unique

Create Your Elevator Pitch

Take a few minutes to draft a 20–30 second explanation of Latinos In Action in your own words.

The goal is not to memorize a script, but to develop an authentic explanation that feels natural to you.

Reflection Question

If a parent or administrator asked you, "What is Latinos In Action?" what would you say in 30 seconds or less? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

title: Understanding the 30/40/30 Model
content:
← Return to Module 2

2.01 The 30/40/30 Model

Learning Objective
Understand the purpose of the 30/40/30 Model and how a balanced classroom creates leadership opportunities and positive peer influence.

What is the 30/40/30 Model?

The 30/40/30 Model is a strategic way to structure the makeup of an LIA class. It is based on the idea that students' strengths can complement the growth areas of other students.

Rather than creating a class made up entirely of high-achieving students or students who need additional support, LIA intentionally creates a balanced learning environment where students can learn from one another.

The Three Student Groups

High Achievers (30%)

  • GPA of 3.0 or higher
  • Taking rigorous courses such as AP, Honors, or Dual Enrollment
  • Involved in extracurricular activities
  • Have clear college or career goals

The Invisible (40%)

  • Average GPA (approximately 2.3–2.9)
  • Limited extracurricular involvement
  • Often overlooked despite their potential
  • Tend to "get lost" within the school system

Untapped Potential (30%)

  • Lower GPAs (approximately 2.0–2.3)
  • May struggle with attendance
  • May not yet have post-secondary goals
  • May include ELL/Emerging Bilingual students

Why Does the 30/40/30 Model Work?

The 30/40/30 Model is a critical component of the LIA program because it creates opportunities for students to learn from one another.

Research shows that students learn through social interactions, observation, collaboration, and positive peer modeling.

By intentionally creating diverse groups of students, LIA helps students develop leadership skills while supporting the academic and personal growth of their peers.

Research Supporting the Model

  • Students learn through social contexts by observing and imitating others.
  • Learning is often most effective when diverse perspectives are present.
  • Diverse groups tend to demonstrate stronger collective problem-solving abilities.
  • Students who need additional support often benefit from positive peer modeling.
  • Both higher-performing and lower-performing students benefit from collaborative learning environments.
Reflection Question

Think about students at your school. Which students might fit into each of the three groups? How could the 30/40/30 Model help create leadership opportunities and support student growth? ← Previous Module Next Module →

title: 4.01 Leadership in LIA
content:
← Return to Module 4

4.01 Leadership in LIA

Learning Objective
Understand why leadership development is a core component of Latinos In Action and how leadership opportunities help students grow academically, personally, and professionally.

Leadership as an Essential of LIA

Leadership is one of the four essential components of the Latinos In Action model and a key element of student success.

LIA believes that leadership is not simply a position or title. Leadership is a set of skills and habits that can be developed through practice, responsibility, and service.

Throughout their LIA experience, students are given opportunities to lead, collaborate, solve problems, and positively influence others.

Why Leadership Matters

Leadership experiences help students build confidence, communication skills, responsibility, and teamwork.

These skills prepare students not only for success in school, but also for college, careers, and community involvement.

By giving students meaningful leadership opportunities, LIA helps students recognize their potential and become active contributors within their schools and communities.

Leadership in Action

Leadership in LIA is learned through action. Students do not simply study leadership concepts; they actively practice leadership through committees, tutoring, service projects, classroom initiatives, and school involvement.

As an LIA teacher, your role is to help create an environment where students can take ownership, make decisions, and develop leadership skills through real experiences.

Watch: Leadership Training

https://youtu.be/Brmlw5xukyo

As you watch, think about how leadership opportunities can be incorporated into your classroom and how students can take ownership of their learning and service activities.

Reflection Question

What leadership qualities do you hope your students will develop through their participation in LIA? ← Previous Module Next Lesson →

title: Leadership Committees & Class Presidency
content:
← Return to Module 4

4.02 Leadership Committees & Class Presidency

Learning Objective
Understand how the LIA Class Presidency and Leadership Committees are structured and how they help students develop leadership skills through active participation.

Student Leadership Structure

One of the unique aspects of Latinos In Action is its student leadership structure.

Rather than having teachers organize every activity and initiative, students are given meaningful leadership opportunities through the Class Presidency and Leadership Committees.

These leadership experiences help students practice communication, organization, teamwork, and problem-solving skills throughout the school year.

The Class Presidency

The LIA Class Presidency serves as the student leadership team for the class.

The President oversees the presidency and helps ensure that leadership committees are functioning effectively. Vice Presidents oversee specific committees, while the Secretary and Historian provide support and help document activities.

Together, the presidency helps guide the vision, goals, and activities of the LIA classroom.

Leadership Committees

Leadership Committees allow students to take ownership of different aspects of the LIA program.

Each committee is led by a Vice President and is responsible for planning, organizing, and carrying out activities related to its area of focus.

Leadership Committees should meet weekly for approximately 20 minutes to plan and discuss their responsibilities.

These committees are a key element of the LIA model and should be treated as a priority throughout the school year.

Leadership Structure Overview

The LIA Class Presidency oversees leadership committees that help students take ownership of the program.

Why Student Leadership Matters

Students learn leadership best by actively practicing it.

By serving in leadership roles, students develop confidence, accountability, teamwork, communication skills, and a sense of responsibility for the success of the program.

The goal is to create a student-led environment where leadership becomes part of the culture of the classroom.

Reflection Question

How might student leadership committees help increase student ownership, engagement, and responsibility within your LIA classroom? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

title: Teacher Responsibilities & Activity Proposals
content:
← Return to Module 4

4.03 Teacher Responsibilities & Activity Proposals

Learning Objective
Understand the teacher's role in supporting student leadership, selecting student leaders, and approving leadership activities.

The Teacher's Role

While LIA is designed to be student-led, teachers play a critical role in supporting and developing student leaders.

As an LIA teacher, you are responsible for creating opportunities for students to lead while providing guidance, support, and accountability.

Your goal is not to do the leadership work for students, but rather to coach and mentor them as they develop leadership skills.

Selecting Student Leaders

The teacher is responsible for ensuring that a Class Presidency is established.

Student leaders may either be selected by the teacher or elected by the students, depending on the needs of the classroom.

Some teachers choose student leaders at the end of the school year so they can begin preparing for their leadership roles before the next year begins.

Once the presidency is established, teachers should assign students to leadership committees and ensure that committees remain balanced and productive.

Supporting Leadership Committees

Leadership committees should meet regularly and have clear responsibilities.

Teachers should monitor committee progress, provide support when needed, and ensure students remain focused on their goals and initiatives.

As programs grow, teachers may choose to create additional committees if existing committees become too large or difficult to manage.

Activity Proposal Form

Before carrying out any activity, event, or initiative, students should complete an Activity Proposal Form and receive teacher approval.

The proposal process helps students think through their plans, communicate their goals, and practice responsible leadership.

Reviewing and approving proposals is an important part of helping students develop planning and decision-making skills.

Leadership Resources

For additional information about leadership committees, presidency responsibilities, and activity planning, please review the LIA Program Manual and Activity Proposal Form.

LIA Program Manual Activity Proposal Form Reflection Question

How can you balance giving students ownership of leadership activities while still providing the guidance and accountability they need to be successful? ← Previous Lesson Next Module →

title: 3.01 Understanding Service Learning and Tutoring

3.01 Service Learning and Tutoring

Learning Objective
Understand why service learning and tutoring are essential components of the LIA model and how they support student leadership development.

Service as a Core Component of LIA

Service is one of the key components of the LIA course and a hallmark of the Latinos In Action model.

LIA students develop leadership skills by serving others through literacy tutoring and community service projects.

These experiences help students become leaders while making a positive impact on their schools and communities.

Why Service Matters

Service learning allows students to apply leadership skills in real-world situations.

Through service, students develop confidence, responsibility, communication skills, and a stronger connection to their communities.

Service also reinforces two of the LIA Pillars: Service and Personal Assets.

The Connection Between Service and Leadership

One of the unique aspects of LIA is that leadership is not taught only through classroom instruction.

Students learn leadership by actively serving others and becoming role models within their schools.

Elementary tutoring is one of the primary ways students develop these leadership skills throughout the school year.

Reflection Question

How can service experiences help students develop leadership skills that cannot be learned through classroom instruction alone? ← Previous Module Next Lesson →

title: Literacy Tutoring in Action
content:
← Return to Module 3

3.02 Literacy Tutoring in Action

Learning Objective
Understand how literacy tutoring works in LIA, the expectations for student participation, and the benefits for both tutors and tutees.

What Is Literacy Tutoring?

All LIA students are expected to participate in weekly literacy tutoring at their Partner Elementary School.

LIA students are paired one-on-one with elementary school students to provide literacy support while serving as positive role models and mentors.

This tutoring experience is one of the defining features of the LIA program and provides meaningful opportunities for leadership and service.

Tutors and Tutees

During tutoring sessions, LIA students serve as tutors while elementary students serve as tutees.

Tutors help younger students develop literacy skills while building positive relationships and encouraging academic growth.

These interactions help elementary students succeed while giving LIA students valuable leadership experience.

Benefits of Tutoring

Literacy tutoring benefits both the tutor and the tutee.

  • Strengthens literacy and communication skills
  • Develops leadership and mentoring abilities
  • Builds confidence and responsibility
  • Promotes bilingual and bicultural awareness
  • Creates meaningful connections between students

Tutoring supports both the Service and Personal Assets pillars of Latinos In Action.

Watch: LIA Tutoring Training

https://youtu.be/VLUL6GoHh7A

As you watch, think about the expectations, responsibilities, and opportunities that tutoring provides for LIA students.

Reflection Question

What leadership skills do you think students develop through tutoring? How might tutoring impact both the tutor and the elementary student? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

title: Planning Tutoring at Your School
content:
← Return to Module 3

3.03 Planning Tutoring at Your School

Learning Objective
Begin planning how elementary tutoring will be implemented at your school and identify key logistical considerations for a successful partnership.

Preparing for Tutoring

Each school's tutoring program will look slightly different based on scheduling, transportation, student enrollment, and elementary school partnerships.

As you prepare to implement tutoring, it is important to begin thinking through the logistics that will help create a successful experience for both your students and their elementary school partners.

Your Regional Program Manager (RPM) and LIA staff will work with you throughout this process.

Key Planning Questions

As you begin planning, consider the following questions:

  • Which elementary schools would be good potential partners?
  • What time does your LIA class meet?
  • Will your class meet daily or on a block schedule?
  • Approximately how many students will participate in tutoring?
  • What transportation or scheduling considerations might need to be addressed?

Tutoring Planning Reflection

Take a few minutes to think about how tutoring might work at your school.

You do not need to have all the answers yet. The goal is simply to begin identifying opportunities and potential challenges so that LIA staff can better support you.

Support From Your RPM

You are not expected to establish tutoring partnerships on your own.

Your Regional Program Manager and the LIA team will work alongside you to help identify elementary school partners, establish schedules, and ensure tutoring is implemented successfully.

The goal is to create a meaningful service-learning experience that benefits both LIA students and elementary students.

Reflection Question

What opportunities and challenges do you anticipate when implementing elementary tutoring at your school? ← Previous Lesson Next Module →

title: Understanding the LIA Curriculum
content:
← Return to Module 5

5.01 Understanding the LIA Curriculum

Learning Objective
Understand the purpose, structure, and implementation of the Latinos In Action curriculum.

The Purpose of the Curriculum

When not participating in tutoring, students engage in a culturally relevant college and career readiness curriculum designed to support their academic success and future goals.

The curriculum helps students develop leadership skills, strengthen personal assets, and prepare for college, careers, and community involvement.

Curriculum Structure

Latinos In Action provides curriculum for both middle school and high school programs.

Each curriculum contains 13 units and is designed to be taught over multiple years rather than completed in a single school year.

Most teachers cover approximately 3–4 units per year, allowing students to participate in LIA for multiple years without repeating content.

Accessing Curriculum Resources

The curriculum can be accessed through the Latinos In Action website by selecting the Login option in the upper-right corner of the website.

Reflection Question

How might the multi-year design of the curriculum benefit students who participate in LIA throughout high school? ← Previous Module Next Lesson →

title: Project-Based Assessments & Digital Portfolios
content:
← Return to Module 5

5.02 Project-Based Assessments & Digital Portfolios

Learning Objective
Understand how project-based assessments and digital portfolios support student learning and growth.

Project-Based Assessments

Each unit includes a project-based assessment that allows students to demonstrate mastery of learning outcomes through authentic tasks and experiences.

These assessments are built directly into each curriculum unit and are identified within lesson plans as Unit Assessments.

Digital Portfolios

Students are encouraged to save important projects, resumes, assessments, and LIA artifacts in a digital portfolio.

Digital portfolios help students showcase their growth and prepare materials that may be useful for college applications, scholarships, and employment opportunities.

Reflection Question

title: Additional Curriculum Activities & Reflective Journaling
content:
← Return to Module 5

5.03 Additional Curriculum Activities & Reflective Journaling

Learning Objective
Understand how supplemental activities and reflective journaling can support the LIA curriculum while keeping college and career readiness as the priority.

Additional Curriculum Activites

LIA teachers may bring additional activities into the curriculum when those activities support the goals of the program.

These activities should supplement the LIA curriculum and help students connect learning to real-world experiences, current events, college readiness, leadership, and service.

Optional Activites

Examples of appropriate supplemental activities include:

  • Guest speakers
  • Field trips to colleges or workplaces
  • Activities connected to the LIA teacher's passions and strengths
  • Current events impacting the community
  • Lessons that address important student needs

Guest speakers should support the LIA curriculum. Teachers should follow LIA policy guidelines when inviting guest speakers to interact with students.

Should Class Time Be Used for Homework

Please avoid using LIA class time primarily as a space for students to complete homework.

While structured peer tutoring and academic support can be beneficial, the LIA curriculum contains valuable lessons that should take priority.

Teachers are encouraged to devote the majority of class time to curriculum so students can learn the skills and information needed to prepare for college, leadership, and future opportunities.

Reflective Journaling

LIA students should journal once a week. Journaling is a hallmark of the LIA program because it helps students become reflective learners and creates a safe space to practice language and communication.

Reflective journaling can support students' language development, self-awareness, and preparation for college and career readiness.

How to Use Journals

Teachers may structure journal writing in several ways:

  • Use suggested journal prompts from lesson adaptations
  • Create original prompts based on student needs
  • Have students respond to current events
  • Ask students to reflect on tutoring experiences
  • Allow students to write about a topic of their choice

Students should keep their journal entries together, either in a notebook stored in the classroom or in a format they are responsible for bringing to class.

Grading journal entries is left to the teacher's discretion. Some teachers may award completion points to increase motivation without needing to read every entry.

Reflection Question

How could reflective journaling help your students become more thoughtful, self-aware, and engaged learners? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

5.04 LIA Events & Ongoing Support

Learning Objective
Understand the professional development opportunities, events, and ongoing support available to LIA teachers throughout the school year.

LIA Events

Throughout the year, Latinos In Action hosts a variety of events that provide leadership development, professional learning, networking opportunities, and celebration experiences for both students and teachers.

These events strengthen the LIA community and help students and educators continue growing throughout the school year.

LIA Conference

The LIA Conference is an end-of-year celebration and learning experience for students and teachers.

Participants attend keynote presentations, workshops, recognitions, performances, and other activities that celebrate the accomplishments of LIA students and educators.

https://youtu.be/ZBLpSKXRZRY

Youth Leadership Boot Camp

The LIA Youth Leadership Boot Camp provides hands-on leadership training for students who serve in leadership positions within their schools.

Students participate in workshops, team-building activities, goal-setting exercises, leadership development sessions, and mentorship opportunities.

The experience helps students strengthen their confidence, leadership abilities, and preparation for the upcoming school year.

Educator Institute

At Latinos In Action, we value our teachers and strive to provide innovative training opportunities through our Educator Institutes.

Educators participate in professional development sessions, collaboration opportunities, networking events, and workshops designed to support successful program implementation.

These institutes provide valuable opportunities to learn from experienced educators and share best practices with other LIA teachers.

Ongoing Support

This training is only the beginning of your LIA journey.

Throughout the year, you will continue receiving support, updates, and professional learning opportunities from Latinos In Action.

  • Biweekly LIA newsletters
  • Regional Program Manager support
  • Classroom visits and coaching
  • Program updates and resources
  • Professional development opportunities

Your Regional Program Manager

Your Regional Program Manager (RPM) is your primary support person throughout the school year.

RPMs regularly check in with teachers, answer questions, provide guidance, and help ensure successful implementation of the LIA program.

Never hesitate to reach out to your RPM whenever you need support or assistance.

Final Phone Call & Next Steps

To conclude your training, you will meet with your Regional Program Manager for a final conversation.

During this meeting, you will have an opportunity to discuss what you learned, ask questions, and receive additional guidance before implementing LIA at your school.

This conversation typically lasts between 30 minutes and one hour, depending on your needs and questions.

title: Being a Culturally Responsive Teacher
content:
← Return to Module 1

1.07 Being a Culturally Responsible Teacher

Learning Objective
Understand the basic idea of Culturally Responsive Teaching and why teachers should look beyond surface-level judgments of students.

What Is Culturally Responsive Teaching?

To help you in this journey of being a champion for your students, LIA uses a Culturally Responsive Teaching approach in the classroom.

Culturally Responsive Teaching recognizes the importance of including students' cultural references in all aspects of learning.

The purpose of this lesson is to introduce one of the fundamental concepts of Culturally Responsive Teaching: developing meaningful and strong relationships with your students.

Looking Beyond the Surface

Sometimes, what we see at first does not tell the full story. The original training uses a truck accident near Hurricane, Utah as an example.

At first, the image appears to show a truck that simply crashed through a barrier. However, when you see the full picture, you realize how close the driver came to a much more serious outcome.

The lesson is that judgments based only on surface-level perspectives are not always accurate. This same idea applies to how we view and understand our students.

Surface-level perspectives do not always show the full story.

Connecting This Idea to Students

Being an effective Culturally Responsive Teacher requires us to pay attention to the way we judge and view others, especially our students.

A student's behavior, appearance, confidence level, language, grades, or participation may only show a small part of who they are. LIA teachers work to understand the deeper story behind each student.

Reflection Question

Think of a time when you misjudged someone or when someone misjudged you. How can that experience help you look beyond surface-level assumptions with your students? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

title: 1.08 Why Strong Relationships?
content:
← Return to Module 1

1.08 Why Strong Relationships?

Learning Objective
Understand why strong teacher-student relationships are essential in LIA and how deeper understanding helps students feel seen, supported, and connected.

The First Day of School

The first day of school is always an interesting day. Unfamiliar students walk into your classroom, and immediately the judgment process begins.

Students try to figure out what kind of teacher you are, and you try to figure out what kind of students you have.

This process is natural, but it is also flawed. Culturally Responsive Teachers understand that what we see on the surface is only a small part of who a student really is.

The Iceberg Example

The judgment of people is often compared to an iceberg.

The tip of the iceberg is the only easily visible part, yet it would be foolish to judge the iceberg's full size based only on what appears above the water.

In the same way, there are certain characteristics we can easily see in students, but stopping there would only give us a surface-level understanding of who they are.

Understanding What Is Beneath the Surface

A Culturally Responsive Teacher strives to learn the qualities, experiences, strengths, challenges, values, and stories that exist beneath the surface.

A teacher who champions students must understand and connect with them through deep relationships.

When you understand your students more fully, you are better able to place them in situations where they can connect with your teaching and succeed in your class.

Connecting Back to My Suitcase

The My Suitcase activity is one way to help you and your students understand each other at a deeper level.

After students complete their suitcases, give them opportunities to share and explain their items with the class. Some teachers choose to have students share over several weeks as time permits.

This type of activity can help build trust, strengthen classroom community, and create meaningful opportunities for connection.

Reflection Question

What are some ways you can learn what is beneath the surface for your students during the first few weeks of school? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

title: CRT Teaching
content:
← Return to Module 1

1.09 CRT Teaching

Learning Objective
Understand how Culturally Responsive Teaching connects classroom instruction to students' lives, identities, and experiences.

A Culturally Responsive Mindset

Culturally Responsive Teaching begins with the belief that a teacher's understanding of students should drive lessons, activities, and assignments.

Students often report that they dislike school because they are bored or do not feel that what they are learning is relevant to their lives.

When teachers connect learning to students' experiences, interests, cultures, and communities, students are more likely to feel engaged and valued in the classroom.

A teacher's understanding of students should shape instruction.

Making Learning Relevant

Contextualizing material is a critical part of engaging students who may already feel like outsiders in traditional public school settings.

For LIA teachers, this means adapting lessons so students can see how the content connects to their lives, goals, communities, and futures.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=nGTVjJuRaZ8

Adapting the Curriculum

LIA provides a curriculum to help you structure your units and lessons. However, you will want to adapt and modify the content to meet the specific needs of your classes.

This is an ongoing process of small adjustments. Over time, you will learn more about your students and make instructional choices that help them connect with the material.

Throughout your LIA experience, you will receive additional instruction about ways to implement Culturally Responsive Teaching.

Reflection Question

How can you adapt a lesson, activity, or assignment so it feels more connected to your students' lives, cultures, goals, or communities? ← Previous Lesson Next Lesson →

1.10 The Four Essentials

Learning Objective
Understand the four essential components of the LIA classroom model and how they work together to support student success.

The LIA Classroom Model

The LIA classroom model has proven effective in schools throughout the United States. When the program is implemented with fidelity, students graduate high school on time and enroll in college at a higher rate than the national average.

While it may feel overwhelming at first to plan and include each essential throughout the school year, these four components work together to create a strong and effective LIA classroom.

The Four Essentials of LIA

This model is based on four essentials:

  1. The 30/40/30 Model
  2. Service Learning and Tutoring
  3. Classroom Leadership Committees
  4. Culturally Relevant and College Readiness Curriculum

The Four Essentials help guide how LIA is implemented throughout the school year.

What Comes Next?

In the following modules, you will learn more about each essential in depth. Each module will help you understand the purpose of the essential, how it supports students, and how you can begin implementing it in your classroom.

You will begin with Essential #1: The 30/40/30 Model.
